o-canada: At the time of the first performance, the Chant National, also by Routhier, was popular among French speakers as an anthem, while "God Save the Queen" and "The Maple Leaf Forever" had been competing since 1867 as unofficial national anthems in English Canada. "O Canada" joined that competition in 1901, when a group of school children sang it for the tour of Canada by the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall, later King George V and Queen Mary. This was the first known performance outside Quebec.

The French lyrics were translated into English in 1906, when the Whaley and Royce company of Toronto published the music with a translation by Thomas Bedford Richardson. The most popular version was written the same year by Robert Stanley Weir, a lawyer and Recorder of the City of Montreal. It was not a translation, and it contained no religious references; a fourth verse of a religious nature was added in 1926, and a slightly modified version was officially published for the Diamond Jubilee of Confederation in 1927.

The song is 28 bars in 4/4 time, to be played maestoso è risoluto, "majestic and resolved", and the original manuscript has been lost. The English and French lyrics set by law are not translations of each other. The line "The True North strong and free" is based on Tennyson's description of Canada in his poem To the Queen, where true means loyal or faithful. The musicologist Ross Duffin has argued that Lavallée built the melody by adapting passages by Mozart, Wagner, Liszt and Matthias Keller.

The tune was thought to have become the de facto national anthem after King George VI remained at attention during its playing at the dedication of the National War Memorial in Ottawa on 21 May 1939. In 1964 Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson said one song would have to be chosen, and in 1967 a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons concluded that "O Canada" should be the national anthem and "God Save the Queen" the royal anthem.

The National Anthem Act took effect on 1 July 1980, with Weir's 1908 version as the basis for the English words, with minor changes, and the French lyrics unchanged. An Act of 2018 changed "in all thy sons command" to "in all of us command". Manitoba and Alberta have taken Latin translations of phrases from the English lyrics as their mottos.
o-come-all-ye-faithful: The earliest printed version appears in a collection by John Francis Wade, an English Catholic who lived in exile in France and made a living copying musical manuscripts. In 1751 he published Cantus Diversi pro Dominicis et Festis per annum, the first printed source for Adeste Fideles, and a manuscript of 1751 by Wade is held at Stonyhurst College in Lancashire. His name is on the earliest printed versions, and modern English hymnals usually credit the text to him. Musicologists agree that it was through Wade that the hymn first appeared in print, but its exact sources remain unproven.

A parody of the chorus was current before 1542, when it appears in Rabelais' Gargantua. The tune has been attributed to Wade, to John Reading and his son, to Handel, to Gluck, to Marcos Portugal, to King John IV of Portugal and to Thomas Arne, whom Wade knew.

Wade's version had four Latin verses, set in the traditional square notation of medieval liturgical music and in triple meter, unlike modern versions. In the later 18th century the French priest Jean-François-Étienne Borderies wrote three further Latin verses, and another anonymous verse is rarely printed. Most of the original lyrics are an almost verbatim expression of Catholic doctrine about Jesus Christ, taking nearly all their content from Bible verses and the Nicene Creed.

Bennett Zon, of Durham University, has proposed that the Latin text was a coded call to the Jacobite cause: that Bethlehem stood for England, and that the phrase Regem Angelorum, king of angels, punned on Anglorum, of the English, naming Charles Edward Stuart. Wade fled to France after the failure of the Jacobite rising of 1745, and his books carried Jacobite imagery. The claims are unproven, and no text shows that Wade wrote the hymn as propaganda.

In 1841 the English Catholic priest Frederick Oakeley translated the hymn into English; he first titled it Ye Faithful, approach ye, for his Margaret Chapel in Marylebone. The common version combines one of Oakeley's translations of the original four verses with William Thomas Brooke's translation of the three added verses, and was first published in Murray's Hymnal in 1852. The hymn was sometimes called the Portuguese Hymn, after the Duke of Leeds heard it at the Portuguese embassy in London in 1795. A German translation appeared in 1823, and it has been translated into many languages. Adeste Fideles is traditionally the final anthem at Midnight Mass in St Peter's Basilica in the Vatican.
o-fortuna: The poem is a complaint against the goddess of fortune. It compares Fortune to the moon, which is changeable, ever waxing and ever waning, and calls her a whirling wheel, monstrous and empty, who first oppresses and then soothes, and who melts poverty and power like ice. The speaker says that Fortune is against him in health and virtue, and that he is driven on and weighed down, always enslaved.

It ends by calling on listeners to pluck the vibrating strings and to weep with him, since Fate strikes down the strong. Scott Horton wrote in Harper's that the text shows how few people at the time felt any control over their destiny, while it also rings with a passion for life and a demand to seize the sweet moments of human existence.

The poem is Latin and Goliardic, written in the 13th century, and its authorship is uncertain. It is contained in the collection known as the Carmina Burana. In 1934 Carl Orff came upon the collection and, working with a Latin and Greek enthusiast, Michel Hofmann, chose and arranged 24 of the poems as a libretto.

He composed his cantata Carmina Burana in 1935–1936, and the Frankfurt Opera first staged it on 8 June 1937. It has 25 movements in five sections, and O Fortuna forms a frame, as the first movement and again as the twenty-fifth, both in sections titled Fortuna Imperatrix Mundi (Fortune, Empress of the World).

Orff was inspired by the poem and by the medieval image of the Rota Fortunae, the Wheel of Fortune, which the goddess spins at random so that some suffer while others find wealth; the repetition in the music suggests the spinning wheel. The piece opens with drums and choir, drops to a whisper and builds in a steady crescendo, modal until the last nine bars, when the final syllable moves from D minor to D major.

A performance takes a little over two and a half minutes. Carmina Burana was successful from its first staging and became Orff's best-known work. O Fortuna has appeared in many films and advertisements, a use that may have begun with the trailer of the film Excalibur in 1981, and Horton wrote that its popularisation may have spoiled it.
o-sole-mio: According to the traditional account, Eduardo di Capua composed the music in April 1898 in Odessa, while touring with his father's band. It later emerged that the melody was an elaboration of one of 23 melodies he had bought from Alfredo Mazzucchi in the preceding year. For nearly 75 years after publication the music was generally attributed to di Capua alone. The words, in Neapolitan, are by Giovanni Capurro, and the title translates literally as my sun or my sunshine.

In November 1972, shortly after her father's death, Mazzucchi's daughter lodged a declaration with Italy's Office of Literary, Artistic and Scientific Property. It sought to have him recognised as co-composer of 18 of di Capua's songs, including this one. In October 2002 Maria Alvau, a judge in Turin, upheld the declaration. She ruled that Mazzucchi was a legitimate co-composer, because the songs included melodies he had composed and sold to di Capua in June 1897 with written authorisation to use them freely. As a result the song had not yet entered the public domain in any country that was a party to the Berne Convention during the relevant period, as it would have done in Italy had di Capua been the sole composer.

The song has been translated into other languages. Charles W. Harrison recorded the first English version in 1915, and in 1921 William E. Booth-Clibborn wrote the hymn Down from His Glory to the same music. In 1949 Tony Martin recorded There's No Tomorrow, with new words, to the melody. Elvis Presley heard it while stationed in West Germany with the U.S. Army, and after his discharge asked for new lyrics, which became It's Now or Never.

Many singers have recorded the original, among them Enrico Caruso, Beniamino Gigli, Mario Lanza and Luciano Pavarotti. At the opening ceremony of the 1920 Summer Olympics in Antwerp the song was played in place of the Italian national anthem, whose sheet music had not been delivered to the band. In the 1980s a television advertisement for Cornetto ice cream, broadcast in Britain, set its Just One Cornetto jingle to the melody.
o-tannenbaum: As early as the 16th century songbooks included a text that gave rise to a folk song, O Tannenbaum, du trägst ein' grünen Zweig, meaning O fir tree, you wear a green branch. In the 1856 edition of the Deutscher Liederhort the collector Ludwig Erk identified three distinct melodies for it in different regions of Germany. The tunes were only recorded in the 18th and 19th centuries, but a line sung to one of them was quoted in 1605 by Melchior Franck in the quodlibet Nun fanget an.

In 1820 the educator August Zarnack published the second volume of his folk songs for schools, with Der Tannenbaum as No. 51. Its text is a lover's complaint in which the fidelity of the fir tree is contrasted with the fickleness of a maiden. Zarnack set it to a melody earlier published with Es lebe hoch der Zimmermannsgeselle, and he may have written much or all of the text himself, as folklorists of German Romanticism sometimes did.

The lyrics known today were written by Ernst Anschütz, a teacher and organist in Leipzig, and published in his Musikalisches Schulgesangbuch of 1824. He kept Zarnack's first verse and added two more that link the tree's faithful colouring to the joy and hope of the Christmas season. In German the song therefore does not refer to Christmas until its second verse. Anschütz published it with the same Zimmermannsgeselle tune, but it came to be associated with the melody of the old student song Lauriger Horatius.

Some versions today change treu, faithful, to grün, green, and may alter the line Wie oft hat nicht zur Weihnachtszeit to Wie oft hat schon zur Winterzeit. If the third verse, with its allusions to religion, is left out, the text can be made effectively secular.

As the custom of decorating Christmas trees spread in this period, the song became one of the most popular Christmas songs in both German and English, although it is not explicitly about such a tree. Its tune has also carried many other texts. They include The Red Flag, the anthem of the British and Irish Labour Parties, and the state songs Maryland, My Maryland, Michigan, My Michigan and The Song of Iowa. A campaign song of 1884 for Grover Cleveland, Democrats, Good Democrats, used it as well, and the Boy Scouts of America and Girl Scouts of the USA sing it to the melody in Scout Vespers and Softly Falls.
oahu: Oʻahu is 71 km long from east to west and about 48 km across at its longest north to south, with an area of 1,545.4 km2. It grew from the sea floor over about four million years from the Hawaii hotspot, and today consists of the remnants of two extinct shield volcanoes, the Waiʻanae and Koʻolau Ranges, with a broad valley between them. The highest point is Kaʻala, at 1,220 m. The name is often translated as "The Gathering Place", a rendering suggested in 1922 by Thomas Thrum; the Hawaiian phrase ʻo ahu could be read as "gathering of objects", and the term has no other confirmed meaning.

It is uncertain when Oʻahu was first settled. Early studies suggested Polynesian explorers from the Marquesas as early as the 3rd century CE, but more modern analyses indicate that the first settlers probably arrived around 900 to 1200 CE. The first great king, Maʻilikūkahi, the lawmaker, began a 304-year dynasty, and in 1773 the throne passed to Kahahana. Captain James Cook sighted Oʻahu on 19 January 1778, the first recorded encounter of the islands by non-Polynesian people, but bypassed it. The next year Captain Charles Clerke landed at Waimea Bay, but left the same day.

In 1783 Kahekili II, king of Maui, conquered Oʻahu and made his son Kalanikūpule its king, turning it into a puppet state. Kamehameha I defeated Kalanikūpule at the Battle of Nuʻuanu in 1795 and founded the Hawaiian Kingdom, which was not fully unified until Kaumualiʻi surrendered Kauaʻi and Niʻihau in 1810. Waikīkī was a major settlement, and Kahekili's residence, but Honolulu eclipsed it with its more accessible harbour, and in 1845 Kamehameha III moved his capital there from Lahaina. In January 1893 American businessmen, with US Marines from the USS Boston, launched a coup against Queen Liliʻuokalani, abolishing the monarchy and establishing the Republic of Hawaii, which later lobbied for annexation to the United States.

On the morning of 7 December 1941 the Imperial Japanese Navy attacked Pearl Harbor, bringing the United States into the Second World War. The attack damaged or destroyed 12 American warships and 188 aircraft and killed 2,335 American servicemen and 68 civilians.

Oʻahu has a population of about one million, roughly 70% of that of the Hawaiian Islands, and the state capital, Honolulu, lies on its south-eastern coast. The island and the uninhabited Northwestern Hawaiian Islands form the City and County of Honolulu. The ʻIolani Palace, built for King Kalākaua, still stands and is the only royal palace on American soil. Waikīkī, Pearl Harbor, Diamond Head and Hanauma Bay are well-known features, and after the Second World War the island became a destination for tourism.
oaths-of-strasbourg: Charlemagne passed his realm to his son Louis the Pious, who passed it to his firstborn son Lothair I. Lothair's brothers, Charles the Bald and Louis the German, refused to recognise him as their suzerain. When Lothair attempted to invade their lands they allied against him and defeated him at the Battle of Fontenoy in June 841. In February 842 they met near modern Strasbourg to affirm their alliance by swearing a joint oath. The civil war ended the following year with the Treaty of Verdun, in which the three claimants partitioned the empire among themselves. The brothers swore not as kings, a term the account never uses, but as lords, with their entourages acting as witnesses.

In his oath Louis the German promised to protect his brother Charles as one ought to protect one's brother, so long as Charles did the same for him, and never to make a pact with Lothair against Charles's interests. Louis swore in an early form of Old French so that Charles's soldiers could understand him, and Charles recited his in Old High German so that Louis's soldiers could understand. The armies then swore a second oath, each undertaking to give no aid against the other brother if their own lord kept his oath.

The oaths are known through the historian Nithard, a grandson of Charlemagne who had campaigned alongside Charles the Bald. His account is firsthand but biased, since it reflects the allies' view and casts Lothair as aggressor and villain.

Nithard's text survives in two manuscripts at the National Library of France. The older was copied around the year 1000, probably for an abbey in Picardy. It was later bought around 1650 by the Swedish Queen Christina, taken to Rome, and acquired after her death by the Vatican Library. After Napoleon's forces captured Rome it was taken back to Paris. The second manuscript is a fifteenth-century copy of the first.

The oaths had little political importance, since the Treaty of Verdun superseded them, but they matter greatly to linguistics. The Romance portion is the oldest extant document in France written deliberately and consistently in a form of Romance language. Its language has been called nearly undifferentiated conservative pre-French, and scholars have variously placed it in Picard, Lyonnais, Lorraine or Poitevin.
oaxaca: Oaxaca is one of the 31 states of Mexico. It borders Guerrero, Puebla, Veracruz and Chiapas and has 533 kilometres of Pacific coastline. Several mountain chains meet there, so the terrain is among the most rugged in Mexico, with narrow valleys and canyons between ranges. Elevations run from sea level to 3,759 metres. Most Indigenous people live in the Central Valleys region, and 16 Indigenous peoples are officially recognised, of whom the Zapotecs and the Mixtecs are the most numerous. The isolating terrain is credited with helping these cultures survive better than most others in Mexico. The name comes from Huaxyacac, the Nahuatl name of a tree called guaje in Spanish, first applied to the Valley of Oaxaca by Nahuatl-speaking Aztecs.

Evidence of human habitation about 11,000 years BCE has been found in the Guilá Naquitz cave near Mitla. It holds some of the earliest known evidence of domesticated plants on the continent, including maize cob fragments, and was recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2010. By 2000 BCE agriculture was established in the Central Valleys, with sedentary villages. The diet of maize, beans, chocolate, tomatoes, chili peppers and squash lasted until the Spanish Conquest.

Spaniards reached Oaxaca very soon after the fall of Tenochtitlan. Zapotec leaders, hearing of the conquest, offered an alliance. Gonzalo de Sandoval, Francisco de Orozco and Pedro de Alvarado overcame the main Aztec stronghold four months after Tenochtitlan fell, and Hernán Cortés then sought the title of Marquis of the Valley of Oaxaca. The state was created in 1824. During the Mexican War of Independence the area stayed loyal to the Crown and the capital remained in royalist hands until the war ended. Under Porfirio Díaz modernisation brought lighting, railways and new farming techniques, and its benefits went mostly to national and international corporations.

The capital is Oaxaca de Juárez, and the state has about 3.5 million people. The state's 570 municipalities include 418 governed by the system of usos y costumbres, which recognises local forms of self-governance. At least a third of the population speak Indigenous languages. The capital and nearby Monte Albán together are a World Heritage Site, and Mitla is another archaeological site of the valleys. Oaxacan cooking is known for its seven moles, and the Guelaguetza festival is held each July.
oban: Oban, in Scottish Gaelic An t-Òban, meaning the little bay, is a resort town and seaport in the Argyll and Bute council area. It is the largest town between Helensburgh and Fort William. It stands on the Firth of Lorn, where the bay forms a near-perfect horseshoe protected by the island of Kerrera and, beyond it, the Isle of Mull. To the north lie the long, low island of Lismore and the mountains of Morvern and Ardgour.

Humans have used the site since at least Mesolithic times, as shown by remains of cave dwellers found in the town. Dunollie Castle, just outside, overlooks the entrance to the bay and has been fortified since the Bronze Age. At Dunstaffnage, to the north, excavations in 2010 found evidence of people living in the area from the Neolithic to the Early Historic periods, including a farmstead occupied between the late 7th and 9th centuries.

Before the 19th century the town sustained only minor fishing, trading, shipbuilding and quarrying. The modern town grew around the distillery founded in 1794. It became a burgh of barony by royal charter in 1811 and a Parliamentary Burgh in 1833. Interest in Sir Walter Scott's poem The Lord of the Isles, published in 1814, brought visitors. The last stretch of the Callander and Oban Railway opened on 30 June 1880, reviving local industry and tourism, and McCaig's Tower, funded by John Stewart McCaig to give work to stonemasons, was begun in the 1890s and left unfinished at his death in 1902.

In the Second World War, Merchant and Royal Navy ships used Oban as an important base in the Battle of the Atlantic, and a Royal Air Force flying-boat base operated at Ganavan and on Kerrera. During the Cold War the first Transatlantic Telephone Cable, TAT-1, came ashore at Gallanach Bay and carried the Hot Line between the US Presidents and USSR General Secretaries.

Since the 1950s the principal industry has been tourism, and Oban is also an important ferry port, the hub for Caledonian MacBrayne ferries to many of the islands of the Inner and Outer Hebrides, known as the Gateway to the Isles. The local culture is Gaelic, and Oban is considered the home of the Royal National Mòd, first held there in 1892. The Argyllshire Gathering, a Highland Games, is held annually, and the Oban distillery, on a site where whisky has been made since 1794, stands behind the seafront. St Columba's Cathedral, designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott and built between 1932 and 1959, is the mother church of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Argyll and the Isles.
obelisk: Obelisks were first built by the ancient Egyptians, who called them tekhenu. The English word comes from the Greek obeliskos, a diminutive of obelos, meaning a spit, nail or pointed pillar. Egyptian obelisks were set in pairs at temple entrances. They symbolised the sun god Ra, and under Akhenaten an obelisk was said to be a petrified ray of the Aten, the sun disk. The earliest temple obelisk still in its original position is that of Senusret I of the Twelfth Dynasty at Al-Matariyyah in Heliopolis, about 20.7 metres tall.

Others made their own. Assyrian kings raised obelisks as public monuments recording their achievements. The Black Obelisk, found at Kalhu in 1846, was erected by Shalmaneser III and shows tribute-bearers and two subdued rulers, Jehu the Israelite and Sua the Gilzanean.

After Rome took control of Egypt around 30 BCE, obelisks were shipped out in large numbers; more than twice as many stand outside Egypt as remain in it. Emperor Caligula brought the Vatican obelisk to Rome in 37 CE. In 357 CE Emperor Constantius II had two removed from Karnak to mark the twentieth year of his reign. One, now the Lateran Obelisk, is the tallest standing Egyptian obelisk at 32.2 metres, and the other went to Constantinople in 390 CE under Emperor Theodosius I.

In 1586 Pope Sixtus V had the Vatican obelisk moved to Saint Peter's Square. The engineer Domenico Fontana did it with nearly 1,000 men, 140 horses and 47 cranes, and described the work in a book published in 1590.

Obelisks were still being taken from Egypt in the nineteenth century, when three went to London, New York and Paris. Modern obelisks, mostly built of masonry or concrete rather than a single stone, serve as commemorative monuments, among them the Washington Monument in Washington, D.C. (1884).

How the ancient monoliths were raised has been tested by experiment. In 1999 a team including Roger Hopkins and Mark Lehner raised a 25-ton obelisk in a Massachusetts quarry by slowly removing sand from a pit beneath it. A papyrus of about 3,000 years ago, which tells a scribe to empty the sand beneath the monument of his lord, seems to support that method. A stele of 520 metric tons found at Axum is thought to have broken during an attempt to erect it.
oberkommando-der-wehrmacht: The OKW was set up by executive decree on 4 February 1938, after the Blomberg-Fritsch affair led to the dismissal of Werner von Blomberg, Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces and head of the Reich Ministry of War, and of Werner von Fritsch, Commander-in-Chief of the Army.

Adolf Hitler, who had been waiting for a chance to gain personal control of the military, used the powers granted to him by the Enabling Act to dissolve the ministry and replace it with the OKW, directly subordinate to him as Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces. Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel was its chief, with the rank of a Reich Minister, and Lieutenant General Alfred Jodl was Chief of Operations Staff. Many officers disregarded Keitel, and Hermann Göring, Commander-in-Chief of the Air Force, circumvented him to reach Hitler.

By June 1938 the OKW had four departments, among them the Wehrmacht operations staff under Jodl, the Wehrmacht propaganda troops under General Hasso von Wedel, which numbered 15,000 men at their peak in 1942, and the Amt Ausland/Abwehr, which handled foreign intelligence and counter-intelligence. The OKW had nominal oversight of the high commands of the army, navy and air force, but there was no direct chain of command between it and them. With the outbreak of war it also exercised tactical control of the Waffen-SS.

Rivalry with the services, mainly the Army High Command (OKH), kept the OKW from becoming a unified general staff. In practice Hitler used it as his personal military staff, turning his ideas into orders such as the Führer Directives. Norway was the first OKW war theatre, and by 1942 the OKW directed the west, North Africa and Italy, while the OKH held the Eastern Front.

Hitler set the commands against each other so that military decisions stayed in his hands, at times down to the battalion level, which with delays and his growing indecision helped bring about Germany's defeat. On 19 December 1941 he dismissed Walther von Brauchitsch and took over command of the army himself. Only on 28 April 1945 did he place the OKH directly under the OKW.

At Nuremberg the OKW was indicted but acquitted of being a criminal organisation, because the Tribunal held that the General Staff and High Command was neither an organisation nor a group within the Charter. Keitel and Jodl were nevertheless convicted of war crimes and sentenced to death by hanging. In the High Command Trial of 1947–48 fourteen Wehrmacht officers were charged, especially over the Commissar Order, the killing of prisoners of war and participation in the Holocaust.
oberwart: Oberwart lies in Burgenland in southeast Austria, on the banks of the Pinka River, and is the capital of the district of the same name. It has almost 8,000 inhabitants and is the third largest town in Burgenland, after Eisenstadt and Neusiedl am See. In Hungarian it is Felsőőr and in Croatian Gornja Borta. It is the cultural capital of the small ethnic Hungarian minority of Burgenland, who live in the Upper Őrség or Wart microregion.

The settlement was established in the 11th century by Hungarian frontier guards, the őrs, together with Unterwart and Siget in der Wart, and was first mentioned in 1327. Its community received noble privileges from King Charles I of Hungary in the 14th century. The Ottoman army partly destroyed the village in 1532. The Reformation arrived in the 16th century, and although most of the region had to return to the Roman Catholic faith under the Counter-Reformation, the free noble village remained Calvinist. The Diet of 1681 made it an articular place, the only legal place of Protestant worship for the whole region.

The villagers took part in the uprisings of István Bocskay in 1605 and of Count Francis II Rákóczi in 1705, and in 1706 an Austrian army under General Sigbert Heister sacked the village. After the Treaty of Trianon in 1920 Felsőőr was annexed by Austria, but its Hungarian population opposed the decision and organised a movement for an autonomous province, Lajtabánság. The Austrian army occupied the village in November 1921. After Austria's annexation by Nazi Germany in 1938 about 140 Jewish inhabitants were deported. In April 1945 the Red Army took the town after a week of fierce fighting. On 5 February 1995 the Austrian terrorist Franz Fuchs killed four young Romani men near a Romani housing area in Oberwart with a booby trap.

Hungarians were the most populous group until 1951, reaching a peak of 3,138 people, 75 per cent of the population, in 1920, and a low of 204 in 1971. About 1,100 ethnic Hungarians now live in the town, mostly in the Calvinist parish, the oldest Calvinist congregation in Austria. The Christian Reading Club of Young Men, founded in 1889, remains an important cultural association. The Baroque Reformed Church was built in 1771–73 by Christoph Preising, and the old parish church of the Ascension was rebuilt in Gothic style in 1463. On 2 September 1984 the song Live Is Life by Opus was recorded at a concert in Oberwart.
obotrites: The name Obotrites, also spelled Obodrites or Abodrites, is commonly traced to a Slavic root bodr-, meaning cheerful, lively or brave, so that Bodriči would signify the spirited ones. Germanic sources, like those for other Slavic groups, often called them Wends. Adam of Bremen called them the Reregi because of their trade emporium at Reric. An anonymous list compiled at Regensburg in 830, known as the Bavarian Geographer, names the Nortabtrezi, taken to be the Obotrites, with 53 civitates.

The main tribes of the confederation were the Obotrites proper, from Wismar Bay to Lake Schwerin, the Wagrians of eastern Holstein, the Warnower of the upper Warnow and the Mildenitz, and the Polabians proper between the Trave and the Elbe. Associated tribes included the Linonen near Lenzen, the Travnjane near the Trave, the Drevani in the Hanoverian Wendland and the Ukrani in Prenzlau.

As allies of the Carolingian kings and of the Ottonian emperors who followed them, the Obotrites fought from 808 to 1200 against the kings of Denmark, and on occasion against the Franks and other Christian forces. The Danes, who wished to rule the Baltic independently of the empire, were their main enemy. Under Prince Thrasco the Obotrites defeated the Saxons at the Battle of Bornhöved in 798. In 983 they destroyed Hamburg under their king Mstivoj, and at times they levied tribute from the Danes and Saxons. Under Niklot they resisted a Christian assault during the Wendish Crusade.

German missionaries such as Vicelinus converted the Obotrites to Christianity. In 1170 they acknowledged the suzerainty of the Holy Roman Empire, which led to Germanisation and assimilation over the following centuries. Until the late 15th century most villagers in the area still spoke Slavic dialects, the Polabian language, which German later displaced. Polabian survived until the beginning of the 19th century in the Hanoverian Wendland.

In 1167 Duke Henry the Lion restored Pribislav to power as Prince of Mecklenburg, which ended the Obotrite regnal style and founded the House of Mecklenburg, which became German in language and culture. The ruling clan kept its power through the Germanisation and ruled the country, apart from a short interruption in the Thirty Years' War, until the end of the monarchies in Germany in the November Revolution of 1918. Before that the Obotrites had been dominated by the Naconids.
obrenovic-dynasty: The House of Obrenović, or Obrenović dynasty, traced its male line to Baba Višnja (1737–1817). Its progenitor in power was Miloš Obrenović, who led the Serbian Uprising of 1815–1817 against the Ottoman Empire. The uprising led to the formation of the Principality of Serbia in 1817. Like Montenegro, and unlike Greece, Bulgaria or Romania, Serbia did not import a member of an existing European royal family to take its throne. The Obrenović family, like its rivals the Karađorđević, was indigenous.

The dynasty ruled Serbia from 1815 to 1842 and again from 1858 to 1903. It was traditionally allied with Austria-Hungary and opposed the House of Karađorđević, which Russia supported. Its rulers included Prince Miloš I (1783–1860), his sons Prince Milan II (1819–1839) and Prince Mihailo III (1823–1868), and in the later line King Milan I (1854–1901) and King Alexander I (1876–1903). Alexander was the last of the family to reign.

Its rule ended in a coup d'état by military conspirators, often known today as the Black Hand. They invaded the royal palace and murdered King Alexander I, who died without an heir. The National Assembly of Serbia then invited Peter Karađorđević to become king of Serbia.

Unlike most European dynasties, which used regnal numbers to tell apart rulers who shared a given name, the Obrenović dynasty gave each ruling prince the next number in a single series. There was therefore never a Milan I, a Milan III, a Michael I or a Michael II: Milan II and Michael III were simply the second and third ruling princes of the house. The practice was discontinued when Prince Milan IV proclaimed himself king and declared the principality of Serbia a kingdom in 1882. Ljubica Vukomanović was the wife of Prince Miloš I and mother of Prince Milan II and Prince Michael III.
obuda: Óbuda, in German Alt-Ofen, meaning Ur-Buda or Old Buda, is, together with Buda and Pest, one of the three cities that were unified to form the Hungarian capital city of Budapest in 1873. Together with Békásmegyer it now forms part of the city's third district, although the name is also sometimes used for northern Buda as a whole. The neighbourhood proper is centred on Fő tér beside the Szentlélek tér station. Óbuda Island, which lies in the Danube beside it, hosts the annual Sziget Festival, a major music and cultural festival.

Settlements dating from the Stone Age have been found in Óbuda. The Romans built Aquincum there, the capital of the province of Pannonia. Hungarians arrived after 900, and the site served as an important settlement of major tribal leaders and later of kings. It was the location of royal and ecclesiastical foundations. After the catastrophic Mongol invasion of 1241–42, King Béla IV built a new capital in Buda, somewhat south of Óbuda. In the fourteenth century Óbuda featured a convent of the Poor Clares.

The obscured historical remains of Óbuda, together with the role the place played in nineteenth-century poetry, have made it the subject of various historical disputes. A commemorative plaque on the building erected on the site of the former Jewish Elementary School in Óbuda, in Óbuda, remembers victims of the Holocaust.

The Aquincum Museum displays jewels, glassware, metal tools and wall paintings from the lives of the Romans of Aquincum, and its outdoor site holds remnants of the town: courtyards, baths, a market place, shrines, large columns, sculptures and a stone sarcophagus. Other Roman ruins in Óbuda include baths that served the legionnaires stationed there, the Hercules Villa and two amphitheatres, the Aquincum Civil Amphitheater and the larger Aquincum Military Amphitheatre. The Vasarely Museum in the Zichy Palace shows work by Vasarely, and the Kassák Museum is devoted to the avant-garde writer Lajos Kassák (1887–1967).
obwalden: The earliest trace of human presence in Obwalden is a stone knife of the 8th millennium BCE, found at Brand by Lungern. A Roman estate built in the late 1st century CE at Alpnach remained in use until a fire destroyed its main building in 270. Around 700 the Alamanni began to migrate in, settling around the lakes while the Gallo-Romans lived on the plateau; over the 8th to 11th centuries the two populations intermarried and became Germanized. The land became part of the Holy Roman Empire after the winter campaign of Emperor Conrad II in 1032-33.

In the early Middle Ages monasteries, especially Murbach-Lucerne and Beromünster Abbey, held much of the land, and Engelberg Abbey acquired rights over the parishes in the 14th century. On 16 April 1291 Rudolph I of Habsburg bought Unterwalden from Murbach Abbey. Fearing for their freedoms, Nidwalden formed the Eternal Alliance with Uri and Schwyz on 1 August 1291; Obwalden is not named in the text, though it appears on the seal. In 1309 Emperor Henry VII granted Unterwalden imperial immediacy. Unterwalden fought at the Battle of Morgarten, and during the 14th century the communities grew powerful at the expense of the nobility. In 1382 the Landsgemeinde excluded the Lords of Hunwil from political and court offices.

In 1481 the Swiss cantons, quarrelling over the spoils of the Burgundian Wars, met at Stans. According to legend the hermit Niklaus von der Flüe of Obwalden sent a message to the delegates, the contents of which are unknown, and it calmed tempers and led to the Stanser Verkommnis. Obwalden stood firmly against the Reformation. On 1 April 1798 it was the first of the original cantons to accept the Helvetic Republic, but it was then forced to reject it, and French armies crushed its rising. Engelberg Abbey and its community joined Obwalden in 1815, and the Landsgemeinde was abolished in 1998.

Obwalden is a canton of central Switzerland with its capital at Sarnen, and contains the geographical centre of the country. It has seven municipalities and an exclave around Engelberg. Since the Federal Constitution of 1999 it has been a full canton, though it still shares representation in the Council of States with Nidwalden. Tourism is a major sector, centred on Pilatus, Titlis and resorts such as Engelberg.
occitania: Occitania is the cultural area where the Occitan language was historically spoken and where it persists today as a local language. It covers much of the southern third of France, except the French Basque Country and French Catalonia, together with the Aran Valley in Spain, Monaco, and the Occitan Valleys of Italy. In Roman times most of it was called Aquitania, with the earlier conquered lands known as Provincia Romana, and under the late empire both were grouped in the Seven Provinces. Its extent varies with the criteria used, and the most widespread definition is a contiguous, compact Occitan-speaking territory.

Written texts in Occitan appeared in the 10th century, first as legal texts and then in literary, scientific and religious works; spoken dialects are older, at least from the 8th century. The culture flourished in the High Middle Ages with the troubadours, who often wrote of courtly love and sometimes of religious and social tolerance. William IX, Duke of Aquitaine, and Bertran de Born are counted among its best-known exponents. Dante called the language lingua d'òc, and the terms Occitania and lingua Occitana appear in Latin texts between 1242 and 1290.

From the 11th century the counts of Barcelona expanded towards Languedoc and Provence through family ties of the feudal nobility, which led to a long confrontation with the counts of Toulouse. They finally allied against the Cathar Crusade, promoted by France and the Papacy early in the 13th century. The defeat at the Battle of Muret in 1213 and the Treaty of Corbeil in 1258 ended Catalan influence in Occitania and began its replacement by the French House of Capet.
The modern concept of Occitania became current in the 19th century. The Felibritge was founded in 1854, the Escòla Occitana in 1919 at Toulouse, and the Institute of Occitan Studies followed.

The region has a population of about 16 million, and the number of native or proficient speakers of Occitan is put at between 200,000 and 800,000. Occitan is an official language in the Aran Valley, a protected language in Italy since 1999, and in France taught in schools without legal recognition. The name Occitanie has also been used since 28 September 2016 for an administrative region of France, which covers only a small part of Occitania.
occupation-of-japan: American planning for a post-war occupation of Japan began as early as February 1942. On 15 August 1945 Emperor Hirohito announced the surrender in a radio broadcast, having accepted the Potsdam Declaration after the atomic bombings and the Soviet entry into the war. The occupation was led by the American military, with support from the British Commonwealth and under the supervision of the Far Eastern Commission. General Douglas MacArthur was Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, and General Matthew Ridgway succeeded him in 1951. The Soviet Union took little part. Nearly one million American soldiers served in the occupation over seven years. The Allies never took direct control of civil administration, and the Japanese government continued to operate.

MacArthur's first task was to organise food distribution, since most of the population was starving after the destruction of the cities. Around 5.1 million Japanese returned from abroad in the fifteen months after October 1945. MacArthur kept Hirohito on the throne, arguing that a prosecution would be unpopular, although some Allied leaders wanted him tried as a war criminal. At SCAP's insistence the emperor renounced his divinity in a New Year's message.

Reforms followed. Japan's armed forces were disbanded by December 1945, political prisoners were freed, State Shinto was abolished and the first trade union law was passed. Of 717,415 wartime officials screened, 201,815 were barred from public office. Women gained the vote, and 39 women won seats in the election of 10 April 1946. Land reform bought about 38 percent of cultivated land from landlords and resold it to those who farmed it. The 1947 constitution, based on a draft by American civilians within SCAP, made the emperor a symbol and in Article Nine renounced war. Tribunals such as the International Military Tribunal for the Far East tried war criminals, though MacArthur granted immunity to many, including Hirohito and members of Unit 731.

From 1947 a Reverse Course shifted American priorities from punishing and reforming Japan to political stability, economic recovery and, within Article Nine, rearmament in support of Cold War aims. Of 325 companies planned for break-up, only the 11 largest zaibatsu were dissolved, and most of those purged returned to public life by 1951. The National Police Reserve, founded in 1950, became the Self-Defense Forces in 1954.

The Treaty of San Francisco, signed on 8 September 1951, took effect on 28 April 1952, ending the occupation and restoring full sovereignty, except for Okinawa and Iwo Jima. Iwo Jima was returned in 1968 and most of Okinawa in 1972. A US-Japan Security Treaty let American troops remain.
octavio-paz: Octavio Paz was born near Mexico City on 31 March 1914 into a prominent liberal family of Spanish and indigenous Mexican roots. His grandfather Ireneo Paz fought in the War of the Reform and became a journalist, and his library introduced the boy to literature. His father supported Emiliano Zapata during the Revolution, and the family suffered financial ruin afterwards. Paz published his first poems in 1931 and founded a literary review, Barandal, in 1932. In 1937 he attended the Second International Writers' Congress in Spain, where he showed solidarity with the Republican side, and visited Paris, where he met the surrealist movement.

Paz entered the Mexican diplomatic service in 1945 and was sent to Paris, where he wrote El laberinto de la soledad (The Labyrinth of Solitude). In 1962 he was named Mexico's ambassador to India. In 1968 he resigned from the diplomatic service in protest against the Mexican government's massacre of student demonstrators in Tlatelolco. Back in Mexico he founded the magazine Plural, which ran from 1970 to 1976, and after the government closed it he founded Vuelta, which he edited until his death. He received the Jerusalem Prize in 1977, the Miguel de Cervantes Prize in 1981 and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1990. He died of cancer on 19 April 1998 in Mexico City.

His early poetry was influenced by Marxism, surrealism and existentialism, and by Buddhism and Hinduism. His poem Piedra de sol (Sunstone), written in 1957, was praised in the presentation speech of the Nobel Prize. Later poems concern love and eroticism, the nature of time and Buddhism. As an essayist he wrote on Mexican politics, Aztec art and anthropology. The Labyrinth of Solitude describes his countrymen as hidden behind masks of solitude, with an identity lost between a pre-Columbian and a Spanish culture, and it influenced other Mexican writers such as Carlos Fuentes.

He supported the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War but became disillusioned on learning of the murder of a friend by the Stalinist secret police. In Plural and Vuelta he exposed violations of human rights in Communist regimes, which brought him open enmity from parts of the Latin American left.
october-manifesto: The Russian Empire kept its autocratic government while, from the early 1890s, the finance minister Sergei Witte led a state-driven programme of industrialisation. Industrial growth was not matched by political reform, and an expanding working class grew discontented, while peasants, still 80 per cent of the population, faced marked agrarian problems. On 22 January 1905 guards fired on peaceful protesters bringing a petition to the Tsar outside the Winter Palace, an event known as Bloody Sunday. Mass strikes followed, crippling communications, transport and public services, and peasants began to burn manors.

Tsar Nicholas II resisted reforms that limited the autocracy, and is quoted as saying he could not squander a legacy that was not his to squander. He gave way only after his first choice to head a military dictatorship, Grand Duke Nicholas, threatened to shoot himself if the Tsar did not accept Witte's proposal. The Manifesto on the Improvement of the State Order was issued on 30 October 1905 (17 October by the old Russian calendar) and was proclaimed in all the churches.

It promised civil freedoms based on the inviolability of the person and freedom of conscience, speech, assembly and association. It extended participation in the State Duma to classes without voting rights and laid down that no law should take effect without the Duma's confirmation. It also introduced universal manhood suffrage. The freedom of religion clause angered the Russian Orthodox Church, since it allowed conversion to evangelical Protestantism.

The strikes and much of the violence ended almost as soon as the Manifesto was published, and it divided the opposition: the Kadets and the Octobrists were appeased. Some opposed it, and the second Kishinev pogrom against the Jewish community on 19 and 20 October began as a protest against it. The Duma was flawed from the start, since the Tsar could veto any legislation or dissolve it. Within months the autocracy reasserted its power, executions of armed revolutionaries numbered more than a thousand, and by 1906 and 1907 much of Russia was under martial law. The Manifesto preceded the empire's first Constitution, adopted in 1906.
october-revolution: The revolution followed the February Revolution of 1917, which toppled Tsar Nicholas II and brought in the Russian Provisional Government. That government stayed weak and divided and continued to fight the First World War, which grew steadily less popular. Industrial production in 1917 had fallen by over 36 per cent from its 1914 level, and by autumn up to half of the enterprises in the Urals and the Donbas had closed, leading to mass unemployment. Real wages had fallen to about half of their 1913 level.

Opposition gathered round the soviets, the councils of workers and soldiers. Demonstrations in May and July demanded all power to the soviets, and in the July Days the government ordered an armed attack on demonstrators, killing hundreds. After General Lavr Kornilov's failed march on Petrograd in late August, the left revived. Bolshevik membership had risen from 24,000 in February to 200,000 by September.

On 10 October 1917 (23 October in the modern calendar) the Bolshevik Central Committee voted ten to two that an armed uprising was inevitable. On 24 October the government closed several newspapers, including the Bolshevik Rabochiy put, and soldiers loyal to it destroyed the paper's printing equipment. The next day the uprising began in earnest, as Bolshevik sailors entered the harbour and thousands of soldiers joined them. Red Guards under the Military Revolutionary Committee occupied government buildings.

The Winter Palace, defended by about 3,000 cadets, officers, Cossacks and women soldiers, was not strongly resisted. Artillery cadets and then 200 Cossacks left it, the cruiser Aurora fired a blank shot at 9:45 in the evening, and insurgents entered the building from 10:25. The ministers were taken in the early hours of 26 October. The initial seizure of Petrograd cost almost no lives. Later Soviet histories, films and a mass reenactment of 1920 showed fierce fighting that did not take place.

The Second Congress of Soviets, with 670 elected delegates, of whom 300 were Bolsheviks and nearly 100 Left Socialist-Revolutionaries, adopted a decree transferring power to the soviets. Lenin became chairman of the Council of People's Commissars, after first proposing Trotsky. Soviet power spread to Moscow by 15 November, and on 10 November a decree abolished estates, titles and civil ranks.

Because the new government was not universally recognised, the country fell into a civil war that lasted until late 1922 and led to the creation of the Soviet Union. The Bolsheviks were strongest in the cities, with more mixed support in the countryside. Soviet historians presented the event as the triumph of the working class, while Western observers often called it a coup that used the soviets only until they were no longer useful.
oda-clan: Oda Nobunaga first claimed that the family descended from the Fujiwara clan and later from Taira no Sukemori of the Taira clan. According to the clan's official genealogy, after Sukemori was killed at the Battle of Dannoura in 1185, his son Taira no Chikazane was entrusted to a Shinto priest at a shrine in Otanosho in Echizen Province and became the founder of the Oda.

Modern scholars find no evidence for the Taira descent. One theory holds that the family came from the Inbe clan, Shinto priests in Otanosho. Another suggests that Nobunaga claimed Taira ancestry to justify his seizure of power, drawing on a belief of the time that the Minamoto and Taira clans were destined to alternate in rule, though it has been questioned whether people then really held this belief.

In the middle of the Muromachi period the Oda served the Shiba clan, military governors of Echizen. When Shiba Yoshishige was appointed governor of Owari Province the Oda followed him there, and Oda Jōshō became deputy governor. After the Ōnin War the Shiba split into two warring factions, and from around 1466 the Oda did the same, with Iwakura Castle and Kiyosu Castle as the strongholds of the two sides.

As the Shiba declined, Oda Tatsusada rebelled against them in 1513, failed and was killed. Oda Nobutomo then made the Shiba his puppets. During the Tenbun period Oda Nobuhide overtook the main family, captured Nagoya Castle in 1538 and became the strongest lord in Owari. Oda Nobunaga, operating from Nagoya Castle, besieged and killed Nobutomo, his uncle, in 1555, and his branch then brought the whole province under its control before turning on the Imagawa, Saitō, Azai, Asakura and Takeda clans. Nobunaga was forced to suicide by his vassal Akechi Mitsuhide in the Incident at Honnō-ji in 1582.

The Oda did not disappear after Nobunaga. One branch became hatamoto, direct retainers of the Tokugawa shogun, and others ruled as minor daimyo. At the end of the Edo period these were the domains of Tendō in Dewa Province and Kaibara in Tanba Province, each rated at 20,000 koku, and Yanagimoto and Kaiju in Yamato Province, each at 10,000 koku. Under the daimyo Oda Nobutoshi the Oda of Tendō signed the pact that created the Ōuetsu Reppan Dōmei.

When the feudal domains were abolished in 1871, after the Meiji Restoration, the heads of all four houses were made viscounts in the new hereditary peerage. Descendants of the clan live throughout Japan today, mainly in the south and south-west.
oda-nobunaga: Oda Nobunaga was born on 23 June 1534 in Owari Province, the heir of Oda Nobuhide, head of the powerful Oda clan and a deputy shugo, and his lawful wife. He is traditionally said to have been born at Nagoya Castle, though recent scholars favour Shobata Castle. As a youth he was known for bizarre dress and eccentric behaviour and was nicknamed Ōutsuke, 'great fool'. When Nobuhide died unexpectedly in 1551, part of the clan opposed Nobunaga's succession; he assembled a force of 1,000 men to intimidate his enemies, and in 1552 he repelled an attack by his uncle Oda Nobutomo, who had the support of the governor of Owari.

In 1560 Imagawa Yoshimoto marched on Kyoto with an army of 25,000 men, and the clash weakened the Imagawa clan, which lost control of the Matsudaira clan. In 1561 Nobunaga allied with Matsudaira Motoyasu, who became Tokugawa Ieyasu. After defeating Saitō Tatsuoki, he conquered Mino Province in 1567 and then Ise. He entered Kyoto in honour of the Ashikaga shogun Yoshiaki, whom he installed, but a coalition formed against him, including Asakura Yoshikage, Azai Nagamasa, Takeda Shingen and the militant Ikkō-ikki movement, which was centred on the Jōdo Shinshū sect. Nobunaga overthrew Yoshiaki and ended the Ashikaga Shogunate in 1573.

He built Azuchi Castle on Lake Biwa between 1576 and 1579; screens depicting it were given to Pope Gregory XIII. He fought the Mōri clan and the Uesugi clan, conquered Iga in 1581, and with Tokugawa Ieyasu destroyed the Takeda at the Battle of Tenmokuzan in 1582. Historians note that he was among the first daimyō to use large numbers of firearms, and that he fostered free trade. He used the seal Tenka Fubu, 'spreading military power throughout the world', to express his aim of ending the Warring States period.

By 1582 Nobunaga controlled most of Honshu. That year his retainer Akechi Mitsuhide ambushed him at Honnō-ji in Kyoto, and Nobunaga committed seppuku on 21 June. Toyotomi Hideyoshi defeated Mitsuhide at the Battle of Yamazaki and completed the unification with Tokugawa Ieyasu. The period of Nobunaga's and Hideyoshi's power is called the Azuchi–Momoyama period, after Nobunaga's Azuchi Castle and Hideyoshi's Fushimi Castle at Momoyama. Nobunaga's rule is also remembered for the brutal suppression of those who would not yield to him. According to the Jesuit Luís Fróis, he held no particular religious belief but respected religious institutions that stayed out of politics.
odaenathus: Septimius Odaenathus was born around 220 into an aristocratic Palmyrene family that had received Roman citizenship in the 190s under the Severan dynasty. He was the son of Hairan, and a tomb inscription gives his descent from Wahb Allat and Nasor. Palmyra was an autonomous city in the province of Syria Phoenice, ruled by a council with no tradition of hereditary monarchy. After the rise of the Sasanian Empire in 224 disrupted its trade, the council probably elected a lord, called ras, to lead a stronger army. Odaenathus held that office, created for him, as early as the 240s, and by 258 he bore the Roman rank of consularis.

Shapur I defeated and captured the emperor Valerian near Edessa in 260. According to the Augustan History, Odaenathus was declared king of Palmyra as soon as the news reached the city. He fell on the retreating Persians between Samosata and Zeugma in late summer 260. When the usurper Fulvius Macrianus took his sons as joint emperors against Gallienus, Odaenathus waited until it was clear that Gallienus would win, then marched on Emesa, where Quietus was killed and Balista executed in autumn 261.

From 262 he crossed the Euphrates and recovered Carrhae and Nisibis, then reached the walls of Ctesiphon, which withstood a short siege. About 263 he took the title King of Kings of the East and crowned his son Herodianus as co-king. By then he effectively controlled the Levant, Roman Mesopotamia and eastern Anatolia, and he ruled in practice as an independent monarch.

He was assassinated together with Herodianus in late 267, near Heraclea Pontica or Emesa. The sources disagree on the killer: a namesake, an unnamed nephew or a cousin named Maeonius. John of Antioch accused Gallienus, though the evidence for a Roman conspiracy is weak. His son Vaballathus succeeded him under the regency of his widow Zenobia, who used the power he had built to form the Palmyrene Empire in 270. He is regarded as the founder of the Palmyrene royal dynasty.
odawa: According to Anishinaabeg tradition, and the record of the birch bark scrolls, the Odawa came from the eastern areas of North America, a region called Dawnland on the East Coast. Guided by the luminescent miigis beings, the Anishinaabe moved inland along the Saint Lawrence River. At the Third Stopping Place near the Straits of Mackinac, the southern group divided into the Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi. Archaeological evidence suggests that the Saugeen complex people of the Bruce Peninsula, a group influenced by the Hopewell tradition, may have evolved into the Odawa.

They considered Manitoulin Island and the Bruce Peninsula their original homeland. With the Ojibwe and Potawatomi they formed the Council of Three Fires. The name Odawaa is believed to come from adaawe, to trade.

In 1615 Samuel de Champlain met 300 men of a people he called les cheueux releuez near the mouth of the French River. The Odawa became so important in the fur trade of New France that, before 1670, colonists in Quebec often called any Algonquian speaker of the Great Lakes an Odawa, and many interior nations became known to Europeans by names the Odawa used for them, such as Winnebago and Sioux. In the mid-seventeenth century they allied with other Algonquian peoples against the Mohawk in the Beaver Wars, though epidemics did more harm than warfare.

After the French built Fort Detroit in 1701, many Odawa moved there from Manitoulin Island. In the Seven Years' War they allied with France, and in 1763, after the British victory, the chief Pontiac led a rebellion against the British but could not stop settlement of the region. In the 1790s Chief Egushawa fought the United States in the Northwest Indian War, which ended in defeat at Fallen Timbers. By the Treaty of Greenville of 1795 the Odawa and their allies ceded most of Ohio, and after the Indian Removal Act of 1830 four bands ceded their reserves in 1831 and moved to Kansas.

The Odawa language, Daawaamwin, is a divergent dialect of Ojibwe noted for frequent syncope. About 500 people in Ontario and Michigan speak it. The Odawa are federally recognised as tribes in the United States and as First Nations in Canada, with about 15,000 people living in Ontario, Michigan and Oklahoma. The Ottawa River, and through it the city of Ottawa, Ontario, take the name of the Odawa, though their home territory lay well to the west of both.
odawara: Odawara lies in the Ashigara Plains, at the south-western tip of the Kantō region and in the far west of Kanagawa Prefecture. The Hakone Mountains border it on the north and west, the Sakawa River on the east and Sagami Bay of the Pacific Ocean on the south. Its climate is humid subtropical, with warm summers and cool winters and light or no snowfall.

The area has been settled since prehistoric times, and archaeological evidence points to a high population density in the Jōmon period. Under the Ritsuryō system of the Nara period it became part of Ashigarashimo District in Sagami Province, and in the Heian period it was divided into estates controlled mostly by the Hatano clan and its branches. During the Genpei War the Battle of Ishibashiyama was fought near the present city.

In the Sengoku period Odawara developed as a castle town and was the capital of the domains of the later Hōjō clan, which covered most of the Kantō region. Toyotomi Hideyoshi defeated the Hōjō in the Battle of Odawara in 1590, despite the castle's reputation as impregnable, and the territory passed to Tokugawa Ieyasu. Under the Tokugawa shogunate Odawara was the centre of Odawara Domain, ruled by a succession of daimyō, and prospered as Odawara-juku, a post station on the Tōkaidō highway linking Edo with Kyoto.

After the Meiji Restoration the domain briefly became Odawara Prefecture, which was merged with the short-lived Ashigara Prefecture before joining Kanagawa Prefecture in 1876. Economic and political life in Kanagawa shifted to Yokohama, and Odawara lost population, a decline worsened when the first route of the Tōkaidō Main Line passed to the north through Gotemba. The Great Kantō earthquake of 1923 caused ninety percent of the buildings in Odawara to collapse, and fires burned the rubble. The opening of the Tanna Tunnel in 1934 brought the main line through the city, which was raised from town to city status on 20 December 1940. On 15 August 1945 it was the last city in Japan to be bombed by Allied aircraft in World War II.

Odawara is a commercial centre for western Kanagawa and a transit point for the Hakone hot springs and the Fuji-Hakone-Izu National Park. It is known for kamaboko fish paste, stockfish, umeboshi salted plums and traditional herbal medicines. Its best-known monument is Odawara Castle, and the Odawara Hōjō Godai Festival is held on 3 May. The economist and philosopher Ninomiya Sontoku of the Edo period was born there.
ode-to-joy: Friedrich Schiller was a German poet, playwright and historian. In 1808 a slightly revised version of the ode, published after his death, changed two lines of the first stanza and left out the last stanza, which had asked for rescue from the chains of tyrants, mercy in the high courts and forgiveness for all sinners. This 1808 text forms the basis for Beethoven's setting.

Later in life Schiller regarded the poem as a failure. In an 1800 letter to Christian Gottfried Körner he called it detached from reality and of value perhaps for the two of them but not for the world. Scholars have speculated whether he first wrote an Ode to Freedom and changed it to Joy, but the musicologist Alexander Rehding points out that scholarly consensus holds there is no factual basis for this.

The ode is a long poem in stanzas, each followed by a chorus. It addresses Joy as a daughter of Elysium, a power that binds together what custom has divided, so that all men become brothers. It praises friendship and love, calls on millions to embrace one another, and looks for a loving Father above the stars. It calls for courage in suffering and truth to friend and foe, and ends with a plea for pardon.

The ode is best known for its use by Ludwig van Beethoven in the final movement of his Ninth Symphony, completed in 1824. Beethoven's text is not based entirely on Schiller's poem and introduces a few new sections. Other composers set the poem too, among them Franz Schubert in 1815, Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky in 1865 and Pietro Mascagni in 1882.

Beethoven's melody, but not Schiller's text, was adopted as the Anthem of Europe by the Council of Europe in 1972 and by the European Union in 1985. It was also used for the national anthem of Rhodesia from 1974 until 1979. During the military dictatorship in Chile women sang a Spanish version outside prisons, and in Berlin on Christmas Day 1989, after the fall of the Berlin Wall, Leonard Bernstein conducted it with choir and orchestra members from East and West Germany.
odenwald: The Odenwald is a low mountain range lying between the Upper Rhine Plain and the Bergstraße to the west, the Main and the Bauland to the east, the Rhine-Main Lowlands to the north and the Kraichgau to the south. The part south of the Neckar valley is sometimes called the Little Odenwald. Its basement of gneiss, granite, diorite and gabbro formed in the Variscan orogeny more than 300 million years ago, while in the eastern part red sandstone is what remains of the later sediments. Extinct volcanoes such as the Otzberg, the Daumberg and the Katzenbuckel date from 50 to 60 million years ago. The Katzenbuckel, at 626 metres, is the highest peak.

About 2500 BCE the Linear Pottery culture settled along the northern and southern edges of the Odenwald, while most of the interior stayed under virgin forest. Celts settled southern Germany about 400 BCE and were driven west across the Rhine by Germanic peoples. About 100 CE the older Odenwald line of the Neckar-Odenwald Limes was built under the Roman emperor Trajan, running from Wimpfen to Wörth on the Main, and parts of the region lay in Germania Superior. About 159 the Limes was moved about 30 kilometres east. Roman rule fell in 260, and the Alamanni and then the Franks settled the land between the Main and the Neckar.

In the 7th and 8th centuries Irish-Scottish and Anglo-Saxon monks, among them Pirmin and Boniface, brought Christianization. Carolingian rulers charged four Benedictine monasteries, Lorsch, Fulda, Mosbach and Amorbach, with opening the empty woods to settlement, and Amorbach became the most important for the eastern Odenwald. The origin of the name is debated: proposals link it to Odin, to a Roman unit named Civitas Auderiensium, to an Old High German word for thinly settled land or for enfeoffment, or to a chief named Odo.

The Odenwald belongs to the German states of Hesse, Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg, with the northern and western parts in southern Hesse and a small part in Lower Franconia. Heidelberg and Darmstadt lie at its edges. It is crossed by more than 10,000 kilometres of hiking trails and has many historic castles, which once controlled the Bergstraße and the valleys of the Weschnitz, Gersprenz, Mümling and Neckar. Local legend places the murder of Siegfried from the Nibelungenlied somewhere in the Odenwald, and many communities claim the spot. The Felsberg's Felsenmeer of weathered boulders was used as a quarry by the Romans.
oder-neisse-line: Oder–Neisse line is an unofficial term for the modern border between Germany and Poland. The line generally follows the Oder and Lusatian Neisse rivers and meets the Baltic Sea in the north. A small portion of Polish territory lies west of it, including the cities of Szczecin and Świnoujście, known in German as Stettin and Swinemünde. The border is 472 km long, the shortest possible between the two countries, and it divides several cities in two, among them Görlitz and Zgorzelec and Frankfurt and Słubice.

The lower Oder in Silesia was the western border of Piast Poland from the 10th until the 13th century, and from about the time of the First World War some proposed restoring that line. At the Tehran Conference in late 1943 Joseph Stalin raised the extension of Poland's western frontier to the Oder, and Franklin D. Roosevelt agreed in general that it should reach that river. At Yalta in February 1945 the Soviets for the first time openly supported a frontier on the Western rather than the Eastern Neisse. Winston Churchill objected that it would be a pity to stuff the Polish goose so full of German food that it got indigestion.

The question was left to the Potsdam Conference. On 2 August 1945 the Potsdam Agreement placed the German territories east of the line under Polish administrative control, in anticipation of a final peace treaty, and decided that Germans remaining there should be expelled. Silesia, Pomerania and the southern part of East Prussia went to Poland; northern East Prussia, with Königsberg renamed Kaliningrad, went to the Soviet Union. Much of the German population, estimated at 12 million in autumn 1944, had already fled the advancing Red Army. In Poland the territories were called the Recovered Territories, a term widely used in the propaganda of the People's Republic of Poland.

East Germany and Poland's Communist government signed the Treaty of Zgorzelec in 1950, recognising the line as the Border of Peace and Friendship. West Germany under Konrad Adenauer refused to accept it as permanent, and later accepted it with reservations in a treaty with Poland. After the revolutions of 1989 Poland and the reunified Germany confirmed the line in the border treaty of 1990, ratified in 1992.
oder-river: The Oder, Odra in Czech and Polish, rises in the Czech Republic and flows through western Poland. For 187 kilometres it forms the border between Poland and Germany as part of the Oder–Neisse line. It ends in the Szczecin Lagoon north of Szczecin and then divides into three branches, the Dziwna, the Świna and the Peene, which empty into the Bay of Pomerania of the Baltic Sea. Its basin covers 119,074 square kilometres, 89 per cent of it in Poland. The largest city on the river is Wrocław, and Szczecin is a major maritime port near its mouth. It is navigable over a large part of its length, up to Koźle.

To the Romans the river was the Viadrus or Viadua, a branch of the Amber Road from the Baltic Sea to the Roman Empire. Before Slavs settled along its banks it was an important trade route. The Dagome iudex described the western frontier of the Duchy of Poland under Duke Mieszko I in 990 as running along the Oder, although in most sections the border lay west of the river.

In the 10th century almost the whole course of the Oder lay inside the new Polish state, except for the area around the source, which was under Bohemian rule. Opole became the capital of Upper Silesia and Wrocław the capital of Lower Silesia. From the 13th century the Oder valley was central to the German Ostsiedlung, and its towns became German-speaking over the following centuries. Control of parts of the river passed from Poland to Brandenburg, Bohemia, and later Hungary, Sweden, Prussia and Germany.
The Finow Canal, first built in 1605, joined the Oder to the Havel, and Frederick the Great had the river diverted into a straight channel through the Oderbruch marshes in 1746–53.

At the Tehran Conference in 1943 the Allies decided that Germany's new eastern border would run along the Oder. After the Second World War the former German areas east of the Oder and the Lusatian Neisse passed to Poland by decision of the Allies at the Potsdam Conference, and the Oder–Neisse line became the border between the Soviet occupation zone and Poland. About 8 million Germans remaining east of the line were expelled by the Polish and Soviet administrations. East Germany confirmed the border in 1950, West Germany in 1970, and reunified Germany and Poland recognised it by treaty in 1990.
odessa: Odesa lies in the Black Sea Lowland, on the southwestern shore of the Gulf of Odesa on the northwestern coast of the Black Sea. It is about 31 km north of the mouth of the Dniester, some 443 km south of Kyiv, and about 40 km east of the border with Moldova. It is a warm-water port. The city is sometimes called the Pearl by the Sea or the Southern Capital.

A large Greek settlement stood on the site no later than the middle of the 6th century BCE, and a necropolis of the 5th to 3rd centuries BCE has long been known. Some scholars believe it was a trading settlement founded by the Greek city of Histria, though whether the bay is the ancient Port of the Histrians is not settled. A Slavic port, Kotsiubijiv, is first mentioned in 1415 as part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. After 1529 the area, known as Khadjibey, belonged to the Ottoman Empire, which rebuilt the fortress there in the mid-18th century under the name Yeni Dünya, meaning New World, until its defeat in the Russo-Turkish War ended in 1792.

A decree of Catherine II in 1794 ordered a naval harbour and trading place at Khadjibey, and in 1795 it was officially renamed Odessa, after a Greek colony of Odessos that supposedly lay in the area. The first census, in 1797, counted 3,455 people, and by 1803 there were 9,000. Its first commercial bank opened in 1801. From 1819 to 1858 it was a free port.

In 1905 Odesa saw a workers' uprising supported by the crew of the battleship Potemkin, commemorated in Sergei Eisenstein's film The Battleship Potemkin, which includes a scene on the great stone staircase now known as the Potemkin Steps. In 1941 Romanian and German troops attacked the city, and the Siege of Odessa began on 5 August and lasted 73 days. In the 1991 referendum 85.38 per cent of Odesa Oblast voted for Ukrainian independence.

Odesa is the third most populous city of Ukraine and a major seaport and transport hub, with the Port of Odesa and the oil terminal at Port Pivdennyi. It is the administrative centre of Odesa Oblast. Its industries include shipbuilding, oil refining and chemicals. Its historic city centre, notable for its multiculturality and 19th-century urban planning, is a World Heritage Site.
odia-language: Odia descends from Odra Prakrit, which itself evolved from Magadhi Prakrit, the language spoken in eastern India over 1,500 years ago and used in early Jain and Buddhist texts. It appears to have had relatively little influence from Persian and Arabic compared with other major Indo-Aryan languages. Its history is divided into Proto-Odia, Old Odia, Middle Odia and Modern Odia, the last running from the 18th century onward.

Inscriptions from the third quarter of the 9th century, from the reign of the early Eastern Gangas, show Odra Prakrit words used alongside Sanskrit. The earliest inscription in Old Odia is the Urajam inscription of the Eastern Gangas, dated 1051, and Old Odia in connected lines appears in an inscription of 1249. The earliest prose is found in the Madala Panji, the chronicle of the Jagannath Temple at Puri.

Odia is an Indo-Aryan language and the official language of Odisha, where native speakers make up 82 per cent of the population. It is also spoken in parts of West Bengal, Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. The 2011 census counted 37.52 million speakers in India, 93 per cent of them in Odisha, and the Odia diaspora brings the number worldwide to about 50 million. Its varieties include Baleswari in the north, Kataki in the centre, Ganjami in the south, Sambalpuri in the west and Desia in the south-west.

It is written in the Odia script, a Brahmic abugida in which every consonant carries an inherent vowel. The script has developed over nearly a thousand years, and its curved shape is attributed to writing on palm leaves, which tear if too many straight lines are used. A cursive form, the Karani script, was used for administration and for palm leaf manuscripts.

Odia has a continuous literary tradition. Sarala Das wrote an Odia Mahabharata, and the Panchasakha, five poets including Balarama Dasa and Jagannatha Dasa, produced translations and adaptations of Sanskrit works, among them an Odia Bhagabata and the Jagamohana Ramayana. Much classical literature was written to be sung and is tied to Odissi music. Upendra Bhanja was the leading poet of the period from about 1700 to 1850.

Christian missionaries cast the first Odia printing type in 1836, and Amos Sutton produced a Bible, a dictionary and a grammar in the following years. The first Odia newspaper, Utkala Deepika, appeared in 1866. In the 19th century some Bengali scholars claimed that Odia was only a dialect of Bengali. Fakir Mohan Senapati, Radhanath Ray and Madhusudan Rao brought a modern outlook to its literature, and four Odia writers have received the Jnanpith award.
odisha: Odisha lies in eastern India, bordering Jharkhand and West Bengal to the north, Chhattisgarh to the west and Andhra Pradesh to the south, with a coastline on the Bay of Bengal. Its coastal plain, which includes the lake Chilika, is rich in silt deposited by six major rivers: the Subarnarekha, Budhabalanga, Baitarani, Brahmani, Mahanadi and Rushikulya. The region is also known as Utkala, a name that appears in India's national anthem. The terms Odisha and Orissa derive from the ancient Prakrit Odda Visaya, found in the Tirumalai inscription of Rajendra Chola I, dated to 1025.

Acheulian tools of the Lower Paleolithic point to early human settlement. Kalinga is mentioned in ancient texts such as the Mahabharata and the Vayu Purana, and Baudhayana describes it as not yet influenced by Vedic traditions. Its borders coincide with those of modern Odisha. The Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga in 261 BCE, the eighth year of his reign. His own edicts record about 100,000 people killed and 150,000 captured, and he is said to have turned to pacifism and Buddhism.

Cuttack became the capital of the region around 1135 under Anantavarman Chodaganga. In the 15th century Sarala Das, who translated the Mahabharata into Odia, called the land Odisha, and the inscriptions of Kapilendra Deva of the Gajapati Kingdom (1435–67) on temple walls in Puri use the same name. The British Indian government demarcated the modern boundaries, and the Orissa Province was established on 1 April 1936 from the Odia-speaking districts of Bihar and Orissa Province, the Madras Presidency and the Central Provinces. After 1948 the capital was Bhubaneswar.

Odisha is a state of India with over 41 million inhabitants. Odia, spoken by 82.70 per cent of the people at the 2011 census, is its official language and one of the classical languages of India. The Jagannath Temple at Puri, about 200 feet high, and the Lingaraja Temple at Bhubaneswar are major Hindu pilgrimage sites, and part of the Konark Sun Temple survives.
odo-of-france: Odo was the eldest son of Robert the Strong, Duke of the Franks, Margrave of Neustria and Count of Anjou, who died at the Battle of Brissarthe in 866. Odo and his brother Robert were still young, so King Charles the Bald put Hugh the Abbot in charge of the counties their father had held. Odo became Count of Paris in 882 and was also lay abbot of St Martin of Tours. In 882 or 883 he married Théodrate of Troyes.

A large army of Northmen sailed up the Seine in July 885 and reached Paris on 24 November. Odo and Bishop Joscelin, who had refortified the city, beat off an assault, and a siege followed. After the bishop died on 16 April, Odo made a sortie to seek aid. Charles the Fat's commander Henry of Alemmania died trying to relieve the city, and Charles paid the Vikings to move on to Burgundy. Evidence suggests that Odo's rise came through alignment with the emperor, whose court he visited.

Charles the Fat was deposed at the end of 887 in a revolt led by Arnulf of Carinthia, leaving a power vacuum in the Carolingian empire. Odo had inherited the property of Bishop Joscelin and Hugh the Abbot and held military command of Neustria and three lay abbacies. The West Frankish nobles chose him as king, and Walter, Archbishop of Sens, crowned him at Compiègne in February 888. Fulk, Archbishop of Reims, resisted and invited Guy of Spoleto to take the crown, without success. Odo defeated a Viking force at Montfaucon, and Arnulf then recognised him. A second coronation followed at Reims in November.

His power was limited outside his family lands, and he rarely left northern France. He gave his brother Robert most of his honours, including Paris and Poitiers. From 892 a party in favour of Charles formed around Fulk and others, and revolts broke out in the south and in Flanders. Fulk crowned the fourteen-year-old Charles the Simple at Reims in 893 with Pope Formosus's support. Odo won a surprise attack that autumn and besieged Reims, and Arnulf backed first Charles and then Odo. After negotiation Odo ceded part of the realm to Charles in 896.

A definitive peace followed in which Odo made Charles his successor. Odo died at La Fère on 1 January 898, and Charles succeeded him. His reign marked the definitive separation of West Francia from the Carolingian Empire, which was never reunited. He was the first king of the Robertian dynasty, the parent house of the House of Capet.
odoacer: Odoacer's origins are uncertain. A fragment of the historian Priscus describes him as a man of the Sciri, the son of Edeco and brother of Hunulf. John of Antioch reported that he was 60 when he died in 493, which gives a birth around 433. Sources call him a Scirian, a Rugian, a Goth or a Thuringian, and many historians accept Scirian heritage; none of the ancient sources calls him a Hun. By 470 he was an officer in what remained of the Roman army.
