In 475 Orestes, appointed commander by the emperor Julius Nepos, rebelled, drove Nepos from Italy and proclaimed his young son Romulus Augustulus emperor. The Germanic foederati, who had been quartered in Italy for years, asked Orestes for lands of their own, and when he refused they turned to Odoacer. Orestes was killed at Placentia, and the foederati proclaimed Odoacer rex on 23 August 476. He advanced to Ravenna and compelled Romulus to abdicate on 4 September, sparing him with a pension of 6,000 solidi, according to the Anonymus Valesianus.

The Senate then sent an embassy to the Eastern emperor Zeno, saying that one monarch sufficed to rule the world, and Zeno granted Odoacer the title of patrician and authority to govern Italy as dux Italiae. Odoacer ruled with the cooperation of the Roman Senate, nominating senators to the consulship and other high offices. Although an Arian Christian, he had good relations with the church hierarchy. After Nepos was murdered on 9 May 480, he executed the assassins and established his rule in Dalmatia.

Zeno came to see Odoacer as a rival, and promised Theodoric the Great and his Ostrogoths the Italian peninsula if they removed him. Theodoric defeated Odoacer at the Isonzo, at Verona and on the Adda, and besieged him in Ravenna. A treaty negotiated by John, bishop of Ravenna, on 25 February 493 provided that the two would share Ravenna and rule jointly. Theodoric entered the city on 5 March and killed Odoacer with his own sword at a banquet on 15 March, and then had Odoacer's followers hunted down.

Odoacer's wife Sunigilda was stoned to death, his brother Onoulphus was killed by archers in a church, and his son Thela, exiled to Gaul, was killed after trying to return. The historian J. B. Bury saw Odoacer's seizure of power as one stage in the dismemberment of the Empire rather than its fall.
odoric-of-pordenone: Little is known of Odoric's life, and legend has clouded it. He was born at Villanova, a hamlet now part of Pordenone in Friuli. One tradition makes him the son of a soldier serving Ottokar II of Bohemia; another makes him the son of a prominent local family, which recent historians tend to discount. A forensic examination of his partly mummified body in 2002 showed that he was about 50 at death, pointing to a birth around 1280. The earliest record of him as a Franciscan is a document he signed in 1296.

Odoric seems to have had no diplomatic mission; he says he went to win a harvest of souls. From Venice he went to Constantinople, Trebizond, Tabriz and Persia, and from Hormuz sailed to India. He travelled down the Malabar coast, visited the shrine of Thomas the Apostle and saw the procession of Jagannath at Puri. By junk he reached northern Sumatra, Java and Borneo, where he was the first European with a recorded visit. In China he saw Guangzhou and Hangzhou and went by the Grand Canal to Khanbaliq, where he stayed three years, between 1323 and 1328.

He returned overland and reached home about the end of 1329 or early in 1330, after some 50,000 kilometres. In May 1330, at the friary of St Anthony in Padua, he told his story to Friar William of Solagna, who wrote it down in simple Latin.

Odoric fell ill at Pisa on his way to the papal court at Avignon and returned to Friuli, where he died on 14 January 1331. Reports of miracles spread and veneration grew, and Pope Benedict XIV approved it in 1755. The Relatio was first printed at Pesaro in 1513; it describes Hangzhou as a city greater than any in the world, and mentions fishing with tame cormorants and the binding of women's feet, which Marco Polo omits. Many of the reports of Asia in Mandeville's Travels are versions of his eyewitness descriptions.
odrysians: The Thracians had no writing tradition of their own, so the history of the Odrysians rests on archaeology, coins and the accounts of Greek historians. The Persian presence in Thrace was short-lived but probably stimulated trade and early state formation, and Thracian coinage began about 500 BCE. The Odrysians first appear in Herodotus after the Persian failure in Greece, with their core territory in the valleys of the Hebros river and its tributaries Tonzos and Arda. Thucydides calls Teres I the first powerful king of the Odrysae and the founder of a great Odrysian empire over a large part of Thrace, though many tribes stayed independent.

Teres had died by the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War in 431 BCE, and his son Sitalces, an ally of Athens, extended Odrysian influence from the Strymon to the Black Sea and the mouth of the Danube. Thucydides held that the state exceeded in revenue and prosperity all the nations between the Ionian Sea and the Black Sea. By 400 BCE it showed signs of fragmentation, and Cotys I led a brief revival until his murder in 360 BCE.

The kingdom then split among Cersebleptes, Amadocus II and Berisades, a division confirmed by a treaty in 357 BCE. Philip II of Macedon conquered the three kingdoms in 340 BCE. About 330 BCE Seuthes III revived a much smaller Odrysian state with a new capital, Seuthopolis, which lasted until the second quarter of the 3rd century BCE. Later evidence for an Odrysian state is slight. The heartlands came to be known as the Sapaean kingdom, a Roman client state converted into the province of Thracia in the mid-first century CE.

The Odrysian kingdom was a tribal amalgam, and before Seuthopolis it had no fixed capital. Its kingship was influenced by the Persian court and resembled that of Macedon. Kings had to justify their rule by military prowess, religion and gifts, and the exchange of gifts, a practice adopted from Persia, was central: Thucydides recorded that a tribute of 400 talents under Seuthes I was shared among the king and the chief men. Armies were largely horsemen, and Sitalces' infantry was mostly ill-organised levies. Greek mercenary commanders such as Xenophon served Odrysian kings, and Greek became the language of administrators. Residences and temples have been found around Starosel in the Sredna Gora mountains.
odysseus: The etymology of the name Odysseus is unknown, and a non-Greek or Pre-Greek origin has been suggested. In Book 19 of the Odyssey his grandfather Autolycus names the child, saying that he has been angered with many, men and women, so the boy shall be called Odysseus; the name is thus tied to the verb odussomai, meaning to be wroth against. According to the Iliad and the Odyssey his father is Laertes and his mother Anticlea. A non-Homeric tradition made Sisyphus his true father. His wife is Penelope and his son Telemachus.

Most sources for his exploits before the Trojan War, chiefly the mythographers Pseudo-Apollodorus and Hyginus, postdate Homer by many centuries. When Helen of Troy was abducted, Menelaus called on the suitors to honour their oaths. Odysseus tried to avoid going, since an oracle had foretold a long-delayed return home if he went, and feigned madness by yoking a donkey and an ox to his plough. Palamedes, at the behest of Agamemnon, placed the infant Telemachus in front of the plough. Odysseus turned it aside, exposing the ruse.

In the Iliad Odysseus is one of the most influential Greek champions and, with Nestor and Idomeneus, one of the most trusted counsellors. When Agamemnon tested the army's morale by announcing his intention to depart, Odysseus restored order, and he later persuaded Agamemnon not to withdraw. He was one of the three envoys sent in the failed embassy to Achilles, and he helped Diomedes in the night raid in which Rhesus was killed. After Patroclus was slain he counselled Achilles to let the men eat and rest before returning to battle.

The Odyssey tells of the ten years of travel that followed the war. Leaving Troy with twelve ships, he first raided Ismarus, a city of the Cicones, allies of the Trojans. The raiders took goods, livestock and women, sparing only Maron, a priest of Apollo, and his family, who gave Odysseus a barrel of wine. The Cicones returned with help from their neighbours, and after losing six of his men Odysseus was forced to flee.

Later sources, mostly genealogical, gave him many further children in order to link him with the foundation of Italic cities. Hellanicus of Lesbos wrote that Rome was founded by Aeneas and Odysseus together. Evidence points to a cult of Odysseus on Ithaca, with public games called the Odysseia and a gathering place, the Odysseion. Strabo records an altar to him on the island of Meninx, modern Djerba.
odyssey: There is no consensus on when the Odyssey and the Iliad were composed. The Greeks began adopting a modified Phoenician alphabet in the 8th century BCE, and if the Homeric poems were among its earliest products they would have been composed towards the end of that century. Scholars agree that the epics developed in an oral tradition over hundreds of years. In the early twentieth century Milman Parry and Albert Lord showed that they have the marks of oral poetry, which lets even an illiterate poet improvise large poems. The poem was performed for audiences by a singer called an aoidos or rhapsode, and by the mid-6th century BCE it was part of the Greek literary canon.
In antiquity Homer's authorship was taken as true, though most scholars now assume that the two epics were composed independently, and the Homeric Question about their authorship still divides them.

The poem has 24 books and 12,109 lines of dactylic hexameter. It opens in medias res, with Odysseus, king of Ithaca, still absent ten years after the Greeks won the Trojan War. His journey home lasts another ten years, and all his crewmates are killed. At home 108 suitors court his wife Penelope, who says she will remarry when she has finished weaving a shroud for Odysseus's aged father Laertes, and each night secretly unweaves it. Athena sends his son Telemachus to seek news of his father, and he visits Nestor and Menelaus; this part, Books 1 to 4, is called the Telemachy.

Homecoming, nostos, is the central theme, with wandering, guest-friendship, testing and omens. The Phaeacians show exemplary guest-friendship, while Polyphemus and Calypso show poor guest-friendship. Back in Ithaca, Athena turns Odysseus into a beggar so that he can test who is loyal. Penelope tests him in turn by saying she will move their bed, which was made from a living tree, a fact that only the real Odysseus would know.

In the Byzantine Empire the epics remained school texts through the Middle Ages. Livius Andronicus made a Latin version, the Odusia, which became a school text for Latin students. The first printed edition in Greek appeared in Milan in 1488, and the first complete English translation in 1616. The epics formed the basis of education in the ancient Mediterranean, and Western humanists adopted that curriculum. A poll of experts by BBC Culture in 2018 named it literature's most enduring narrative.
oecd: The OECD is the successor of the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC), established in April 1948 among the European recipients of Marshall Plan aid for the reconstruction of Europe after the war. Only Western European states belonged to it, and its main function was to allocate American aid. It was headquartered in the Château de la Muette in Paris.

After Marshall aid ended in 1952 the OEEC turned to economic issues. Its coordinating role was challenged by the Rome Treaties of 1957, which created the European Economic Community and Euratom. By then some leading countries felt that the OEEC had outlived its purpose but could be adapted to a more global mission. After meetings in Paris beginning in January 1960, it was agreed to create a body that would also devise policies to assist less developed countries.

The Convention on the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development was signed on 14 December 1960, and the OECD officially superseded the OEEC in September 1961. It consisted of the European OEEC members plus the United States and Canada, who had been observers. There were twenty official founding members. Japan joined in 1964, and over the following decade Finland, Australia and New Zealand did as well.

The OECD created agencies such as the OECD Development Centre in 1961, the International Energy Agency in 1974 and the Financial Action Task Force on Money Laundering. After the Revolutions of 1989 it began helping Central European countries prepare market reforms. In 1990 it set up the Centre for Co-operation with European Economies in Transition, and in 1991 it launched the Partners in Transition programme for Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Poland. Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, together with South Korea and Mexico, became members between 1996 and 2000. East Germany joined on 3 October 1990 through reunification.

Article 1 of the Convention states the aims: the highest sustainable economic growth and employment and a rising standard of living in member countries while maintaining financial stability, sound economic expansion in member and non-member countries, and the expansion of world trade. The OECD describes itself as a forum whose members are committed to democracy and the market economy. It is funded by contributions from members and is an official United Nations observer.

It conducts multilateral surveillance through peer reviews and policy assessments. In taxation it publishes a Model Tax Convention, which serves as a template for allocating taxation rights between countries, and has issued Transfer Pricing Guidelines since 1995.
oecusse: Oecusse, also called Oecusse-Ambeno, is a municipality and the only special administrative region of Timor-Leste. It lies on the north coast of the western part of Timor and is separated from the rest of the country by West Timor, which surrounds it on all sides except the north, where it faces the Savu Sea. Its area is 813.6 km2 and its capital is Pante Macassar. Ambeno was the historic Timorese kingdom that occupied most of the present territory, while Oecusse was the traditional name of Pante Macassar and its environs; the name Oecusse comes from the Uab Meto words for water and a clay jug, or perhaps a ruler named Kussi.

Oecusse was among the first parts of Timor where the Portuguese settled and is usually considered the cradle of Timor-Leste. Around 1556 the Dominican friar António Taveiro began missionary work on the north coast, and in 1569 the village of Lifau appears on a European map. In 1641 Dominican priests baptised the royal families of Ambeno, Mena and Amanuban. From the 1650s the Topasses, a Eurasian population, grew in strength, controlled the sandalwood trade and used Lifau as a stronghold. In 1702 Lifau became the capital of the colony, with its first governor from Goa; the capital moved to Dili in 1769 because of attacks by the Topass leader Francisco Hornay III.

The Treaty of Lisbon of 1859 divided the island between Portugal and the Netherlands and left Oecusse as an enclave inside Dutch territory. In 1912 João da Cruz, the Liurai of Ambeno, revolted against the Portuguese; the revolt was put down and the Ambeno kingdom lapsed. Indonesian forces invaded Oecusse on 6 June 1975, a few months before the invasion of the rest of Timor-Leste. The region became part of the independent state on 20 May 2002.

Articles 5 and 71 of the 2002 constitution provide for a special administrative and economic regime, and a law of 2014 created the Special Administrative Region. It has four administrative posts and 18 sucos, and the Census of 15 October 2022 gave a population of 80,176. The Atoni Pah Meto are the dominant ethnic group and Uab Meto is the native language, while Tetum is the main language of public life; 99.3 per cent of inhabitants are Roman Catholic, many also following older customs known as adat.
oedipus: In the best-known version of the myth, Oedipus was born to King Laius and Queen Jocasta of Thebes. Laius had been told by the oracle of Apollo at Delphi that any son born to him would kill him. He had the child's ankles pierced and tethered, and a servant was to abandon the baby on the mountain. The servant instead passed him to a shepherd from Corinth, and the infant was adopted by King Polybus and Queen Merope of Corinth. His name, "swollen foot", came from the injuries to his feet.

Years later the oracle at Delphi told Oedipus that he was destined to murder his father and marry his mother. To avoid this, he did not return to Corinth but travelled to Thebes. Where three roads crossed, near Daulia, he met a chariot driven by Laius, his birth father, and killed him in a quarrel over who had the right to go first.

Oedipus found Thebes in the grip of the Sphinx, which killed travellers who could not answer her riddle: what walks on four feet in the morning, two in the afternoon and three at night. He answered correctly that it was man, and the Sphinx killed herself, though in some versions he kills her. Jocasta's brother Creon had announced that whoever rid the city of the Sphinx would become king and marry the widowed queen, so Oedipus married his mother. They had four children, the sons Eteocles and Polynices and the daughters Antigone and Ismene.

Many years later a plague struck Thebes. Oedipus learned that the killer of Laius must be brought to justice, and the blind prophet Tiresias exposed him as the culprit. A messenger from Corinth revealed that Oedipus was adopted, and the herdsman who had been told to leave the infant to die confirmed the truth.

Events after the revelation depend on the source. In Sophocles, Jocasta hanged herself, and Oedipus blinded himself with a pin from her gown and was exiled; his daughter Antigone guided him until he died at Colonus, welcomed by King Theseus of Athens. In Euripides, Jocasta did not kill herself and Oedipus was blinded by a servant of Laius, and some older sources, including Homer, have him continue to rule Thebes. His sons Eteocles and Polynices killed each other in a fight over the throne, and Creon took it.

Written mention begins in the 5th century BCE. Aeschylus won first prize in 467 BCE with a trilogy on the myth, of which only Seven Against Thebes survives. Sophocles's three Theban plays were written for separate festivals many years apart. Sigmund Freud took the name Oedipus complex from the myth.
offa-of-mercia: Offa was the son of Thingfrith and a descendant of Eowa, a son of Pybba, who ruled Mercia early in the 7th century. His grandfather Eanwulf was a first cousin of King Æthelbald, who had ruled Mercia since 716 and by 731 was overlord of all the provinces south of the Humber. Æthelbald was assassinated in 757, reportedly murdered at night by his own bodyguards. Beornred took the throne briefly, and Offa put him to flight. It is possible that Offa did not gain the throne until 758, since a charter of 789 places him in the thirty-first year of his reign. No contemporary biography of Offa survives.

Offa first secured Mercia's traditional dependencies, the Hwicce and the Magonsæte. After 762 he exploited instability in Kent, where he granted land at Rochester in 764, and he controlled Sussex by 771. In the 780s he allied with Beorhtric of Wessex, who married his daughter Eadburh. In East Anglia he became overlord, and in 794 the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that he ordered King Æthelberht's head struck off, perhaps for rebellion.

He persuaded Pope Adrian I to divide the archdiocese of Canterbury and create one at Lichfield, which may have been meant to let an archbishop consecrate his son Ecgfrith as king in 787. He repeatedly fought the Welsh, and Offa's Dyke, about 64 miles of earthwork along the border, is attributed to him by the monk Asser.

Around 789 Charlemagne proposed that his son marry one of Offa's daughters. Offa asked in return for a Frankish bride for Ecgfrith, which angered Charlemagne, who broke off contact and forbade English ships his ports. Relations were later restored. Offa's coins carry fine portraits and show his wife Cynethryth, the only Anglo-Saxon queen ever depicted on a coin.

Offa died on 29 July 796. His son Ecgfrith reigned for less than five months before Coenwulf became king. Historians once saw Offa's reign as a step towards a unified England, but this is no longer the majority view. In the words of Simon Keynes, Offa was driven by a lust for power, not a vision of English unity, and what he left was a reputation, not a legacy.
offenbach-am-main: Offenbach am Main lies on the left bank of the river Main in Hesse and borders Frankfurt, of whose urban area it is part. Its inner city consists of the historic centre and the expansions of the 19th century. Three formerly independent suburbs were incorporated in the first half of the 20th century: Bürgel in 1908, then Bieber in 1938 and Rumpenheim in 1942. In 2019 the city council divided the whole city into 21 districts, where only nine had been officially districts before.

The first documented mention of a suburb of Offenbach dates from 770, and a document of the Holy Roman Emperor Otto II of 977 gives the first mention of the place itself. During the Middle Ages it passed through many hands. In 1486 Count Ludwig of Isenburg finally took control for his family, and in 1556 Count Reinhard of Isenburg moved his residence to Offenbach and built the Isenburg Palace, completed in 1559. It burned in 1564 and was rebuilt in 1578.

In 1635 Offenbach was given to the Landgraves of Hesse-Darmstadt, but it returned to the Isenburg-Birstein count, later prince, in 1642. It remained in that principality until 1815, when the Congress of Vienna gave the city to the Austrian Emperor Francis I. A year later it was passed to the Grand Duchy of Hesse-Darmstadt, and the monarchy there ended in 1918.

French Protestants, the Huguenots, came in the 17th century and helped to make the town prosperous. They brought knowledge of tobacco and turned Offenbach into a centre for rolling cigars. The town was more cosmopolitan than Frankfurt, and Goethe and Mozart visited it several times. Jews settled there from the late 16th century. Of 871 residents in 1829, the 40 Jewish families made up nearly a quarter of the population, and they had their own cemetery. The Jewish community was destroyed in the Holocaust.

In the Second World War a third of the city was destroyed by Allied bombing, which claimed 467 lives. The city expanded to the south in the 1960s with the district of Lauterborn, and the office district of Kaiserlei was built on the border with Frankfurt.

In the 20th century the economy rested on machine-building, leather-making, typography and design, and the automobile and pharmaceutical industries. Offenbach was a European centre of typography, with the firm Gebr. Klingspor, and the Linotype company, which produced the typefaces Optima and Palatino. Figures of traditional design included the typographer Rudolf Koch. The city has the German Leather Museum, the Klingspor Museum of typography and calligraphy, a design university and the German Meteorological Service. The Isenburg Palace is now used by the design university.
ogaden: The Ogaden is a vast, largely semi-arid plateau south and southeast of the Ethiopian Highlands, on the border between Ethiopia and Somalia. It is one of the historical names for the modern Somali Region, which Somalis also call Soomaali Galbeed, Western Somalia. It is the westernmost region inhabited by Somalis in the Horn of Africa, and its plains extend towards the southeastern highlands, near cities such as Harar and Dire Dawa. The name is usually traced to the Somali clan called Ogaden, whose progenitor Abdirahman Absame bore the nickname Ogaadeen, meaning one who takes care of another; an alternative etymology, possibly folk, combines the Harari word for road with Aden.

Few texts survive on the early inhabitants. The region was the home of the Harla, a people now extinct, and became one of the earliest footholds of Islam in Africa. It formed part of the Ifat Sultanate in the 13th century and later of the Adal Sultanate, for which Harar was the effective capital. In the first half of the 16th century the Ethiopian–Adal War broke out, when Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, Imam of Adal, launched a jihad against Abyssinia; Somali and other Muslim communities in the region joined it. The Ajuran Sultanate, successor to Ifat and Adal in the region, ruled from Qalafo on the upper Shabelle until its decline in the 17th century.

Before the late 19th century the Ogaden was inhabited by organised Somali communities and was independent of Ethiopian imperial rule. Emperor Menelik II conquered Harar in 1887, and raids from it into the Ogaden in the 1890s brought looting and the burning of settlements. In 1897 Britain ceded part of the British Somaliland protectorate to Ethiopia in the Anglo-Ethiopian Treaty, on which Ethiopia bases its claim; the Somali Republic rejected the treaty as invalid after its independence in 1960. The Dervish movement of Sayyid Mohamed Abdullah Hassan arose in resistance. After the Italian conquest of Ethiopia in 1936 the Ogaden was attached to Italian Somaliland, and the British ceded it to Ethiopia in 1948, with the last parts of Haud transferred in 1955.

Almost thirty Somali clans live in the region, the Ogaden clan of the Darod forming the majority. At the founding conference of the new region, held in Dire Dawa in 1992, the name was divisive: the Ogaden National Liberation Front wanted it called Ogadenia, while the other clans opposed naming a region of many clans after one, and it was named the Somali Region.
ogaden-war: The Ogaden is a vast plateau overwhelmingly inhabited by Somali people, the westernmost region settled by Somalis in the Horn of Africa. Before the late 1880s its Somali clans were free of the control of the Ethiopian Empire. Then Emperor Menelik II launched invasions into Somali-inhabited territories, and in the Anglo-Ethiopian Treaty of 1897 the British ceded large parts of Somali territory to Ethiopia. A rebellion known as Nasrallah, or the Ogaden Liberation Front, broke out in 1963, followed by an interstate war between Ethiopia and Somalia in 1964.

In October 1969 Major General Mohamed Siad Barre led a military coup in Somalia. After the Derg overthrew Emperor Haile Selassie in September 1974, drought and military oppression worsened conditions in the Ogaden. The Somali government helped to organise the Western Somali Liberation Front, which by June 1977 had forced the Ethiopian army out of much of the region and into fortified towns.

The Somali National Army invaded the Ogaden in July 1977. According to Gebru Tareke it fielded about 31,000 to 39,000 men with 250 tanks and 600 artillery pieces, against 35,000 to 47,000 Ethiopian regular troops and militiamen, whose best units were fighting the Eritrean War of Independence in the north. Somali forces took the Jijiga area on 30 August 1977.

The Soviet Union, which had armed Somalia, disapproved of the invasion and backed Ethiopia instead. A massive airlift of supplies worth 1 billion dollars, Cuban soldiers and airmen, and Soviet advisers led by General Vasily Petrov saved Ethiopia from defeat. On 23 January 1978 Cuban armoured brigades inflicted the worst losses Somali forces had suffered in a single action. The Ethiopian and Cuban force prevailed at Harar and Jijiga and pushed the Somalis out of the Ogaden, and on 23 March 1978 Ethiopia declared that the last border post had been regained.

Somalia lost almost a third of its regular soldiers, three-eighths of its armoured units and half of its air force, and the disorganised, demoralised army revolted, a revolt that spiralled into the Somali Civil War. The Western Somali Liberation Front kept up guerrilla resistance. A second Ethiopian offensive in December 1979 attacked the means of survival of the population, including the poisoning of wells and the killing of cattle, and thousands of Somali civilians were killed. Executions and rape of civilians and refugees by Ethiopian and Cuban troops were widespread during the war. An estimated 800,000 people crossed into Somalia, and by 1979 official figures counted 1.3 million refugees there.
ogooue: The Ogooué, also called the Ogowe or the Nazareth River, is some 1,200 km long and is the principal river of Gabon in west-central Africa. It is the fourth largest river in Africa by volume of discharge. Its watershed drains nearly the entire country, with some tributaries reaching into the Republic of the Congo, Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea. The basin covers 223,000 square kilometres, of which 189,500, or 85 per cent, lie within Gabon.

The river rises in the north-west of the Batéké Plateau near Kengue in the Republic of the Congo, runs north-west and enters Gabon near Boumango. From Lastoursville up to Ndjolé rapids make it unnavigable, and from Ndjolé it runs west to enter the Gulf of Guinea near Ozouri, south of Port-Gentil. Its delta is about 100 km long and 100 km wide. Among its many tributaries the Iyinda is the most important. The first European explorer to trace the river to its source was Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, who travelled in the area in the 1870s.

The river is navigable from Ndjolé to the sea, and it is used to bring wood to the harbour at Port-Gentil. Its basin mostly consists of undisturbed rainforest, with some savanna grassland where the mid-year dry season is longest, and it is home to high biodiversity. All three African crocodile species occur in the river: the Nile crocodile, the dwarf crocodile and the slender-snouted crocodile. A site of 30,000 hectares in the delta, including much of Mandji Island, is an Important Bird Area. The basin holds several major conservation reserves, including Lopé National Park. Towns along the river include Lambaréné, Ndjolé, Booué, Lastoursville, Moanda and Franceville, near the Congo border.
ohio: Ohio takes its name from the Ohio River on its southern border, which comes from a Seneca word meaning good river, great river or large creek. The state covers about 116,100 square kilometres, with rolling glaciated plains across most of it, rugged unglaciated hills on the Allegheny Plateau in the southeast and 502 kilometres of Lake Erie coastline to the north. Nearly all of the river belongs to Kentucky and West Virginia, since a 1980 Supreme Court ruling placed the boundary at the northern low-water mark of 1792. The border with Michigan was adjusted after the Toledo War.

Spear points of the Folsom and Clovis types show that nomads lived in the Ohio Valley as early as 13,000 BCE. The settled Adena culture appeared between 1,000 and 800 BCE, and its best-known remnant is the Great Serpent Mound in Adams County. Around 100 BCE the Adena evolved into the Hopewell tradition, whose large earthworks survive at Marietta, Newark and Circleville and whose trading network spanned a third of the continent. The Hopewell disappeared from the valley about 600 CE. The Fort Ancient people, the Whittlesey culture and the Monongahela culture all disappeared in the 17th century, and their origins are unknown.

After the Beaver Wars of the mid-17th century the Iroquois Confederation claimed much of the Ohio country as hunting and beaver-trapping ground. Epidemics and war left it gradually repopulated by Algonquian peoples, many in multi-ethnic societies, who by the 18th century took part in the European fur trade. Ohio was organised as part of the Northwest Territory, defined in the Enabling Act of 1802, and was the first state admitted under the Northwest Ordinance and the first free state admitted after independence. Statehood came in 1803. Ohio University, founded in 1804, was its first college, and Oberlin College, founded in 1833, admitted African Americans in 1835 and women in 1837.

The capital and most populous city is Columbus; Cleveland and Cincinnati are the other major cities. The 2020 census counted 11,808,848 residents. Ohio is known as the Buckeye State and as the Mother of Presidents, having been the birthplace of seven presidents, and the Wright brothers designed and built their first successful airplane there. Among its surviving earthworks, the Serpent Mound and the Hopewell mounds remain the most visible traces of its early peoples.
ohio-river: The Ohio River is 981 miles (1,579 km) long. It begins at the confluence of the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers at what is now Point State Park in Pittsburgh and flows south-westwards to its mouth on the Mississippi at Cairo, Illinois, serving as the boundary between the Midwestern and Southern United States. It is the largest tributary by volume of the Mississippi. The name comes from the Seneca word Ohi:yo', meaning good river. The Falls of the Ohio below Louisville, a drop of 26 feet in two miles, long obstructed larger commercial navigation until the Louisville and Portland Canal bypassed the rapids in 1830.

For thousands of years Native Americans used the river as a major transport and trading route. In the five centuries before European colonisation the Mississippian culture built regional chiefdoms and earthwork mounds in the valley, among them the Angel Mounds near Evansville. The Osage, Omaha, Ponca and Kaw lived in the Ohio Valley and, under pressure over the fur trade from the Haudenosaunee, migrated west of the Mississippi in the 17th century. Arnout Viele, sent by the governor of New York in 1692 to trade with the Shawnee, is credited as the first European to explore western Pennsylvania and the upper Ohio Valley.

After the French and Indian War the river divided Britain's trans-Appalachian Indian Reserve into colonial lands to the south and Native American lands to the north. In the late 18th century it became the southern boundary of the Northwest Territory, and it was later part of the border between free and slave territory. Where the river was narrow, thousands of enslaved people escaped across it to the North, many helped by free Black and white people of the Underground Railroad. The Silver Bridge at Point Pleasant collapsed into the river on 15 December 1967, killing 46 people.

The river is extensively industrialised and populated, and regular barge traffic carries oil, steel and other goods. It is maintained by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers as part of the Mississippi River System.
ohrid: Ohrid lies in the south-western part of North Macedonia, on the shore of Lake Ohrid at an elevation of 695 metres. It is the largest city on the lake. In antiquity it was Lychnidos; by 879 it was called Ohrid, and Byzantine writers often called it Achrida. It is known for once having 365 churches, one for each day of the year, a legend supported by the 17th-century Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi, and has been called the Jerusalem of the Balkans.

The earliest inhabitants of the region were the Illyrian tribes of the Enchele and Dassaretii, and Lychnidos, as the town was then called, was the capital of the Dassaretii. In Roman times the town lay on the Via Egnatia, which connected the Adriatic port of Dyrrachion with Byzantium. The Polyconch Basilica of the 5th century shows an early adoption of Christianity, and bishops from Lychnidos took part in several ecumenical councils.

South Slavs began to arrive in the 6th century, and Bulgaria conquered the city around 840. Clement of Ohrid established the Ohrid Literary School in 886, one of the two major cultural centres of the First Bulgarian Empire. Between 990 and 1015 Ohrid was the empire's capital and stronghold, and from 990 to 1018 the seat of the Bulgarian Patriarchate. After Basil II's reconquest in 1018 the patriarchate was reduced to an Archbishopric of Ohrid under the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople.

In the 13th and 14th centuries the city changed hands between the Despotate of Epirus, the Bulgarian, Byzantine and Serbian empires and Albanian rulers. Stefan Uroš IV Dušan took it in 1334. The Ottomans under Bayezid I captured it in 1395 and made it the seat of the Sanjak of Ohrid. Ohrid became an important trade centre in the 18th century. It remained Ottoman until 29 November 1912, when the Serbian army took it in the Balkan Wars. Bulgaria occupied it in 1915 to 1918 and again in 1941 to 1944, and since 1991 it has been part of North Macedonia.

Ohrid had 38,818 residents at the 2021 census and is the seat of Ohrid Municipality. Tourism is predominant. The city and Lake Ohrid were accepted as Cultural and Natural World Heritage Sites by UNESCO in 1979 and 1980, one of only 40 World Heritage sites that are both.
ohringen: Öhringen is the largest town in the district of Hohenlohe, in the state of Baden-Württemberg, in south-west Germany, near Heilbronn. It lies in the flat valley of the small river Ohrn, in the western, deeper part of the Hohenlohe plain between the Keuper hills of the Swabian-Franconian Forest and the valley of the Kocher. The limestone of the subsurface is widely karstified, and the loess over the Lower Keuper has made fertile farmland, so that cereals, sugar beet, orchards and vineyards give the surroundings their character. The local dialect shows Rhenish Franconian and Swabian influence, since the town stands on the south-western edge of the East Franconian language area.

To the Romans the place was Vicus Aurelii. The old Roman frontier wall, the limes, runs to the east, and numerous remains and inscriptions from the Roman settlement have been found, including traces of three camps. A building that belonged to a monastery, now a library, was erected in 1034, and the Spitalkirche of St Anna and Elisabeth was built in 1376. The cemetery chapel of St Anna dates from 1520.

Later the town became the seat of a line of the Hohenlohe princes. Their former residence, the Schloss on the medieval marketplace, is now the town hall, beside a Renaissance town hall and the Upper Gate of 1792. The wider town grew in the 1970s, when the nearby villages including Cappel, Michelbach am Wald and Ohrnberg were incorporated in a regional reform. Among people born in Öhringen are Wendel Hipler, who led the peasants' parliament in Heilbronn in the sixteenth century, and Otto Röhm, who developed one of the first polymethylmethacrylates and invented the brand Plexiglas.

Öhringen has a population of 24,374, counted in 2019. Its Protestant collegiate church, the Stiftskirche, stands near the castle and holds carvings in cedar wood from the 15th century and many tombs and monuments. The Weygang Museum covers local history, with a tin and faience collection. The town is a secondary centre of the Heilbronn-Franken region and is on the railway line to Schwäbisch Hall and Crailsheim.
oil-well: Chinese records give the earliest known oil wells, drilled in 347 CE to depths of up to about 240 metres with bits attached to bamboo poles. The oil was burned to evaporate brine and make salt, and by the 10th century bamboo pipelines connected oil wells with salt springs. Some sources claim oil fields near Baku were exploited from the 9th century, and Marco Polo described oil collected from seeps there, saying a hundred shiploads might be taken from one fountain at a time.

The modern wells began in the 19th century. In 1846 a well was drilled with percussion tools to 21 metres at Bibi-Heybat near Baku, and in 1846-1848 the first modern oil wells were drilled on the Absheron Peninsula by the Russian engineer Vasily Semyonov. Ignacy Łukasiewicz drilled one of the first modern wells at Bóbrka in 1854, the first commercial well in North America began work at Oil Springs, Ontario, in 1858, and the first offshore well was drilled in 1896 off California.

The earliest modern wells were drilled by percussion, a bit on a cable being raised and dropped. In the 20th century rotary drilling largely replaced cable tools and reached much greater depths in less time; the Kola Borehole went below 12,000 metres. Until the 1970s most wells were essentially vertical, and directional drilling now allows horizontal wells.

An oil well is a drillhole designed to bring petroleum to the surface, usually with some natural gas. A rig rotates a drill string with a bit, and drilling mud cools the bit, lifts cuttings and holds back the pressure of fluids in the rock. Steel casing, cemented in place, lines the hole in stages. Wells are classed as wildcat, exploration, appraisal, production and development wells, and injection wells pump water or gas into a field to keep up pressure. Poorly maintained or abandoned wells can leak methane and other substances into air, water and soil.
oirats: The Oirats, also called Oirds and formerly Eluts or Eleuths, are the westernmost group of Mongols, whose ancestral home lies in the Altai region of Siberia, Xinjiang and western Mongolia. The Secret History of the Mongols, a 13th-century chronicle, counts them among the forest people and says they lived under a shaman-chief known as bäki. They fought Genghis Khan in his early rise but were defeated, and they submitted fully after the death of his rival Jumukha. Historically they comprised four major tribes, the Dzungar, Torghut, Dörbet and Khoshut, and the name may derive from Dörben Öörd, meaning the Allied Four.

After the fall of the Yuan dynasty the Oirats reconvened as a loose alliance and gradually spread eastwards into lands held by the Eastern Mongols. The Ming dynasty helped their rise after 1410. The ruler who led them furthest, Esen Taishi, led them from 1438 to 1454 and unified Mongolia under his puppet khan Taisun Khan. In 1449 his cavalry destroyed Ming defences at the Great Wall and captured the Zhengtong Emperor at Tumu, whom Esen returned the following year after a failed ransom attempt. Esen was killed soon after claiming the title of khan, and Oirat power declined.

The Oirats converted to Tibetan Buddhism around 1615. In 1637 Güshi Khan of the Khoshuts defeated a Khalkha prince at the request of the Gelug school and in the early 1640s was proclaimed Khan of Tibet by the 5th Dalai Lama, founding the Khoshut Khanate. In the 17th century the Dzungar Khanate, ruled by Choros noblemen, arose in the east. The Qing Empire defeated the Dzungars in the 1750s, and some scholars estimate that about 80 per cent of the Dzungar population, which had reached 600,000 in 1755, was wiped out in the conquest of 1755–1757.

In 1607 Oirats led by Kho Orlok of the Torghuts and Dalai Tayishi of the Dörbets moved west to the Volga and founded the Kalmyk Khanate, and by 1630 had reached the steppes of southeastern Europe. They came under Russian control in 1724. In January 1771 about 170,000 Kalmyks left the Volga for Dzungaria under Ubashi Khan. The modern Kalmyks of Kalmykia are Oirats. In the 17th century the Khoshut monk Zaya Pandita devised the Clear Script for the Oirat language, still used by some Oirats in China.
oireachtas: The word oireachtas comes from the Irish airecht or oireacht, a deliberative assembly of freemen, ultimately from airig, a freeman. Its first recorded use as the name of a legislative body was within the Irish Free State. Earlier Irish parliaments are treated as its predecessors.

The Parliament of Ireland was founded in the thirteenth century as the legislature of the lordship of Ireland and lasted until 1801. From Poynings' Law in 1494 until its repeal in 1782 it was subordinate to the Parliament of England. The Constitution of 1782 gave it greater independence, and under Henry Grattan it was known as Grattan's Parliament. In 1800 it approved its own abolition by the Act of Union, in force from 1 January 1801.

The next legislature was the unicameral Dáil Éireann, set up by Irish republicans in 1919. In 1920 the British government created a home rule Parliament of Southern Ireland, which most Irish politicians boycotted and which was abolished in 1922. The Oireachtas of the Irish Free State then took shape under its constitution. It consisted of the King, represented by a Governor-General, and two houses, the Dáil and the Seanad. The Free State Senate was abolished in May 1936 and the role of the monarch was removed in December 1936. The modern Oireachtas came into being on 29 December 1937, when the Constitution of Ireland was adopted.

Radio broadcasts of the Oireachtas began with ceremonial addresses, the first being that of John F. Kennedy during his 1963 state visit. Regular radio broadcasting of edited proceedings began in October 1986. Television coverage of the Dáil, Seanad and committees began in 1990, 1991 and 1993 respectively. The Houses of the Oireachtas Commission, set up by statute in 2003, employs the support staff of both houses.

The Oireachtas consists of the President of Ireland and two houses, which sit in Leinster House in Dublin, an eighteenth-century ducal palace. The Dáil has greater powers. It is elected by proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote, and the Seanad has 60 members: 11 nominated by the Taoiseach, 6 elected by university constituencies and 43 from vocational panels.

A bill must pass the Dáil and, in most circumstances, the Seanad, though the Dáil can override a Seanad refusal after 180 days, and then be signed by the president. Amendments to the constitution must also be put to a referendum. The Oireachtas may not enact a law providing for the death penalty, and a law is invalid to the extent that it conflicts with the constitution.
ojibwe: The Ojibwe are an Anishinaabe people, and several distinct nations, including the Saulteaux, Nipissings and Oji-Cree, also consider themselves Ojibwe. Their name is known in French as Ojibwa and in English as Chippewa, and its meaning is not known. According to Ojibwe oral history and birch bark scrolls, the people originated at the mouth of the Saint Lawrence River on the Atlantic coast of what is now Quebec, and migrated and traded widely across the continent. In their account, seven great miigis, or cowrie shells, appeared in the Land of the Dawn to teach the mide way of life, and six of them remained to establish the doodem, or clans. The Ojibwe belong to the Council of Three Fires with the Odawa and Potawatomi.

The first historical mention of the Ojibwe is in the French Jesuit Relation of 1640. Through friendship with French traders they gained guns and European goods and began to dominate their traditional enemies to the west and south. They drove the Sioux from the Upper Mississippi region towards the present-day Dakotas and forced the Meskwaki down from northern Wisconsin. By the end of the 18th century the Ojibwe controlled nearly all of present-day Michigan, northern Wisconsin and Minnesota, including most of the Red River area, as well as the northern shores of lakes Huron and Superior on the Canadian side, westward to the Turtle Mountains of North Dakota.

Decades of fur trading with the French made their language one of the key trade languages of the Great Lakes and the northern Great Plains. European powers, Canada and the United States have colonised Ojibwe lands, and the Ojibwe signed treaties with settler leaders to share land in exchange for compensation.

The Ojibwe are organised in bands, and most, except for the Great Plains bands, have historically lived settled lives. They fished and hunted, cultivated maize and squash, and harvested manoomin, or wild rice. Their typical dwelling is the wiigiwaam, made of birch bark, juniper bark and willow saplings. They are known for birchbark canoes, birchbark scrolls, copper mining and trade, and the making of maple sugar.

Traditionally kinship followed the father's clan. The Midewiwin society keeps scrolls with pictorial writing that record oral history, songs, maps, geometry and mathematics, and their beliefs have been passed down through its teachings. Their language, Anishinaabemowin or Ojibwemowin, belongs to the Algonquian family. Fluent speakers have declined sharply and are mostly elders, and a movement to revive the language has grown since the early 21st century. The dreamcatcher developed from the Ojibwe spider web charm.
oka-river: The Oka is the largest right tributary of the Volga. It flows through the regions of Oryol, Tula, Kaluga, Moscow, Ryazan, Vladimir and Nizhny Novgorod and is navigable as far upstream as the town of Kaluga. Its catchment area is 245,000 km2. Moscow sits on one of its tributaries, the Moskva, from which the capital's name is thought to be derived. There is no consensus about the origin of the name Oka, which could be cognate with the Sanskrit ogha, meaning stream or current.

The river was the homeland of the Eastern Slavic Vyatichi. By the 5th century the land around it was inhabited by different Slavic tribes, the Baltic Galindians lived in the western part of the basin, and Turkic tribes and Vikings and other peoples from Scandinavia were there as well; artefacts of Scandinavian origin have been found along the Oka and Volga route. The river gave its name to the Upper Oka Principalities, upstream from Tarusa. In 1221 Grand Duke Yuri II of Vladimir founded Nizhny Novgorod to protect the Oka's confluence with the Volga, and it later became one of the largest Russian cities.

From the Mongol conquest until about 1633 the Oka was the last line of defence against steppe raiders. The Zasechnaya cherta, a chain of fortification lines built later to protect the Grand Duchy of Moscow and then the Tsardom of Russia from Crimean and Nogai raids, lay south of the original line along the Oka. In the 15th and 16th centuries the Qasim Khanate, a Muslim polity, occupied the middle reaches around the city of Kasimov.

Before the building of railways in the mid-19th century and of the Moscow Canal in the 1930s, the Oka and the Moskva formed an important route from Moscow to the Volga. Travel was slow because of the meanders: in 1703 it took Cornelis de Bruijn around ten days to sail from Moscow to Nizhny Novgorod, and boats going upstream had to be pulled by burlaks.

The Oka is 1,500 km long. Its banks hold the medieval monasteries of Murom, the mosques and minarets of Kasimov, the fortified kremlins of Kolomna and Serpukhov, the excavated ruins of Old Ryazan and the memorial houses of Vasily Polenov and Sergey Yesenin. The Prioksko-Terrasny Biosphere Reserve lies on the left bank opposite Pushchino and is known for its wisent breeding nursery. A military field song of 1943, named after the river, was written by Leon Pasternak of the Polish 1st Tadeusz Kościuszko Infantry Division, founded near the river.
okavango-delta: The Okavango Delta lies in the central part of the endorheic basin of the Kalahari Desert, where the Okavango River reaches a tectonic trough at an elevation of 930 to 1,000 metres. The river is formed by the Cubango and Cuito rivers in Angola and enters the delta near Mohembo, where it divides into channels, floodplains, lagoons and permanent swamps. Nearly all the water reaching the delta is lost to evaporation and transpiration or seeps into the aquifer below, while a small part leaves by the Thamalakane and Boteti rivers.

The delta is very flat, varying less than 2 metres in height across about 15,000 square kilometres. Rain falling on the Angolan highlands in January and February travels some 1,200 km in about a month and spreads over the delta between March and June, so that flood levels peak from June to August, during Botswana's dry winter. About 70 percent of the thousands of islands began as termite mounds. Chief's Island, the largest, was historically reserved as a hunting area for the chief.

The Okavango Delta peoples consist of five groups: the Hambukushu, the Dceriku, the Wayeyi, the Bugakhwe and the ǁanikhwe. The first three have traditionally combined millet and sorghum farming, fishing, hunting, gathering and pastoralism, while the last two, who are Bushmen, have lived by fishing, hunting and gathering. The delta has been under the political control of the Batawana, a Tswana nation, since the late 18th century. Led by the house of Mathiba I, they established complete control in the 1850s as the regional ivory trade expanded. Most Batawana lived at the edges of the delta because the tsetse fly threatened their cattle, though many lived in the swamps from 1896 to the late 1930s.

The delta is home to all of the big five game animals, over 400 bird species, and 71 species of fish; the red lechwe is its most abundant large mammal. Its flora includes 1,068 plants, with papyrus growing in the deeper channels. The Moremi Game Reserve lies on its eastern side. On 22 June 2014 the delta became the 1,000th site inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, as one of the few interior delta systems without an outlet to the sea.
okayama: Okayama lies in the southern part of Okayama Prefecture, in the Chūgoku region of western Japan. The central urban area stands on the Okayama Plain, formed by sediment carried by the Asahi and Yoshii rivers as they flow into the Seto Inland Sea. To the north, the city forms a corner of the Kibi Plateau, a series of gentle hills, and to the south Kojima Bay opens onto the Kojima Peninsula.

In the late 16th century, during the Sengoku period, Ukita Naoie consolidated a stronghold at Ishiyama beside the Asahi River. His successor, Ukita Hideie, shifted the main enclosure to the hill called Okayama and completed Okayama Castle, traditionally dated to 1597. River channels were redirected to serve as moats, and a castle town was laid out on a north to south axis. After the Battle of Sekigahara, Kobayakawa Hideaki became lord of the Okayama Domain and reconfigured the outer defences, including the Hatsuka-bori, an outer moat reputedly finished in twenty days. Ikeda Tadatugu, lord of Himeji Domain, then became lord of Okayama, and the Ikeda clan ruled and expanded the castle town.

On 29 August 1871 the Meiji government replaced the feudal domains with centralised authority, and Okayama became the capital of Okayama Prefecture. The city was founded on 1 June 1889, and the San'yō Main Line and other railways greatly aided its growth. The Sixth Higher Middle School and Okayama Medical College were established there. In the Second World War it was a garrison city of the Imperial Japanese Army; air raids on 29 June 1945 burned much of the urban core, destroyed the castle keep and killed more than 1,700 people.

After the war the central districts were rebuilt on the former castle-town grid, and the keep was reconstructed in 1966. The San'yō Shinkansen reached Okayama in 1972, and the Seto-Ōhashi Bridge, opened in 1988, linked it with Shikoku by rail and road. Okayama became a designated city on 1 April 2009.

Okayama has roughly seven hundred thousand inhabitants and is the capital of the prefecture. Kōraku-en, built by Ikeda Tsunamasa over fourteen years and completed in 1700, is counted among the three best traditional gardens in Japan and lies south of the castle grounds. The city is known as the setting of the fable Momotarō, and kibi dango, balls of millet and rice flour, are a well-known local sweet. Okayama University began as a medical school in 1870.
okayama-prefecture: Okayama Prefecture borders Tottori Prefecture to the north, Hyōgo Prefecture to the east and Hiroshima Prefecture to the west. Its south faces the Seto Inland Sea, across from Kagawa Prefecture on the island of Shikoku, to which it is joined by the Great Seto Bridge, and it includes 90 islands in the sea, while the north is characterised by the Chūgoku Mountains. The city of Okayama is the capital and largest city, and other major cities include Kurashiki, Tsuyama and Sōja. Most of the population lives around Kurashiki and Okayama, and the small villages of the northern mountains are aging and declining in population. Two national parks lie partly in the prefecture, Daisen-Oki and Setonaikai.

Before the Meiji Restoration of 1868 the area was divided between the provinces of Bitchū, Bizen and Mimasaka. Okayama Prefecture was formed and named in 1871 as part of the large-scale administrative reforms of the early Meiji period, and its borders were set in 1876.

The prefecture is known for Bizen-yaki, Bizen pottery, and for the swords of Bizen Osafune and Bitchu Aoe. It is closely associated with the folklore hero Momotarō. The tale is said to have roots in the legend of Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto and Ura: Prince Ura of Kudara lived in Kinojo, the castle of the devil, and troubled the villagers, so the emperor's government sent Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto, identified with Momotarō, to defeat him. The city of Okayama holds an annual Momotarō Festival.

Kurashiki is a historic town with a preserved historical area, the Bikan Historical Area, and the Ohara Museum of Art. The prefecture also has the Kōraku-en garden and Okayama Castle in the city of Okayama, Bitchū Matsuyama Castle at Takahashi, Ki Castle at Sōja and the Shizutani School at Bizen.
okinawa-island: Okinawa Island is about 106 kilometres long and on average 11 kilometres wide, with an area of 1,206.98 square kilometres. It lies roughly 640 kilometres south of Kyushu and 500 kilometres north-east of Taiwan. The north is sparsely populated and holds the Yanbaru, one of the largest tracts of subtropical rainforest in Asia, with many endemic species, among them the Okinawa rail; the south-central and southern parts are markedly urbanised, especially Naha. The climate is humid subtropical.

Early history is defined by shell mound cultures, divided into Early, Middle and Late periods; rice was not cultivated until the Middle Shell Mound period. From about the 12th century came the Gusuku period, named for the distinctive Ryukyuan castles, whose nature as holy places, stone-ringed dwellings or rulers' castles is still discussed. The Sanzan period began in 1314, when Hokuzan and Nanzan declared independence from Chūzan, and the three kingdoms competed for recognition as vassals of Ming China. In 1429 King Shō Hashi completed the unification and founded the Ryūkyū Kingdom, with its capital at Shuri Castle.

In 1609 the Japanese Satsuma Domain invaded Ryukyu, capturing the king and his capital, and the kingdom ceded the Amami Islands and became a vassal of Satsuma while remaining a tributary of China. In 1879 Japan annexed the archipelago, established Okinawa Prefecture and abolished the monarchy at Shuri; the deposed King Shō Tai was forced to move to Tokyo.

The Battle of Okinawa, from 1 April to 22 June 1945, was the bloodiest ground battle of the Pacific War. About 95,000 Japanese troops and 20,195 Americans were killed, and the Cornerstone of Peace lists 149,193 people from Okinawa, about a quarter of the civilian population, killed or dead by suicide. The United States then controlled the Ryukyu Islands until their return to Japan.

Okinawa Island is the seat of Okinawa Prefecture, with Naha as its capital, and its population was estimated at 1,384,762 in 2009. Gusuku and related remains, among them Shuri Castle and Nakagusuku Castle, are listed by UNESCO as World Heritage Sites. The island hosts many United States military installations, which cover about a quarter of it.
okinawa-prefecture: Okinawa Prefecture is the southernmost and westernmost prefecture of Japan. It consists of three main island groups, the Okinawa Islands, the Sakishima Islands and the Daitō Islands, spread across a maritime zone about 1,000 kilometres from east to west and 400 kilometres from north to south. Of its 160 islands, 49 are inhabited. The largest and most populous is Okinawa Island, which holds the capital, Naha. The land area is 2,281 square kilometres, and the climate is subtropical, with warm temperatures and high rainfall through the year.

Human activity on the islands goes back a long way: the Yamashita Cave Man is dated to about 32,000 years ago and the Minatogawa Man to about 18,000 years ago. From the 12th century the islands entered the Gusuku period, when an agrarian society grew on the limestone plateaus. Local chieftains called Aji built fortified residences known as gusuku and expanded their influence through foreign trade. The later Ryukyu Kingdom was a trading hub that kept tribute relations with the Ming and Qing courts and retained its own statehood.

After the Meiji Restoration, Japan abolished the domains and set up prefectures in 1871. The Mudan Incident of that year, in which the crew of a drifting Ryukyuan ship was killed in Taiwan, became a pretext for Japan to assert control. In 1872 the kingdom was reclassified as the Ryukyu Domain, a step known as the Ryukyu Disposition, and in 1879 it became Okinawa Prefecture. The last king, Shō Tai, was moved to Tokyo. Ryukyuan opponents of the change petitioned the Qing dynasty, and Ulysses S. Grant was asked in 1879–1880 to mediate, without result.

On 1 April 1945 the United States Army and Marine Corps landed on Okinawa with about 185,000 troops. They met fierce resistance and won on 22 June. About one third of the civilian population died in the fighting, and the dead of all nationalities are commemorated at the Cornerstone of Peace. The caves of the coral island served as refuges for civilians during the battle. The islands were then under American administration until 1972.

Okinawan culture shows the influence of its historical trading partners, above all Kyushu and China. Its music centres on the sanshin, a three-stringed instrument related to the Chinese sanxian and ancestor of the Japanese shamisen, and on eisa, a drumming dance. Karate originated on the islands. Six Ryukyuan languages remain, mutually unintelligible with Japanese. Shuri Castle in Naha and the Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu are on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The American bases cover about 10 per cent of the prefecture's land.
oklahoma: Oklahoma covers 69,895 square miles (181,030 square kilometres) near the geographical centre of the 48 contiguous states. Most of it lies in the Great Plains, the Cross Timbers and the Interior Highlands, with ancient mountain ranges, prairie, mesas and eastern forests. It borders Texas, Kansas, Missouri, Arkansas, New Mexico and Colorado. Its southern and western boundary with Texas, the Red River and the 100th meridian, was first set in the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819 between the United States and Spain.

Indigenous peoples were present by the last ice age. Ancestors of the Wichita, Tonkawa and Caddo lived in the area, and Spiro Mounds was a major Mississippian mound complex that flourished between 850 and 1450 CE. Plains Apache people settled the Southern Plains between 1300 and 1500. The Spanish expedition of Francisco Vázquez de Coronado crossed the region in 1541, and French explorers claimed it in the early eighteenth century. The Comanche and Kiowa entered from the west in that century, and the Quapaw and Osage moved into the east. The United States acquired the territory in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, and it was part of the Arkansas Territory from 1819 to 1828.

The name comes from the Choctaw words okla, meaning people, and humma, meaning red. Chief Allen Wright of the Choctaw Nation suggested it in 1865 during treaty negotiations over Indian Territory, imagining a state wholly for American Indians. It became the usual name of Oklahoma Territory and was officially approved in 1890, two years after that area was opened to settlers. The Indian Appropriations Act of 1889 authorised the Land Rush of 1889 that opened land formerly held by Indian nations; settlers who staked claims early gave the state its nickname, the Sooner State.

The northern border was set at the 37th parallel by the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, which the Cherokee and Osage disputed until the Drum Creek Treaty of 1870. The Panhandle, once part of the Republic of Texas, remained a no-man's land until Oklahoma acquired it on gaining statehood in 1907. The first newspaper in the region, the Cherokee Advocate, appeared in 1844 in Cherokee and English.

Oklahoma City is the capital and largest city, and Tulsa the other main economic centre. Oklahoma is a constitutional republic with executive, legislative and judicial branches and 77 counties; its legislature has a 48-member Senate and a 101-member House. It has 38 federally recognised tribes with headquarters in the state, and 25 Indigenous languages are spoken there. The 2020 census counted 3,959,353 residents.
oktoberfest: In October 1810 Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria married Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen, and Munich officials invited the public to celebrate on fields outside the city walls. The site was named Theresienwiese, "Therese's Meadow", the following year, and is still called the Wiesn. The first festival featured a horse race modelled on the medieval Scharlachrennen once run at the Karlstor. Major Andreas Michael Dall'Armi of the National Guard proposed it, although the coachman Franz Baumgartner later claimed the credit.

Sendlinger Hill, now Theresienhöhe, served as a natural grandstand for about 40,000 spectators. Sixteen pairs of children in regional costume opened the programme, thirty horses ran a course of 3,400 metres and a student choir closed the event. Baumgartner's horse won, and he received a gold medal from the minister Maximilian von Montgelas. The race was repeated in 1811, forming the core of the tradition.

An agricultural show was added in 1811. The fair was cancelled in 1813 during the War of the Sixth Coalition, and skittles, swings and climbing poles appeared when it returned in 1814. Carnival booths came in 1818, and in 1819 Munich's city council took control and decreed that it be held annually. In the 19th century the opening moved into late September for warmer evenings. A costume and marksmen parade has marched to the Theresienwiese since 1850, and the festival was cancelled for cholera epidemics in 1854 and 1873 and for wars in 1866 and 1870.

The centenary in 1910 saw about 120,000 litres of beer drunk. The festival was cancelled during the First World War and in 1923–24, and between 1933 and 1945 the Nazi regime used it for propaganda; in 1933 Jewish people were barred from working there. It was suspended from 1939 to 1945, and a modest autumn fest was held in 1946–48. On 26 September 1980 a pipe bomb exploded near the main entrance, killing 13 people and injuring more than 225.

Since 1950 the Mayor of Munich has opened the festival by tapping the first keg with a twelve-gun salute and the cry "O'zapft is!", meaning "It's tapped!". Since 1994 it has usually lasted 16 days, from the first Saturday after 15 September to the first Sunday in October, and it draws around seven million visitors a year. Only beer brewed within Munich's city limits may be sold, by the six breweries of the Club of Munich Brewers, in large temporary tents each associated with one of them.

A Greek delegation that visited in 1832 later cited the festival as a model for the Zappas Olympics, precursors of the modern Olympic Games. About 8,000 people now walk the costume parade, led by the Münchner Kindl.
okubo-toshimichi: Ōkubo Toshimichi was born on 26 September 1830 at Kagoshima in the Satsuma Domain. His father was a low-ranking samurai whose family lived in straitened circumstances, and his maternal grandfather, a physician, had studied Western science. Ōkubo grew up with his boyhood friend Saigō Takamori, three years his senior, studying Zen Buddhism and the Ōyōmei school of philosophy. His father was exiled in 1849 after the Takasaki Uprising, a conflict over the succession to the daimyō, and Ōkubo himself was removed from his post in the han archives, so that the family endured poverty until 1853.

The new daimyō Shimazu Nariakira, an interested reformer, recognised his talents and pardoned him. When Nariakira died in August 1858, Ōkubo and Saigō lost their footing, and the setback is said to have made Ōkubo a serious, determined and calculating reformer.

After the assassination of Ii Naosuke in 1860 Ōkubo rose in Satsuma and, closer to Shimazu Hisamitsu, favoured a moderate union of court and shogunate. In 1862 he arranged for Hisamitsu to lead Satsuma troops to Kyoto, and the British bombardment of Kagoshima in August 1863 convinced him of Western military superiority. His policy shifted to opposition to, and finally the overthrow of, the shogunate. With the court noble Iwakura Tomomi he was central to the coup of 3 January 1868, which proclaimed imperial rule. He pressed for Edo to become the capital, renamed Tokyo in September 1868, and in August 1871 he helped to bring about the abolition of the han and establishment of prefectures.

From 1871 to 1873 he was vice ambassador on the Iwakura Mission to the United States and Europe, and met Otto von Bismarck in March 1873. On his return he opposed the proposed invasion of Korea in October 1873, a dispute that led to the resignation of Saigō. He became Home Minister on 29 November 1873 and drove state-led industrialisation, founding agricultural schools and supporting textiles and the Mitsubishi shipping company. He directed the suppression of the Saga Rebellion of 1874 and of the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877, and in 1874 negotiated a settlement with China after the Formosan Expedition.

On 14 May 1878 six disaffected samurai ambushed Ōkubo's carriage at Kioichō in Tokyo, killed his coachman and cut his throat. Their note charged him with suppressing popular rights and monopolising authority; the consensus is that avenging Saigō's death also motivated them. They were executed on 27 July.

Ōkubo is regarded as one of the founders of modern Japan, and some historians compare his role to Bismarck's in Prussia. His authoritarian methods drew criticism, but his government laid the groundwork for later leaders. He was awarded the Junior First Rank posthumously in 1901.
olaf-ii-of-denmark: Olaf was born Olaf Hákonsson in December 1370. When his grandfather Valdemar IV of Denmark died, he was still a small child, and a Danehof at Slagelse proclaimed him king of Denmark the following year. His mother, Queen Margaret, served as regent. At her insistence the proclamation added the title true heir of Sweden, since both his father and his paternal grandfather, Magnus IV, had been kings of Sweden until they were forced to abdicate. Olaf was also hailed as king in Scania, including the towns controlled by the Hanseatic League since the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370.

Margaret signed a coronation charter on his behalf. In it Olaf agreed to meet the Danehof at least once a year and to return properties that Valdemar IV had confiscated. He was to come of age at fifteen, but even when he reached his majority in 1385 his mother ruled through him. On the death of his father in 1380 he had inherited Norway, so that Denmark and Norway were joined in a personal union ruled from Denmark. Apart from short interregna the two kingdoms shared a king until the dissolution of Denmark-Norway and the forced union of Norway with Sweden through the Treaty of Kiel in 1814.

Olaf died unexpectedly at Falsterbohus in August 1387, aged sixteen, and was buried at Sorø Abbey on Zealand, where his grandfather and later his mother were also buried. Rumours arose at once that he had been poisoned, and in 2015 the forensic scientist Jørgen Lange Thomsen proposed that he died of Brugada syndrome. His death ended the male line of the House of Bjälbo.

Margaret then united all three Scandinavian kingdoms in a personal union. After Olaf no Norwegian king was born on Norwegian soil for more than 550 years, until Harald V, born in 1937, became king in 1991. In 1402 a man impersonated him as the False Olaf.
olaf-ii-of-norway: Olaf Haraldsson was the son of Åsta Gudbrandsdatter and Harald Grenske, a petty king in Vestfold, who died while Åsta was pregnant. According to later Icelandic sagas, Harald descended from King Harald I Fairhair, so Olaf was a great-great-grandson of the founder of the Norwegian kingdom. Åsta later married Sigurd Syr, and their children included Harald Hardrada. During his lifetime Olaf was known as Olaf the stout.

According to Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla, whose facts are dubious, he landed on the Estonian island of Saaremaa in 1008 and won a battle there. Skaldic poetry suggests he led an attack that took down London Bridge, though Anglo-Saxon sources do not confirm it, and he is said to have aided the sons of Æthelred the Unready against Cnut.

Olaf was King of Norway from 1015 to 1028. Traditionally he has been seen as leading the Christianisation of Norway, but most scholars now believe he had little to do with it. Stone crosses suggest the coasts were deeply influenced by Christianity long before him. He did import bishops from England, Normandy and Germany and probably tried to enforce Christianity in the inland areas. The church laws later ascribed to him probably were not his.

Modern historians generally agree that Olaf was inclined to violence and brutality, and that he used Christianity to gain more power for the monarchy and centralise control. Judged on the bare facts, he appears to have been a fairly unsuccessful ruler, whose power rested on an alliance with Cnut the Great, who was driven into exile when he claimed power of his own, and whose attempt at reconquest was swiftly crushed.

Olaf died in the Battle of Stiklestad on 29 July 1030. Bishop Grimketel, who had come with him from England, performed his canonisation about a year later, and he was enshrined in Nidaros Cathedral. He became Norway's patron saint and is also patron saint of the Faroe Islands. He came to be called Rex Perpetuus Norvegiae, Norway's Eternal King, a title that goes back to the thirteenth century.

Historians point to three factors in his later status: the myth of his role in the conversion, dynastic relations and a later need for legitimacy. His illegitimate son Magnus the Good took power in Norway and promoted his father's cult, which became typical of Scandinavian monarchies. The axe in Norway's coat of arms symbolises him, and Olsok, on 29 July, is his day of celebration.
olaf-iii-of-norway: Olaf was a son of King Harald Hardrada and Tora Torbergsdatter. He joined his father's invasion of England in 1066 but was only 16 at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066 and stayed to guard the ships at Riccall, so he did not fight. After the defeat he sailed with the remains of the Norwegian force to Orkney, where they wintered, and returned to Norway in the summer of 1067. He then shared the kingdom with his brother Magnus II, who had become king the previous year. When Magnus died in 1069, Olaf became sole ruler.

Norway enjoyed a rare extended period of peace under Olaf. He renounced an offensive foreign policy and protected the kingdom's sovereignty through agreements and marriage connections. When the Danish king Svend Estridsen prepared to attack after the defeat of 1066, Olaf made peace with him and married his daughter Ingerid, and he also made peace with William the Conqueror of England. According to Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla, he founded the city of Bergen, and he took measures so that key cities could better serve as royal residences.

Unlike his father, who quarrelled with the Archbishopric of Bremen, Olaf fully recognised the archbishop's authority over the Norwegian church. Bishops, who had travelled with the king's court, established fixed residences in Oslo, Nidaros and Bergen, and the king took the initiative for churches including Christ Church in Bergen and Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim. He is credited with instituting the system of guilds, and the law of the Gulating was probably first written down in his time.

Olaf died of illness on 22 September 1093 at Haukbø in Rånrike, then part of Norway, and was buried at Nidaros Cathedral. His marriage to Ingerid was childless, and he was succeeded by Magnus III, called Barefoot, acknowledged as his illegitimate son. Medieval sources describe him as tall, fair and silent in public but cheerful at drinking parties and peaceful throughout his reign. A Norwegian silver coin found in Maine in 1957, the Maine penny, has been dated to his time, though how it reached a Native American village there is unclear and disputed. An abstract equestrian statue of him by Knut Steen was unveiled in Bergen on 21 May 1998.
olaf-tryggvason: Olaf was the son of Tryggvi Olafsson, king of Viken, and is numbered as Olaf I. Historical information about him is sparse. He appears in some contemporary English sources and skaldic poems, and the oldest narrative source, Adam of Bremen's Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum of about 1070, mentions him briefly. Most of what is told of his life comes from late sagas, among them Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla of about 1230, whose credibility modern historians debate. The date and place of his birth are uncertain; one late 12th-century source places it in the Orkney Islands.

According to Heimskringla, his mother Astrid fled with him from his father's killers and sailed for Kievan Rus', but Estonian vikings captured the ship and Olaf was sold as a slave. Six years later his uncle Sigurd Eirikson found him in Estonia and brought him to the court of Vladimir the Great, where he was made chief of the king's men-at-arms.

Heimskringla says Olaf then raided settlements and ports, and in 982 married Queen Geira, who ruled part of Wendland. After her death he plundered from Friesland to the Hebrides. In 991 he was one of the commanders of the first large-scale Viking attack on England in a generation, which defeated the English at the Battle of Maldon. The sagas place his conversion to Christianity in the Isles of Scilly, after a seer foretold a mutiny, a wound and a baptism that came true. By another account Saint Ælfheah of Canterbury baptised him near Andover in 994; the historian Henrietta Leyser holds that he was already baptised and that Andover confirmed his faith, as part of a treaty in which he agreed to stop raiding England.

In 995 Olaf sailed for Norway, where many had risen against Jarl Haakon, the ruler under the Danish king. The rebels accepted Olaf as king, and Haakon was killed by his own thrall, Kark. Olaf demanded that the regions that had sworn allegiance to the Danish king be baptised, and they complied most reluctantly. He is said to have built the first Christian church in Norway in 995, and in 997 he founded his seat of government at Trondheim, a site defended by the River Nid.

It has been suggested that he hoped to rule a united Christian Scandinavia. He made an enemy of Sigrid the Haughty, queen of Sweden, whose pagan faith led her to refuse his proposal, and he married Tyra, the sister of Sweyn Forkbeard. According to the sagas, an expedition in 1000 to claim Tyra's lands led to an ambush off the island of Svolder by the combined Swedish, Danish and Wendish fleets and the ships of Haakon's sons. He died on 9 September 1000.
olaudah-equiano: In his 1789 memoir Equiano says he was born around 1745 in the village of Essaka, thought to be Isseke in today's Anambra State, Nigeria. He was the youngest of six surviving sons, and at the age of eleven he and his sister were seized from the family compound. Six months later he reached the coast and was taken on a slave ship with 244 other enslaved Africans to Barbados, and then to Virginia. There Michael Henry Pascal, a lieutenant in the Royal Navy, bought him and renamed him Gustavus Vassa, after the sixteenth-century King of Sweden. He had already been called Michael on the slave ship and Jacob by his first owner.

Pascal took him to England and kept him as a valet through the Seven Years' War. He was baptised at St Margaret's, Westminster, on 9 February 1759. That parish register describes him as a Black child born in Carolina, aged twelve, and in 1999 Vincent Carretta cited it as evidence of an American birth. Other scholars hold that the weight of evidence favours an African birth.
