In December 1762 Pascal sold him to James Doran, who took him to Montserrat, where he was sold to Robert King, a Quaker merchant of Philadelphia. King allowed him to trade on his own account, selling fruit, glass tumblers and other goods between Georgia and the Caribbean. Equiano bought his freedom in 1766, and by about 1768 he had gone to Britain. He worked at sea, and in 1773 travelled to the Arctic in HMS Racehorse in an expedition towards the North Pole.

Settled in London, he became involved in the abolitionist movement in the 1780s. In 1783 he was the first to tell Granville Sharp about the Zong massacre. He became one of the Sons of Africa, and a member of the London Corresponding Society, which campaigned for democratic reform. In 1791 and 1792 he toured the British Isles with his book.

The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African appeared in 1789 and went through nine editions in his lifetime. It describes his African childhood, the voyage on a slave ship, the brutality of slavery in the West Indies, Virginia and Georgia, and the risks of kidnapping that free people of colour faced. It is credited with helping shift opinion in favour of the Slave Trade Act of 1807. Equiano married Susannah Cullen at Soham in 1792, and they had two daughters. He died on 31 March 1797, a year after his wife.
old-babylonian-empire: The Old Babylonian Empire, also called the First Babylonian Empire, comes after the end of Sumerian power with the destruction of the Third Dynasty of Ur and the Isin-Larsa period that followed. Its origins are hard to pinpoint, because Babylon itself yields few intact archaeological materials owing to a high water table. The evidence that survives includes royal and votive inscriptions, literary texts and lists of year-names, while economic and legal documents are few.

Little is known of the kings from Sumuabum through Sin-muballit, except that they were Amorites rather than Akkadians and added little to the territory. Sumuabum conquered Dilbat and Kish and began a wall around Babylon, which his successor Sumualailum completed. Sin-muballit defeated Rim-Sin I, which protected Babylon from further invasion, and passed the throne to his son Hammurabi.

Hammurabi ruled Babylon from 1792 to 1750 BCE. At first his realm consisted of a few towns near Babylon: Dilbat, Sippar, Kish and Borsippa, and Babylon was only one of several important powers beside Isin and Larsa. By 1762 BCE he had captured Eshnunna, inheriting its trade routes, and his armies then took Assyria and parts of the Zagros Mountains. In 1761 BCE Babylon gained control over Mari, giving it virtually all the territory of Mesopotamia that had been under the Third Dynasty of Ur. In his thirtieth year he conquered Larsa from Rim-Sin I and gained Nippur, Ur, Uruk and Isin.

The archives of Zimri-Lim, king of Mari, are a main source for the diplomacy of Hammurabi's reign. They survived because Hammurabi burned the palace down, which buried the tablets. His successors from Samsuiluna to Samsuditana left few records. Samsuiluna defeated Rim-Sîn II but lost major parts of the conquered land and kept real authority only over the core of Babylonia. The dynasty came to an end as the empire lost territory and money, and attacks by Hittites expanding out of Anatolia led to the destruction of Babylon. The Kassite period followed.

The Code of Hammurabi comes from this dynasty and is among the oldest written laws and the best known artifacts of the ancient world. It is written in cuneiform on a diorite stele 2.25 metres high. At the top the king receives his kingship from the sun god Shamash, and below is the collection of laws. The text says that the god Marduk commanded Hammurabi to provide just ways for the people of the land, and it presents the laws as the divine role given to him. Babylon came to dominate Mesopotamia for over a thousand years.
old-believers: Old Believers, or Old Ritualists, are communities that keep the liturgical and ritual practices of the Russian Orthodox Church as they stood before the reforms of Patriarch Nikon of Moscow between 1653 and 1656. The reforms aimed to remove every difference between Russian use and Greek use, and they touched hundreds of pages of matters of form but not theology. After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 many Russians held that foreign Orthodox churches were contaminated by heresy and Moscow was the Third and Last Rome, and the Stoglav Synod of 1551 had enshrined practices such as crossing oneself with two fingers and a double Alleluia.

The old rite and its followers were anathematised in 1667. Early opponents regarded the new ritual as heralding the Last Judgment and the church and state as servants of the Antichrist. Fleeing persecution, they settled in remote areas or abroad, and educated believers founded monastic communities there.

Under Catherine the Great, from the mid-eighteenth century, Old Believers gained almost complete tolerance, and large urban communities appeared in which members took a leading part in Russian economy and society. They had rejected the Westernization measures of Peter the Great. In 1820 Alexander I created a Secret Committee for Schismatic Affairs, and a crackdown followed that continued under Nicholas I. The government ranked the groups as most harmful, harmful and less harmful, and none was tolerated. Full religious freedom came only after 1905. At the start of the twentieth century demographers estimated between 10 million and 20 million Old Believers.

The Bolshevik government at first treated them sympathetically as a force hostile to the old order. In 1923 priestly Old Believers found a bishop, Nikola Pozdnev, and founded the Russian Old-Orthodox Church. The Stalin era decimated the communities, and a wave of refugees established centres in the West.

Old Belief has no central organisation. The priestly popovtsy accepted priests who left the state church and abjured the reforms, so they kept the liturgy and sacraments. The priestless bezpopovtsy denied that any Nikonite ordination was valid, kept only baptism and penance and appointed lay leaders. Old Believers saw themselves as God's elect, lived in secluded settlements with strict morals, kept long services and fasts, and taught children Church Slavonic so that they could read scripture. Their main early centres lay in the Kerzhenets basin, Starodub, Vetka, the Don Cossacks' lands and Karelia.
old-french: Old French descended from Vulgar Latin, the common spoken language of the Western Roman Empire, which differed from Classical Latin in sound, word forms and vocabulary. The two remained mutually intelligible until the 7th century, when Classical Latin ceased to be a daily spoken language and had to be learned as a second language. Gaulish left a small mark: classical Latin equus was replaced by caballus, derived from Gaulish caballos, and an estimated 200 words of Gaulish origin survive in Modern French, among them chêne 'oak tree' and charrue 'plough'.

Old French was not a unified language but a group of Romance dialects, mutually intelligible yet diverse, known collectively as the langues d'oïl in contrast to the langues d'oc of Occitania in the south. It was spoken natively across the northern half of the Kingdom of France and in Upper and Lower Lorraine, including Anjou and Normandy, which in the 12th century were ruled by the Plantagenet kings of England. The Norman dialect spread to England and Ireland, and during the Crusades Old French was also spoken in the Kingdom of Sicily, the Principality of Antioch and the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

The language kept a two-case system, a nominative and an oblique, longer than Spanish or Italian did, marking case on the masculine article and noun: the nominative li enfes beside the oblique l'enfant. In later Old French the distinction faded, and the oblique form usually survived into Modern French. Its spelling was more phonetic than that of later centuries. In the late 12th century, whose form can be taken as standard, every written consonant was pronounced and a final e was sounded.

The Oaths of Strasbourg of 842, treaties and charters entered into by King Charles the Bald, are among the earliest documents in the Gallo-Romance that prefigures French; the Eulalia sequence is the second oldest and is valued for its consistent spelling. The Canticle of Saint Eulalie, from the second half of the 9th century, is generally accepted as the first literary text, and the first works in Old French were saints' lives. Around 1100 the conditions Charles Homer Haskins called the Renaissance of the 12th century produced a profusion of works in many genres. In the mid-14th century Old French gave way to Middle French, the dialect of the Île-de-France, and a standardised Classical French spread across France only in the 17th and 18th centuries.
old-great-bulgaria: Old Great Bulgaria, also called Magna Bulgaria and Patria Onoguria, the Onogur land, was a seventh-century Turkic nomadic state of the Onogur-Bulgars on the western Pontic-Caspian steppe, in what is now southern Ukraine and south-west Russia. Byzantine writers such as Agathon, Nikephoros I and Theophanes link the Bulgars with the Onogurs, whose name may mean ten arrows and so a federation of ten tribes. The origin of the name Bulgar is not fully understood; it may derive from a Turkic verb meaning to stir or mix.

Between 630 and 635 Khan Kubrat united the Onogur Bulgars with the Kutrigurs and Utigurs under one rule. According to the Nominalia of the Bulgarian khans he belonged to the Dulo clan, and the Byzantine emperor Heraclius gave him the title of honorary patrician. Some scholars call the state the Onogundur-Bulgar Empire.

Kubrat's capital is presumed to have been the old city of Phanagoria on the Taman Peninsula, and some scholars think the state reached the Pannonian Plain and included some of the Pannonian Avars. Kubrat overthrew Avar domination and extended Onogur influence among the Bulgars of Pannonia. His grave was found in 1912 at Pereshchepina in Ukraine. In the mid-seventh century the state expanded west into Avar territory and was centred on Poltava.

After Kubrat's death, according to Patriarch Nikephoros I, his eldest son Batbayan was left in charge, but under strong Khazar pressure the other sons ignored their father's advice to stay together and left with their own tribes. The state disintegrated under Khazar attack in 668, though an Avar-Slavic alliance in the west also defeated the Bulgars. Some Bulgars remained under Khazar rule.

The successor states are the First Bulgarian Empire and Volga Bulgaria. Asparukh led 30,000 to 50,000 Bulgars to a new home, and after the Battle of Ongal founded the First Bulgarian Empire, which the Byzantine Empire recognised in 681. Kotrag took the western steppe and a branch settled at the confluence of the Volga and Kama, where Volga Bulgaria arose; its people converted to Islam in the ninth century. Kuber ruled a mixed population at Sirmium and led his people to Macedonia, while Alcek and his followers, around 662, were given land in Molise by the Lombards. Paul the Deacon says that they kept their own tongue.
old-javanese: Old Javanese, also called Kawi, is an Austronesian language and the oldest attested phase of the Javanese language. It was natively spoken in the central and eastern parts of Java, in what are now the provinces of Central Java, Yogyakarta and East Java. As a literary language it was used across Java and on Madura, Bali and Lombok. Its most important shaping force was its Austronesian heritage in vocabulary, sentence structure and grammar, shared with its sister languages in Southeast Asia.

Sanskrit influence was deep, and it was almost exclusively Sanskrit: no other Indian language left traces, unlike in Old Malay. P. J. Zoetmulder's Old Javanese-English Dictionary of 1982 has about 25,500 entries, no fewer than 12,500 of them borrowed from Sanskrit. In any given literary work about 25% of the vocabulary comes from Sanskrit.

Old Javanese has six vowels and twenty consonants in Latin transliteration. Verbs are built with affixes that mark voice, aspect and mood: the active voice with the prefix (m)aN- or the infix -um-, the passive with the prefix ka- or the infix -in-. Verbs do not formally distinguish present and past time. In a basic clause the predicate comes first, the subject follows, and a particle, most commonly ta, separates them, as in lunghā ta sira, meaning he leaves.

It was written in the Kawi script, a Brahmic script related to the Pallava and Kadamba scripts of South India, from the 8th to the 16th century. Traditionally Kawi is written on lontar, prepared palm leaves.

Medieval poems in Old Javanese, called layang kawi or kakawin, continued to circulate in the courts of Kartasura, Surakarta and Yogyakarta and were held in high regard. From the 18th century literature inspired by them was written in Modern Javanese. Kakawin works include the Ramayana of about 870, Mpu Kanwa's Arjunawiwaha of about 1030, the Bharatayuddha of Mpu Sedah and Mpu Panuluh of 1157, and the Nagarakertagama of Mpu Prapanca of 1365. Mpu Tantular's Kakawin Sutasoma gave Indonesia its national motto, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, which is more correctly rendered as scattered, remaining as one.

Kawi is not truly extinct as a spoken language. It is used in wayang performances and in parts of Javanese weddings, such as the ceremonies of Peningsetan and Panggih. The first scholar to treat Kawi seriously was Wilhelm von Humboldt, who considered it the father of all Malay-Polynesian languages.
old-prussians: The Old Prussians lived on the south-eastern shore of the Baltic Sea between the Vistula Lagoon and the Curonian Lagoon, in what is now part of Poland, the Kaliningrad Oblast of Russia and southern Lithuania. They spoke Old Prussian, an Indo-European language of the Baltic branch, and worshipped pre-Christian deities. Archaeology confirms an uninterrupted presence from the Iron Age, from the fifth century BCE. Prussian is an exonym: the tribes used the names of their regions, such as Sambians and Bartians, and never formed a common political organisation, which weakened them severely.

Recorded Baltic history begins in the 10th century. Adalbert of Prague was slain in 997 during a missionary effort among the Prussians, and the Polish dukes made repeated attempts at conquest that met strong resistance. In 1166 the Prussians led a Polish army into marshy ground, where nearly all of it perished. In 1209 Pope Innocent III commissioned the Cistercian monk Christian of Oliva to convert them, and Konrad I of Masovia, harassed by Prussian raids, called in the Teutonic Order.

In 1230 Grand Master Hermann von Salza and Konrad launched the Prussian Crusade, and the Order created its own monastic state in the conquered territory. In an attack of 1233 over 21,000 crusaders took part, and the Prussians suffered a decisive defeat at the Sirgune River. The crusades lasted sixty years, and revolts, including a major one in 1286, were defeated. Germans and Dutch settlers colonised the land, Poles and Lithuanians settled in the south and east, and the surviving Old Prussians were assimilated over the following two centuries.

The smallest social unit was the laūks, a small settlement of households and fields separated from others by forest and marsh. According to Peter of Dusburg, who wrote in 1326, the Prussians worshipped the sun, moon, stars and thunder, and held certain forests, fields and waters sacred. The highest priest, the Kriwe-Kriwajto, lived in a sacred grove called the Romove. Old Prussian was probably extinct by the beginning of the 18th century, but translations of the Bible, poems and other texts allow scholars to reconstruct it, and the ethnonym was later adopted by the German-speaking inhabitants of the region.
old-saybrook: Old Saybrook lies in Middlesex County on the west bank of the Connecticut River, where it flows into Long Island Sound. It covers 56.0 square kilometres, about 30 per cent of it water, and is joined to Old Lyme on the east bank by the Raymond E. Baldwin Bridge, which carries Interstate 95. Its population was 10,481 at the 2020 census.

Dutch settlers set up a short-lived trading post here in 1624, Kievits Hoek, or Plover's Corner. The Saybrook Colony was founded in late 1635 by a group claiming the land by a deed from Robert Rich, 2nd Earl of Warwick, with John Winthrop the Younger as governor, aided by Colonel George Fenwick and Captain Lion Gardiner. It struggled because its investors, supporters of Oliver Cromwell, stayed in England during the English Civil War, and in 1644 Fenwick agreed to merge it with the Connecticut Colony, whose settlers bought the land and fort. The seal Fenwick brought from England gave the design of the Flag of Connecticut.

Pequots besieged the fort from September 1636 to March 1637, after Massachusetts Bay attacked Manisses, Pequot and Western Niantic villages. They killed and wounded more than 20 settlers over eight months, and the siege escalated the Pequot War. In 1659 Major John Mason, who had commanded the fort from 1647, led most of the settlers to found Norwich. The Collegiate School of Connecticut was chartered at Old Saybrook on 9 October 1701 and moved to New Haven in 1716, becoming Yale. The town was created from Saybrook in 1852, and in 1854 its northern part became Essex.

The former town hall of 1901, a theatre until the 1940s, reopened in 2009 as the Katharine Hepburn Cultural Arts Center; the actress lived in the borough of Fenwick. The Lynde Point and Saybrook Breakwater lighthouses are on the National Register of Historic Places, and the train station, opened in 1873, has Amtrak service.
ole-romer: Ole Rømer was born in Aarhus on 25 September 1644, the son of a merchant and skipper, Christen Pedersen, who had taken the name Rømer to show that he came from the island of Rømø. He graduated from the cathedral school in Aarhus in 1662 and moved to Copenhagen to study at the university. His mentor there was Rasmus Bartholin, who published his discovery of the double refraction of light by Iceland spar in 1668 while Rømer was living in his home. Bartholin had been given the task of preparing Tycho Brahe's astronomical observations for publication, and Rømer was able to learn mathematics and astronomy from them.

In 1671 Rømer joined Jean Picard to observe about 140 eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io on the island of Hven, while Giovanni Domenico Cassini observed the same eclipses in Paris; comparing the times gave the difference in longitude between the two places. In 1672 he went to Paris and worked as Cassini's assistant. He observed that the intervals between eclipses of Io grew shorter as the Earth approached Jupiter and longer as it moved away.
Cassini announced on 22 August 1676 that light seemed to take ten to eleven minutes to cross the radius of the Earth's orbit, but Rømer was the one who set out to prove it.

Rømer himself never published his results; a report appeared in the Journal des sçavans on 7 December 1676. Christiaan Huygens later deduced a speed from his data. The idea was not fully accepted until James Bradley measured the aberration of light in 1727. In Paris Rømer was also tutor to the Dauphin and helped build the fountains at Versailles.

Rømer returned to Denmark in 1681 as professor of astronomy at the University of Copenhagen. As royal mathematician he introduced the first national system of weights and measures in Denmark on 1 May 1683, adopting a more accurate national standard in 1698, and he defined a Danish mile of 24,000 Danish feet.

In 1700 he persuaded the king to introduce the Gregorian calendar in Denmark and Norway, which Tycho Brahe had urged in vain a hundred years earlier. He invented the meridian circle, the altazimuth and the passage instrument. In 1705 he became the second Chief of the Copenhagen Police, dismissing the whole force at the start, and he introduced Copenhagen's first street lights, oil lamps. He died in 1710 and was buried in Copenhagen Cathedral.
oleg-of-novgorod: According to the Primary Chronicle, Oleg was a kinsman of Rurik and was entrusted by him with the care of both his realm and his young son Igor. His relation to Rurik is debatable, and several modern scholars reject it. The Novgorod First Chronicle states that Oleg was not related to Rurik at all, but was a Scandinavian client-prince who served as Igor's army commander. His name is given in Old Norse as Helgi, and the Primary Chronicle calls him the Prophet, an epithet alluding to the sacred meaning of the Norse name.

The Primary Chronicle has Oleg succeed Rurik as ruler of Novgorod in 879. In 881 and 882 he took control of Smolensk and then seized Kiev by tricking and killing Askold and Dir, an act commonly taken as the founding of Kievan Rus'. He was the first prince (knyaz) of Kiev in this account, though not yet a grand prince: later Muscovite chroniclers used that title, the earliest sources do not. In 883 he made the Drevlians pay tribute to Kiev.

In 907 a campaign against Constantinople followed, with the Drevlians taking part. Historians read its outcome differently. Vladimir Shikanov holds that the Rus' were defeated at Cape Tricephalus and that the treaty of 911 was a gift to barbarians, with the chronicle disguising the defeat, whereas Vladimir Pashuto considers the treaty beneficial to Rus' in every respect.

According to legend, which Alexander Pushkin romanticised in his ballad The Song of the Wise Oleg, pagan priests prophesied that Oleg would take death from his stallion. He sent the horse away, and years later learned it had died. When he touched its skull with his boot, a snake slithered out and bit him. A variant appears in the 13th-century saga of Örvar-Oddr. The Primary Chronicle places his grave in Kiev, while Novgorodian sources point to a funerary barrow in Ladoga.

The traditional chronology is contested. The Novgorod First Chronicle dates his death differently from the Primary Chronicle. The Schechter Letter, written by a Jewish Khazar, describes a Rus' warlord named Helgu, often interpreted as Oleg, active long after the traditional date of his death, and Constantine Zuckerman and David Christian have argued that it requires the early chronology of the Rus' to be re-determined. A tale dated to the second half of the 17th century also names Oleg as founder of Moscow.
olesnica: Oleśnica lies in the Silesian Lowlands east of the Trzebnickie Hills, on the Oleśnica River, a tributary of the Widawa, about 30 kilometres northeast of Wrocław. It is the administrative seat of Oleśnica County. Its name comes from the Polish word olsza, alder. It stood on an important trade route to Greater Poland, Kalisz, Łódź and Warsaw, and it was the site of an important printing press and a gymnasium.

A Piast castle with a nearby abbey and trading settlement is first mentioned in a deed of 1189. On 22 February 1255 Duke Henry III the White granted the town its privileges, and from the 13th century the area was largely settled by Germans. The town became capital of the Duchy of Oleśnica, partitioned from the Duchy of Głogów, and Duke Konrad I made it his residence. In 1329 Konrad accepted the overlordship of the Bohemian Crown while keeping wide autonomy. The Hussites invaded in 1432, and later Polish–Hussite negotiations took place there. The local Piast line ended with the death of Duke Konrad X the White in 1492.

In 1495 the duchy was sold to Duke Henry I of Münsterberg, son of the Bohemian king George of Poděbrady, and his grandson John established a gymnasium in 1530. When the Podiebrad family died out in 1647 the Swabian dukes of Württemberg inherited the duchy, and in 1792 the Welf dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg. After the First Silesian War it came under Prussian suzerainty in 1742, and in 1884 the duchy was incorporated into Prussia. In the 17th century the Polish-German language border ran close to the town, and the Polish writers Adam Gdacius and Jerzy Bock published their works there.

Fighting for the town between 21 and 25 January 1945 and arson afterwards destroyed about 60 to 80 per cent of its buildings. Oleśnica became part of Poland again after the Potsdam Conference, the remaining German-speaking population was expelled, and the town was resettled with Poles. The large 16th-century ducal castle, whose inner courtyard arcades are a masterpiece of Renaissance architecture, still marks the town. It also holds the only surviving chained library in Central Europe, and its traditional wheat and rye gingerbread is officially protected.
olga-of-kiev: The Primary Chronicle gives Olga's origin as Varangian and her birthplace as Pleskov. Little is known of her life before her marriage to Prince Igor I of Kiev, the son and heir of Rurik, and the birth of their son Sviatoslav. According to the historian Alexey Karpov she was no more than 15 years old when she married.

In 945 Igor went to the Drevlian capital, Iskorosten, to force the Drevlians to pay tribute. They paid, but on the way home he decided the sum was too small and returned with only a small escort. The Drevlians murdered him. The Byzantine chronicler Leo the Deacon says he was tied to tree trunks and torn in two, a detail that the historian D. Sullivan suggests Leo may have invented.

Olga took power as regent for her three-year-old son Sviatoslav and was the first woman to rule Kievan Rus'. The Primary Chronicle tells how she answered a Drevlian proposal that she marry their Prince Mal. She had one embassy of twenty men buried alive in their boat, burned a second party of leading men in a bathhouse, and had Drevlians killed at a funeral feast beside Igor's tomb, five thousand according to the chronicle. After a year-long siege of Iskorosten she asked for three pigeons and three sparrows from each house and set the city alight by tying burning sulphur to the birds. The historian Boris Akunin finds only the killing of the first envoy plausible.

She changed the collection of tribute and set up trading posts, hunting grounds and boundary posts, among them the administrative and trading centres called pogosti. In the 950s she travelled to Constantinople to visit Emperor Constantine VII. The sources disagree about the visit. The Book of Ceremonies mentions no baptism, John Skylitzes says she was baptised there, and the Primary Chronicle adds a marriage proposal that she refused, since baptism made the emperor her godfather. Church Slavonic sources give 957 for her baptism.

She sent an embassy to the Holy Roman Emperor Otto I in 959, asking for a bishop and priests, but Adalbert of Magdeburg was expelled by Sviatoslav's pagan allies. Sviatoslav refused to be baptised, though he did not hinder those who were. According to the Primary Chronicle Olga died of illness in 969 and was buried by her priest Gregory without a pagan funeral feast.

Her grandson Vladimir adopted Christianity in 988. Olga is venerated as a saint in the Eastern Orthodox Church with the epithet Equal to the Apostles, her feast day being 11 July. The Russian Orthodox Church officially named her a saint in 1547, though John Fennell argued that she was most likely canonised in 1284.
olinda: Olinda lies on the Atlantic coast of Pernambuco in north-eastern Brazil, six kilometres north of the centre of Recife, in whose metropolitan region it now stands. The landscape is made of plains and hills, some of them steep, with an average elevation of 16 metres, and the municipality lies in the Atlantic Forest ecoregion. It is drained mostly by the Paratibe River, the rest by the Capibaribe. The climate is tropical monsoon, with average monthly temperatures consistently above 18 °C and abundant rain for most of the year.

For several thousand years Indigenous peoples occupied this coast, and the hills of present-day Olinda held settlements of the Caeté and Tupinambá, who were frequently at war. French mercenaries are thought to have been the first Europeans to reach the region. The Portuguese exploited the rivalries between the peoples and built a stronghold on a former Caeté village on a high hill. Olinda was founded in 1535 by Duarte Coelho Pereira and raised to the rank of a town on 12 March 1537. It became the seat of a Catholic prelature in 1614 and of the Diocese of Olinda in 1676.

Sugarcane dominated the regional economy, and the import of slaves from Africa to work the plantations made Olinda a colonial stronghold. During the Iberian Union of 1580 to 1640 the area around Olinda and Recife was occupied by the Dutch, who gained access to the sugar plantations. John Maurice, Prince of Nassau-Siegen, was appointed governor of the Dutch possessions in Brazil in 1637 and landed at Recife, the chief Dutch stronghold. After the union ended in 1640 Portugal re-established its authority over the lost territories. Olinda declined in importance after the Dutch invasion, and Recife became the capital of Pernambuco in 1827. Slavery on the sugar plantations remained a source of wealth until the Lei Áurea abolished it in 1888.

Olinda is noted as one of the best-preserved colonial cities in Brazil, and its historic centre was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. Its cathedral, São Salvador do Mundo, remains the primary seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Olinda and Recife, and the Basílica Abacial do Mosteiro de São Bento is also part of the heritage site. The city's Carnaval is held in the streets, with frevo, maracatu and other music of the north-east, and admission is free. Tourism, commerce and crafts are the main economic activities.
olive-oil: Olive oil is a vegetable oil obtained by pressing whole olives, the fruit of Olea europaea, a traditional tree crop of the Mediterranean Basin. Olive trees have been cultivated around the Mediterranean since the 8th millennium BCE, and wild olives, which originated in Asia Minor, were collected by Neolithic people as early as that time. The exact date and place of domestication are unclear. The modern olive tree may have originated in ancient Persia and Mesopotamia and spread to the Levant and later to North Africa, though some scholars argue for an Egyptian origin.

Archaeological evidence in Galilee shows that olives were being turned into oil by 6000 BCE, and at a now-submerged settlement south of Haifa by 4500 BCE. The archives of the city-state of Ebla also mention oil production.

Besides food, olive oil served for religious rituals, medicines, fuel in oil lamps, soap-making and skincare. The Spartans and other Greeks rubbed themselves with oil while exercising in the gymnasia. Its cosmetic use began early in the 7th century BCE, spread to all the Greek city-states together with athletes training naked, and lasted close to a thousand years despite its great expense.

The olive tree has long symbolised peace between nations. In Greek mythology the city of Athens was named after the goddess Athena because her gift of an olive tree was held to be more precious than the salt spring offered by Poseidon. In Jewish observance, pure oil from the first pressing was the only fuel permitted for the seven-branched menorah, in the Mishkan and later in the Temple in Jerusalem. Various Christian churches use it in consecration ceremonies.

Olives were traditionally ground into paste by large millstones, and the paste was then pressed. In the ancient Levant three methods produced different grades. The finest oil came from ripe olives harvested from the top of the tree and lightly pressed, since what flows from light pressure is very sweet and thin, while inferior oil came from olives left to soften or shrivel. Pomace, the remaining solid waste, has been used as fuel since Roman times, as it burns hotter and with less smoke than charcoal. Olive oil is one of the three core food plants of Mediterranean cuisine, with wheat and grapes.
oliver-cromwell: Oliver Cromwell was born in Huntingdon on 25 April 1599 to Robert Cromwell and his second wife Elizabeth Steward. The family's estate came from an ancestor who married the sister of Thomas Cromwell, Henry VIII's chief minister, and it profited from the Dissolution of the Monasteries. He married Elizabeth Bourchier on 22 August 1620, a match that linked him to the Puritan gentry of Essex and the merchants of London. He sat for Huntingdon in 1628 and made little impression. He became a religious Independent in the 1630s, and afterwards believed his successes were the work of divine providence.

Returned for Cambridge to the Short and Long Parliaments in 1640, Cromwell raised a cavalry troop when civil war began in 1642. His cavalry were a major factor in the Parliamentarian victory at Marston Moor in July 1644. The Self-Denying Ordinance of 1645 forced members to choose between office and command, and Cromwell alone was kept in his. He led his wing at Naseby in June 1645, which smashed the King's main army. In 1648 he defeated the invading Scottish Engagers at Preston, and after the King's execution he commanded the campaign in Ireland in 1649 and 1650, then won at Dunbar on 3 September 1650 and at Worcester on 3 September 1651.

Barebone's Parliament voted itself out on 12 December 1653, and John Lambert's Instrument of Government made Cromwell Lord Protector. He was sworn in on 16 December in plain black clothing, without regalia, signed himself Oliver P and was addressed as Your Highness.

Cromwell died at Whitehall on 3 September 1658, probably of sepsis after a urinary infection and a bout of malarial fever. His son Richard succeeded him, and the Stuart Restoration followed in 1660. On 30 January 1661 his body was hanged at Tyburn, and his head was displayed on the roof of Westminster Hall until at least 1684.

His reputation remains debated. His report on Drogheda in September 1649 lists the killing of 3,000 military personnel and many inhabitants. Some historians argue that he acted harshly only against those in arms, while others note that the worst of the mass evictions and deportations of over 50,000 people to Bermuda and Barbados came under other generals after he left. Winston Churchill described him as a military dictator, while others view him as a hero of liberty.
oliver-goldsmith: Details of Goldsmith's birth are uncertain. He told a biographer that he was born on 10 November 1728, and his birthplace is given either as Pallas, near Ballymahon in County Longford, where his father was Anglican curate of Forgney, or as the house of his maternal grandparents near Elphin in County Roscommon. When he was two his father became rector of Kilkenny West in County Westmeath, and the family lived at Lissoy until his father's death in 1747.

In 1744 he entered Trinity College Dublin. He neglected his studies in theology and law and fell to the bottom of his class, and in 1747 he was expelled with four other undergraduates for a riot in which they tried to storm the Marshalsea Prison. He graduated as a Bachelor of Arts in 1749 without distinction. After trying various professions, he studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh from 1752 to 1755, then toured Flanders, France, Switzerland and northern Italy, living by his wits and by playing the flute.

He settled in London in 1756 and briefly worked as an apothecary's assistant and a school usher. Always in debt and addicted to gambling, he produced a large output as a hack writer on Grub Street for London publishers. His few painstaking works won him the company of Samuel Johnson, and in 1764 he became one of the earliest members of Johnson's circle, The Club. Through a fellow member, Edmund Burke, he met Sir George Savile, who later found him a post at Thornhill Grammar School in Yorkshire.

In 1760 he began publishing letters in the Public Ledger as The Citizen of the World, purportedly by a Chinese traveller in England named Lien Chi, who commented ironically on British society; the series, inspired by Montesquieu's Persian Letters, brought him fame. The Vicar of Wakefield followed in 1766, the story of a devout vicar, Charles Primrose, and his family, reduced to poverty and prison. The Deserted Village (1770) expresses a fear that clearing villages to make landscape gardens would ruin the peasantry. She Stoops to Conquer, a satirical comedy of mistaken identities, was first performed in 1773.

Goldsmith died in London on 4 April 1774, aged 45; his death may have been partly due to his own misdiagnosis of a kidney infection. He was buried in Temple Church, where a monument was destroyed in an air raid in 1941. Another stands in Westminster Abbey with an epitaph written by Johnson. Among his papers was found the prospectus of a planned encyclopedia, the Universal dictionary of the arts and sciences, which his death prevented. In the 19th century he was regarded as a seminal figure of sentimental literature, and Charles Dickens, Jane Austen and Mary Shelley mentioned his characters in their novels.
oliver-tambo: Oliver Reginald Kaizana Tambo was born on 27 October 1917 in the village of Nkantolo in eastern Pondoland, in what is now the Eastern Cape. His father, who had four wives and ten children, named him Kaizana after the German Kaiser Wilhelm II, Britain's enemy in the First World War, in protest at the British annexation of Pondoland. Tambo herded cattle from the age of three, boarded with families near school, and was educated at the Anglican Holy Cross Mission, where he excelled; financial help from the Goddard family and an older brother paid for his schooling. He then attended St Peter's College in Johannesburg, graduating in 1938.

He wanted to study medicine but black students were not admitted, so he took up sciences at the University of Fort Hare. In 1940 he and others, including Nelson Mandela, were expelled for taking part in a student strike for an elected students' council. In 1942 he returned to teach science and mathematics at his old school in Johannesburg.

In 1944 Tambo, Mandela and Walter Sisulu founded the ANC Youth League, which urged boycotts, civil disobedience and strikes in its Program of Action. Tambo became the ANC's secretary-general in 1955, deputy president in 1958 and was served a five-year banning order in 1959. After the Sharpeville massacre of 21 March 1960 the ANC sent him abroad, and he crossed into Bechuanaland. He travelled across Africa, meeting leaders such as Julius Nyerere, Kwame Nkrumah and Gamal Abdel Nasser, and settled in Muswell Hill, north London. After Albert Luthuli died in 1967 he became acting president, and he was re-elected in 1985.

Tambo was directly responsible for organising guerrilla units. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission identified him as the person who gave final approval for the Church Street bombing of 20 May 1983, which killed 19 people and injured between 197 and 217. The ANC said the target was military, while lawyers for victims said many of the dead were administrative staff. He returned to South Africa on 13 December 1990 after more than thirty years in exile, and in 1991, weakened by a stroke in 1989, he gave the presidency to Mandela and became National Chairman.

Tambo died on 24 April 1993 after complications following a stroke, aged 75, and was buried in Benoni, Gauteng. His house in Muswell Hill was bought by the South African government in 2010 as a historic monument. Johannesburg International Airport was renamed after him on 27 October 2006.
oljeitu: Öljaitü, also known as Mohammad-e Khodabandeh, was the eighth Ilkhanid ruler. His name means blessed in Mongolian. He was the son of the Ilkhan Arghun and his third wife, the Keraite Christian Uruk Khatun, and the brother of Mahmud Ghazan. Born during his father's viceroyalty in Khorasan, he was given the name Khar-banda, meaning mule driver, raised a Buddhist and baptised in 1291 with the name Nikolya, after Pope Nicholas IV. He later converted to Sunni Islam with Ghazan and took the name Muhammad. Named heir in 1299, he moved against possible rivals on hearing of Ghazan's death: his emissary killed Prince Alafrang, son of Gaykhatu, on 30 May 1304.

Öljaitü was crowned on 19 July 1304 and appointed Rashid al-Din and Sa'd al-Din Savaji as his viziers. In 1305 he received ambassadors from the Yuan dynasty, the Chagatai Khanate and the Golden Horde, which established a peace among the Mongols. He campaigned against the Kartid ruler of Herat and in Gilan, where his commander-in-chief Qutluqshah was defeated and killed. Rashid al-Din completed the Jami al-Tawarikh on 14 April 1307. The citadel of Irbil, held by rebel Christians, fell on 1 July 1310 and its defenders were massacred. In 1312 Sa'd al-Din Savaji was arrested for corruption and executed.

His last campaign against the Mamluks failed, though he reportedly briefly took Damascus. He sent embassies to Philip IV of France, Pope Clement V and Edward I of England in 1305, again in 1307 and to Edward II in 1313, renewing the Mongol hope of an alliance against the Mamluks, and gave the Venetians trading rights by a treaty in 1306. Byzantine Emperor Andronicus II gave him a daughter in marriage, and in 1308 Öljaitü sent 30,000 men against the Ottomans in Bithynia. In 1315 his son Abu Sa'id was made governor of Khorasan and Mazandaran.

Öljaitü died at Soltaniyeh in December 1316 and was succeeded by his son Abu Sa'id. Rashid al-Din Hamadani was accused of having poisoned him and was executed. He professed Buddhism, Christianity and Islam during his life. Influenced by Shi'a theologians such as Al-Hilli, and alienated by Sunni factional strife, he changed to Shi'a Islam in 1310; a Mamluk historian wrote that he became Sunni again in his last years. He oversaw the completion of the city of Soltaniyeh in 1306, and his tomb there, 300 km west of Tehran, remains the best known monument of Ilkhanid Persia.
ollantaytambo: Ollantaytambo (Quechua: Ullantaytampu) lies about 72 kilometres by road north-west of Cusco, at an altitude of 2,792 metres, in the province of Urubamba in the Cusco region. The town stands along the Patakancha River, close to its junction with the Willkanuta River, and the main Inca ceremonial centre rises on a hill called Cerro Bandolista. Human occupation of the site may go back as far as 3,500 years, and some buildings predate the Incas. In and around the town are traces of settlements of the Huari civilisation (600 to 1000 CE), and the fortress of Pumamarka controlled access to Ollantaytambo along what later became the Inca Trail.

Around the middle of the 15th century the Inca emperor Pachacuti conquered and razed an existing town of Ollantaytambo and incorporated the town and nearby region into his personal estate. He rebuilt it with sumptuous constructions and undertook extensive terracing and irrigation in the Urubamba Valley. The town lodged the Inca nobility, while retainers of the emperor, the yanakuna, farmed the terraces. After his death the estate passed to the administration of his family clan, the panaqa.

During the Spanish conquest of Peru, Manco Inca, leader of the Inca resistance, made it a temporary capital and fortified the town and its approaches. In 1537, on the plain of Mascabamba, he defeated a Spanish expedition in the Battle of Ollantaytambo, blocking its advance from high terraces and flooding the plain. He did not consider his position tenable, and the following year he withdrew to Vilcabamba, where he established the Neo-Inca State. In 1540 the native population was assigned in encomienda to Hernando Pizarro. Hiram Bingham III stopped here in 1911 on his journey in search of Machu Picchu.

The town has an orthogonal layout of four longitudinal streets crossed by seven parallel ones, and dates from the late 15th century. It has some of the oldest continuously occupied dwellings in South America, although later building altered it; colonial buildings, for example, covered the central plaza. The Temple Hill, commonly called the Fortress, is a misnomer, since its main functions were religious; its Temple sector holds the Sun Temple, never completed, with the Wall of the Six Monoliths of rose rhyolite from quarries at Kachiqhata, about 5 kilometres away.

Cut-stone agricultural terraces climb the surrounding hills. They allowed the Incas to farm different ecological zones, and the sunken terraces called Callejón form a microclimate 2 to 3 °C warmer than the ground above. Storehouses on the hills held the harvest.
olmecs: The name Olmecs comes from the Nahuatl Ōlmēcatl, meaning rubber people, from ōlli, natural rubber. The Olmec heartland is a swampy lowland on the Gulf coast, broken by low hills, ridges and volcanoes, with the Sierra de los Tuxtlas rising in the north. Pre-Olmec cultures had flourished there since about 2500 BCE, and the Olmecs may have derived in part from the neighbouring Mokaya or Mixe–Zoque cultures. They seem to have had their roots in early farming cultures of Tabasco, which began between 5100 and 4600 BCE. Ritual deposits at the shrine of El Manatí show activity at least as early as 1600 to 1500 BCE.

The first Olmec centre, San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán, was almost abandoned around 900 BCE, when La Venta rose to prominence. Many San Lorenzo monuments were destroyed around the 950s BCE, which may point to an internal uprising or, less likely, an invasion. The latest view is that rivers changing course may have been responsible. Other centres included Tres Zapotes and Laguna de los Cerros.

By about 400 BCE the major centres had been abandoned, and between 400 and 350 BCE the population of the eastern half of the heartland dropped sharply. Scholars have not determined why. Archaeologists think serious environmental changes in the river system, on which farming, hunting and transport depended, probably made the region unsuited to large farming populations. Elements of Olmec tradition lived on in successor societies.
Olmec culture was unknown to historians until the mid-19th century. In 1869 José Melgar y Serrano published a description of a colossal head at Tres Zapotes, the first Olmec monument found in place.

Olmec art is the hallmark of the culture, worked in jade, clay, basalt and greenstone. Seventeen colossal heads have been unearthed, ranging from 3.4 metres high to 1.47 metres, and the largest weigh between 25 and 55 tonnes. No two are alike, and they are generally accepted as portraits of rulers, perhaps dressed as ballplayers. Jade was a mark of rank among the ruling classes.

Little is directly known of Olmec political structure. Site surveys show considerable centralisation, first at San Lorenzo and then at La Venta. San Lorenzo and La Venta were largely ceremonial centres; most Olmecs lived in villages on higher ground, in houses with storage pits and gardens. Obsidian, which the heartland lacks, came mostly from Guatemala, and greenstone and marine shell also travelled far.

The Olmecs are credited, sometimes speculatively, with early bloodletting, the Mesoamerican ballgame and perhaps writing, as in the Cascajal Block, whose status as writing some scholars doubt. Their ethnic and linguistic affiliation is unknown; one proposal, by Lyle Campbell and Terrence Kaufman, is that they spoke a language ancestral to Mixe–Zoquean.
olof-skotkonung: Olof Skötkonung, sometimes called Olaf the Swede, was the son of Eric the Victorious and, according to Icelandic sources, of Sigrid the Haughty. He is the first Swedish ruler about whom there is substantial knowledge, though knowledge of his life rests mostly on the accounts of Adam of Bremen and Snorri Sturluson, which some scholars criticise. His epithet Skötkonung has been explained as meaning tributary king, or from the Swedish skatt, taxes or treasure, or from the ancient ceremony of scotting.

Adam of Bremen says that Sweyn Forkbeard had been expelled from Denmark by Eric the Victorious, and that when Eric died, Sweyn returned and married his widow. Olof then attacked and expelled Sweyn, but the conflict was settled and the two kings became allies. Around 1000 Olof joined Sweyn and the Norwegian jarls Eric and Sven against the Norwegian king Olaf Tryggvason in the Battle of Svolder. Olaf Tryggvason disappeared during the fight, and the victors divided Norway: Olof gained part of Trøndelag and the modern Bohuslän.

When Olaf II of Norway re-established the Norwegian kingdom in 1015, war broke out again. In 1018 Olof's cousin Ragnvald Ulfsson urged him at the thing of Uppsala to make peace and marry his daughter Ingegerd to the Norwegian king. Olof instead married Ingegerd to Yaroslav I the Wise, and his other daughter Astrid went to Norway and married Olaf II. The Swedes and Geats were displeased with his self-willed rule, and he agreed to share power with his son Anund Jacob.

Olof was the first king in Sweden known to have minted coins, and a few hundred survive as contemporary evidence for his reign. They were struck at Sigtuna in imitation of English pennies; the earliest call him King in Sigtuna and the later ones King of the Swedes, which may reflect a wider base of power around 1000.

He was the first Swedish king to remain a Christian until his death. A Westrogothic law of about 1240 says he was baptised at Husaby in Västergötland by the missionary Sigfrid, though the circumstances are unclear. Adam of Bremen says he planned to tear down the Uppsala temple but had to give up the plan because many Swedes were still pagan, and he installed a bishopric in Västergötland instead. His reign is considered in Sweden to mark the transition from the Viking Age to the Middle Ages.
olomouc: Olomouc lies on the Morava River, about 61 kilometres north-east of Brno and 200 kilometres south-east of Prague, mostly on the flat fertile land of the Upper Morava Valley. It is the ecclesiastical metropolis of Moravia and a historical co-capital of the region. The origin of its name is unknown. The most frequent theory derives it from a personal name, Olmút, giving Olmút's castle or court. A legend of a Roman fort founded under Julius Caesar arose in the Renaissance, and nothing confirms it.

As early as the 7th century a gord of the early Slavs developed in the present-day quarter of Povel, probably an administrative centre. It was conquered in the early 9th century and vanished. A new centre, where the Great Moravian governor resided, grew at Předhradí, survived the fall of Great Moravia about 907 and gradually became the capital of Moravia. The bishopric of Olomouc was founded in 1063, possibly re-founded, and was raised to an archbishopric in 1777. It was one of the richest in the area. In 1306 King Wenceslas III stopped there on his way to Poland, where he was assassinated, and with his death the Přemyslid dynasty died out.

The city was officially founded in the mid-13th century and was the biggest town in Moravia, competing with Brno for the position of capital. According to the account, the Mongols, after the Battle of Legnica, raided Moravia but were defeated at the fortified town of Olomouc. In 1454 the city expelled its Jewish population. In the second half of the 15th century, considered its golden age, Matthias Corvinus was elected anti-king of Bohemia there in 1469, and in 1479 he and Vladislaus II concluded the Peace of Olomouc, dividing the country.

Swedish troops occupied the city for eight years during the Thirty Years' War and left it in ruins, and it lost its predominant place to Brno. Frederick the Great besieged it unsuccessfully for seven weeks in 1758. In 1848 Emperor Ferdinand abdicated in Olomouc, and in 1850 Austrian and German statesmen concluded the Punctation of Olmütz, restoring the German Confederation under Austrian leadership.

The historic centre is well preserved and protected as an urban monument reservation. The Holy Trinity Column, listed by UNESCO in 2000, is valued for its Baroque style and symbolic value. The Jewish community returned after the expulsion order was rescinded following 1848, and built a synagogue in 1897. It was destroyed on Kristallnacht in 1938, and fewer than 300 of the city's Jews survived the Holocaust.
oltenia: Oltenia is a historical province in western Wallachia, between the Danube, the Southern Carpathians and the Olt river, from which its name derives. Craiova is its main city and traditional seat of power. The first medieval seat was Turnu Severin, anciently Drobeta, near the site of Trajan's Bridge. In Latin it was called Vallachia Cisalutana, meaning Cis-Oltine Wallachia. Under Habsburg rule it was officially the Banat of Craiova and commonly Lesser Wallachia, and sometimes Imperial Wallachia.

Dacians first inhabited the region, which the Roman Empire took in 106. In 129, under Hadrian, it formed Dacia Inferior, and Marcus Aurelius's reform made it Dacia Malvensis, with its capital at Romula, colonised with legion veterans. The Romans withdrew their administration south of the Danube at the end of the 3rd century, and Goths, Taifals and then Huns ruled in turn. From 681 it was, with interruptions, part of the Bulgarian Empire. In 1233 the Kingdom of Hungary formed the Banate of Severin in the west, which lasted until the Battle of Mohács in 1526.

Around 1247 a polity emerged under Litovoi. When Wallachia arose in the 14th century, its voivode was represented in Oltenia by a ban, the Great Ban of Craiova, the highest office in the Wallachian hierarchy. The Craiovești family held it most from the late 15th century to about 1550, and the title lasted until 1831. Wallachia accepted Ottoman suzerainty in the 15th century; many bans cooperated with the Turks, while rulers such as the Oltenian-born Michael the Brave fought them.

Under the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 Oltenia was split from Wallachia and annexed by the Habsburg monarchy as the Banat of Craiova, though the Austrians held it de facto by 1716. It was the only part of the Danubian Principalities, apart from Bukovina later, to experience Enlightened absolutism. Welcomed at first, the Austrians lost goodwill by imposing administrative, fiscal and judicial reforms that withdrew privileges from nobles and enforced taxes on peasants. In 1761 the bans' residence moved to Bucharest, and in 1821 Oltenia was at the centre of Tudor Vladimirescu's uprising.

Oltenia is part of Romania and takes in the counties of Gorj and Dolj entirely and parts of Mehedinți, Vâlcea, Olt and Teleorman. Its traditional emblem, a gold lion holding a sword over a bridge, stands in the lower dexter quarter of the Romanian coat of arms; the bridge is that of Apollodorus of Damascus at Drobeta Turnu Severin. An official Romanian administrative region of Craiova, also called Oltenia, existed from 1952 to 1968.
olympe-de-gouges: Marie Gouze was born on 7 May 1748 in Montauban in south-western France. Her father is uncertain: she may have been the daughter of her mother's husband, Pierre Gouze, a butcher, or of the Marquis de Pompignan, a relationship she encouraged rumours of and which is considered plausible but historically unverifiable. On 24 October 1765 she was married, against her will, to Louis Yves Aubry, a caterer. Their son Pierre was born on 29 August 1766, and Aubry died that November in a flood of the river Tarn. She never married again, calling marriage 'the tomb of trust and love', and she took the name Olympe de Gouges.

In 1768 a Lyon businessman, Jacques Biétrix de Rozières, funded her move to Paris. There she frequented salons and met writers and future politicians such as Brissot and Condorcet. She published a novel in 1784 and began a prolific career as a playwright; a record of the papers seized at her arrest lists about 40 plays.

Her work expressed indignation at social injustice. She wrote on the slave trade, divorce, marriage, debtors' prisons, children's rights and work schemes for the unemployed, and with Condorcet she is considered one of France's earliest public opponents of slavery. She published under her own name, unlike many women playwrights at the Comédie Française. She published 68 pamphlets; her first political brochure appeared in November 1788, and in early 1789 her Remarques Patriotiques proposed social security, care for the elderly and a jury system.

In 1791, answering the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, she wrote the Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen, which follows the same seventeen-article structure. It contains her statement that a woman has the right to mount the scaffold and must equally have the right to mount the speaker's platform. She followed it with a Contrat Social proposing marriage based on equality between the sexes.

De Gouges welcomed the Revolution but grew disenchanted when equal rights were not extended to women. She was associated with the moderate Girondins and opposed the execution of Louis XVI. After the Montagnards imprisoned prominent Girondins on 2 June 1793, her increasingly vehement writings culminated in the poster Les Trois urnes, which led to her arrest. She was guillotined on 3 November 1793. On 15 November Pierre Gaspard Chaumette cited her as a warning to women who meddled in politics. Largely forgotten afterwards, she was rediscovered through a political biography by Olivier Blanc in the mid-1980s, and a square in Paris was named after her in 2004.
olympias: Olympias was born around 375 BCE, probably at Passaron in Epirus, the eldest daughter of Neoptolemus I, king of the Molossians. Her brother was Alexander I of Epirus. Her family, the Aeacidae, claimed descent from Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, and were perhaps the only people of Epirus universally recognised as Greek. According to Plutarch she was first named Polyxena and took the name Myrtale before her marriage as part of an initiation into a mystery cult.

In 358 BCE Arybbas, who had succeeded Neoptolemus I as king of the Molossians, made a treaty with the new king of Macedonia, Philip II, and the alliance was sealed by the marriage of his niece Olympias to Philip in 357 BCE. In 356 BCE Philip's racehorse won at the Olympic Games, and Olympias, until then called Myrtale, took the name Olympias. That summer she gave birth to Alexander.

According to the sources, the marriage was stormy, because of Philip's volatility and Olympias' ambition and jealousy. In 337 BCE Philip married a Macedonian noblewoman, Cleopatra, niece of Attalus, to whom he gave the name Eurydice, and Olympias went into exile in Epirus with Alexander. When Philip was murdered in 336 BCE by Pausanias, one of his bodyguards, Olympias was suspected of having countenanced the killing.

During Alexander's campaigns she corresponded with him and wielded great influence in Macedonia, causing trouble for the regent Antipater. After Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BCE, his wife Roxana bore a son, Alexander IV. In 317 BCE Olympias allied with the regent Polyperchon against Antipater's son Cassander, who had made Philip III Arrhidaeus king. Her army won over the army of Adea Eurydice, the wife of Philip III, and in October 317 BCE she captured and executed the pair.

Cassander besieged Olympias in Pydna. Her life had been promised in the terms of capitulation, but he decided to have her killed, and when the fortress fell the soldiers sent to kill her refused to harm the mother of Alexander the Great. Accounts of her death differ: Pausanias says she was stoned to death by the families of her victims, while Justinus says she went out to meet her enemies in royal attire with two maids and made them stab her publicly. Cassander is also said to have denied her body burial rites. Roxana and Alexander IV were executed a few years later, in 309 BCE.
oman: Oman lies between latitudes 16 and 28 degrees north. A gravel desert plain covers most of the centre, with the Hajar Mountains along the north and the Dhofar Mountains along the south-east coast, where the main cities stand: Muscat, Sohar and Sur in the north and Salalah in the south. The peninsula of Musandam, on the Strait of Hormuz, is an exclave cut off from the rest of Oman by the United Arab Emirates. The climate is hot and dry inland and humid on the coast, and the Dhofar Mountains receive monsoon rain from late June to late September.

Stone tools found at Al Aybut Al Awal in Dhofar, dated to about 106,000 years ago, support the view that early human groups moved from Africa into Arabia in the Late Pleistocene. The Bronze Age Umm an-Nar and Wadi Suq periods left many remains, including monumental architecture. Sumerian tablets of about 2300 BCE call the region Magan, a source of copper and diorite for Mesopotamia, and the Magan civilisation is said to have lasted until 550 BCE. The oldest known written mention of the name Oman comes from a tomb at Mleiha, dated to about 220 BCE.

From the 17th century Oman became a regional power, expelled the Portuguese from its coastal possessions and built an empire that competed with the Portuguese and British in the Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean. In the 19th century its influence reached across the Strait of Hormuz and south to Zanzibar. The Al Bu Said dynasty has ruled continuously since 1744. In the 20th century Oman came under British influence while remaining formally sovereign, and after the Dhofar rebellion and the coup of 1970 it became the modern state under Qaboos bin Said.

Oman is a sultanate with its capital and largest city at Muscat. Arabic is the official language and Islam the state religion. The Basic Statute of the State, issued in 1996, serves as its constitution. The country has about 5 million people and belongs to the United Nations, the Arab League and the Gulf Cooperation Council.
omar-al-mukhtar: Omar al-Mukhtar was born in 1858 at Zanzur, near Tobruk, in Ottoman Cyrenaica, into the Mnifa tribe, which belonged to the Senussi. He lost his father early and grew up in poverty. A sheikh adopted him, and after early schooling at the local mosque he studied for eight years at the Senussi university at Jaghbub. He became an expert on the Quran and an imam, and was chosen to settle disputes between tribes.

In 1895 he travelled south with al-Mahdi as-Senussi to Kufra and Chad, where he became sheikh of the zawiya of Ayn Kalk, and in 1899 he was among the Senussi sent to defend Chad against French expansion. After al-Mahdi's death in 1902 the new leader, Ahmed Sharif as-Senussi, recalled him and made him sheikh of the troubled zawiya of Laqsur in Cyrenaica.

In October 1911, during the Italo-Turkish War, the Italian navy reached the Libyan coast, demanded the surrender of Tripoli and Benghazi and bombarded them for three days when the Ottomans withdrew inland. Al-Mukhtar organised and led the resistance in Cyrenaica. He knew the desert well, and his small groups attacked outposts, ambushed troops and cut supply lines before vanishing into the terrain. After the Italian governor Ernesto Bombelli formed a counter-guerrilla force that dealt the rebels a severe setback in April 1925, al-Mukhtar changed his tactics. In 1929 he rejected a compromise reached with Marshal Pietro Badoglio.

General Rodolfo Graziani took command in March 1930. After a large offensive failed, Graziani, with Badoglio, Emilio De Bono and Benito Mussolini, resolved to move the 100,000 people of the Jebel Akhdar into concentration camps and to fence the Libyan-Egyptian border. Begun early in 1931, these measures cut the fighters off from help and supplies.

Wounded in battle near Slonta, al-Mukhtar was captured on 11 September 1931 and hanged before his followers in the Soluch camp on 16 September, aged 73, on the orders of an Italian court. Even Graziani described him as intelligent, religious, uncompromising and poor. Omar al-Mukhtar University was founded in 1961, the film Lion of the Desert (1981) depicts his last years, and he is regarded as the national hero of Libya and a symbol of resistance in the Arab and Islamic worlds.
omar-ali-saifuddien-mosque: The Omar Ali Saifuddien Mosque is one of the two state mosques of Brunei, the other being the Jame' Asr Hassanil Bolkiah Mosque. According to stories, the Italian artist and architect Rudolfo Nolli created it from an initial drawing by Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien III. A committee chaired by Pengiran Bendahara Pengiran Anak Muhammad Yasin was set up in 1952 to find a site. Padang Besar was first proposed, but the Sultan asked for the present location near the Brunei River, for the sake of the people of Kampong Ayer.

Construction began on 4 February 1954 and used 1,400 tonnes of concrete and 640 tonnes of steel, on foundation piles of 24 to 37 metres. The Sultan opened the mosque on 26 September 1958, in conjunction with his 42nd birthday celebration, and it cost US$5 million. The opening was the first news reported over the radio in the country.

The style is primarily influenced by Mughal architecture, with Islamic and Bruneian elements. The mosque measures 69 by 26 metres and can hold 3,000 worshippers. The golden dome rises over the prayer hall and is covered with a mosaic of more than three million Venetian glass pieces. The 51-metre main minaret, the highest in the country, stands with four lesser minarets, which together represent the five pillars of Islam. Nolli designed the pillars with a Bruneian motif, a thick rope called kalat. The floors and columns are covered in Italian marble, and carpets from Saudi Arabia and Belgium cover the prayer hall.

The mosque stands in a man-made lagoon, in which lies a concrete re-creation of the 16th-century Mahligai, the royal barge of Sultan Bolkiah, accessible since 1967. It is based on the traditional longboats used by the indigenous people of Borneo for warfare, memorial services and royal celebrations.

The mosque is a place of worship and a popular tourist destination. It hosted the mass thanksgiving prayer of 31 December 1983 on the declaration of Independence Day and remains the main venue for the solemnisation of royal weddings and mass prayers on National Day. Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah married there in 1965 and Crown Prince Al-Muhtadee Billah in 2004. A first renovation, completed in January 1994, added air conditioning and decorative glass with verses from the Quran in the small windows of the domes.
omar-khayyam: Omar Khayyam was born in 1048 at Nishapur, a metropolis in the province of Khorasan in the Seljuk Empire, of Persian stock. His full name was Ghiyath al-Din Abu al-Fath Umar ibn Ibrahim Nishapuri. It has often been assumed, though it is open to doubt, that his forebears were tent-makers, since khayyam means tent-maker in Arabic. The historian Bayhaqi, who knew him personally, gave the details of his horoscope, which modern scholars used to establish his date of birth as 18 May 1048. Khayyam was known in his lifetime as a mathematician, and he considered himself a student of Avicenna.

In 1074-5 Sultan Malik-Shah commissioned Khayyam to build an observatory at Isfahan and to reform the Persian calendar. A panel of eight scholars worked under his direction, making large-scale astronomical observations and revising the astronomical tables. The calendar fixed the first day of the year at the moment the centre of the Sun crosses the vernal equinox, marking Nowruz. It was named the Jalali calendar in the sultan's honour and inaugurated on 15 March 1079. It used a 33-year cycle of 25 ordinary years of 365 days and 8 leap years of 366 days, and remained in use across Greater Iran from the 11th to the 20th centuries. The observatory fell into disuse after Malik-Shah died in 1092.

His surviving mathematical works include a commentary on Euclid's postulates, completed in December 1077, and a Treatise on Algebra, most likely completed in 1079. He seems to have been the first to conceive a general theory of cubic equations and to solve every type of cubic geometrically, so far as positive roots are concerned, using conic sections. In treating the parallel axiom he refuted earlier attempts at proof and considered the acute, obtuse and right angle cases of what is now called the Khayyam-Saccheri quadrilateral. He also wrote on Archimedes' principle, on music theory, and in philosophy, where he wrote on existence, free will and determinism.

A tradition attributes quatrains, or rubaiyat, to him. The earliest allusion to his poetry comes from the historian Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, a younger contemporary, and the earliest quatrains are quoted in works of about 1160 and 1230. Because quotations in 13th- and 14th-century texts are of doubtful authenticity, sceptical scholars point out that the whole tradition may be pseudepigraphic. Edward FitzGerald's English translation of 1859, at first unsuccessful, became extremely well known by the 1880s and led to Omar Khayyam Clubs and a cult of the Rubaiyat.
omar-torrijos: Omar Efraín Torrijos Herrera was born on 13 February 1929 in Santiago, in the province of Veraguas, the sixth of twelve children. Both his parents were teachers. At eighteen he won a scholarship to the military academy in San Salvador and graduated as a second lieutenant. He joined the National Guard in 1952, became a captain in 1956 and a major in 1960, took a cadet course at the School of the Americas in 1965, and was Executive Secretary of the Guard in 1966.

In 1968 Torrijos was sent to El Salvador as a military attaché after accusations of involvement in election fraud. That year Major Boris Martínez and Colonel José Humberto Ramos overthrew the recently elected president, Arnulfo Arias. Torrijos, named commandant of the National Guard, and Martínez were the true leaders from the start; they barred political activity and closed the legislature. On 23 February 1969 Torrijos ousted Martínez and Ramos and exiled them to Miami, and he promoted himself to brigadier general. He was never officially president but held titles of his own, including Maximum Leader of the Panamanian Revolution.

His government promoted land reform, education and social welfare, redistributing 180,000 hectares of uncultivated land and adopting a new constitution and a labour code. In 1972 an Assembly of Community Representatives approved a constitution and elected Demetrio Lakas as president, while Torrijos remained the actual head of government. After a long dispute over the Panama Canal he negotiated the Torrijos–Carter Treaties, signed on 7 September 1977, which gradually passed control to Panama until 31 December 1999, though the United States kept a right to defend the canal's neutrality. In 1978 he stepped down as head of government but stayed the de facto ruler, and in 1979 he organised the Democratic Revolutionary Party.

Torrijos died at the age of 52 on 31 July 1981, when his Panamanian Air Force Twin Otter crashed at Cerro Marta, near Penonomé. Four aides and two pilots also died. His death caused national mourning, especially in poor areas, and he was followed as commander of the National Guard by Florencio Flores and then Rubén Darío Paredes. His death before the planned transition could be completed caused a political crisis that brought Manuel Noriega to power. It also produced charges and speculation that he had been assassinated; no documents supporting them have been produced. His son Martín Torrijos was president from 2004 to 2009.
omdurman: Omdurman, in Arabic Umm Durmān, lies on the west bank of the River Nile, opposite and north-west of Khartoum, in the State of Khartoum. The name means Mother of Durman, but who she was is unknown. It is an important road hub, and the Nile adds to its transport links. The climate is hot and arid, with only the summer months seeing noticeable rain, about 155 millimetres a year, and temperatures routinely above 40 °C in mid-summer. It is one of three connected cities, joined to Khartoum and Khartoum Bahri by several bridges over the Blue and White Nile rivers.

After the siege of Khartoum, and after the building of the Mahdi's tomb following his death from typhus, the city grew rapidly. In September 1898 a British army of twenty thousand men under General Horatio Herbert Kitchener, with Maxim guns and Martini-Henry rifles, invaded Sudan. At the Battle of Omdurman, fought in the nearby village of Kerreri, it faced more than 52,000 poorly armed Sudanese defenders, and the battle was over in five hours. At least 10,000 Sudanese were killed, against fewer than four hundred British casualties, forty-eight of them dead. Kitchener then ordered the desecration of the Mahdi's tomb, and in Winston Churchill's words carried off the Mahdi's head in a kerosene can as a trophy.

The following year British forces defeated the Khalifa Abdallahi ibn Muhammad at the Battle of Umm Diwaykarat, which secured British control over Sudan. Kitchener restored Khartoum as the capital, and from 1899 until 1956 Sudan was governed jointly by Great Britain and Egypt. Most of Omdurman was destroyed in the battle, but the Mahdi's tomb was restored and refurbished.

Omdurman is the second most populous city in Sudan. Its public universities include Karary University and Omdurman Islamic University, and its private ones include the Ahfad University for Women and Omdurman Ahlia University. Its location in the centre of the country, almost within the national capital, connects it by road to the cities and capitals of Sudan's other states.
omo-river: The Omo River, also called the Omo-Bottego, is the largest Ethiopian river outside the Nile Basin. Its course lies wholly inside Ethiopia, and it empties into Lake Turkana on the border with Kenya, forming the principal stream of the endorheic Turkana Basin. It is formed by the confluence of the Gibe River, by far its largest tributary, and the Gojeb River, and its whole basin is sometimes called the Omo-Gibe basin. The river is 760 kilometres long and falls about 700 metres, from 1,060 metres at the confluence of the Gibe and Wabe rivers to 360 metres at lake level. It is a rapid stream in its upper reaches, broken by the Kokobi and other falls.

The Omo formed the eastern boundary of the former kingdoms of Janjero and Garo. The Italian explorer Vittorio Bottego first reached the river on 29 June 1896, during his second African expedition, and died on 17 March 1897, after which the river was renamed in his honour. Herbert Henry Austin and his men reached the delta on 12 September 1898 and found that an Ethiopian expedition under Ras Wolda Giyorgis had planted flags on the north shore of Lake Turkana on 7 April. A second Ethiopian expedition under Lieutenant Alexander Bulatovich reached the lake on 21 August 1899. Frenchmen in that party mapped many of the delta's meanders, a map used until the 1930s.

The lower valley has been a crossroads for various cultures and ethnic groups, and peoples such as the Mursi, Suri, Nyangatom, Dizi and Me'en are studied for their diversity. The seasonal flood brings fertile silt, and many peoples along the lower Omo, including the Turkana, Dassanach, Hamer, Karo, Kwegu and Bodi, draw a great part of their food from flood-retreat cultivation.

The basin is important to archaeology: over 50,000 fossils have been identified from the lower valley, 230 of them hominid, dating to the Pliocene and Pleistocene. Fossils of Australopithecus and Homo and quartzite tools, the oldest about 2.4 million years old, have been found. A French expedition made the first discoveries in 1901, and an international team made the most significant finds between 1967 and 1975, among them an Australopithecus jawbone about 2.5 million years old. The valley was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1980.

The river passes the Mago and Omo National Parks, where hippopotamuses, crocodiles and puff adders live. Lake Turkana is generally recognised to receive about ninety per cent of its water from the Omo. Several hydroelectric stations and dams stand in the basin, among them Gibe III, a roller-compacted concrete dam 246 metres high.
omri: Omri was the sixth king of Israel. The Hebrew Bible says nothing about his lineage and gives no tribal origin for him, as it also does not for his predecessor Zimri. One possibility, though unproven, is that he was of the tribe of Issachar. His name is puzzling to scholars, and an Amorite, Arabic or Hebrew origin has been proposed. According to the biblical narrative, Omri was commander of the army of King Elah when Zimri, commander of half the king's chariots, murdered Elah and made himself king.

The troops at Gibbethon chose Omri as king instead, and he led them to Tirzah and besieged it. When Zimri saw that the city had fallen, he shut himself in the royal palace and set it ablaze, after a reign of only seven days. Half the people, however, supported Tibni against Omri, and it took Omri four years to subdue him and be undisputed king. By the biblical count he reigned twelve years, six of them in Tirzah. Modern scholars offer several different dates for his reign.

Omri bought a hill from Shemer for two talents of silver and built the new capital of Samaria there, reigning in it until his death and being buried in it. His son Ahab succeeded him. The Bible is silent about his other actions but says he did more evil than all the kings before him.

The Moabite Mesha Stele, now in the Louvre, indicates that Omri expanded his holdings to include northern Moab east of the Jordan, and it refers to the oppression of Moab by Omri, king of Israel. Assyrian kings called Israel the House of Omri, Bit-Humria, and the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III has been read as naming Jehu as son of Omri, though that reading has been questioned in favour of Omride. Many scholars consider Omri the first truly historical figure in the Bible, though this is debated.

The dynasty he founded ended almost fifty years of constant civil war over the throne. There was peace and cooperation with Judah, and marriages bolstered relations with Sidon. This allowed Israel to expand its influence in Transjordan and brought economic prosperity, but the peace with Sidon also brought Phoenician religious ideas that led to conflict between traditionalists, represented by the prophet Elijah, and the court of Ahab and Jezebel.
omsk: Omsk lies in the south of the West Siberian Plain, on the banks of the north-flowing Irtysh at its confluence with the Om River, which gives the city its name; in the dialect of the Baraba Tatars the hydronym means the quiet one. It stands about 450 km north of Astana and 2,230 km east of Moscow. Omsk is the junction of the northern and southern branches of the Trans-Siberian Railway, and its river port gives access to the waterways of the Irtysh and the Ob.

The fortress at Omsk arose from the need to secure the trade route to China. The Siberian governor, Prince Matvey Gagarin, obtained the tsar's consent in May 1714 to build fortresses along the Irtysh. By the end of 1716 the first fortress, an earthen pentagon with stores, barracks and officers' houses, stood at the mouth of the Om. Omsk was granted town status in 1782, and in 1822 it became the administrative capital of Western Siberia. As the frontier receded the town became a major centre of Siberian exile; Fyodor Dostoyevsky served his sentence in an Omsk prison from 1850 to 1854. The Trans-Siberian Railway of the 1890s made it a logistic hub.

After the October Revolution the Provisional All-Russian Government was established in Omsk in 1918 under Admiral Kolchak, and the city was proclaimed capital of Russia, its central bank keeping the former empire's gold reserves. The Red Army forced Kolchak to retreat east to Irkutsk, and Bolshevik forces entered Omsk in 1919. The Second World War gave the city new life, because industry was evacuated there from the front. In the 1950s the development of Siberian oil led to a refinery complex, now the largest in Russia.
