Omsk is the administrative centre and largest city of Omsk Oblast and has more than a million inhabitants. It is the third largest city in Siberia, after Novosibirsk and Krasnoyarsk. It is the seat of the bishop of Omsk and Tara.
omurtag: Omurtag, also known as Murtag or Murtagon, bore the title Kanasubigi and is known as the Builder. After the death of Khan Krum there was a short period of political instability. Byzantine sources name three nobles, Dukum, Ditzeng and Tsog, as persecutors of Christians, and Dukum may be identical with Omurtag. They were either Krum's generals with a major role in government but without the throne, or regents to the infant Omurtag. Historians usually accept Vasil Gyuzelev's view that Omurtag succeeded his father after short disturbances.

In the summer of 814 the Byzantine Emperor Leo V the Armenian attacked the Bulgarian troops in Thrace and won a battle near Burtodizos, probably modern Babaeski; Omurtag escaped on a swift horse. News of a possible alliance between the Byzantines and Louis the Pious of the Franks led to a 30-year peace treaty with the Byzantine Empire in 815, partly inscribed on a column found near Seltsi. It fixed the border in Thrace from the Black Sea coast near Debelt to the Maritsa river, without Plovdiv, and provided for exchanges of prisoners. It was renewed in 820 under Michael II, and Omurtag later sent an army to help Michael II against the rebel Thomas the Slav.

In 818 the Slavic Timočani, Abodrites and Braničevci rebelled against Bulgarian rule and sought the support of Louis the Pious. After diplomacy failed, Omurtag issued an ultimatum in 826 and in 827 sent a fleet along the Danube and the Drava, which restored Bulgarian control over parts of southeastern Pannonia. At home he ended the autonomy of the Slavic tribes and divided the state into large provinces called comitati, whose governors, appointed by the Kanasubigi, held military and civil authority. He also repressed Christians, especially the Byzantine prisoners settled by Krum, and disinherited his eldest son Enravota, who was sympathetic to Christianity.

Omurtag undertook large-scale construction to restore his capital Pliska, destroyed by the Byzantines in 811, and to develop regional centres, palaces and fortifications. Inscriptions at Chatalar and Tarnovo record the rebuilding of Pliska, a new palace with a large throne room and a temple of Tangra. An alley of stone columns bore the names of conquered towns in Thrace. His Tarnovo Inscription reads in part: Let the one who comes later upon seeing this inscription remember the one who had made it. And the name is Omurtag, Kanasubigi.
on-liberty: According to John Stuart Mill's autobiography, On Liberty was first conceived as a short essay in 1854. As the ideas developed, the married couple expanded, rewrote and jointly corrected it, and Mill says it was more directly their joint production than anything else bearing his name. The final draft was nearly complete when Harriet died suddenly in 1858, and he published it under his name alone, dedicated to her memory. It also drew on Wilhelm von Humboldt's On the Limits of State Action. A stylometric analysis in 2022 suggested that Harriet Taylor Mill's contribution was large enough for her to be regarded as co-author.

The essay opens with the struggle between authority and liberty and warns of a tyranny of the majority, which the authors consider worse than the tyranny of government because it is not limited to a political function. It proposes a single standard: power may rightfully be used over a member of a civilised community, against his will, only to prevent harm to others, and over himself, his body and mind, the individual is sovereign. The authors base this on utility, not natural rights.

The second chapter argues that opinions should never be suppressed: a silenced opinion may be true, may hold part of the truth, and an accepted truth left uncontested risks becoming a prejudice. The third values individuality, comparing human nature to a tree that must grow on all sides. The fourth separates what concerns the individual from what concerns society, and the last applies the principles to trade, taxation, education and marriage.

The essay was very popular in the years after its publication, and Thomas Hardy recalled that undergraduates of the 1860s knew it almost by heart. Thomas Carlyle, James Fitzjames Stephen and Matthew Arnold criticised it for leaving the door open to barbarism. Later critics, among them Nigel Warburton, questioned whether its defence of liberty fits its utilitarian foundation. It remains regarded as a classic of political thought and a seminal work of British liberalism, and a copy of it is the symbol of office of the president of the Liberal Democrat Party in England.
on-the-origin-of-species: Darwin wrote to Charles Lyell of his ideas in January 1842 and in June roughed out a 35-page "Pencil Sketch"; by July 1844 it had grown into a 230-page "Essay", to be published if he died prematurely. In 1856 he began a full treatise, his "big book" on natural selection. On 18 June 1858 he received a parcel from Alfred Russel Wallace, then in the Maluku Islands, describing a mechanism similar to his own. Lyell and Joseph Dalton Hooker arranged for papers by both men to be read at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858, and they drew little reaction.

Darwin then began an abstract of his work on 20 July 1858. John Murray published it on 24 November 1859, in a first printing of 1,250 copies at fifteen shillings; 500 were taken by Mudie's Library. A second edition of 3,000 copies followed on 7 January 1860, and the book went through six editions in Darwin's lifetime. The fifth, of 1869, first included the phrase "survival of the fittest", coined by Herbert Spencer.

The opening chapter treats animal breeding and plant cultivation, using fancy pigeons, all descended from the rock dove, as an illustration of artificial selection. Chapter III introduces natural selection and asks how varieties become distinct species. Darwin admitted that the laws of inheritance were unknown, and he accepted that the use and disuse of parts could be inherited.

Several chapters take up difficulties: the absence of transitional forms, and a geological record that Darwin argued, following Lyell, was extremely imperfect. He argued from biogeography that differences between regions could not be explained by environment alone, and from classification that resemblance reflects descent with modification. He kept human origins to one sentence: "Light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history."

The book aroused international interest and a widespread debate, with no sharp line between scientific, ideological and religious issues. Much of the first reaction was hostile, partly because few reviewers understood the theory, but Darwin was a respected scientist and had to be taken seriously. Bishop Samuel Wilberforce disagreed with it in the Quarterly Review in 1860. By 1875 most scientists accepted that evolution had occurred, though few thought natural selection important.

During the "eclipse of Darwinism" from the 1880s to the 1930s other mechanisms were given more credit. The modern evolutionary synthesis of the 1930s and 1940s, in which R. A. Fisher, Sewall Wright and J. B. S. Haldane joined selection to Mendelian genetics, made natural selection central to evolutionary theory.
onake-obavva: Obavva belonged to the Holaya community. Her husband, Kahale Mudda Hanuma, was the guard of a watchtower in the rocky fort of Chitradurga, which the troops of Hyder Ali besieged during the reign of Madakari Nayaka. As the story is told, a chance sighting of a man entering the fort through a hole in the rocks gave Hyder Ali the plan of sending his soldiers in by the same way.

The guard on duty near the hole had gone home for his meal. When he wanted water, Obavva went to fetch it in a pot from a pond near the hole, halfway up the hill, and there saw the soldiers trying to enter. She struck each on the head with the pestle as he came through and quietly moved the body aside, so that those behind suspected nothing. Mudda Hanuma returned to find her standing with the bloodstained pestle among the enemy dead.

She was found dead later the same day, either from shock or killed by enemy soldiers. Her act saved the fort on that occasion, but Madakari Nayaka could not withstand Hyder Ali's attack in 1779, when Chitradurga was lost to him.

In Karnataka she is honoured beside Abbakka Rani, Keladi Chennamma and Kittur Chennamma as one of the foremost women warriors of the state. Since 2021 the Government of Karnataka has celebrated 11 November as Onake Obavva Jayanti. A sports stadium in Chitradurga bears her name, and a statue of her by the sculptor Ashok Gudigar stands in front of the District Commissioner's office there. Her deed is shown in a song sequence of the film Nagarahavu, directed by Puttanna Kanagal, in which the actress Jayanthi played her, and in the 2019 Kannada film Chitradurgada Onake Obavva, with the actress Tara in the role.
ondjiva: The Ondjiva mission station was founded in 1891 by Friedrich Meisenholl and August Wulfhorst of the Rhenish Mission Society, with the help of Friedrich Bernsmann and the permission of King Weyulu Hedimbi. The missionaries believed Ondjiva lay in the territory of German South West Africa, which later proved not to be so. The next year they founded the station of Omupanda. Meisenholl stayed about four years before serious illness forced him to leave, and Wilhelm Stahlhut replaced him in the mid-1890s. Three of Stahlhut's children died in Africa, and he died of blackwater fever at Outjo on 1 May 1900. In August 1915 King Mandume had the mission station burned, and the Germans fled to Ondonga in South West Africa.

Ondjiva later became a Catholic mission and the see of the bishop of the Ondjiva Diocese. It has traditionally been a centre of the Kwanyama, whose standardised dialect, Oshikwanyama, belongs to the Oshiwambo language. The Angolan Civil War, which lasted from 1975 to 2002, largely destroyed the town. Its administration operated from Huíla Province and in theory ruled Cunene Province in exile. Most residents had left by 1989, and by 1999 fewer than 5,000 people lived there. Reconstruction began after peace came in 2002.

Ondjiva, formerly Vila Pereira d'Eça, is the administrative capital of Cunene Province, in the extreme south of Angola about 42 kilometres from the border with Namibia. It is a commune in the municipality of Cuanhama and had a population of 121,537 in 2014. After the war many people returned and others arrived from other parts of Angola, notably Huíla Province. The town has twelve neighbourhoods and is served by Ondjiva Pereira Airport. A planned rail connection to Namibia on the Moçâmedes Railway remains unbuilt.
ondo-state: Ondo State lies in south-western Nigeria and was created on 3 February 1976 from the former Western State. It borders Ekiti State to the north, Kogi State to the north-east, Edo State to the east, Delta State to the south-east, Ogun State to the south-west and Osun State to the north-west, with the Atlantic Ocean to the south. The coast includes mangrove-swamp forest near the Bight of Benin. Its climate is tropical wet and dry. The Idanre inselberg hills, over 1,000 metres high, are the highest point in the western half of Nigeria.

The state capital, Akure, was formerly the capital of the ancient Akure Kingdom. The population is predominantly Yoruba, made up of subgroups known as the Idanre, Akoko, Akure, Ikale, Ilaje, Ondo, Ese Odo, Owo and Ose peoples. Ijaw people, including the Apoi and Arogbo, live in the south-eastern swamps close to the Edo State border. In Oke-Igbo town, near the Osun State border, a small population speaks a variant of Yoruba similar to the Ife dialect.

The vast majority of the population are Christians, among them members of the Anglican Province of Ondo and Catholics in the Diocese of Ondo, which dates from 1943. Minorities practise Islam and traditional Yoruba religion.

The state is divided into 18 local government areas, the major ones being Akoko, Akure, Okitipupa, Ondo, Ilaje, Idanre and Owo, and most citizens live in towns. Its economy rests on cocoa production, farming, asphalt mining and activities connected with its long coastline, and its mineral resources include bitumen, coal, oil and gas, granite, limestone and kaolin. Universities include the Federal University of Technology Akure, the Adekunle Ajasin University at Akungba Akoko and the Ondo State University of Science and Technology at Okitipupa. Federal highway A121, part of Trans-African Highway 8 from Lagos to Mombasa, crosses the state from Ogun State through Ore to Edo State, and highway A122 runs from Osun State through Akure to Edo State.
one-thousand-and-one-nights: One Thousand and One Nights is a collection of Middle Eastern folktales compiled in Arabic during the Islamic Golden Age. It was collected over many centuries by various authors, translators and scholars across West Asia, Central Asia, South Asia and North Africa. Some tales go back to ancient and medieval Persian, Arabic and Mesopotamian literature, but most were originally folk stories of the Abbasid and Mamluk eras. The frame story comes from the Pahlavi Persian work Hezār Afsān, meaning A Thousand Tales, which in turn relied partly on Indian elements. The earliest mentions of the Nights describe it as an Arabic translation from that Persian book.

The tenth-century Fihrist of Ibn al-Nadim in Baghdad mentions Hezār Afsān. One of the oldest Arabic manuscript fragments, a few handwritten pages from Syria dating to the early ninth century, was discovered by the scholar Nabia Abbott in 1948. It bears the title Kitab Hadith Alf Layla, The Book of the Tale of the Thousand Nights.

In the frame story the king Shahriyar is told tales by his wife Scheherazade, one for each night of storytelling, and some stories are framed within others while some are self-contained. The bulk of the text is in prose, with verse used for songs, riddles and heightened emotion. If a canonical text with every story in a fixed order ever existed, it no longer survives. Editions range from a few hundred nights to 1001 or more, and the corpus now comprises more than 550 tales. Variants of the ending agree that Shahriyar pardoned Scheherazade and spared her life.

The Nights use the frame story and the story within a story, techniques with roots in earlier Persian and Indian storytelling such as the Sanskrit Panchatantra, and its tales also make use of foreshadowing, repetition and the device of the unreliable narrator.

Four printed Arabic editions, all of the 19th century, are taken as canonical: Calcutta I, Bulaq, Breslau and Calcutta II. Calcutta I was printed by the British East India Company in 1814 to 1818. The first European version, in French, was made by Antoine Galland between 1704 and 1717 in twelve volumes. It included tales such as Aladdin's lamp and Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves that appear in none of the original manuscripts; Galland said he heard them from the storyteller Hanna Diyab. The first English edition, of about 1706 to 1721, gave the work the title The Arabian Nights' Entertainments.
oni-georgia: Oni lies in a deep gorge on the left bank of the Rioni river, some 830 metres above sea level and 210 kilometres north-west of Tbilisi. It belongs to the Racha-Lechkhumi and Kvemo Svaneti region of Georgia and is, historically and ethnographically, part of Racha, a highland province of western Georgia. It is also the administrative centre of the Oni district.

The area has been inhabited since the Bronze Age. Archaeology has found artefacts of Colchian culture, among them Colchian coins of the sixth to third centuries BCE. Oni is first chronicled in the fifteenth century, though a legend credits its founding to King Pharnajom of Iberia in the second century BCE. It stood at a crossroads between the northern Caucasus, Kartli, Imereti and Lower Racha, and developed into a typical late medieval commercial town, contested between the kings of Imereti and the princes of Racha.

Imperial Russia absorbed the town in 1810, and in 1846 it became the administrative centre of the Racha Uyezd of the Kutaisi Governorate. In the Soviet period it was joined with surrounding villages to form the Oni district. The earthquake of 29 April 1991 measured 7.0 on the moment magnitude scale, with a maximum intensity of IX on the MSK scale, the most powerful recorded in the Caucasus Mountains, and it did significant damage to the town's infrastructure.

The Oni Synagogue was built in the 1880s by a Polish architect, with Greek Jews from Thessaloniki as the builders. It recalls a large Jewish community, Georgia's third largest after those of Tbilisi and Kutaisi, most of whom emigrated to Israel after the fall of the Soviet Union; a few families remain. Most of the population is Georgian and Orthodox Christian, and the largest minority is Ossetian. The town and its surroundings hold ruined medieval forts and Georgian Orthodox churches, and the Racha Regional Museum has about 14,000 objects in archaeology, ethnography, numismatics, natural history, fine art, manuscripts and printed books.
ontario: Ontario is the southernmost province of Canada, bordered by Manitoba to the west, Hudson Bay and James Bay to the north and Quebec to the east and northeast. To the south lie the United States, from Minnesota to New York. Almost all of its 2,700-kilometre international border follows rivers and lakes of the Great Lakes drainage system. The Canadian Shield covers over half of the land area and is rich in minerals but mostly unsuited to farming, while most people and most arable land are in Southern Ontario. The province has about 250,000 freshwater lakes.

Paleo-Indians first settled the land about 11,000 years ago. French exploration followed the founding of Quebec in 1608, and the French named the region the Pays d'en Haut, the Upper Country, a dependency of Canada that existed for defence and trade rather than settlement, in which Indigenous peoples were the vast majority of the population.

In 1782–1784 about 5,000 United Empire Loyalists entered the land after the American Revolution, and Britain granted them 200 acres each. The British also resettled displaced Iroquois at the Six Nations reserve at the west end of Lake Ontario in 1784. Upper Canada was created in 1791, and John Graves Simcoe was appointed its first lieutenant governor in 1793. After rebellions, Lord Durham recommended responsible government and the reunion of Upper and Lower Canada. The colonies were merged as the Province of Canada, with Upper Canada becoming Canada West. Responsible government was achieved in 1848, and heavy immigration in the 1840s more than doubled its population by 1851.
The name Ontario was adopted at Confederation in 1867. After Canada acquired Rupert's Land, a boundary dispute led to the province's northern limit being set at the 51st parallel north.

Ontario is the most populous province of Canada, with over 14 million people, and the second-largest by total area after Quebec. Its capital, Toronto, is the country's most populous city, and Ottawa, the national capital, lies within its borders. Its legislature is the Legislative Assembly of Ontario, established by the British North America Act of 1867. The Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto, founded in 1912, is the largest museum in Canada. The name is thought to have Indigenous origins, either Ontarí:io, a Huron word meaning great lake, or skanadario, beautiful water.
opava: Opava lies on the Opava River, near the border with Poland and about 27 kilometres north-west of Ostrava. The river takes its name from old Celtic words for water, and the town takes its name from the river, in German as Troppau, from zu Oppa, meaning on the Oppa, and in Polish as Opawa. Most of its territory lies in the Opava Hilly Land within the Silesian Lowlands, and the Opava and Moravice rivers meet within it. It is one of the historical centres of Silesia and was a historical capital of Czech Silesia.

The town is first mentioned in writing in 1195 and received town privileges in 1224. In 1269 the Duchy of Troppau was established with the town as its capital. The Hussites ruled the duchy from 1427 to 1431, and in 1485 it was acquired by Matthias Corvinus and ruled by Hungarians until 1526. In 1613 Karl I of Liechtenstein became Duke of Troppau and merged the duchy with the Duchy of Krnov. The title of Duke of Troppau continues in the Liechtenstein family.

Most of Silesia was annexed by the Kingdom of Prussia during the War of the Austrian Succession, after 1740. The part that remained with the Habsburg monarchy became known as Austrian Silesia, with its capital at Troppau from 1742 to 1918. The Congress of Troppau met there from 24 October to 23 December 1820. By the Austrian census of 1910 the town had 30,762 inhabitants, of whom 92 percent gave German as their native language, 6.9 percent Czech and 0.9 percent Polish.

In 1919 the town became part of Czechoslovakia, whose government established the name Opava. It was ceded to Nazi Germany in 1938 under the Munich Agreement and administered as part of Reichsgau Sudetenland. The Soviet Red Army occupied it on 22 April 1945, at the cost of enormous war damage. In 1945 and 1946 the German population was expelled under the Beneš decrees and the city was resettled with Czechs.

Opava is a regional centre of education and culture. The Silesian University was established in 1991, and the Silesian Museum, founded in 1814, is the oldest public museum in the Czech Republic. The Silesian Theatre dates from 1805. The city's two main landmarks are the city hall tower, known as Hláska, built in 1614 to 1618, and the Co-Cathedral of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, the largest building in the Czech Republic in Silesian Brick Gothic style, whose southern tower, 102 metres high, is the tallest in Silesia. The Chapel of the Holy Cross, from 1394, is also a national cultural monument.
opec: In 1949 Venezuela invited Iran, Iraq, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia to exchange views and explore closer communication among petroleum-exporting nations, as the world recovered from World War II. In February 1959 the multinational oil companies unilaterally cut their posted prices for Venezuelan and Middle Eastern crude oil by 10 per cent. Weeks later, at the Arab League's first Arab Petroleum Congress in Cairo, Saudi Arabia's Abdullah Tariki met Venezuela's observer Juan Pablo Pérez Alfonzo.

The Baghdad Conference of 10 to 14 September 1960 was held at the initiative of Tariki, Pérez Alfonzo and the Iraqi prime minister Abd al-Karim Qasim. Representatives of Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela met to discuss raising the price of their crude oil and answering the companies' unilateral actions, despite strong United States opposition. The organisation was founded on 14 September 1960.

In a series of steps in the 1960s and 1970s OPEC restructured the world's oil production in favour of producing states and away from an oligopoly of Anglo-American firms known as the Seven Sisters. Coordination within OPEC made it easier for states to nationalise oil production and set prices in their favour. The oil market was tight in the early 1970s, which lowered the risk of nationalisation, and a wave of nationalisations followed in Libya, Algeria, Iraq, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela. In 1973 members unilaterally raised oil prices, which led to the 1973 oil crisis.

After 1973 OPEC added to its goals the selling of oil for the socio-economic growth of poorer nations, and the OPEC Special Fund was established in January 1976. After prices approached US$40 a barrel in 1979 and 1980, industrial nations turned to coal, gas and nuclear power and developed non-OPEC oilfields in Siberia, Alaska, the North Sea and the Gulf of Mexico.

The OPEC Conference is the supreme authority and consists of delegations normally headed by the oil ministers of member countries. The secretary general is its chief executive. It ordinarily meets at the Vienna headquarters at least twice a year, and generally works by unanimity and one member, one vote, with each country paying an equal fee. Saudi Arabia, the largest exporter, has enough capacity to act as the swing producer and is regarded as the de facto leader.

Members differ widely in export capacity, costs and reserves, so agreeing on policy is often difficult. Economists often cite OPEC as a textbook example of a cartel, though some sources take a broader view. Its formation marked a turning point toward national sovereignty over natural resources.
operation-bagration: By June 1944 Germany's Army Group Centre had been left exposed. Defeats of Army Group South at Kursk, Kiev and in the Dnieper-Carpathian and Crimean offensives, and the retreat of Army Group North, left its lines protruding towards the east. The German High Command expected the next Soviet blow to fall against Army Group North Ukraine under Field Marshal Walter Model, and it lacked the intelligence to discover the Soviets' true intentions. Soviet deception measures, known as maskirovka, sustained that mistake.

The Stavka committed about 1,670,300 combat and support personnel, 5,818 tanks and assault guns and 7,799 aircraft. Army Group Centre had 486,000 combat personnel, only 495 operational tanks and assault guns and almost no mobile reserves. On Hitler's orders its main towns, among them Vitebsk, Minsk and Babruysk, were declared fortified towns to be held at all costs, which made the army vulnerable.

Soviet partisans began attacking railways behind the German lines on 19 and 20 June, and the main offensive opened with an artillery bombardment of unprecedented scale. The assault broke through almost everywhere. By 28 June the German 4th Army had been destroyed, along with most of the 3rd Panzer and 9th Armies. Soviet tanks broke into Minsk in the early hours of 3 July, and the city was cleared on 4 July, trapping the German 4th Army and many remnants of the 9th Army.

The Stavka ordered the advance to continue far beyond Minsk. Polotsk was cleared on 4 July, Vilnius was reached by 7 July, Lublin fell on 24 July, Białystok on 27 July and Brest on 28 July, and Kaunas came under Soviet control in early August. Soviet forces reached the Vistula and gained bridgeheads west of Sandomierz, and the German line along the Narew held until January 1945.

The Soviet Union destroyed 28 divisions of Army Group Centre. The overall engagement is the largest defeat in German military history, with around 450,000 German casualties, and it set the stage for the isolation of 300,000 German soldiers in the Courland Pocket. It forced Germany to fight on two major fronts for the first time, just over two weeks after Operation Overlord.

The Red Army used deep battle and maskirovka to their full extent for the first time, though with heavy losses, and reached the Vistula and Warsaw. In the reconquered lands it found cities destroyed, villages depopulated and much of the population killed or deported. About 57,000 German prisoners were paraded through Moscow.
operation-barbarossa: Germany and the Soviet Union signed the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact on 23 August 1939, a non-aggression agreement whose secret protocol divided eastern Europe into spheres of influence, and in 1940 they concluded a trade pact. After the Soviet occupation of Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina in July 1940, the German High Command began planning an invasion, which Adolf Hitler approved in December. Hitler renamed the plan, first called Operation Otto, after the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. The aims were ideological as well as material: the destruction of communism and the conquest of land that Generalplan Ost would repopulate with Germans, removing the Slavic peoples by deportation, enslavement and genocide. Joseph Stalin, despite intelligence of an attack, did not order mobilisation, fearing to provoke Germany.

On 22 June 1941 more than 3.8 million Axis troops invaded along a front of 2,900 kilometres. The attack paralysed Soviet command within hours. Army Group North overran the Baltic lands and, with Finnish forces, began the siege of Leningrad on 8 September, which lasted until 1944. Army Group Centre took Minsk on 28 June, closing a ring around Białystok and Minsk, and captured Smolensk on 16 July; the pocket there closed on 5 August with upwards of 300,000 Red Army soldiers captured.

Army Group South completed the encirclement of Kiev on 16 September, and Soviet losses there were 452,720 men. It took Kharkov on 24 October. Operation Typhoon, the drive on Moscow, began on 30 September, but supply problems, mud, the winter and determined resistance stalled it at the outskirts of the city by 5 December, when the Soviets began a major counteroffensive.

The failure of Barbarossa reversed the fortunes of Nazi Germany. The Red Army absorbed the Wehrmacht's strongest blows and bogged it down in a war of attrition for which Germany was unprepared. Hitler took personal control of the German army on 19 December 1941, and the offensives of 1942 and 1943, Case Blue and Operation Citadel, were made on narrower fronts and failed.

The Axis captured five million Red Army soldiers and deliberately starved or otherwise killed 3.3 million of these prisoners, along with millions of civilians. German death squads and collaborators murdered over a million Soviet Jews. The Eastern Front killed over 26 million Soviet people, and about 1,710 Soviet towns and 70,000 villages were razed.
operation-blue-star: In 1973 Sikh activists presented the Indian government with the Anandpur Sahib Resolution, a list of demands for greater autonomy for Punjab, which was rejected. The Akali Dal leader Harchand Singh Longowal said Sikhs wished to live within India as Sikhs, but Prime Minister Indira Gandhi viewed the resolution as secessionist. In July 1982 Longowal invited Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale of the Damdami Taksal to live in the Golden Temple complex, where he settled with about 200 armed followers. In December 1983 he moved into the Akal Takht, and former army officers, among them Major General Shabeg Singh, advised his men.

The operation ran from 1 to 10 June 1984. On 3 June a curfew was imposed on Punjab, communications and electricity were cut and the press was censored, while the temple was crowded with pilgrims marking the martyrdom anniversary of Guru Arjan Dev. The army began its assault in the early morning of 4 June. Underestimating the militants' firepower, it first used light weapons and then turned to tanks, helicopters and artillery.

Eyewitnesses reported many civilian deaths in the pilgrim rest houses on 5 June. By 6 June the militants had run out of most of their ammunition, and fighting ended around 1 a.m. on 7 June, when the army entered the Akal Takht and found the bodies of Bhindranwale, Shabeg Singh and Amrik Singh. The army first put the dead at 554 militants and civilians and 83 of its own soldiers; independent estimates were much higher. The government said that militants used pilgrims as human shields.

The Akal Takht was razed and many relics destroyed. The government issued a White Paper on 10 July 1984, which critics called unreliable. Punjab then saw Operation Woodrose, in which soldiers searched villages and made mass arrests. Sikhs worldwide saw the operation as an attack on their faith, and it is regarded as the beginning of the insurgency in Punjab. On 31 October 1984 two of her Sikh bodyguards assassinated Indira Gandhi, and anti-Sikh riots followed, mainly in Delhi.
operation-torch: After the United States entered the Second World War on 7 December 1941, British and American leaders agreed at the Arcadia Conference on a policy of Germany first, but differed on how to carry it out. The Americans favoured a limited landing in Europe in 1942 and a main thrust in 1943. The British pressed for a less ambitious plan, noting that American forces would take time to build up and that shipping was short. Winston Churchill proposed an invasion of North Africa, and President Franklin D. Roosevelt, wanting to support the Soviets, agreed over the opposition of his military chiefs. In August 1942 Dwight D. Eisenhower was appointed commander of the Allied expeditionary force.

The Allies believed the Vichy French Armistice Army would not fight, partly on information from the American consul Robert Daniel Murphy in Algiers. The Americans had recognised Pétain's government in 1940, while the British recognised Charles de Gaulle's French National Committee. Because de Gaulle had few supporters in North Africa, the Free French were kept out of the operation.

Three task forces landed on 8 November 1942. The Western Task Force, American troops under Major General George S. Patton, came ashore at Safi, Mehdiya-Port Lyautey and Fedala in Morocco, and met unexpected resistance and bad weather. Casablanca was taken after a short siege. The Centre Task Force under Major General Lloyd Fredendall landed near Oran, where shallow water and sandbars damaged landing ships, and Oran surrendered after bombardment by British battleships. The Eastern Task Force met less opposition at Algiers. French Resistance fighters seized the city in the early hours, but lost it again when no American troops appeared in the morning. On 11 November British troops landed unopposed at Bougie.

Admiral François Darlan, who was in Algiers on a private visit, first refused to join the Allies, then made a deal with Eisenhower on 10 November, which recognised him as High Commissioner. In return he ordered French forces in North Africa to stop resisting, and fighting ceased almost at once. When Adolf Hitler learned of the deal, he ordered the occupation of Vichy France, and German and Italian forces invaded on 11 November. The French fleet at Toulon was scuttled on 27 November by its own commander, Jean de Laborde, rather than join the Allies.

Darlan was assassinated by a monarchist six weeks later, and the Free French gradually came to dominate the government. French North African troops later fought in Italy, where Maghrebis, mostly Moroccans, made up over 60 per cent of the French Expeditionary Corps.
opium-wars: In the eighteenth century China enjoyed a trade surplus with Europe, exporting porcelain, silk and tea for silver. Foreign trade was restricted under the Canton System, which confined Western merchants to one port and to licensed Chinese merchants. As British demand outran Chinese demand for British goods, merchants began exporting opium grown in India, and by the late eighteenth century the British East India Company was expanding its cultivation in Bengal and selling it to private merchants, who passed it to Chinese smugglers.

Emperors issued edicts against opium in 1729, 1799, 1814 and 1831, but imports grew, helped by officials who shared the profit, and reached 30,000 chests by 1833. The trade drained silver from China, and the Qing government saw addiction as a threat to the workforce and to moral order. After the Company's monopoly ended in 1834, the Daoguang Emperor charged Lin Zexu with ending the trade.

In 1839 Lin wrote an open letter to Queen Victoria and ordered the seizure of all opium in Canton. In May 1840 the British government decided to send an expedition to obtain reparations for the traders' losses and security for the trade, and the Royal Navy's ships and guns inflicted a series of decisive defeats on Chinese forces. The Treaty of Nanking of 1842, the first of the unequal treaties, ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain, opened Shanghai, Canton, Ningbo, Fuzhou and Xiamen as treaty ports and required China to pay twenty-one million dollars.

The Second Opium War, fought by Britain and France from 1856, began after Chinese authorities boarded the Arrow at Canton on 8 October 1856; accounts differ over whether a British flag was flying. The Taiping Rebellion was then under way. The Treaty of Tientsin of 1858 opened ten more ports, legalised the opium trade and allowed foreigners to travel in China. Fighting resumed, and in October 1860 British and French forces took Beijing and looted and burned the Old Summer Palace.

The Convention of Peking in 1860 confirmed the treaty. The treaties weakened Chinese sovereignty, and they are central to the period that Chinese writers call the century of humiliation; later nationalist movements, including the Chinese Communist Party, drew on this history to justify efforts to restore sovereignty. Of the twelve bronze animal heads looted from the Old Summer Palace, seven have been found and returned to China.
opole: According to excavations, the first settlement was founded in the 8th century on the Ostrówek, the northern part of the Pasieka Island in the middle of the Oder. In the early 10th century it grew into one of the main strongholds of the Opolans, a Lechitic tribe. Duke Mieszko I conquered the land of the pagan Opolans in 992. After 1163 Silesia was divided between two Piast lines, and Opole became a duchy in 1172, often combined with the Duchy of Racibórz.

In the early 13th century Duke Casimir I of Opole moved the settlement to the right bank of the Oder, and a new town was established under German law between 1211 and 1217, settled by people from the earlier settlement and by German merchants from the west. In 1327 the duchy came under the sovereignty of the Kingdom of Bohemia, and in 1521 it inherited the Duchy of Racibórz. After the last Piast duke, Jan II the Good, died, the Habsburgs took control in 1532. They pawned the duchy to several rulers, among them monarchs of Poland, and in November 1655 King John II Casimir Vasa issued the Universal of Opole from the city, calling on Poles to rise against the Swedes.

Frederick II of Prussia conquered most of Silesia in 1740, confirmed by the Peace of Breslau in 1742. Oppeln became a regency seat in 1816, a railway reached it in 1843, and the first factories followed in 1859. At a plebiscite on 20 March 1921, 94.7 per cent of the votes cast in the city were for Germany. In 1945 it was transferred to Poland under the Potsdam agreements. Part of the local population was allowed to remain after being verified as Poles, while many Poles displaced from the eastern territories settled there.

Opole is the capital of Opole Voivodeship and its largest city, with a metropolitan area of 146,522 inhabitants. The Piast Tower, the only part left of the medieval castle of the dukes, survived a demolition of the castle in 1928 to 1931. The Holy Cross Cathedral holds the Piast Chapel with the tomb of Jan II the Good. The National Festival of Polish Song has been held in the city annually since 1963, and the University of Opole is among its higher education institutions.
oppidum: Oppidum is a Latin word meaning a defended administrative centre or town. In the Commentarii de Bello Gallico, Julius Caesar called the larger Celtic settlements he met in Gaul in 58 to 52 BCE oppida, without defining the word. They were important economic sites, where goods were produced, stored and traded, and political centres, the seats of authorities whose decisions affected large numbers of people, such as the appointment of Vercingetorix as head of the Gallic revolt in 52 BCE. Caesar named 28 oppida, and he also counted some unfortified settlements, so his usage was not strict.

In archaeology the term now names a category of settlement. Paul Reinecke, Joseph Déchelette and Wolfgang Dehn first used it in that sense for Bibracte, Manching and Závist. Dehn proposed four criteria: a minimum size of 30 hectares, a site usually on a height, a surrounding wall, and a date in the last two centuries BCE. Later definitions have been looser, with a notional minimum of 15 to 25 hectares and some fortified sites as small as 2 hectares, and the term is also used loosely for any fortified prehistoric settlement.

Oppida originated in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, and most were built on fresh sites, usually on high ground that let them dominate trade routes. They were far larger than earlier hill forts, which were mostly a few hectares, and some held up to 10,000 inhabitants. Their ramparts were built on an immense scale. The 7 km murus gallicus at Manching is estimated to have needed some 2,000 people working for 250 days, and the wall at Bibracte may have required the clearing of 40 to 60 hectares of mature oak woodland. Such walls were probably as much for show and for controlling the movement of people and goods as for defence.

Forms varied by region. Central Europe used dry stone Kelheim ramparts, the east used timber-supported walls, Gaul the murus gallicus, and Britain earth dump ramparts. Camulodunon, modern Colchester, tribal capital of the Trinovantes, used two rivers and long earthworks, and Stanwick in England covers 350 hectares. Caesar noted that each Gallic tribe had several oppida of unequal importance, and according to Fichtl, Gaul in the 1st century BCE was divided into about sixty civitates, mostly organised around one or more oppida, some of which were effectively capitals.

Oppida continued in use until the Romans conquered Iron Age Europe. North of the Danube, which stayed unconquered, they were abandoned by the late 1st century CE. In conquered lands the Romans used their infrastructure to administer the empire, and many became full Roman towns, often by moving from the hilltop to the plain.
oracle-bone-script: The inscriptions were made by carving characters into oracle bones, usually the shoulder bones of oxen or the plastrons of turtles. They mainly record the results of official divinations for the Late Shang royal family. In these divinations, which took the form of scapulimancy, the bones were exposed to flames, creating patterns of cracks that were then interpreted. Both the prompt and the interpretation were inscribed on the bone used for the divination. Inscriptions range from 10 to over 100 characters, a few dozen being typical, and their subjects include war, ritual sacrifice and agriculture, as well as births, illnesses and deaths in the royal family. Each of the last nine Shang kings is named in them, beginning with Wu Ding.

The tradition of writing behind the script is generally agreed to be older than the first known examples, since the attested script is already mature. Many characters had been simplified and made linear, and semantic extension and phonetic loaning had clearly been used for some time, perhaps for centuries. Yet no clearly identifiable writing earlier than the 13th century BCE has been found, and the symbols on Neolithic pottery, jade and bone have not been shown to be ancestors of the Anyang script.

The bronze inscriptions, which keep a more pictorial style, are thought to be closer to typical Shang writing on bamboo books than the angular bone forms, which were simplified because the hard surface was difficult to engrave.

Wang Yirong recognised the characters as ancient Chinese writing in 1899. Liu E published the first collection of rubbings in 1903, and Luo Zhenyu identified the names of the Shang kings, which showed the bones to be Shang artefacts. Wang Guowei showed that the Shang kings' commemorative cycle matched the list in Sima Qian's Records of the Historian, and Dong Zuobin established a chronology.

Over 30,000 distinct characters are found on the fragments, which may represent about 4,000 individual characters in their various forms. Scholars believe they can decipher between 1,500 and 2,000 of them. Some characters are attested only here, such as one for spring that has no known modern counterpart. After the Zhou overthrew the Shang, divination with milfoil became more common and far fewer inscriptions date to the Western Zhou, though a cache found in 1977 held thousands of Zhou-era bones, and an ancestral temple for Duke Dan of Zhou, uncovered in 2004, held over 2,000 inscriptions.
oral-kazakhstan: Oral, also known as Uralsk in Russian, lies in north-western Kazakhstan at the confluence of the Ural and Chagan rivers, close to the Russian border. It stands on the western bank of the Ural and is therefore considered geographically part of Europe. It is the capital of West Kazakhstan Region. Oral has been an important trade stop since its founding, and barge traffic has passed up and down the Ural between the Caspian Sea and the Ural Mountains for centuries.

Cossacks founded the city in 1613 and named it Yaitsk, after the Yaik, which was then the name of the Ural river. In 1773 Yemelyan Pugachev led the first Cossack rebellion against the local Russian commander, General Traubenberg, who was murdered together with several other officers. Pugachev captured the city and besieged its fortress from 30 December 1773 to 17 April 1774, until tsarist troops under Mantsurov retook it. As a punishment because the Yaik Cossacks had sided with the insurrection, Catherine II declared on 15 January 1775 that the Yaik would be renamed the Ural River and Yaitsk would be known as Ural'sk.

Alexander Pushkin visited the city in September 1833 with his friend Vladimir Dahl while he was researching his History of Pugachev and his novel The Captain's Daughter. During the Russian Civil War the city was besieged by Cossacks from 1917 to 1922, and Mikhail Frunze, Vasily Chapaev and Georgy Zhukov took part in its defence. It was renamed Oral after Kazakhstan became independent in 1991.

Oral is an agricultural and industrial centre. It is one of the main points where rail traffic from Europe enters Siberia. Its climate is humid continental, with long cold winters and warm, often hot summers.
oral-rehydration-therapy: In 1953 Hemendra Nath Chatterjee reported in The Lancet the treatment of 186 patients with mild cholera using an oral glucose-sodium electrolyte solution of 4 g of sodium chloride, 25 g of glucose and 1000 mL of water, given by mouth and rectally with other drugs, without controls. In the early 1960s Robert K. Crane described the co-transport of sodium and glucose in the intestine, which suggested that absorption might continue during cholera. In 1967 and 1968 Norbert Hirschhorn and Nathaniel F. Pierce showed that people with severe cholera can absorb glucose, salt and water enough to stay hydrated. In 1968 David R. Nalin and Richard A. Cash reported that an oral solution cut the need for intravenous fluid by eighty per cent.

The therapy rests on the fact that water continues to be absorbed from the gut even while fluid is lost through diarrhoea or vomiting. Sodium enters intestinal cells together with glucose, and without glucose intestinal sodium is not absorbed, which is why oral rehydration salts contain both. The recommended formulation includes sodium chloride, sodium citrate, potassium chloride and glucose. In 2003 the World Health Organization and UNICEF recommended lowering the osmolarity of the solution from 311 to 245 mOsm/L, which reduced stool volume in children by about a quarter.

In 1971 fighting in the Bangladesh Liberation War displaced millions and cholera broke out among refugees. When intravenous fluid ran out in the camps, the physician Dilip Mahalanabis, working with the Johns Hopkins International Center for Medical Research and Training in Calcutta, had an oral solution prepared and given by family members. More than 3,000 people received it, and mortality was 3.6% against 30% among those given intravenous fluid. In 1980 the World Health Organization recognised the therapy, and the nonprofit BRAC sent teams from village to village to teach mothers to mix water, sugar and salt at home.
oran: Oran is a coastal city in north-western Algeria, 432 kilometres west-south-west of Algiers. The name Wahran is thought to come from a Berber expression meaning place of lions, and the hypothesis linking it to the Libyco-Berber root for lion is regarded as the most plausible.

Phoenician settlement in the region dates to the Punic period, between the 6th and 1st centuries BCE, and a small Roman settlement, Unica Colonia, existed near the site until the Vandals, the Mauro-Roman kingdom and the Arabs in turn took the region. The present city was founded around the start of the 10th century by Berbers of the Maghrawa confederation. It prospered under the Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min, who built thirty vessels to connect it with Andalusia, and under the Zyyanid dynasty of Tlemcen, which used its port as an outlet to Spain.

Count Pedro Navarro captured the city for Spain on 17 May 1509, on the orders of Cardinal Cisneros. Spanish rule lasted until 1708, when Mustapha Ben Youssef, bey of Mascara and a vassal of the dey of Algiers, took advantage of the War of the Spanish Succession to drive the Spanish out. Spanish forces returned in 1732. On the night after 8 October 1790 an earthquake killed more than 3,000 people in less than seven minutes, and Charles IV, finding the occupation costly and perilous, agreed with the dey of Algiers to leave. The bey Mohammed el Kebir besieged the city, and the Spanish evacuated by February 1792. Oran then became the seat of the beylik, which lasted until the French captured it in 1831.

Under French rule Oran became the second largest Algerian city, and many Europeans settled there, forming a majority of its population by the early 20th century. In July 1940 the British navy shelled French warships in the port, and the Allies took the city in November 1942 in Operation Torch. During the Algerian War of 1954 to 1962 Oran had one of the highest shares of Europeans of any North African city. In July 1962 the Oran massacre killed at least 95 and as many as 365 people, and most Europeans and Algerian Jews left for France.

Oran is the capital of Oran Province and, with a population of 803,329 in 2008, the second city of Algeria after Algiers. Under French rule it was the capital of the Département of Oran. The Pasha Mosque, built in 1796 by the bey with ransom money paid for the release of Spanish prisoners, dates from the time of the beylik.
orange-revolution: The movement is often traced to the kidnapping and murder in 2000 of Georgiy Gongadze, founder of the newspaper Ukrayinska Pravda, and to the Cassette Scandal that followed, which damaged the standing of President Leonid Kuchma. Rumours persisted that Kuchma had ordered the killing. Kuchma, who had served two terms from 1994 and could not run again under the constitution, supported Prime Minister Viktor Yanukovych against Viktor Yushchenko of the Our Ukraine bloc, a former prime minister who had led the government from 1999 to 2001.

The campaign took place in a charged atmosphere. The Yanukovych team and the outgoing administration were accused of using state power to intimidate Yushchenko and his supporters, and in September 2004 Yushchenko suffered dioxin poisoning under circumstances that remained unclear. He survived and returned to campaigning.

Protests began on the eve of the second round of voting, held on 21 November 2004. Exit polls gave Yushchenko a lead of up to 11 percent, while the official count gave Yanukovych the win by 3 percent. Domestic and foreign observers reported many incidents of fraud. Negotiations between Yushchenko and Kuchma broke down on 24 November, and Yanukovych was certified as the winner by the Central Election Commission. Yushchenko urged his supporters in Kyiv to begin mass protests, general strikes and sit-ins.
On 1 December 2004 the Verkhovna Rada passed a vote of no confidence in the Cabinet of Ministers, which Yanukovych refused to recognise. The Supreme Court ordered a new run-off for 26 December.

In the re-run, held under close scrutiny, Yushchenko received 51.99 percent and Yanukovych 44.20 percent. Yanukovych's legal challenges were dismissed, and on 10 January 2005 the Election Commission declared Yushchenko the winner.

Yushchenko took the oath in the Verkhovna Rada on 23 January 2005 and was then inaugurated publicly on Maidan Nezalezhnosti before hundreds of thousands of supporters. As part of the settlement, constitutional changes shifted powers from the presidency to parliament; they took effect in 2006 and were overturned by the Constitutional Court on 1 October 2010. Yanukovych won the presidential election of 2010 after Yushchenko received 5.45 percent.

Analysts have noted the role of the internet and mobile phones in organising the protests, and some suggest it was the first internet-organised mass protest. Opinion about the revolution stayed divided along largely geographical lines, with western and central Ukraine more favourable than the south and east.
orange-river: The Orange rises in the Drakensberg mountains on the border between South Africa and Lesotho, at an altitude of over 3,000 m; in Lesotho its upper course is known as the Senqu. It flows westward through South Africa, passing into the Gariep Dam and later the Vanderkloof Dam, and meets its main tributary, the Vaal River, south-west of Kimberley. It then crosses the arid southern Kalahari and Namaqualand, reaches Namibia at 20°E, forms the border for 550 km and enters the Atlantic between Oranjemund and Alexander Bay.

Its catchment, including the Vaal, covers 973,000 km2, equal to about 77% of the land area of South Africa, although 38% of it lies outside the country. Rainfall is about 2,000 mm a year at the source but under 50 mm at the mouth. In the lower river the Augrabies Falls drop the water 56 m over a course of 18 km.

Some of the earliest precolonial inhabitants called the river ǂNūǃarib, referring to its black colour, or Kai!Arib, "Great River", from which the Afrikaans name Gariep derives. The early Dutch name was a translation, Groote Rivier. Colonel Robert Gordon, commander of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) garrison at Cape Town, named it the Orange River on a trip to the interior in 1779, in honour of William V of Orange. A popular belief that the name describes the colour of the water is incorrect. Its tributary the Vaal takes its name from ǀHaiǃarib, "pale river".

In 1867 the first diamond found in South Africa, the Eureka Diamond, was picked up near Hopetown on the Orange. Two years later a much larger stone, the Star of South Africa, was found in the same area and set off a diamond rush. This was soon eclipsed by the rush to mine kimberlite directly at Kimberley in 1871, although alluvial diamonds continued to be found in the river. Hippopotami, once abundant there, were hunted to extermination in the 19th century.

The river supplies water for irrigation and hydroelectric power. The Orange River Project, built by Hendrik Verwoerd's government during the apartheid era, centres on the Gariep Dam near Colesberg: from there water flows west to the Vanderkloof Dam and south through the Orange-Fish Tunnel to the Eastern Cape. The Vanderkloof power station was the first in South Africa built entirely underground. The Lesotho Highlands Water Project delivers water to the Vaal River system. Its mouth is a Ramsar site, and since the end of apartheid the name Gariep has found greater favour in official South African correspondence, while Orange has greater international recognition.
orange-vaucluse: Orange is a commune in the Vaucluse department of the Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region in south-eastern France, about 21 kilometres north of Avignon. It lies on the departmental border with Gard, which follows the Rhône. The name derives from a Proto-Celtic form meaning in front of the ear and was originally unrelated to the orange fruit, with which it was later conflated during the Middle Ages. The Latin form Arausio is attested in the first century CE.

A Celtic settlement named after a local sacred spring stood on the site. In 105 BCE a major battle was fought there between two Roman armies and the Cimbri and Teutones. Roman Arausio covered about 70 hectares and was the capital of a wide area of northern Provence, with a monumental temple complex and a forum as well as its theatre and arch. It was sacked by the Visigoths in 412, had been a diocese since the end of the third century, and hosted synods in 441 and 529. The Second Council of Orange condemned what later came to be called Semipelagianism.

From the 12th century Orange was a minor principality, a fief of the Holy Roman Empire. When William the Silent, count of Nassau, inherited the title Prince of Orange in 1544, the principality joined the holdings of the House of Orange-Nassau, which drew it into the Protestant side of the Wars of Religion. The forces of Louis XIV captured it repeatedly in the late 17th century, and it was finally ceded to France in 1713 by the Treaty of Utrecht. The title stayed with the Dutch princes.

Orange is known for its Roman architecture. Its theatre is described as the most impressive still existing in Europe, and the Triumphal Arch carries an inscription dedicated to the emperor Tiberius in 27 CE; the arch, theatre and surroundings were listed by UNESCO in 1981. The museum displays the largest Roman cadastral maps ever recovered, etched on marble. The theatre, restored in 1869, hosts the annual Chorégies d'Orange opera festival.
oranjestad-sint-eustatius: Oranjestad, English Orange Town, is the capital and largest town of the island of Sint Eustatius in the Caribbean Netherlands. It is a historic harbour town divided into two main sections. Lower Town is a strip of buildings just above sea level along the waterfront, bordering the island's safest beach, and holds the harbour and numerous colonial-era ruins. Upper Town has a restored historic core and is the island's main commercial and residential centre.

The first colonist arrived on the island between 1625 and 1629. Sint Eustatius produced sugar and cotton, but above all it developed into a centre of the North American slave trade. In 1780 its population was estimated at 20,000 people, including the enslaved. In 1781, during the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War, the island was captured and plundered by George Rodney, and all the archives were destroyed. By 1786 the island was home to 7,600 people, of whom 3,000 were white, 600 coloured and 4,000 enslaved, and by 1829 the population had fallen to 2,273.

The main historical site is Fort Oranje, a well-maintained 17th-century cliff-side fort in the centre of the town, with cannons, intact bastions and a courtyard overlooking the waterfront. Nearby are a museum, the ruins of one of the oldest synagogues in the Western Hemisphere and a Jewish cemetery. Other features include a Dutch Reformed church built in 1755, partly in ruins, and restored 18th-century merchants' houses, the oldest being the Gezaghebber House, the former Lieutenant Governor's residence, on Kerkstraat. Parts of 18th-century buildings on the bay side were swept into the sea and can be seen while snorkeling in Oranje Bay.
orbetello: Orbetello was an Etruscan settlement dating from the 7th century BCE, and the massive polygonal city walls that still exist were built when it was refounded in the 4th century BCE. After the Romans defeated Vulci and confiscated its territory in 280 BCE, the Roman reorganisation of the area centred on the Latin colony of Cosa, founded near present-day Ansedonia in 273 BCE. The Domitii Ahenobarbi had a substantial property at Orbetello, which the emperor Domitian inherited through his wife Domitia Longina, and he built other sumptuous villas nearby for his courtiers.

In the Middle Ages the Aldobrandeschi family held it until the 14th century, when the city of Orvieto acquired it. After several struggles with the Orsini of Pitigliano and with Orvieto, it was captured by the Sienese Republic. When Siena fell and its territory passed to Tuscany, Philip II of Spain retained Orbetello, Talamone, Monte Argentario and the island of Giannutri, under the name of the Reali Stati dei Presidii, until 1713. Many Spanish names remained among the inhabitants. During the Franco-Spanish War the French besieged the town, which led to the inconclusive naval Battle of Orbetello on 14 June; in July a Spanish army forced the French to lift the siege.

The district passed by treaty to the emperor in 1713, to the king of the Two Sicilies in 1736, to the kingdom of Etruria in 1801 and to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany in 1814. It joined the newly unified Kingdom of Italy in 1860. In 1927–33 Italo Balbo's air cruises started from the lagoon.

Orbetello is a town in the province of Grosseto in Tuscany, about 35 kilometres south of Grosseto, on a lagoon that is home to an important nature reserve. Its sights include the ancient city walls and the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta, built over an Etruscan-Roman temple and restructured in 1375 in Tuscan-Gothic style, which holds notable 15th-century frescoes. The Spanish Forte delle Saline stands at Albinia, and the remains of the Roman city of Cosa lie at Ansedonia.
order-of-assassins: Hasan-i Sabbah, born in Qom around 1050, studied with the Fatimids in Cairo. By subterfuge he and his followers captured Alamut Castle in the Alborz mountains of Persia in 1090. He adapted it for defence and for the indoctrination of followers, spread his influence to nearby towns through agents, and spent most of his days at Alamut writing religious works, never leaving it again. Lambsar Castle, taken soon after under Kiya Buzurg Ummid, became the largest Isma'ili fortress. From these a network of strongholds grew across Persia and Syria, including Masyaf, Abu Qubays, al-Qadmus and al-Kahf.

The first agent Hasan sent to Syria, al-Hakim al-Munajjim, set up a cell in Aleppo in the early 12th century. Its first known killing was that of Janah ad-Dawla, emir of Homs, in 1103. Over nearly two hundred years the Assassins killed hundreds of people, including three caliphs, among them the Abbasid caliphs al-Mustarshid in 1135 and ar-Rashid in 1138, as well as Raymond II, Count of Tripoli, in 1152, and Conrad of Montferrat in 1192. Saladin escaped two attempts on his life in 1175 and 1176. Hasan died in 1124 and was succeeded by Kiya Buzurg Ummid. In 1126 the Seljuks under Ahmad Sanjar attacked without decisive result, and in 1127 Assassins killed his vizier, Mu'in ad-Din Kashi.

In the 1130s and 1140s the Syrian Isma'ilis acquired al-Qadmus, al-Kahf, Masyaf and Qala'at al-Khawabi. In 1210 Hassan III became imam and returned to Sunni practice, claiming allegiance to Sunnis, and the Syrian Assassins paid tribute to the Knights Hospitaller. The Mongols began assaulting fortresses in 1253, and in 1256 the last Isma'ili imam surrendered at Maymun-Diz and ordered his people to demolish their castles. Alamut capitulated, Lambsar fell in 1257 and Masyaf in 1267. The Mamluk sultan Baibars annexed the Syrian fortresses between 1270 and 1273.

Contemporary sources call the Assassins batiniyya. The name Assassin is often said to come from the Arabic hashishin, users of hashish, a term first applied to them by rival Mustali Isma'ilis and used abusively. Marco Polo's story that young followers were drugged with hashish and shown a paradise is the best known explanation of their loyalty, though there is little evidence that hashish was used. Assassination was used selectively, in public places, to frighten rivals. The scattered fortresses were called dar al-hijra, a land of refuge, and the strongholds at Masyaf and Ulayqa were later rebuilt, the Isma'ilis remaining there as subjects of the Mamluks.
order-of-santiago: The Order of Santiago is a religious and military order named after the patron saint of Spain, Santiago (Saint James the Greater). Its first aims were to protect pilgrims on the Way of St. James, to defend Christendom and to remove the Muslims from the Iberian Peninsula. Santiago de Compostela was neither its cradle nor its principal seat. Two cities, León and Uclés, contend for the honour of its birth, and the rivalry between two branches of the royal dynasty in 1157 to 1230 obscured its beginnings.

Both Ferdinand II of León and Alfonso VIII of Castile required that the order's seat lie in their own state, and the disputes ended only in 1230 when Ferdinand III united the crowns. Thereafter Uclés was regarded as the headquarters. The order received its first rule in 1171 from Cardinal Jacinto, the later Pope Celestine III, and was recognised by Pope Alexander III's bull of 5 July 1175. Its first grand master, Pedro Fernández de Castro, died in 1184.

Unlike Calatrava and Alcántara, which followed the severe rule of the Benedictines of Cîteaux, Santiago adopted the milder rule of the Canons of St. Augustine, and its character was both hospitaller and military. Married knights were allowed from the beginning, with the king's permission. At its height the order held more possessions than Calatrava and Alcántara together: 83 commanderies and 200 parishes in Spain, with about 400 knights, and lands in Portugal, France, Italy, Hungary and Palestine. The commandery at Abrantes in Portugal, dating from 1172, became a distinct order in 1290.

The knights fought alongside the royal armies, notably in the conquest of the Algarve. A Council of Thirteen elected the grand master and could depose him. In 1499 Ferdinand the Catholic induced the pope to give him the administration of the order, and in 1523 Pope Adrian VI united the office of grand master to the Crown for good. Charles V set up the Council of Orders, which ended the order's autonomy but not its prestige.

Each province was divided into encomiendas, local units under a knight commander, which supported the knights living there and equipped spearmen for the order's army. Revenue came from land, pastures, industries, tolls, taxes and tithes. Entry was easy at first but after the mid-thirteenth century a candidate had to prove noble descent by blood, and many groups were excluded. Women were admitted from the beginning. The order's insignia is a red cross ending in a sword.
order-of-the-golden-fleece: The order was established on 10 January 1430 at Bruges by Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, on the occasion of his wedding to Isabella of Portugal. It marked the wealthy domains united in his person, which ran from Flanders to Switzerland. Membership was limited, at first to 24 knights, raised to 30 in 1433 and 50 in 1516, besides the sovereign. The sovereign undertook to consult the order before going to war, disputes among knights were settled within it, and knights could claim trial by their fellows on charges of rebellion, heresy and treason. Heretics were excluded, so it became an exclusively Catholic honour during the Reformation.

The badge, a sheepskin, hung from a collar of firesteels in the shape of the letter B, for Burgundy, linked by flints. The choice of the Golden Fleece of Colchis as a Christian symbol caused controversy, since Jason's deeds were open to reproach, and the order's chancellor, the bishop of Châlons, identified it instead with the fleece of Gideon.

After Charles the Bold died in 1477 and the House of Burgundy became extinct, the order passed to the Habsburgs. Maximilian of Habsburg, who had married the heiress Mary of Burgundy, was knighted at Bruges on 30 April 1478 and appointed sovereign. He expelled the knights who had been disloyal in the War of the Burgundian Succession. Charles V was made head of the order at the age of nine and identified strongly with it. Sovereignty then passed to the Habsburg kings of Spain until Charles II died childless in 1700.

The War of the Spanish Succession split the order into a Spanish and an Austrian branch, since both the Bourbon Philip V and the Habsburgs claimed it. The old Burgundian territories became the Austrian Netherlands, and the treasure and archive went with them to Vienna.

The Spanish order became a state order of merit, while the Austrian remained a Catholic order of knighthood. In 1812 the Spanish government gave the Fleece to the Duke of Wellington, the first Protestant so honoured, and it has since been given to non-Christians. Napoleon's award of it to himself and his brother Joseph during the French occupation of Spain angered Louis XVIII, who returned his collar, and Ferdinand VII revoked the awards in 1813.

The Austrian branch keeps the treasure, including an oath cross of 1401-02 said to hold a splinter of the True Cross. It holds its day on 30 November, the feast of St Andrew, patron saint of Burgundy.
orderic-vitalis: Orderic was born on 16 February 1075 at Atcham in Shropshire, the eldest son of a French priest, Odelerius of Orléans, who served Roger de Montgomery, Earl of Shrewsbury. His mother was English, though her name is unknown. At five he was sent to an English monk, Siward, who taught at the Abbey of SS Peter and Paul at Shrewsbury. At ten he was given as an oblate to the abbey of Saint-Évroul in Normandy, for which his parents paid thirty marks. He knew no French on arrival and for a long time likened himself to Joseph in a strange land, keeping an English cast of mind.

When he came to profess as a monk, his superiors gave him the name Vitalis, finding his English baptismal name hard to pronounce. In his chronicle he put the old name before the new and added the epithet Angligena, meaning English-born. He became a deacon in 1093 and a priest in 1107, and visited places including Cambrai in 1105 and Cluny in 1132. At Saint-Évroul he rose to master scribe, and according to Charles Rozier he also served as librarian and cantor.

His first literary work was a continuation and revision of William of Jumièges's Gesta Normannorum Ducum. Because he used Norman sources but wrote from an English perspective, his account of the Norman Conquest is balanced and sympathetic to both sides.

His superiors ordered him to write the history of Saint-Évroul, and the Historia Ecclesiastica grew into a general history of his age. Books one and two treat Christianity from the birth of Christ and were added in 1136 to 1141, books three to six, mainly composed in 1123 to 1131, deal with Saint-Évroul and William the Conqueror, and books seven to thirteen take up his own times from about 1082, including the First Crusade. His chief interest was Robert Curthose, William Rufus and Henry I. The narrative breaks off in 1141, and he reports that he was old and infirm.

He wrote about secular matters such as inheritance and the right to rule, called the Norman acquisition of English lands plunder and criticised Bohemond I of Antioch for using the crusade to gain power. Modern historians view him as a reliable source. The work as a whole was not widely read in the Middle Ages, though parts of it circulated.
ordino: Ordino is the most northerly parish of the Principality of Andorra, mostly the valley of the Valira del Nord. It borders France and the parishes of La Massana, Canillo and Encamp, and at 85 square kilometres it is the third largest parish. The town lies on the footslopes of Casamanya, a mountain of 2,740 metres almost in the centre of Andorra. Other settlements include El Serrat, La Cortinada, Llorts and Arcalís.

The name Ordino is pre-Roman in origin. It is first documented in the 9th century, in the deed of consecration of the cathedral of La Seu d'Urgell, as Hordinavi or Sant Cebrià d'Hordinavi. The parish church of Sant Corneli i Sant Cebrià, already mentioned in 839, was mainly built in the 12th and 13th centuries, and the Romanesque church of Sant Martí de la Cortinada has 12th-century murals.

Ordino was the industrial centre of Andorra, known for its 16th-century ironworks, the Farga del Serrat and the Farga de l'Areny. It is also regarded as the cultural centre of the country: here Antoni Fiter i Rossell wrote the Manual Digest (1748), called the Bible of Andorra, which sets out the country's story, government and customs. Manor houses such as Fiter-Riba, Casa Rossell and the house of the Areny-Plandolit family, owners of the Farga de l'Areny, represented Andorran society between the 17th and 19th centuries. They were acquired in 1972 and made a museum.

The parish contains the Sorteny National Park, the largest nature area in Andorra, and belongs to UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves. A local legend tells of a bagpiper of Ordino who, on his way to a festival, was chased up a tree by wolves and drove them off by playing; the instrument, the buner, is a symbol of the parish. The International Narciso Yepes Festival of classical music has been held at the National Auditorium in Ordino every October since 1983.
ordono-ii-of-leon: Ordoño was born around 873, the second son of King Alfonso III of Asturias and his wife Jimena. His father sent him to Zaragoza to be educated at the court of the Banu Qasi, and he later served in the government of Galicia. Before 910 he personally led a military expedition against the Muslims in the south of the Iberian Peninsula that reached Seville and looted the neighbourhood of Regel. In 909 Alfonso's children rebelled against him for reasons unknown, and the following year he was obliged to abdicate and divide his kingdom: León went to the eldest, García, Asturias to Fruela and Galicia to Ordoño. Alfonso died at Zamora on 20 December 910.

García kept distant and combative relations with Ordoño. García died childless at Zamora in 914, and Ordoño inherited León. Contemporaries and later writers describe his reign as an energetic one: he subjected the kingdom of León to his control and made the city of León his royal headquarters, which marked the move from the kingdom of Asturias to that of León.

He expanded the Christian realm on two fronts. In the south-west he sacked Mérida and Évora and forced the Muslim governor to buy his retreat. In the east he allied with Sancho I Garcés of Navarre against the emir of Córdoba, Abd-ar-Rahman III, and the Muslims were routed at San Esteban de Gormaz in 917. Arnedo and Calahorra were taken from the Banu Qasi the next year. In 920 Abd-ar-Rahman recovered Osma and San Esteban and defeated the Christians at Valdejunquera. Ordoño blamed the absence of the leading counts of Castile and had them imprisoned at Tebular. He was married three times and died in June 924, leaving young children. His brother Fruela succeeded him.
ordubad: Ordubad lies at an elevation of 949 metres on the northern bank of the central stretch of the Aras River, enclosed on three sides by mountains of the Zangezur range, with many walnut and mulberry trees. It lies 88 kilometres from the city of Nakhchivan, and Tabriz is 94 kilometres to the north-northwest. The name is of Turko-Persian origin and means army town, from Turkic ordu and Persian bad, which implies a foundation under Mongol or Il-Khanid rule. The geographer Hamdallah Mustawfi mentions it in the mid-14th century as one of the five towns of the tumān of Nakhchivan, with fine gardens, producing good grapes, corn and cotton.

The city may have been established by the 14th century, or earlier. It was an important stop on the Silk Road caravan route to China, Europe and India. A feudal town called Gala was founded in the 15th century on top of Ambras, and as trade grew the city spread to the right bank of the Ordubadchay river, where trade centres were built in the 17th and 18th centuries. Local rebels led by Hadji, called Kasab (the butcher), and Bayandar took the city and a nearby fortress, but dissension among them let a small Safavid battalion defeat and kill them. The vizier Khaten bey Ordubadi then appealed to the Shah to waive the taxes on the local people, which was agreed.

Under the Treaty of Turkmenchay of 1828, after the Russo-Persian War of 1826 to 1828, the town passed from Iranian to Russian rule. A census of 1834 counted 11,341 people, Muslims and Armenians, in Ordubad and its 52 villages. Silk was exported from the middle of the 16th century to Venice, Marseille, Amsterdam and other places in Europe, and in the early 20th century Ordubad silk won 13 gold medals at international exhibitions.

Ordubad is the second largest city of Azerbaijan's Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic and the capital of the district of the same name. It is divided into five districts: Ambaras, Kurdtatal, Mingis, Sarshahar and Uch. Its streets run radially, in a fan shape near the centre, around a prominent medieval market square. The Juma Mosque, begun in the 17th century as the office of Hatambek Ordubadi, vizier of Shah Abbas, is a landmark. Qanats, underground canals called kahriz, supply water to houses and orchards. Ordubad was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List on 24 October 2001.
ore-mountains: The Ore Mountains lie along the Czech–German border and separate the historical regions of Bohemia and Saxony. They run from south-west to north-east for about 150 kilometres and are on average about 40 kilometres wide. The highest peak is Klínovec in the Czech Republic, at 1,244 metres. The range is a fault block tilted so that it presents a steep scarp towards Bohemia and a gentle slope on the German side, and its rivers drain south into the Ohře and north into the Mulde or directly into the Elbe. The climate of the higher parts is harsh, with average annual temperatures of only 3 to 5 degrees, and the upper Ore Mountains were nicknamed Saxon Siberia in the 18th century.

The Czech name, Krušné hory, comes from the old Czech krušec, a piece of ore, and the German Erzgebirge has the same meaning. Petrus Albinus used the name Erzgebirge for the first time in his chronicle of 1589, after the discovery of large ore deposits, and in the early 17th century the name Meissen Mountains was used for a while. Europe's earliest known mining district appears to lie in the Erzgebirge, dated to about 2500 BCE; tin from there was traded north to the Baltic and south to the Mediterranean along the Amber Road, and knowledge of tin mining spread from it to other districts such as Brittany, Devon and Cornwall.

Settlement was slow, especially on the Bohemian side, because of the harsh climate and short growing seasons, but the aristocratic Hrabischitz family supported settlements at the foot of the mountains and along mountain streams. The region saw the earliest stages of the early modern change of mining and metallurgy from a craft to a large-scale industry, a process that preceded and enabled the later Industrial Revolution.

Mining shaped the landscape with its tips, dams, ditches and sinkholes, and cleared much of the original dense forest for timber. In 2019 the region, as the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with 22 mines or mining complexes listed. Its culture was formed by mining: the saying Alles kommt vom Bergwerk her, everything comes from the mine, and the greeting Glück Auf! recall it. The region has its own dialect, Erzgebirgisch, and poets such as Christian Gottlob Wild and Anton Günther. The Fichtelberg Cable Car, opened in 1924, was the first in Germany, and Oberwiesenthal is the chief ski resort.
oregon-city-oregon: Oregon City lies on the Willamette River near the confluence of the Clackamas River with the Willamette, in what is now Clackamas County. The land was originally home to the Clowwewalla, Cashhooks and Molalla peoples. The town is divided into a lower area on a bench beside the river and an upper area on a bluff of Canemah basalt. Indian trails once connected the two levels, stairs were built in the 19th century, and in 1915 the town built the water-powered Oregon City Municipal Elevator, converted to electricity in the 1920s.

Dr John McLoughlin of the Hudson's Bay Company established the settlement to use the power of Willamette Falls to run a lumber mill. In the 1840s and 1850s it was the destination for those who wanted to file land claims after travelling the Oregon Trail, of which it was the last stop.
