It was the capital of the Oregon Territory from its establishment in 1848 until 1851, and it rivalled Portland for early supremacy in the area. During the term of Governor John P. Gaines, and against his wishes, the capital moved to Salem.

The city's newspaper, the Oregon Spectator, founded in 1846, was the first American newspaper published west of the Rocky Mountains. Oregon City College was established in 1849 as a Baptist school but was defunct by the 1870s, and in 1849 the city was also the site of the Beaver Coins Mint, which produced the short-lived independent Oregon Territory currency. The diocese of Oregon City, established in 1846, was raised to metropolitan rank as the first Roman Catholic archdiocese in the western United States, under Archbishop François Norbert Blanchet. Its territory included all of the western United States. The population around Oregon City declined because of the California Gold Rush, and the archdiocese's headquarters moved to Portland in 1926.

Oregon City is the county seat of Clackamas County, near the southern limits of the Portland metropolitan area, and is largely a suburb of Portland. For much of its history its economy was dominated by forestry and its paper mills. The centre of the city retains part of its historic character through preserved buildings, among them the McLoughlin House, and the End of the Oregon Trail Interpretive Center and the Museum of the Oregon Territory record its history. The Willamette Falls Locks, in neighbouring West Linn, were the first multi-lift navigational locks in the United States.
oregon-trail: The Oregon Trail was a large-wheeled wagon route connecting the Missouri River to valleys in Oregon Territory. The eastern part crossed what are now Kansas, Nebraska and Wyoming, and the western half Idaho and Oregon. Fur traders and trappers laid it between about 1811 and 1840, when it could be crossed only on foot or horseback. The Lewis and Clark Expedition of 1804 to 1806 had mapped the first land route across the contiguous United States, but the passes it used were far too difficult for wagons.

By 1836, when the first migrant wagon train was organised at Independence, Missouri, a wagon trail had been cleared to Fort Hall, Idaho. Reports of the Great Plains as the Great American Desert made them seem unfit for settlement, while Oregon appeared fertile and free of the diseases of the Mississippi basin.

In the Great Migration of 1843 an estimated 700 to 1,000 emigrants left for Oregon, initially led by John Gantt. When Hudson's Bay Company agents at Fort Hall urged them to abandon their wagons, Marcus Whitman volunteered to lead the wagons on, and the emigrants cut a road through the Blue Mountains. Nearly all reached the Willamette Valley by early October. From 1847 Mormon pioneers under Brigham Young left the main trail at Fort Bridger for the Salt Lake Valley. The discovery of gold in California in January 1848 drew about two thirds of Oregon's male population south, and the traffic of forty-niners rose sharply.

Disease was the main killer on the trail, and cholera killed up to 3 percent of all travellers in the epidemic years from 1849 to 1855. The number of deaths is not known with precision, partly because graves were disguised.

The trail and its offshoots were used by about 400,000 settlers, farmers, miners, ranchers and business people and their families, with traffic especially thick from 1846 to 1869. Use declined after the Panama Railroad opened in 1855 and then after the first transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869, which made the journey faster, safer and usually cheaper. Some emigrants still used the trail into the 1890s. Interstate 80 and Interstate 84 now follow parts of its course, and wagon ruts and registers where emigrants carved their names are preserved.
orenburg: Orenburg lies on the banks of the Ural River near the boundary of Europe and Asia, about 1,480 kilometres south-east of Moscow, and is the administrative centre of Orenburg Oblast. It was called Chkalov from 1938 to 1957, after the Soviet pilot Valery Chkalov, who had never lived in or visited it. The name Orenburg was proposed by its founder Ivan Kirilov and traditionally means a fortress on the River Or. On 7 June 1734 Empress Anna Ioannovna ordered an edict, A Privilege for Orenburg.

In 1734 the Russian Empire began to build a fortified city on its eastern border, in the Southern Urals. Ivan Kirilov, a cartographer and statistician, began developing a settlement at the confluence of the Or and Ural in 1735. He argued that it was needed to open a transit route to Bukhara, Badakhshan, Balkh and India. His successor Vasily Tatishchev thought the place unsuitable and in 1739 prepared a new town on Krasnaya Gora, downstream. That site proved treeless, rocky and far from the river, and on 19 April 1743 Orenburg was built on the third attempt, at a place chosen by Ivan Neplyuev. It became an outpost on the border with the nomadic Kazakhs and the centre of the Orenburg Cossacks.

Orenburg played a major part in Pugachev's Rebellion of 1773–1774. Yemelyan Pugachev besieged the city from nearby Berda from October 1773 to 26 March 1774, and thousands of inhabitants died. Alexander Pushkin visited in 1833 while researching The History of Pugachev, and met Vladimir Dal. The city was the base for General Perovsky's expeditions against the Khanate of Khiva, and an important centre of trade between Kazakhs and Russians, as well as with Bukhara and Khiva. The Kazakh newspaper Qazaq was published there from 1913 to 1918.

In December 1917 Orenburg hosted the Second All-Kazakh Congress, which proclaimed the Alash Autonomy. Alexander Dutov's forces captured the city on 3 July 1918. In 1920 Orenburg became the first capital of the Kazakh Autonomous Socialist Soviet Republic. The First Congress of Kazakh Scholars met there in June 1924 and decided on a reform of the Kazakh alphabet. In 1925 the Kazakh capital moved to Kyzylorda, and Orenburg has been part of Russia since.
oresund: The Øresund forms the Danish–Swedish border, separating Zealand from Scania. It is 118 kilometres long and between 4 and 28 kilometres wide. Together with the Great Belt, the Little Belt and the Kiel Canal it is one of four waterways linking the Baltic Sea to the Atlantic by way of the Kattegat, Skagerrak and North Sea. The strait is geologically young. It formed 8,500 to 8,000 years ago as rising sea levels let salt water enter the Ancylus Lake, a fresh-water body that had been connected to the sea only through the Great Belt. This marked the beginning of the modern Baltic Sea as a salt-water body.

The name is first attested on a runestone of about 1000 CE, in an Old East Norse form. Its first part is øre, a gravel or sand beach, and its second sund, a strait. The same element appears in Helsingør, Skanör and Dragør. The water is unusual: oceanic salt water lies below a depth of 10 to 15 metres, while the surface, fed from the far less salty Baltic, is much fresher in the south.

Political control of the strait has been an important issue in Danish and Swedish history. Denmark held it with the fortress of Kronborg at Elsinore on the western side and Kärnan at Helsingborg on the eastern side, both where the strait is 4 kilometres wide, until the eastern shore was ceded to Sweden in 1658 under the Treaty of Roskilde.

In 1429 King Eric of Pomerania introduced the Sound Dues, which remained in force until 1857. Tolls on waterways, roads and bridges were an accepted way of taxing and could make up a great part of a state's income. For several centuries the Dues were the most important source of income for the Danish Crown, which made Danish kings relatively independent of the privy council and the aristocracy. To escape the tolls Sweden carried out two great projects: the foundation of Gothenburg in 1621 and the building of the Göta Canal from 1810 to 1832. The Copenhagen Convention of 1857 abolished the Dues and made the Danish straits an international waterway.

The Øresund Bridge, between Copenhagen and Malmö, was inaugurated on 1 July 2000 and connects a bi-national metropolitan area. The ferry route between Helsingør and Helsingborg, at the narrowest point, has long been one of the busiest international ferry routes. The strait's islands include Amager, Saltholm and the artificial Peberholm in Denmark, and Ven in Sweden.
organisation-armee-secrete: The Organisation armée secrète (OAS, Secret Army Organisation) was a far-right dissident French paramilitary organisation of the Algerian War, founded in 1961 by Raoul Salan, Pierre Lagaillarde and Jean-Jacques Susini. It was officially formed in Madrid, in Francoist Spain, in January 1961, in response to the referendum of 8 January 1961 on self-determination for Algeria organised by President Charles de Gaulle. It drew together existing anti-FLN networks that called themselves counter-terrorists, self-defence groups or resistance. Its motto was L'Algérie est française et le restera, meaning Algeria is French and will remain so.

The OAS was anti-communist and authoritarian, like many colonists, yet it also included ex-communists, Algerian Jews and former members of the French Resistance as well as Vichy collaborators. In France it recruited mainly among openly fascist groups. By bombings and assassinations in metropolitan France and Algeria between April 1961 and April 1962 it is estimated to have caused 2,000 deaths. Its first victim was the lawyer Pierre Popie. Roger Gavoury, the head of the police in Algiers, was killed on 31 May 1961. The OAS became notorious for stroungas, attacks using plastic explosives.

After the Évian agreements of 19 March 1962 the OAS tried to prove that the FLN was restarting the war, setting off on average 120 bombs a day in March. On 26 March troops fired on settler demonstrators in Algiers, killing 54 in the gunfight of the Rue d'Isly. Raoul Salan was captured in April 1962, and the OAS began a ceasefire on 17 June. Its attempts on de Gaulle included the ambush of 22 August 1962 at Petit-Clamart, planned by Jean Bastien-Thiry, who was not a member and was executed in March 1963.

By 1963 the main OAS operatives were dead, in exile or in prison, and with the arrest of Gilles Buscia in 1965 the organisation effectively ceased to exist. Jailed members were amnestied under a law of July 1968, and generals still alive in November 1982, among them Salan and Edmond Jouhaud, were reintegrated into the army by another amnesty law.

Many members later took part in anti-communist struggles elsewhere. The chaplain Georges Grasset organised a flight route from Paris through Spain to Argentina. The Charles Martel Group, active in France in the 1970s and 1980s, was formed by OAS veterans. The organisation also left its mark on fiction, notably Frederick Forsyth's novel The Day of the Jackal (1971), in which it hires an assassin to kill de Gaulle.
organisation-of-african-unity: The OAU began with the Sanniquellie Pledge at the First West African Summit Conference, held at Sanniquellie, Liberia, from 15 to 19 July 1959. President Tubman of Liberia hosted President Touré of Guinea and Prime Minister Nkrumah of Ghana, and the three pledged to work for a Community of Independent African States. After independence, two groups disagreed on how unity should be reached. The Casablanca bloc, led by Kwame Nkrumah and founded in 1961, wanted a federation of all African countries. The Monrovian bloc, led by Senghor of Senegal, preferred gradual unity through economic cooperation. The dispute was resolved when Emperor Haile Selassie I invited both groups to Addis Ababa, where the organisation was established on 25 May 1963.

The OAU's primary aims were to coordinate and intensify cooperation among African states for a better life, to defend their sovereignty and territorial integrity, and to eradicate colonialism and white minority rule. A Liberation Committee aided independence movements. The OAU gave weapons, training and bases to groups such as the ANC and PAC against apartheid and ZANU and ZAPU against the government of Rhodesia, closed African harbours and airspace to South Africa, and persuaded the United Nations to expel South Africa from bodies such as the World Health Organization. It also helped to set up the African Development Bank and worked with the UN on refugees.

Morocco left on 12 November 1984, after the admission in 1982 of the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic as the government of Western Sahara. By the time of its dissolution 53 of the 54 African states were members. In September 1999 the OAU issued the Sirte Declaration, calling for a new body, and on 9 July 2002 its chairman, the South African president Thabo Mbeki, formally dissolved it and replaced it with the African Union.

The organisation had no armed force of its own and held to a policy of non-interference in the affairs of member states, so it could do little to stop civil wars in Nigeria and Angola or abuses such as those of Idi Amin's Uganda in the 1970s. Critics called it a talking shop and, because it did little to protect citizens from their own leaders, a Dictators' Club. Divisions between the Cold War camps, led by Nkrumah on the socialist side and Félix Houphouët-Boigny of the Ivory Coast on the capitalist side, made agreement on action rare. Kofi Annan praised it for bringing Africans together, and its members often acted together in the UN to defend African interests, especially against lingering colonialism.
organisation-todt: Fritz Todt, an engineer and senior member of the Nazi Party, was named Inspector General of German Roadways after Adolf Hitler decreed a national network of highways on 27 June 1933. The idea of a high-speed road was not Nazi in origin: a private consortium, the HaFraBa, had planned one between northern Germany and Basel from 1926. By 1938 Todt's office had built more than 3,000 kilometres of the Autobahn, drawing first on the open labour market and from 1935 on conscripts of the Reich Labour Service, under a law requiring six months of state service from men aged 18 to 25. In 1938 Todt created the Organisation Todt proper, a consortium of his administrative offices, private contractors and the Labour Service.

After 1938 the work became almost wholly military. The first major project was the Westwall, or Siegfried Line, opposite the French Maginot Line. Todt became Reich Minister of Armaments and Munitions in 1940, and in 1941 the organisation was charged with the Atlantic Wall along the coasts of France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark and Norway, including the Channel Islands, which Germany occupied from 30 June 1940 to 9 May 1945. Todt died in an aeroplane crash on 8 February 1942, and some have speculated, without proof, that he was killed.

Albert Speer succeeded him and managed the organisation, which was incorporated into his Ministry of Armaments and War Production in 1943. It then built launch platforms in northern France for the V-1 and V-2, air-raid shelters and underground armaments factories. Contractors did the technical work, and from late 1942 most contracts supplied materials and labour from the organisation itself. About 1.4 million labourers served in it from 1942, of whom 1.5 per cent were concentration camp prisoners and most of the rest prisoners of war and forced labourers from occupied countries. Two of its camps on Alderney passed to the SS in March 1943 and became the Alderney concentration camps.

Research has found more than 185,000 deaths of forced labourers on its projects. More than 10,000 forced labourers from eastern Europe and some hundred German political prisoners were worked to death building the Blood Road in Norway, and on the road to Donetsk known as Durchgangsstrasse IV some 20,000 Jews in Poland and 25,000 in Ukraine, with about 50,000 Soviet prisoners of war, were worked to death or shot. At the end of the war its members received a blanket amnesty from the Western Allies, and the organisation itself was found not guilty at Nuremberg. A two-decade process over Durchgangsstrasse IV with 1,500 witnesses ended without a conviction.
organization-of-american-states: The idea of an international union in the Americas was first put forward during the liberation of the continent by José de San Martín and Simón Bolívar. At the 1826 Congress of Panama, Bolívar proposed a league of American republics with a common military, a mutual defence pact and a supranational parliamentary assembly. Representatives of Gran Colombia, Argentina, Peru, Bolivia, the United Provinces of Central America and Mexico attended, but the Treaty of Union, League, and Perpetual Confederation was ratified only by Gran Colombia. The plan foundered amid civil war in Gran Colombia, the disintegration of Central America and the rise of national rather than continental outlooks.

At the fourth International Conference of American States, held at Buenos Aires in 1910, the organisation was renamed the Union of American Republics and its Bureau became the Pan American Union. In the 1930s the conferences turned to questions of peace: members agreed at Montevideo in 1933 not to recognise territorial acquisitions obtained by force, and at Buenos Aires in 1936 to enter arbitration where peace was threatened. The 1936 conference also widened membership from American republics to American states, to accommodate Canada, but United States opposition kept Canada out until it joined in 1990.

Later milestones include the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and the Inter-American Development Bank in 1959, the American Convention on Human Rights in 1969 and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights in 1979. In August 1960 the foreign ministers, meeting in Costa Rica, unanimously condemned the Dominican Republic after finding that the regime of Rafael Trujillo had sponsored an attack on the Venezuelan president Rómulo Betancourt. All members broke off diplomatic relations, and an economic blockade hit the sugar exports on which the Dominican economy rested. In January 1962, at Punta del Este, Cuba was excluded by fourteen votes to one, with six abstentions.

The Organization has a General Secretariat, a Permanent Council, the Inter-American Council for Integral Development and a number of committees. Its supreme body, the General Assembly, meets once a year in a different member state; each state has one vote, and most matters are settled by majority. It has five specialised agencies, among them the Pan American Health Organization. Spanish, Portuguese, French and English are its official languages. It began with 21 members, mostly in Latin America, and grew with the newly independent Caribbean states, from Barbados and Trinidad and Tobago in 1967 to Belize and Guyana in 1991.
orhan: Orhan was born in Söğüt, the son of Osman I and his consort Malhun Hatun. Osman died in 1323 or 1324, and Orhan succeeded him. According to Ottoman tradition he proposed to his brother Alaeddin that they share the emerging beylik, but Alaeddin refused, since their father had designated Orhan sole successor, and accepted only the revenues of a single village near Bursa. Most writers credit Alaeddin with laws on dress and with the creation of a paid standing army, the infantry corps called the Yaya.

Orhan conquered most of north-western Anatolia, much of it Byzantine. At Pelekanon in June 1329 his disciplined troops routed the army of Emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos, who never again fought an Ottoman field battle. Nicaea surrendered in 1331 after a siege of three years, Nicomedia fell in 1337, and Scutari in 1338. In 1345 he took the Turkish principality of Karesi after its ruler's death left two rival sons, which brought his lands to the Dardanelles. He also took Ankara from the Ahis.

In the Byzantine civil war of 1341 to 1347, the regent John VI Kantakouzenos gave his daughter Theodora in marriage to Orhan and used Ottoman warriors, allowing them to loot Thrace. Around 1352 Kantakouzenos granted the use of the fortress of Çimpe, and after an earthquake devastated Gallipoli, Orhan's son Süleyman Pasha occupied the town, giving the Ottomans a foothold in Europe. Orhan is also credited with the formation of the Janissaries, a corps of a thousand boys chosen from conquered Christian families. Ibn Battuta ranked him first among the Turcoman kings in wealth, lands and military forces.

In his last years Orhan left most of the powers of state to his second son Murad and lived in seclusion at Bursa. In 1356 a Genoese captain kidnapped his young son Halil, and John V Palaiologos ransomed him for 100,000 hyperpyra. In 1357 his eldest son and likely heir, Süleyman Pasha, died after a fall from his horse near Bolayır. Orhan died soon after, in March 1362 at Bursa, and was buried in the tomb called Gümüşlü Kumbet, with his wife and children. His son Murad I succeeded him and had Halil executed, and under Orhan the Ottomans had moved from a frontier beylik into Europe.
origen: Almost all information about Origen's life comes from the biography in the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius, written almost fifty years after Origen's death from few reliable sources. Origen was born in 185 or 186 in Alexandria. According to Eusebius his father was Leonides, a respected professor of literature and a devout Christian who later became a martyr. Eusebius also claims that, reading Matthew 19:12 literally, Origen castrated himself or had it done. Origen never mentions this in his surviving writings, and in his Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew he condemns any literal reading of the verse.

In his early twenties Origen turned from work as a grammarian to that of a rhetor-philosopher, giving his post as catechist to his younger colleague Heraclas. Styling himself a Christian philosopher brought him into conflict with Demetrius, the bishop of Alexandria.

Around 231 Demetrius sent Origen on a mission to Athens. He stopped at Caesarea, where Bishop Theoctistus ordained him a priest at his own request, and Demetrius condemned the ordination by a foreign bishop as insubordination. Origen settled at Caesarea and founded the Christian School of Caesarea, teaching logic, cosmology, natural history and theology. Between 238 and 244 he visited Athens, where he completed his Commentary on the Book of Ezekiel.

His friend Ambrose of Alexandria gave him a team of secretaries, and he wrote roughly 2,000 treatises. They include On the First Principles, which laid out the principles of Christian theology systematically, and Contra Celsum, a work of apologetics. His Hexapla set the Hebrew text beside four Greek translations and a Greek transliteration in columns, and he wrote hundreds of sermons on almost the entire Bible, often reading passages allegorically. He defended free will and advocated Christian pacifism, and hoped that all people might eventually be saved, while stressing that this was only speculation.

When Emperor Decius ordered Christians persecuted in 250, Origen did not escape. Eusebius describes tortures under the iron collar and in the dungeon, and the governor of Caesarea ordered that he not be killed until he renounced his faith. He refused. After Decius died fighting the Goths at Abritus in June 251 he was released, but his health was broken and he died a few years later. A later legend places his burial at Tyre, though little value can be attached to it.

His teachings were especially influential in the east, among followers such as Athanasius of Alexandria and the three Cappadocian Fathers. Arguments over their orthodoxy caused the First Origenist Crisis in the late 4th century, in which Epiphanius of Salamis and Jerome attacked him. In 543 Emperor Justinian I condemned him as a heretic, and the Church rejected his teaching on the pre-existence of souls.
orihuela: Orihuela lies at the foot of the Sierra de Orihuela in the province of Alicante in the Valencian Community, Spain, on the river Segura. It is the capital of the Vega Baja del Segura, the floodplain of the river near its mouth. The municipality extends down to the Mediterranean coast west of Torrevieja and includes the coastal tourist development of Dehesa de Campoamor. The Romans settled the city and called it Orcelis and then Aurariola, from the Latin for breeze.

In 576 Orihuela was the capital of the Visigothic province of Aurariola, to which it gave its name. On 5 April 713 the Count Teodomiro proclaimed himself King of Tudmir. The city was attacked by Vikings in the first wave across the Mediterranean, in 858 to 861. In 825 the Kingdom of Tudmir became a dependent kingdom under Umayyad control and its capital moved to Murcia, and in 910 it passed to the Emirate of Cordova. Orihuela later belonged to the principality of Murcia, part of the Kingdom of Denia, which became independent in 1086, and in 1212 the area passed to the Kingdom of Murcia.

In 1304 the city stood on the border between Castile and Aragon, and in 1366 it passed to the Kingdom of Valencia. It was declared a city in 1437. A Jewish community lived there in the Middle Ages until the expulsion of 1492. In 1737 Alicante and other towns became independent from the province of Orihuela. In 1810 Napoleon made Orihuela part of the Department of Segura, with its capital at Murcia, and in 1833 it became part of the province of Alicante. During the Cantonal Rebellion of 1873 it was an independent canton after the Battle of Orihuela.

The medieval centre has five National Monuments, and its layout reflects the city's former rank as a university centre and episcopal see. The cathedral was built between the 14th and 16th centuries, and a mountaintop castle of Arab origin stands in ruins above the town. Among other sights are the baroque church of Santo Domingo and the 15th-century church of Santiago Apóstol. The processions of Holy Week and the parades of Moors and Christians in July are well known. Agriculture rests on lemons, oranges, almonds, olives, palm trees, pomegranates, cotton, hemp and vegetables, and there is a silk, wool and food-preserving industry. The poet and playwright Miguel Hernández, born in 1910, is the best known person from the city.
orinoco: The Orinoco is 2,140 kilometres long. Its drainage basin, sometimes called the Orinoquia, covers about 1,000,000 square kilometres, 65 per cent of it in Venezuela and 35 per cent in Colombia. The river's name derives from the Warao for a place to paddle, from güiri, paddle, and noko, place: a navigable place. The course forms a wide arc around the Guiana Shield, in four stretches: the upper Orinoco of 286 kilometres, the middle Orinoco of 805 kilometres, the lower Orinoco of 959 kilometres and the Delta Amacuro of 200 kilometres. At its mouth the river branches into hundreds of waterways through 41,000 square kilometres of swampy forest.

Its main tributary is the Guaviare. The Caroní, the largest of the Venezuelan tributaries, joins it at Puerto Ordaz. A peculiarity of the system is the Casiquiare canal, which starts as an arm of the Orinoco and reaches the Rio Negro, a tributary of the Amazon, forming a natural canal between the two basins.

Christopher Columbus documented the mouth of the Orinoco on 1 August 1498, during his third voyage. German expeditions under Ambrosius Ehinger and his successors explored the river and its eastern llanos tributaries, the Apure and the Meta, in the 16th century. In 1531 Diego de Ordaz sailed up from the Boca de Navios in the delta to the Meta. In 1595 the Englishman Sir Walter Raleigh, searching for the fabled city of El Dorado, captured Antonio de Berrio for information and then sailed down the river, reaching the savanna country.

From April to May 1800 the Prussian-born Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland explored stretches of the Orinoco with the help of indigenous guides. Humboldt wanted to prove that South America's waterways formed an interconnected system from the Andes to the Amazon, and later published on the river's pink dolphins, flora and fauna. The source, at Cerro Delgado–Chalbaud, 1,047 metres above sea level, was found in 1951 by a French-Venezuelan expedition led by the Venezuelan army officer Frank Risquez Iribarren.

The river and its tributaries are the major transport system for eastern and interior Venezuela and the llanos of Colombia. It is navigable for most of its length, and with dredging ocean ships can reach Ciudad Bolívar, 435 kilometres upstream. A Venezuelan mining inspector found one of the richest iron ore deposits near the delta in 1926, and full-scale mining began after the Second World War. The first bridge across the river, the Angostura Bridge at Ciudad Bolívar, was completed in 1967. The basin has more than 1,000 recorded fish species and is home to the boto, the giant otter and the Orinoco crocodile.
oristano: Oristano lies on the northern part of the Campidano plain, in the central-western part of Sardinia. The Byzantines knew it as Aristiánēs Límnē, "Pond of Oristano", and it was founded close to the ancient Phoenician settlement of Othoca, now Santa Giusta. It was made the capital of the province of Oristano on 16 July 1974.

The town gained importance in 1070, when frequent Saracen attacks led Archbishop Torcotorio to make it the seat of the bishopric, previously in the coastal town of Tharros. It also became the capital of the Judicate of Arborea, a Sardinian kingdom, and fortifications were designed, though building went on until the rise of the judge Mariano II.

In medieval times Oristano contended for power over the whole island and fought the other Sardinian kingdoms. The effort culminated in the attempt to conquer all of Sardinia under Mariano IV (1347–75), his son Hugh III (1376 to 1383) and his daughter Eleanor (1383 to 1404). Arborea was the last Sardinian kingdom to end, in 1420, about ten years after the battle of Sanluri. The Aragonese turned it into a marquisate, and after a revolt by the last marquess, Leonardo Alagon, Catalan troops of the Kingdom of Sardinia conquered it in 1478, after the battle of Macomer.

Afterwards the town shared the island's history, under Aragonese and Spanish rule until 1708, Piedmontese rule from 1720 and then a united Italy. In April 1921 David Cova, Emilio Lussu, Camillo Bellieni and other Sardinian veterans of the First World War founded the Sardinian Action Party there.

Oristano has about thirty thousand inhabitants, and its economy rests mainly on services, agriculture, tourism and small industries. The Tower of St Christophoros, built in 1290 and 19 metres tall, is the most striking remnant of the walls of the Judicate, and St Mary's Cathedral, dating from 1130, was rebuilt under Mariano II after a siege. The town holds Sa Sartiglia, an equestrian tournament on Carnival Sunday and Mardi Gras, in which masked horsemen led by Su Componidori gallop at a star-shaped ring hung across the street; a manuscript dates the first tournament to 1543.
orkhon-inscriptions: The inscriptions stand in the Orkhon Valley, on the western Orkhon River near Ögii Lake, about 80 km north of the Erdene Zuu Monastery and about 40 km northwest of Ordu-Baliq. Two memorial steles honour the brothers Bilge Qaghan (683–734) and Kul Tigin (684–731), a politician and a military commander who were descendants of Ilterish Qaghan. Each stone slab was set on a carved stone turtle inside a walled enclosure, with traces of altars and carved human couples, possibly the honoured man and his wife. Bilge Qaghan's stone shows an ibex, the emblem of Göktürk qaghans, and a twisted dragon.

The texts are bilingual, in Middle Chinese and Old Turkic, and the Old Turkic parts were written by Yollıg Tigin, a son of Bilge Qaghan. They recount the origins of the Turks, a golden age, subjugation by the Tang dynasty and liberation by Ilterish Qaghan. Bilge Qaghan lists campaigns to the Shantung plain in the east, Tokuz-Ersin in the south, Timir-Kapig, the Iron Gate, in the west and the land of the Yer-Bayirku in the north, and says the forest of Mount Ötüken is where the kingdom is held together. He claims to have brought a dying people back to life.

The texts take a mixed view of the Chinese. One passage blames Chinese cunning and intrigue for the fall of the old Turkic realm, saying that nobles' sons became bondsmen and their daughters slaves, and that begs took Chinese names and served the emperor for fifty years. Another says Bilge Qaghan was reconciled with the Chinese and received court painters from the emperor to decorate a separate hall. The closing lines ask who could destroy the Turkic state if the sky above did not collapse.

Nikolai Yadrintsev's expedition found the monuments in 1889, and Vasily Radlov published them. The Danish philologist Vilhelm Thomsen deciphered the script in 1893 and published a French translation in 1899 and a fuller Danish interpretation in 1922. These texts, with the Tonyukuk inscriptions, are the oldest surviving attestation of a Turkic language, and Thomsen's work gave a foundation for reading other Turkic writings. The alphabet is thought to derive from, or be inspired by, a non-cursive form of the Sogdian script.

Both inscriptions belong to the Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Since 2000 more than 70 archaeologists from several countries have studied and excavated the area. The site is fenced, with buildings for research and storage, and a museum has been planned.
orkney: Orkney lies 10 miles (16 km) north of Caithness, separated from the Scottish mainland by the Pentland Firth, a seaway about ten kilometres wide. The archipelago measures 80 kilometres from northeast to southwest and covers 975 square kilometres. Twenty of its islands are inhabited. The largest, the Mainland, has an area of 523 square kilometres and holds three quarters of the population, together with both burghs, Kirkwall and Stromness.

Late Upper Palaeolithic stone tools found on Stronsay and at Brodgar suggest that the islands were inhabited around or before 8000 BCE. Norwegian settlers arrived in large numbers in the late 8th and early 9th centuries. Harald Fairhair is said to have annexed the Northern Isles in 875, though that story from the Orkneyinga Saga is regarded by some scholars as apocryphal; the earldom passed from Rognvald Eysteinsson to his brother Sigurd the Mighty, who conquered Caithness and Sutherland.

In 1468 Christian I, as King of Norway, pledged Orkney and Shetland as security for the dowry of his daughter Margaret, betrothed to James III of Scotland. The money was never paid, and Orkney was absorbed by Scotland in 1472. From then on ordinary people emerge more clearly in the record, and an influx of Scottish entrepreneurs helped create a community of farmers, fishermen and merchants.

In the 20th century Scapa Flow was a Royal Navy base. After the Armistice of 1918 the German High Seas Fleet was brought there, and its sailors scuttled the ships. A month into the Second World War a German U-boat sank the battleship HMS Royal Oak; barriers built afterwards, the Churchill Barriers, were made by Italian prisoners of war, who also built the Italian Chapel.

Orkney is one of the 32 council areas of Scotland, administered from Kirkwall by Orkney Islands Council. Its people are called Orcadians and speak a distinctive dialect of Scots. Agriculture is the main economic sector. The Heart of Neolithic Orkney, which includes Skara Brae and the Ring of Brodgar, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
orlande-de-lassus: Orlande de Lassus is also written Orlando di Lasso or Roland de Lassus, and none of these forms is considered incorrect. Little is known of his early years. At twelve he left the Low Countries with Ferrante Gonzaga and went to Mantua, Sicily and later Milan, where he lived from 1547 to 1549. In the early 1550s he worked in Naples, and in 1553 he became maestro di cappella of the Basilica of Saint John Lateran in Rome, a post he held for only a year. He returned to the Low Countries in 1555 and had his early works published in Antwerp.

In 1556 he joined the court of Albrecht V, Duke of Bavaria, who was trying to create a musical establishment equal to the major Italian courts. Lasso settled in Munich, married Regina Wäckinger in 1558 and had two sons who became composers. Composers such as Andrea Gabrieli came to study with him. In 1570 Emperor Maximilian II conferred nobility on him, and Charles IX of France invited him to visit in 1571 and 1573. He declined offers from other courts, writing in 1580 that he did not want to leave his house, his garden and the other good things in Munich.

His last work was the Lagrime di San Pietro, spiritual madrigals published in 1595. He died in Munich on 14 June 1594, the day his employer decided to dismiss him for economic reasons; he never saw the letter.

Lasso wrote in all the Latin, French, Italian and German vocal genres of his day, including 530 motets, 175 Italian madrigals and villanellas, 150 French chansons and 90 German lieder. No instrumental music by him survives. Almost sixty complete masses are known, most of them parody masses built on secular works. The Prophetiae Sibyllarum, twelve motets in a strongly chromatic style, belongs to the manner called musica reservata, and his 1584 setting of the Penitential Psalms, ordered by Charles IX, is among the best-known psalm collections of the Renaissance. A drinking song of his, Un jour vis un foulon, was used by Shakespeare in Henry IV, Part II.
orleans: Orléans stands about 120 kilometres south-west of Paris, at the northern bend of the Loire, where the river curves west towards the Atlantic. It lies within the stretch of the Loire valley that UNESCO inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2000. Because the city sits at the river's most northerly point, it is the Loire's closest point to Paris. The river was formerly an important route of navigation and trade, and it is at the heart of the city's foundation in the second century BCE as a centre of trade.

Cenabum was a stronghold of the Carnutes, where the Druids held their annual assembly, and Julius Caesar destroyed the city in 52 BCE. In the late 3rd century CE it was renamed civitas Aurelianorum, possibly in honour of a Roman emperor of the Aurelian name, and this evolved into Orléans. In the Merovingian era it was capital of the Kingdom of Orléans after Clovis I divided his kingdom. Under the Capetians it became a county and then a duchy held in appanage by the house of Valois-Orléans, which later reached the throne through Louis XII and then Francis I. In 1108 Louis VI was crowned in its cathedral, one of the few French kings crowned outside Reims.

Few bridges crossed the Loire, and Orléans had one, which helped make it one of the three richest cities of medieval France, with Rouen and Paris. The battle at the châtelet des Tourelles on 8 May 1429 allowed Joan of Arc to enter the city and lift the siege by the Plantagenets. Every first week of May since 1432 the city has held the Johannic Holidays in her honour.

Orléans is the prefecture of the Loiret department, in the region of Centre-Val de Loire, with 116,357 inhabitants in 2023. A university was created there in 1306 by Pope Clement V and re-founded in 1966 as the University of Orléans. A Gallo-Roman wall of the 4th century survives beside the cathedral. The city gave its name to the Île d'Orléans in Quebec and, through the regent, the duke of Orléans, to New Orleans.
orontes-river: The Orontes, in Arabic Nahr al-ʿĀṣī, is the chief river of the northern Levant. It rises in springs near Labweh in Lebanon on the east side of the Beqaa Valley, between Mount Lebanon and the Anti-Lebanon Mountains, and runs north through a gorge. It then passes the Lake of Homs, an artificial lake created by a Roman-era dam, and the cities of Homs and Hama before entering the Ghab Plain, with the ancient city of Apamea on its eastern edge. Beyond Jisr al-Shughur it turns west into the plain of Antioch in Hatay Province, Turkey, passes north of Antakya, the ancient Antioch, and enters the Mediterranean south of Samandağ. The river is not easily navigable, and its valley mattered as a road for north–south traffic.

For the ancient Egyptians the river marked the northern edge of Amurru, the region north of Phoenicia. In the Late Bronze Age its valley held several important kingdoms and city-states, among them Alalakh, Niya and Tunip. The Battle of Kadesh, fought around 1274 BCE between the Egyptian army of Ramesses II and the Hittite army of Muwatalli II, took place on the Orontes, as did the Battle of Qarqar in 853 BCE, when Assyria's king Shalmaneser III met an allied army of twelve kings led by Hadadezer of Damascus.

Alexander the Great acquired the valley after the Battle of Issus in 333 BCE, and after his death it passed to the Seleucid Empire, which founded Seleucia ad Belum, Antigoneia and Antioch on the river. Pompey took it in 64 BCE for the new Roman province of Syria. The emperor Diocletian built the Lake Homs dam in 290 CE. The Rashidun Caliphate won the Battle of the Iron Bridge near Antioch in 637 CE and soon controlled the whole valley, and in the 12th century the river formed the boundary between the Principality of Antioch and that of Aleppo.

The river has gone by several names. The Assyrians called it Arantu in the 9th century BCE and the Egyptians Araunti, and the name became Orontes in Greek. Macedonian settlers at Apamea called it the Axius, from which the Arabic name al-ʿĀṣī derives; the word also means insubordinate in Arabic, and a folk etymology ties it to the river's flow from south to north. The Roman satirist Juvenal, writing in the early 2nd century, used the Orontes as a metonym for eastern influence in Rome, saying that the Syrian Orontes had long flowed into the Tiber.
orosius: Orosius was probably born in Bracara Augusta, now Braga in Portugal, then capital of the Roman province of Gallaecia, though the birthplace is disputed. Other theories name Tarragona, A Coruña or Brittany, and the Irish scholar Donnchadh Ó Corráin argued that he was a Briton taken captive by Irish raiders. Whether he used the name Paulus is also uncertain, since Paulus may have been his Christian name and Orosius his native one. Augustine called him a young priest in 415, which places his birth between 375 and 385. He was probably from a family of good standing, grew up when Priscillianism was debated in Hispania, and left Braga suddenly because of the barbarian invasions.

Orosius came to Augustine of Hippo, probably in 414, and wrote to him about the errors of the Priscillianists and Origenists in his Commonitorium. Augustine sent him to Palestine to consult Jerome and to gather information on Pelagius, who had been living there since the synod of Carthage in 411. At the Synod of Jerusalem in June 415 Orosius reported the decisions of Carthage and read Augustine's writings against Pelagius. The Greeks present, who did not understand Latin, were unmoved by Pelagius's question, Who is Augustine to me? Orosius was later entrusted with the relics of Saint Stephen, found on 26 December 415.

On his return he passed through Hippo and gave Augustine Jerome's letters. The plan for his great work arose in that meeting. He wrote the Seven Books of History against the Pagans, most probably in 416 and 417, to defend Christians against the charge that the sack of Rome in 410 was a punishment for abandoning the old gods.

The Histories begin with the creation and run to Orosius's own time, a universal history that has been called the first Christian universalist history, or the last classical one. Its guiding idea is that the past was always worse than the present because it stood further from the true religion. He stresses the suffering of the defeated and the terrors of war, and he opens with a description of the world, imprecise in places, that later historians such as Lucien Febvre and Fernand Braudel valued. His sources included the Old and New Testaments, Caesar, Livy, Justin, Tacitus, Suetonius, Florus and Jerome's translation of Eusebius's Chronicles.

Nothing certain is known of him after 417. He was on Menorca, using Stephen's relics to try to convert members of the Jewish community. Gennadius of Massilia thought he lived at least until 423, and legends of a monastery near Cabo de Palos are thought improbable.
orthez: Orthez is a commune in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department, in the region of Nouvelle-Aquitaine, in south-western France. It lies 40 kilometres north-west of Pau on the railway to Bayonne and straddles the westward-flowing Gave de Pau, with most of the town proper on the right bank. Its Basque name is Ortheze and its Occitan name Ortès. The town also includes the small village of Sainte-Suzanne, an independent commune until 1973, and has rail connections to Tarbes, Pau, Bordeaux and Bayonne.

Orthez was a capital of Béarn, after Morlaàs and before Pau. At the end of the twelfth century it passed from the viscounts of Dax to the viscounts of Béarn, whose chief residence it became in the thirteenth century. Froissart records the splendour of the court of Orthez under Gaston Phoebus in the latter half of the fourteenth century. Jeanne d'Albret founded a Calvinist university in the town, where Theodore Beza taught for some time.

An envoy sent by Charles IX in 1569 to revive the Catholic faith had to stand a siege in the battle of Orthez, and the town was taken by assault by the Huguenot captain Gabriel, count of Montgomery. In 1684 the intendant Nicholas Foucault, acting for Louis XIV, was more successful, as the inhabitants at least ostensibly renounced Protestantism, which remains a strong tradition in the town. A second battle of Orthez took place on 27 February 1814, during the Napoleonic Wars, when the Duke of Wellington defeated Marshal Soult on the hills north of the town. The physicist Gaston Planté, born in Orthez on 22 April 1834, invented the lead-acid battery in 1859. Orthez was the seat of a subprefecture from 1800 until 1926.

The Gave de Pau is crossed by a fourteenth-century bridge with four arches, topped at its centre by a tower. The Tour Moncade, a pentagonal tower of the thirteenth century, was once the keep of a castle of the viscounts of Béarn and is now a meteorological observatory. A church dating from the twelfth, fourteenth and fifteenth centuries and a seventeenth-century building, the remains of the Calvinist university, also survive.

Early in the twentieth century industries included the weaving of hemp and flax, flour-milling, paper and leather, and the preparation of Bayonne hams. The basketball club Élan Béarnais won the Korać Cup in 1984, and the club moved to Pau in 1991. Natives include Gaston III Febus, Jeanne d'Albret, the poet Francis Jammes and the geographer Onésime Reclus.
os-lusiadas: Os Lusíadas, usually translated The Lusiads, was written by Luís Vaz de Camões, who lived from 1524/5 to 1580, and first published in 1572. It is written in the Homeric fashion and is frequently compared to Virgil's Aeneid. It was composed while Camões was an exile in Macau. The heroes are the Lusiads, the sons of Lusus, that is, the Portuguese. He dedicated it to King Sebastian of Portugal.

The ten cantos are in decasyllabic ottava rima, with the rhyme scheme ABABABCC, and total 1,102 stanzas and 8,816 lines. The narration begins in stanza 19 of Canto I, in medias res, with Vasco da Gama's fleet already past the Cape of Good Hope. The gods watch over the voyage: Venus favours the Portuguese, while Bacchus, associated with the east, resents the encroachment on his territory and is opposed to them.

In Canto III Vasco da Gama tells the king of Melinde the history of Portugal, from Lusus and Viriathus through the first dynasty of kings, with episodes such as the Battle of Ourique and the tragic story of Inês de Castro. Canto IV carries the story through the House of Aviz and the Battle of Aljubarrota to the sailing of the fleet, when an old man on the beach, the Old Man of the Restelo, speaks pessimistically of the venture. In Canto V the giant Adamastor appears to the sailors. The fleet reaches Calicut in Cantos VII and VIII, and in Canto IX the sailors rest on the Isle of Love, prepared by Venus, where sea nymphs meet them.

In Canto X the goddess Thetis, now the lover of Gama, prophesies the future of Portuguese exploration and conquest, including the defence of Cochin and the Battle of Diu, and shows him a vision of how the Ptolemaic universe works. She also tells of the voyage of Magellan. The poem ends with further advice to the young King Sebastian. The arrival in India, the most important part of the poem, was placed at the point that divides the work by the golden section, at the beginning of Canto VII.

The work is widely regarded as the most important work of Portuguese-language literature and as Portugal's national epic, much as the Aeneid was for the Romans and the Iliad and Odyssey for the Greeks.
osaka: Osaka is a designated city in the Kansai region of Honshu. Its west side is open to Osaka Bay, and it is otherwise surrounded by more than ten satellite cities, all in Osaka Prefecture except Amagasaki, in Hyōgo Prefecture, to the northwest. When Osaka was established as a city in 1889 it occupied roughly the area of today's Chuo and Nishi wards, 15.27 square kilometres, which grew by incremental expansions into today's 222.30 square kilometres. The largest was a single expansion of 126.01 square kilometres in 1925.

Central Osaka is roughly divided into the downtown and uptown areas of Kita, meaning north, and Minami, meaning south. Kita holds the Umeda district, a major business and retail hub, and Minami, which is in Chūō Ward, holds the Namba and Shinsaibashi shopping areas and the Dōtonbori canal entertainment area. The business districts between them, known as Semba, house the regional headquarters of many large banks and corporations.

In the Jōmon period, about 7,000 BCE, present-day Osaka was mostly submerged, and the Uemachi Plateau formed a peninsula 12 kilometres long and 2.5 kilometres wide, separating Kawachi Bay from the Seto Inland Sea. It is considered one of the first places where inhabitants of Japan settled, because of its fresh water and vegetation and because it could be defended. The earliest evidence of settlement is the Morinomiya ruins in Chuo-ku, with human skeletons, shell mounds, arrowheads, stone tools, fishing hooks and crockery. Permanent habitation on the plains grew in the Yayoi period (300 BCE to 250 CE) as rice farming became popular.

By the Kofun period (300 to 538) the area had developed into an important regional port, and in the seventh and eighth centuries it served briefly as the imperial capital. It continued to flourish in the Edo period (1603 to 1867) and became known as a centre of Japanese culture. After the Meiji Restoration it expanded greatly and industrialised rapidly, and it was the industrial hub of the Meiji and Taishō eras.

Osaka is the capital and most populous city of Osaka Prefecture, with an estimated 2.8 million people. It is the largest component of the Keihanshin metropolitan area. Panasonic and Sharp are headquartered there, and it is home to the Osaka Exchange. Landmarks include Osaka Castle, Dōtonbori, Tsūtenkaku in Shinsekai, Sumiyoshi Taisha Grand Shrine and Shitennō-ji, one of the oldest Buddhist temples in Japan.

The name Ōsaka means large hill or large slope. The oldest written evidence for it dates to 1496, and it is unclear when it gained prominence over Naniwa. The kanji 阪 became the official form in 1868 after the Meiji Restoration, replacing 坂, which was disliked because it can be read as samurai rebellion.
osaka-castle: The inner keep of Osaka Castle stands on a plot of roughly one square kilometre in Chūō-ku, Osaka, on two raised platforms of landfill held by sheer walls of cut rock, each overlooking a moat. The keep is five storeys tall outside and eight inside, set on a high stone foundation. An inner moat, wet to the north-east and dry to the south-west, and an outer moat of four water-filled sections surround it. The grounds cover about 61,000 square metres and contain thirteen structures that the Japanese government has designated important cultural assets, among them the Ote-mon and Sakura-mon gates, several turrets and the Kinmeisui Well.

Toyotomi Hideyoshi began construction in 1583 on the site of the Ishiyama Hongan-ji, a temple of the Ikkō-ikki. The plan was modelled on Azuchi Castle, the headquarters of Oda Nobunaga, which Hideyoshi wanted to match and surpass: a five-storey tower with three more storeys underground and gold leaf on the sides to impress visitors. The inner donjon was complete in 1585 and the whole castle in 1597. Hideyoshi died the next year and the castle passed to his son, Toyotomi Hideyori.

In the winter of 1614 Tokugawa Ieyasu besieged the Toyotomi forces. Though outnumbered about two to one, they held off an army of 200,000 and protected the outer walls, but Ieyasu had the outer moat filled in. When Hideyori began to restore it in summer 1615, Ieyasu's armies returned and routed the defenders on 4 June. Hideyori and his mother Yodo-dono killed themselves, the buildings burned, and the Toyotomi line ended.

The shogunate then took direct control of Osaka in 1619 and rebuilt the castle. The granite walls raised in the 1620s still stand, laid without mortar, and many stones carry the crests of the clans that supplied them. A new keep, begun in 1628, was built in a different part of the main bailey, over the buried base of the Toyotomi tower.

Lightning ignited the gunpowder store in 1660, and in 1665 it burned the keep down. In 1868 the castle surrendered to anti-bakufu imperial loyalists, and many buildings burned in the conflicts around the Meiji Restoration. Under the new government the site became the Osaka Army Arsenal.

A ferroconcrete keep was built in 1931. In the Second World War the arsenal employed 60,000 workers, and on 14 August 1945 American bombing destroyed 90 per cent of it and killed 382 people. A restoration approved in 1995 and finished in 1997 made the keep a concrete reproduction of the original tower, with a museum inside. The castle is open to the public and is crowded during the cherry blossom season.
osama-bin-laden: Osama bin Laden was born into the wealthy bin Laden family of Saudi Arabia. His exact date of birth is unknown: Saudi men of his generation often did not know theirs, and in a 1991 interview he gave the month of Rajab in the Islamic year 1377, which could be 1957 or 1958. Researchers generally agree that he was born in Riyadh. He was raised a Sunni Muslim in the Athari school of theology.

In 1979 the Soviet Union occupied Afghanistan, and bin Laden left college to go to Pakistan with Abdullah Yusuf Azzam to help the Afghan mujahideen. He likely did so with the support of the Saudi government. In 1984 he co-founded Maktab al-Khidamat to recruit foreigners to the resistance, and in 1988 he founded al-Qaeda.

After the Soviet withdrawal he returned to Saudi Arabia, where many praised him as a hero of jihad. During the Gulf War he offered the royal family a mujahideen force, but they accepted 500,000 U.S. troops, and he was expelled in 1991. He went to Afghanistan and then to Sudan. In 1993 al-Qaeda bombed the World Trade Center complex in New York City. Expelled from Sudan, he returned to Afghanistan in 1996, and al-Qaeda allied with the Taliban. In 1996 and 1998 he issued fatwas declaring war on the United States, and in 1998 al-Qaeda bombed U.S. embassies in East Africa.

The attacks of 11 September 2001, planned mainly by bin Laden and Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, were carried out by nineteen al-Qaeda members who hijacked four passenger planes. They struck the World Trade Center towers and the Pentagon, and one plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. The attacks directly killed 2,977 victims. Bin Laden did not unambiguously take responsibility until a video of 2004.

After the United States invaded Afghanistan and deposed the Taliban, bin Laden relocated to Pakistan, and in 2005 he moved into a compound he had built at Abbottabad. U.S. intelligence found it in 2010, and on 2 May 2011 he was killed inside it in a raid by U.S. Navy SEALs, code-named Operation Neptune Spear. Ayman al-Zawahiri succeeded him as emir of al-Qaeda. Polls show that Muslims at large have a negative view of bin Laden, while many Islamists consider him heroic. Elsewhere he is overwhelmingly seen as a symbol of terrorism and mass murder.
oscan-language: Oscan is an extinct Indo-European language of southern Italy, in the Osco-Umbrian or Sabellic branch of the Italic languages, and so a close relative of Umbrian and South Picene. It was spoken by a number of tribes, including the Samnites, the Lucani, the Aurunci and the Sidicini. Several poorly attested varieties of the eastern central Italian highlands, among them Hernican, Marrucinian and Paelignian, are conventionally grouped with it.

Oscan speakers lived in close contact with the people of Latium, and the language had much in common with Latin as well as striking differences. Oscan has p where Latin has qu, as in pis and quis, and b where Latin has v. Where Latin used volo for willing, Oscan used words from a root meaning to desire, as in herest. It is considered the most conservative of the known Italic languages.

Oscan is known from inscriptions as far back as the 5th century BCE, about 800 texts in all. The most important are the Tabula Bantina, the Oscan Tablet and the Cippus Abellanus. The Cippus Abellanus records an agreement between Abella and Nola about building near a temple of Hercules and a shared road. The Tabula Bantina sets out rules for assemblies and for magistrates' trials, with fines for those who break them. Coins inscribed in Oscan at Teanum Apulum in Apulia date from before 300 BCE.

It was written first in an Oscan alphabet derived from the Etruscan, which the Osci probably adopted in the 7th century BCE, though a recognisably Oscan form is attested only from the 5th. Later texts were written in a South Oscan script based on Greek and in the Latin alphabet. In the 3rd century BCE two new signs, Í and Ú, were added to the inventory. Oscan nouns had seven cases and verbs were inflected for tense, voice, mood, person and number.

In the coastal zones of southern Italy Oscan is thought to have lived beside Greek for three centuries, from 400 to 100 BCE, in what has been called an unusual case of stable bilingualism. Over the Roman period both languages were gradually effaced. Oscan declined after the Social War, but graffiti show it remained in colloquial use. Oscan graffiti on Pompeian walls rebuilt after the earthquake of 62 CE must have been written between 62 and 79 CE. Other scholars argue that this is weak evidence for Oscan as an official language, since public inscriptions in Oscan disappeared after Roman colonisation. Latin may have held political, religious and administrative importance while Oscan was regarded as a low language.
oscar-carmona: António Óscar de Fragoso Carmona was born to Maria Inês Côrte-Real de Melo Fragoso and Alvaro Rosario Teixeira Carmona, a Portuguese naval officer from Felgueiras who was part of the Portuguese military attaché's staff in Brazil. A republican and a Freemason, he quickly adhered to the proclamation of the Portuguese First Republic on 5 October 1910, but was never a sympathiser of democratic government and later said he first voted in the 1933 constitutional referendum. He wrote a book of rules for the Cavalry School in 1913 and married Maria do Carmo Ferreira da Silva in January 1914. In 1923 he briefly served as minister of war. Unlike the popular marshal Gomes da Costa, he had not seen action in World War I.

Carmona was very active in the coup d'état of 28 May 1926 that overthrew the First Republic. José Mendes Cabeçadas, the first council president, was succeeded in June by Gomes da Costa. Carmona, foreign minister from 3 June to 6 July, led the most conservative and authoritarian wing of the military regime, which saw the more moderate Gomes da Costa as a liability. On 9 July he led a countercoup with General João José Sinel de Cordes, named himself both president and prime minister and immediately assumed dictatorial powers. He was formally elected in 1928 as the only candidate.

In 1928 Carmona appointed António de Oliveira Salazar minister of finance and in 1932 prime minister, largely turning control of the government over to him. A new constitution in 1933 established the Estado Novo and on paper codified Carmona's powers, but in practice Salazar held the real power and Carmona was little more than a figurehead. He was re-elected without opposition in 1935 and 1942. After World War II the opposition was allowed to contest elections, but Carmona refused to delay them. After rumours that he supported the failed military uprising of 1947, he accepted the title of marshal. In 1949 his opponent General José Norton de Matos withdrew on 12 February after severe persecution.

Carmona died in 1951, after 24 years as president, and was buried in the Church of Santa Engrácia, the National Pantheon in Lisbon. The town of Uíge in Angola was called Carmona after him until 1975, and he appeared on the Angolan escudo banknote issue of 1972.
oscar-romero: Óscar Arnulfo Romero y Galdámez was born on 15 August 1917 in Ciudad Barrios, San Miguel, El Salvador. He attended the local school, which offered only three grades, and was then tutored privately. His father trained him in carpentry, but Romero raised the idea of studying for the priesthood and entered the minor seminary in San Miguel at the age of thirteen. He completed his studies at the Gregorian University in Rome, took a Licentiate in Theology in 1941 and was ordained in Rome on 4 April 1942.

In 1943 his bishop summoned him home. On the way he and a friend, Father Valladares, were detained by the Cuban police, probably because they had come from Fascist Italy, and spent months in internment camps before release from a hospital.

Romero was appointed auxiliary bishop of San Salvador on 25 April 1970 and Bishop of Santiago de María, a poor rural region, on 15 October 1974. On 3 February 1977 he became Archbishop of San Salvador. The government welcomed the appointment, while many priests were disappointed, especially those who supported liberation theology and feared that his conservative reputation would hurt its commitment to the poor. After the murder of his friend and fellow priest Rutilio Grande, Romero became an outspoken critic of the military government.

He broadcast his weekly sermons on the church's radio station YSAX, listing disappearances, tortures and murders each Sunday. By listener surveys 73 per cent of the rural population and 47 per cent of the urban listened regularly. His diocesan weekly Orientación carried lists of cases of torture and repression. His relationship with liberation theology was debated: his biographer Jesús Delgado holds that he supported the Catholic vision of it rather than a materialist one.

On 23 March 1980 Romero called on Salvadoran soldiers, as Christians, to stop carrying out the government's repression. The next evening he was shot while celebrating Mass at the chapel of the Hospital de la Divina Providencia. His funeral on 30 March was attended by more than 250,000 mourners. No one has been convicted of the killing, but the United Nations Truth Commission for El Salvador concluded that Major Roberto D'Aubuisson, a death squad leader, had ordered it.

In 2010 the United Nations General Assembly proclaimed 24 March the International Day for the Right to the Truth Concerning Gross Human Rights Violations and for the Dignity of Victims, in recognition of his role. Pope Francis declared him a martyr on 3 February 2015, beatified him on 23 May 2015 and canonised him on 14 October 2018. A statue of him stands above the Great West Door of Westminster Abbey, among ten twentieth-century martyrs.
osh: Osh lies in the Fergana Valley in the south of Kyrgyzstan and is often called the capital of the south. It has been the administrative centre of Osh Region since 1939. UNESCO estimates it to be more than 3,000 years old. The name is said to derive from the river Vakhsh, personified there as a water goddess who was worshipped, together with sacred fire, in a Zoroastrian shrine in the Eagle Cave on the mountain Sulaiman-Too. The Oxus, the ancient name of the Amu Darya, is cognate with the same river name. The city covers 182.5 square kilometres and is administered apart from any region.

Osh is among the oldest settlements of Central Asia. It was known as early as the 8th century as a centre of silk production along the Silk Road, which crossed the Alay Mountains to reach Kashgar. Its bazaar on the Ak-Buura River stood on the same spot for some 2,000 years. Some researchers think Sulaiman-Too is the Stone Tower that Claudius Ptolemy mentions in his Geography, which marked the midpoint of the ancient Silk Road. Babur, the founder of the Mughal Empire, was born at nearby Andijan, and he built a porticoed pavilion on the mountain's spur, according to his own account.

Russia occupied and annexed the city in 1876 as it overcame the Central Asian khanates in the Great Game with Britain, a conquest completed by the mid-1880s under General von Kaufman and General Mikhail Skobelev. In the 1960s Osh and other southern towns of the Kyrgyz SSR began to industrialise. The population had long included many ethnic Uzbeks, and as Kyrgyz were encouraged to move from the countryside into industrial and public jobs, social tension between the two groups rose.

In 1990, shortly before the end of Soviet power in Central Asia, Osh and its surroundings saw bloody clashes between Kyrgyz and Uzbeks over land. There were about 1,200 casualties, including over 300 dead. In 2010 violence between Kyrgyz and Uzbeks broke out again, in the context of the political upheaval that year.

Osh is the second-largest city of Kyrgyzstan after Bishkek. Sulayman Mountain, the only World Heritage Site in Kyrgyzstan, holds a museum complex carved into the rock. The 16th-century Rabat Abdul Khan Mosque stands in the city. Osh State University is one of the largest in the country, and the city's industrial base was established in the Soviet period.
osijek: Osijek stands on the southern bank of the Drava, 25 kilometres upstream from its confluence with the Danube, at an elevation of 94 metres, and 16 kilometres west of the Croatian border with Serbia. Its name comes from its location on elevated ground, which gave protection from floods in the surrounding swamps, and derives from the Croatian word oseka, meaning ebb tide. It is known as Eszék in Hungarian, Esseg in German and Ösek in Turkish.

Human habitation dates to the Neolithic. The first known inhabitants were the Illyrian Andizetes, and in the second half of the 4th century BCE the Celtic Scordisci captured the settlement. After the Roman conquest of Pannonia, Mursa was garrisoned by the Seventh Legion, which built a castrum and a bridge across the Drava; Hadrian is thought to have founded it anew and raised it to a colony in 133 CE. Several decisive battles were fought near it, and Slavic tribes repopulated the region in the 6th and 7th centuries. The name Osijek is first recorded in 1196. From 1353 to 1472 the town was a possession of the Kórógyi family.

An Ottoman army sacked and nearly destroyed the town on 8 August 1526, just before the Battle of Mohács, and a permanent garrison was established in 1529. In 1566 the Ottoman ruler Suleiman commissioned an eight-kilometre wooden pontoon bridge, regarded in its time as one of the wonders of the world. Osijek became a significant commercial centre for East-West trade. Habsburg forces captured it on 29 September 1687, ending over 150 years of Ottoman rule.

Between 1712 and 1715 the Austrians built the fortress of Tvrđa, designed by Maximilian Gosseau de Henef, with five bastions. The Upper Town was founded in 1692 and the Lower Town in 1698, and in 1786 the three districts were united in one city. German immigrants settled there, giving rise to a local dialect, Essekerisch. Osijek became a Free Royal City in 1809 and was then the largest city in Croatia. The Museum of Slavonia was founded in 1877. After the Second World War the German-speaking population was expelled, and the University of Osijek was established in 1975.

Osijek is the largest city and the economic and cultural hub of Slavonia, the seat of Osijek-Baranja County and the fourth-largest city in Croatia, with 96,313 inhabitants at the 2021 census. During the Croatian War of Independence it was heavily shelled, from August 1991 to June 1992 alone about 800 people were killed, and the Co-cathedral of St. Peter and St. Paul was badly damaged. The Baroque citadel of Tvrđa, the Neo-Gothic co-cathedral, whose tower rises to 90 metres, and a tram network running since 1884 are among its landmarks.
osiris: The first evidence of the worship of Osiris dates from the middle of the Fifth Dynasty, in the 25th century BCE, though he was probably worshipped much earlier: his epithet Khenti-Amentiu, Foremost of the Westerners, goes back at least to the First Dynasty and was used as a royal title. By the end of the Fifth Dynasty the offering formula in tombs, which had begun in the Fourth Dynasty as an offering the king gives and Anubis, read an offering the king gives and Osiris. As his cult spread, kings, once held to ascend to the sun god Ra after death, were associated with Osiris instead, expecting to rise as he did and inherit eternal life.

Osiris is shown as a king with a pharaoh's beard, wrapped as a mummy from the chest down, wearing the atef crown and holding a crook and a flail. He was the brother and husband of Isis. In Plutarch's version his brother Set, with 72 accomplices, tricked him into a box that was sealed and thrown into the Nile; Isis found it in a tree trunk in a palace at Byblos. In one version she revived him briefly by a spell so that she could conceive Horus.

Because he died and rose again, Osiris became linked with the annual flooding and retreat of the Nile and with the growth and death of crops. At his festival worshippers made Osiris Beds, frames in his shape filled with soil and sown with seed, whose sprouting stood for his rising from the dead. One was found in the tomb of Tutankhamun.

The Ikhernofret Stela, set up at Abydos under Senwosret III, about 1875 BCE, records the public rites of Osiris, which lasted five days and included a procession in which his body was carried to his tomb, a mock battle with his enemies, a night vigil and his rebirth at dawn. After death a person faced a tribunal of forty-two divine judges and was welcomed into the kingdom of Osiris if they had lived by the precepts of Maat.

The early Ptolemaic kings promoted a new god, Serapis, who combined traits of Osiris with those of Greek gods and became the patron deity of Alexandria. The cult of Isis and Osiris continued at Philae until at least the 450s CE, and Philae was the last major ancient Egyptian temple to be closed.
oskar-kokoschka: Oskar Kokoschka was born on 1 March 1886 in Pöchlarn, the second child of the goldsmith Gustav Josef Kokoschka and Maria Romana Kokoschka. His father's unstable finances meant constant moves to smaller flats, and Kokoschka drew close to his mother. At a Realschule he excelled only in art, and a teacher who admired his drawings suggested a career in the fine arts. Against his father's will he entered the Kunstgewerbeschule in Vienna, a progressive school dominated by teachers of the Vienna Secession, on a scholarship. He studied there from 1904 to 1909 and was influenced by Carl Otto Czeschka.

In 1908 he showed the lithograph book Die träumenden Knaben and a tapestry at the first Vienna Kunstschau. Their sexualised fantasies provoked a backlash from conservative officials, and he was expelled from the Kunstgewerbeschule. The architect Adolf Loos befriended him and introduced him to the Viennese avant-garde, whose members he painted in portraits between 1909 and 1914. Loos often ordered these and bought them if the sitter did not, which left Kokoschka free. The portraits use harsh colour, scratched lines and visible brushwork, and give prominence to hands. In 1910 he moved to Berlin, where Herwarth Walden employed him as an illustrator for the magazine Der Sturm and Paul Cassirer took him up.

His affair with Alma Mahler, begun in 1912, ended two years later, and The Bride of the Wind of 1913 expresses it. He volunteered as a cavalryman in the First World War and was seriously wounded in 1915. He taught in Vienna from 1911 to 1913 and at the Dresden Kunstakademie from 1919 to 1923. The Nazis deemed him degenerate, and he left Austria for Prague in 1934, took Czechoslovak citizenship in 1935 and fled to the United Kingdom in 1938. There he painted political allegories, among them The Crab and The Red Egg, which refers to the Munich Agreement of 1938.

In 1912 he delivered the essay On the Nature of Visions, which set out a relation between inner vision and optical sight; art historians take it, with Kandinsky's ideas on spirituality in art, as a basis for Viennese Expressionism. His short play Murderer, the Hope of Women (1909) is often called the first Expressionist drama, and Paul Hindemith set it as an opera. His autobiography, A Sea Ringed with Visions, appeared in 1962. In teaching he drew on the educator Jan Amos Comenius and held that pupils reason best through the five senses.

He became a British subject in 1947, settled at Villeneuve in Switzerland in 1953 and regained Austrian citizenship only in 1978. The Tate Gallery held a retrospective in 1962, and he won the Erasmus Prize in 1960. He died at Montreux on 22 February 1980, aged 93.
oslo: Oslo occupies an arc of land at the northernmost end of the Oslofjord. The fjord, which the Nesodden peninsula nearly bisects opposite the city, lies to the south; in every other direction the city is surrounded by green hills and mountains. Within its limits are 40 islands, the largest being Malmøya, and 343 lakes, of which Maridalsvannet is the largest and a main source of drinking water.

In the Viking Age the area lay in Viken, the northernmost province of Denmark, and control over it shifted between Danish and Norwegian kings until Denmark gave up its claim in 1241. According to the Norse sagas Oslo was founded around 1049 by Harald Hardrada, but archaeologists have found Christian burials from before the year 1000, evidence of an earlier urban settlement, and the city marked its millennium in 2000. It became a bishopric in 1070. Under Olaf III (1067–1093) it was a cultural centre for Eastern Norway, and Hallvard Vebjørnsson, its patron saint, is shown on the city's seal.

Hovedøya Abbey was built in 1174, and churches and abbeys came to own large tracts of land. At the end of the 12th century Hanseatic League traders from Rostock moved in and gained major influence. Oslo became a capital under Haakon V around 1300, but personal unions with Denmark from 1397 to 1523 and from 1536 to 1814 reduced its standing.

A fire destroyed the city in 1624, during the reign of Christian IV, and a new city was built closer to Akershus Fortress and named Christiania in his honour. The old site east of the Aker river remained as a suburb called Oslo. Christiania was the capital of Norway during the union with Sweden from 1814 to 1905; government usage spelled the name Kristiania from 1877, and the municipality adopted that spelling in 1897. In 1925 the name Oslo was given to the whole city, and the old suburb became Gamlebyen. In 1948 Oslo merged with the much larger municipality of Aker, creating the present city.

Oslo is the capital of Norway and the seat of its government and parliament, the Storting. It is both a municipality and a county, with 724,290 inhabitants in the municipality on 1 January 2025 and roughly 1.5 million in the wider urban region. Frogner Park holds the sculptures of Gustav Vigeland, and the Bygdøy peninsula is the site of the Fram Museum, the Viking Ship Museum and the Kon-Tiki Museum.
oslo-accords: The Oslo Accords build on the Camp David Accords of 1978, whose framework envisioned autonomy only for the local Palestinian inhabitants of the West Bank and Gaza. Israel then regarded the Palestine Liberation Organization as a terrorist organisation and refused to talk with it, preferring to negotiate with Egypt, Jordan and elected representatives of the inhabitants.

That changed with secret talks in Oslo, Norway. Israeli negotiators including Yossi Beilin, Yair Hirschfeld, Ron Pundak, Uri Savir and the lawyer Joel Singer dealt with the PLO's Ahmed Qurei, under the leadership of Yasser Arafat. The Norwegian facilitators Terje Rød-Larsen and Mona Juul worked with Foreign Minister Johan Jørgen Holst and Deputy Foreign Minister Jan Egeland. In Letters of Mutual Recognition dated 9 September 1993 the PLO recognised the State of Israel, and Israel recognised the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people, no more and no less.

The Oslo I Accord, the Declaration of Principles on Interim Self-Government Arrangements, was signed in Washington in 1993. It set a five-year transitional period, beginning with withdrawal from the Gaza Strip and the Jericho area, with talks on a permanent settlement based on United Nations Security Council Resolutions 242 and 338 to begin by the third year. The agreements did not define the nature of Palestinian self-government or the borders of the territory it would govern.

The Palestinian Authority was established by the Gaza–Jericho Agreement of 1994, and Israel withdrew that year from Jericho and most of the Gaza Strip. The Oslo II Accord, the Interim Agreement, was signed at Taba, Egypt, in 1995. In January 1997 Israel withdrew from 80 per cent of Hebron under the Hebron Protocol, and the Wye River Memorandum of October 1998 promised further redeployments, of which only the first stage was carried out.

Less than six months after the Declaration, an Israeli extremist killed 29 Palestinians in the Cave of the Patriarchs massacre, and Hamas answered with its first lethal suicide bombing. Opposition to the accords came from many Palestinians, among them Edward Said, who called them a Palestinian Versailles, and from far-right Israelis: Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated in 1995 by a right-wing Israeli extremist for signing them.

The interim period ended on 4 May 1999 without a comprehensive agreement. The core issues, Israeli settlements, Jerusalem, security, borders and the Palestinian right of return, had been deferred. The Oslo process came to an end after the failure of the Camp David Summit in 2000 and the outbreak of the Second Intifada. Many scholars have judged the accords harshly, pointing to an asymmetrical balance of power and the continuing Israeli control of Palestinian lives.
oslofjord: The Oslofjord begins at the small village of Bonn in Frogn Municipality, runs north to Oslo, and then curves east and south until it becomes part of the Skagerrak strait at an imaginary line between the Torbjørnskjær and Færder lighthouses. The Skagerrak connects the North Sea and the Kattegat, which leads to the Baltic Sea. In the geological sense it is not a fjord, but in Norwegian the word covers many kinds of waterway, inlets of this sort among them. The inner and outer fjord are separated by the Drøbak Sound, 17 km long and 1 km wide. The innermost part is Bunnefjorden, and the islands there include Hovedøya, known for monastery ruins, and Gressholmen, known for its rabbits.
