The oldest settlements around the fjord date from the Stone Age and the Bronze Age. Three of the best preserved Viking ships, among them the Gokstad ship, were unearthed on its eastern and western shores. In historical times the bay was known as Viken, the bay, which is the name of the present region. Its Old Norse name was Fold, which gave rise to the counties of Vestfold and Østfold and the district of Follo. From 1624 until 1925 it was called Christianiafjorden, or Kristianiafjorden, after the capital, whose name was Christiania; the Ch became K in 1877.

The fjord was the scene of a key event in the German invasion of Norway in April 1940, the Battle of Drøbak Sound. The invasion plan envisaged landing 1,000 troops by ship at Oslo. Colonel Eriksen, commander of the Oscarsborg fortress near Drøbak, which was mainly maintained for historical purposes, sank the German heavy cruiser Blücher in the narrows. This delayed the rest of the invading force long enough for the royal family, government, parliament and national treasury to leave Oslo, so that Norway never surrendered to the Germans. During the war the Germans had installations at several points on the coast, including one on Hovedøya that held 1,100 soldiers.

About 1.96 million people live around the fjord including Oslo, most of them on the mainland, although it also holds hundreds of populated islands. The painter Edvard Munch had a cottage and studio in Åsgårdstrand on its shore, and the fjord appears in several of his paintings, including The Scream and Girls on the Pier.
osman-i: Very little is certain about Osman. No written source survives from his reign, and the Ottomans did not record his life until the fifteenth century, more than a hundred years after his death. One historian has called the period of his life a black hole. The oldest accounts include the Destan-ı Tevarih-i Al-i Osman of Ahmedî, the Behcetü't-Tevârîh of Şükrullah and the Tevarih-i Âl-i Osman of Âşıkpaşazâde, and they survive in copies. Later Ottoman tradition made his ancestors descendants of the Kayı tribe of the Oghuz Turks, but many scholars regard that as a later fabrication meant to strengthen dynastic legitimacy. His name may originally have been Turkish, perhaps Atman, and later changed to the Arabic ʿOsmān.

His date of birth is unknown. Some sources give 13 February 1258, and the sixteenth-century historian Kemalpaşazade gave 1254/5. The few sources agree that he was born at Söğüt, which his father Ertuğrul took as the capital of his beylik. According to Ottoman tradition, Ertuğrul pledged allegiance to the Anatolian Seljuks, who gave him Söğüt on the Byzantine frontier, though that connection was largely invented by court chroniclers a century later. The Karamanid historian Shikari called Osman a lowborn Yörük and shepherd.

The Ottoman principality was one of many Anatolian beyliks that emerged in the second half of the thirteenth century. It lay in Bithynia, well placed for attacks on the vulnerable Byzantine Empire, and Söğüt stood on a defensible hill on the road from Constantinople to Konya. Osman became emir upon his father's death, around 1281. Some historians think the succession was not peaceful, and that he killed his uncle Dündar Bey for disobedience. Almost nothing is known of his early activities except that he controlled the region around Söğüt and raided Byzantine lands from there.

The first datable event is the Battle of Bapheus, in which he defeated a Byzantine force sent against him. He appears to have enlarged his territory at Byzantine expense while avoiding conflict with his more powerful Turkish neighbours. His conquests included Bilecik, Yenişehir, İnegöl and Yarhisar, and Yenişehir became the capital. After a victory near Nicaea he began to settle his forces closer to Byzantine areas. By 1308 he had extended his control north along the Sakarya River and south-west towards the Sea of Marmara.

He married the daughter of the dervish leader Sheikh Edebali, and later Ottoman writers told a story of a dream he had in the sheikh's house. Osman died in 1323 or 1324. His small Turkoman principality became a vast empire in the centuries after his death, which lasted until the sultanate was abolished in 1922.
osnabruck: Osnabrück lies on the river Hase in a valley between the Wiehen Hills and the northern tip of the Teutoburg Forest. Although it belongs to Lower Saxony, it is historically, culturally and linguistically considered part of Westphalia. The origin of its name is disputed, and the city gave its name to the textile fabric osnaburg.

Osnabrück began as a marketplace beside the bishopric founded by Charlemagne in 780. Some time before 803 it became the seat of the Prince-Bishopric of Osnabrück, probably the oldest bishopric in Lower Saxony. It was first called a city in 1147, and a decade later Frederick Barbarossa granted it fortification rights. It joined the Hanseatic League in the 12th century. In 1582, under Mayor Hammacher, 163 women were executed as alleged witches, most of them burned alive, and 276 women and two men were executed in all between 1561 and 1639, a period of unrest that also saw the Reformation and the Thirty Years' War.

The first Lutheran services were held in 1543, but the Catholic churches continued to operate and the city never became wholly Lutheran. A Catholic bishop was elected in 1623, and troops of the Catholic League occupied the city in 1628. The Gymnasium Carolinum became a Jesuit university in 1632, which closed a year later when Swedish troops took the city. Peace negotiations were held in Osnabrück and Münster from 1643 to 1648, and the Peace of Westphalia recognised Osnabrück as bi-confessional: the prince-bishopric was to be held alternately by a Catholic and a Lutheran bishop, the Protestant chosen from the descendants of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg.

The Napoleonic period saw the city change hands several times. It passed to the Electorate of Hanover in 1803, briefly to Prussia in 1806, was in the Kingdom of Westphalia from 1807 to 1810, then in the First French Empire, and after 1815 in the Kingdom of Hanover. Prussia annexed it after the Austro-Prussian War of 1866. In 1930 the Nazi Party won nearly 28 per cent of the vote in the city. Jews and Romani people were deported during the Second World War. British troops entered the city on 4 April 1945 with little resistance, after extensive bombing.

The old town was reconstructed after the Second World War in designs that follow the original medieval architecture, and most of the towers of the old fortifications are still visible. Osnabrück was the home of the largest British garrison outside the United Kingdom. It has a university and a university of applied sciences.
ossetians: The Ossetians, also called Ossetes or Ossets, are an Iranian people indigenous to Ossetia, a region on the northern and southern sides of the Caucasus Mountains. They speak Ossetian, an Eastern Iranian language and a remnant of the Scytho-Sarmatian dialect group once spoken across the Pontic–Caspian Steppe; it is not mutually intelligible with any other Iranian language. The names Ossetians and Ossetia come from the Russian Osetin, borrowed from the Georgian Oseti, 'the land of the Osi', a term used since the Middle Ages for the Iranian-speaking population of the central Caucasus. It derives ultimately from As, the self-designation of an Alanic tribe of the Sarmatians.

They descend from the Alans. Between 350 and 374 the Huns destroyed the Alan kingdom between the Don and the Volga; some Alans fled west and took part in the invasions of the Roman Empire, while others went south and settled in the Caucasus, where they established the medieval kingdom of Alania.

From the 8th century a consolidated Alania existed in the northern Caucasus, a centralised monarchy with a strong military force and an economy that benefited from the Silk Road. It reached its peak in the 11th century under the ruler Durgulel, who established relations with the Byzantine Empire. The Mongols first met the Alans in 1222, and a second campaign in 1238 and 1239 captured much of the Alan plain, after which Alania ceased to exist as a political entity. The Alans withdrew into the mountains, where they formed three groups, the Iron, the Digoron and the Kudar.

Ossetia became part of the Russian Empire in 1774. In 1922 the South Ossetian autonomous oblast was created within the Georgian SSR, while North Ossetia remained in the Russian SFSR, and in 1994 North Ossetia added the name Alania to its official title.

Before the 10th century the Ossetians were pagan; Byzantine missionaries partly converted them early in the 10th century, and by the 13th century most of the urban population had become Eastern Orthodox through Georgian missionary work. Islam spread among the Digor in the 1500s and 1600s through contact with the Kabarday Circassians. Most Ossetians are Eastern Orthodox Christians, while many follow the folk religion Uatsdin, also called Assianism, which has temples known as kuvandon and ritual animal sacrifices. The Narts, a cycle of mythology, form the basis of Ossetian folk literature.
ostergotland: Östergötland is one of the traditional provinces of Sweden, bordering Småland, Västergötland, Närke, Södermanland and the Baltic Sea. In older English literature it is also called Ostrogothia. A fertile, largely agricultural plain, the Östgöta Plain, runs from west to east through its middle, while the south is hilly with countless lakes and the north is hilly and forested. Off the eastern shore lies an archipelago of islands and islets. The province is traditionally divided into two halves, east and west of the river Stångån, and the Göta Canal crosses it from the Baltic Sea at Mem to Lake Vättern at Motala.

The earliest mention of Östergötland, as the Ostrogoths of Scandza, appears in the Getica of the scholar Jordanes. Its traditions reach back into the Viking Age and the undocumented Iron Age, when the region had its own laws and kings. It kept its own laws, the Östgötalagen, into the Middle Ages, and about 50,000 ancient remains of different kinds survive, among them 1,749 grave fields.

Östergötland belonged to the Christian heartland of the late Iron Age and early medieval Sweden, and the Sverker and Bjälbo dynasties played a pivotal role in the consolidation of the kingdom. Vreta Abbey, dating from the early 12th century, was the first convent established in Sweden, and Vadstena Abbey became the dominant convent of medieval Sweden. Linköping received its royal charter in 1287 and Norrköping in 1384. Since the 13th century Swedish princes and princesses have been created dukes and duchesses of provinces, and since 1772 these have been honorary titles only.

Linköping is the largest city, with Norrköping second. Linköping Cathedral is the second largest church in Sweden and is very well preserved from the Middle Ages. Among the castles open to the public are Ekenäs Castle, one of the best preserved Renaissance castles in Sweden, and Vadstena Castle, built by the Vasa dynasty between 1545 and 1620. The Rök runestone, now beside the church in Rök, carries the longest known runic inscription in stone and is considered the first piece of written Swedish, marking the beginning of Swedish literature.
osterode-am-harz: Osterode am Harz, often simply called Osterode, is a town in south-eastern Lower Saxony on the south-western edge of the Harz mountains. It was the seat of government of the district of Osterode and lies on the German Timber-Frame Road. The Söse River flows through the town from the reservoir of the Söse Dam, about 5 kilometres upstream; the dam, built in 1931, holds 25.5 million cubic metres and its water supplies drinking water as far away as Bremen.

Osterode was granted town rights in the early 13th century. Defensive walls were built in the 13th century and extended by 1330. In 1510 riots broke out and the townspeople murdered the mayor; Duke Philip I held a court session, the leaders of the riots were sentenced, town property was confiscated and municipal privileges were revoked. A fire struck the town in 1545, and in the Thirty Years' War of 1618-1648 marching troops, marauders, looting, high war taxes and epidemics devastated it. Since 1665 it has belonged to the domain of the House of Hanover, which also ruled Great Britain.

In 1807 it became part of the Napoleonic Kingdom of Westphalia, in 1813 it passed to the Kingdom of Hanover, in 1866 it was annexed by Prussia, and from 1871 it formed part of the German Empire. Its population was 7,467 in 1905. The Great Depression collapsed numerous local businesses, and in 1933 the Nazi Party gained a majority in the town. From 1939 to 1941 the Oflag XI-A prisoner-of-war camp for Polish officers stood there, and from 1944 to 1945 there was a subcamp of the Buchenwald concentration camp. American troops captured Osterode in April 1945.

The town granary, built between 1719 and 1722 to supply the mining villages of the Upper Harz with grain, is among its most imposing buildings. After a comprehensive renovation it serves as the town hall, and a bas-relief of the 18th-century coat of arms of Great Britain decorates it. The Museum im Ritterhaus shows documents of the town's history from the Middle Ages, and the Lichtenstein Cave near Dorste, an archaeological site, yielded the bones of a man dated to about 1000 BCE. Osterode is the starting point of the 100-kilometre Harzer Hexenstieg, a hiking trail to Thale. The sculptor Tilman Riemenschneider was brought up locally.
ostfold: Østfold lies in eastern Norway on the eastern side of the Oslofjord, between the fjord and Sweden. Its landscape is largely flat, with woodland in the north and along the Swedish border, a major lake system in the centre and a densely populated lowland along the coast. Norway's longest river, the Glomma, flows through the county and reaches the Oslofjord at Fredrikstad. Its towns include Moss, Sarpsborg, Fredrikstad and Halden. The name means 'the region east of the Fold', Fold being the old name of the Oslofjord; it was first recorded in 1543.

Østfold is among the oldest inhabited regions of Norway, with petroglyphs and burial mounds throughout. In the Viking Age it was part of Vingulmark, which in turn belonged to Viken, and it was partly under Danish rule until the time of Harald Fairhair. In the Middle Ages the county was known as Borgarsysla, after Borg, now Sarpsborg.
Under Danish rule the king divided the area into many baronies, which were merged into one county in 1662 under the name Smaalenenes Amt; the old name Østfold returned in 1919.

In 1768 the barony of Heggen og Frøland was transferred to Østfold from Akershus. In 2018 archaeologists announced the discovery of a buried Viking ship about 20 metres long at Gjellestad, together with other burial mounds and the remains of five longhouses, found using ground-penetrating radar.

Østfold was part of the county of Viken for four years, a change that was controversial, and it was re-established as a separate county on 1 January 2024, without the municipality of Rømskog, which had been merged into Aurskog-Høland. Its administrative seat is Sarpsborg. Fredrikstad has shipyards, Sarpsborg has the Borregaard biorefinery, and the granite mines of the county supplied stone to the sculptor Gustav Vigeland. The county's coat of arms, from 1958, shows lines that represent sunrays at sunrise in the east and the worship of the Sun in the Bronze Age, depicted in rock carvings found there.
ostpolitik: After 1945 Germany was divided into the Federal Republic and the German Democratic Republic, and both at first claimed to represent the whole German nation. The Christian Democratic Union governed West Germany from 1949 to 1969 and refused contact with the East German government. The Hallstein Doctrine stipulated that the Federal Republic would withdraw diplomatic contact from any country that established relations with the GDR; it was first applied in 1957 against Yugoslavia. By the 1960s the policy was failing: when the Federal Republic established relations with Israel in 1965, the Arab states broke off relations with it and recognised the GDR. Egon Bahr proposed change through rapprochement in a 1963 speech.

Willy Brandt, the Social Democratic mayor of West Berlin and later chancellor, held that the Hallstein Doctrine neither weakened the communist government nor eased the lives of Germans in the GDR. He believed that collaboration would foster German-German encounters and trade that would undermine communist rule in the long term, and he stressed that the policy did not neglect the ties with Western Europe and the United States or membership in NATO. Henry Kissinger was among American advisers who had urged Bonn to be more flexible, though some in the West feared a more independent German policy.

In 1970 Brandt signed the Treaty of Moscow, renouncing the use of force and recognising the existing European borders, and later that year the Treaty of Warsaw, which recognised the People's Republic of Poland and the Oder–Neisse line. The most controversial agreement was the Basic Treaty of 1972 with East Germany, which established formal relations between the two German states for the first time. In April 1972 the opposition leader Rainer Barzel came two votes short in a vote of no confidence, and it later emerged that the GDR had paid two CDU deputies to vote against him. The Bundestag approved the treaty on 11 May 1973, opening the way for both states to join the United Nations.
ostracism: Ostracism was not in use throughout the whole period of Athenian democracy, roughly 506 to 322 BCE, but only in the fifth century BCE. The standard account, in Aristotle's Constitution of the Athenians, attributes its establishment to Cleisthenes, which would place it from around 506 BCE. Its first victim, however, was not expelled until 487 BCE, nearly twenty years later, and over the next sixty years some twelve or more individuals followed him, though the list may be incomplete.

The first people ostracised in the decade after the Persian defeat at Marathon in 490 BCE were connected with the tyrant Peisistratos, whose son Hippias had later landed at Marathon with an invasion force. Tyranny and Persian aggression were paired threats to the new democracy, and ostracism was used against both. Victims include Aristides in 482 BCE and Cimon in 461 BCE.

The word comes from ostraka, the pottery sherds used as voting tokens. Each year the Assembly was asked whether it wished to hold an ostracism, in the sixth month of the state's year. If a majority agreed, the vote took place two months later in a barriered section of the agora, where citizens, many of them illiterate, gave a name to a scribe or scratched it on a sherd. Nine archons and the council of the five hundred supervised the count. The man named on most sherds was banished, provided a quorum was met; Plutarch gives it as at least 6,000 votes.

The man ostracised had ten days to leave Athens and faced death if he returned, but his property was not confiscated and he lost no status. After ten years he could come back without stigma, and the Assembly could recall him earlier. Cimon, ostracised in 461 BCE, was recalled during an emergency. There was no charge and no defence.

The last known ostracism, that of Hyperbolos, took place in the later fifth century BCE. Plutarch tells that the people were disgusted when Nicias and Alcibiades turned the vote against Hyperbolos instead of one of themselves, and abandoned the procedure for ever. It was in part replaced by the graphe paranomon, a regular court action that could reach many politicians at once and with greater severity, and the threats of the late fifth century came from oligarchic coups, such as that of the Four Hundred in 411 BCE and of the Thirty in 404 BCE, against which ostracism was no defence. Megara, Miletos, Argos and Syracuse are known to have had forms of ostracism.
ostrava: Ostrava lies about 270 kilometres east of Prague, mostly in the low Ostrava Basin, where the Oder, Opava, Ostravice and Lučina rivers meet. Its highest point is 280 metres above sea level. The city has about 281,000 inhabitants, and the wider conurbation, with towns such as Bohumín, Havířov and Karviná, about 500,000. It straddles the border of the historic lands of Moravia and Silesia, on the ancient trade route from the Baltic Sea to the Adriatic known as the Amber Road, and its position there helped the town to grow.

The first written mention of Silesian Ostrava, as a settlement, dates from 1229, and Moravian Ostrava is first named as a township in 1267. The place took its name from the Ostrá, now the Ostravice, which still divides the city into Moravian and Silesian parts. The oldest known depiction of the city's coat of arms, a rearing silver horse, is on a seal of 1426. The coloured version first appears in 1728.

The coalfield made Ostrava an industrial engine of the Austrian empire. Steam trams ran from 1894 and were electrified in 1901, and the turn of the twentieth century was the time of the city's largest boom, to which its theatres, banks and department stores belong. Hermann Zwierzina became the first mayor of Moravian Ostrava in 1861. In the twentieth century the city was known as the steel heart of Czechoslovakia for its mining and metallurgy. After the fall of communism in 1989 its industries were restructured, and the last coal was mined in the city in 1994.

Ostrava is the capital of the Moravian-Silesian Region and the third largest city of the Czech Republic by population and area. In the Lower Vítkovice area a former coal mining, coke production and ironworks complex keeps its historic industrial architecture. The city has four urban monument zones, among them the historic centre round Masaryk Square, with its 16th-century Old City Hall and a Marian plague column of 1702. It is the seat of the Technical University of Ostrava and the University of Ostrava, and hosts festivals such as Colours of Ostrava and the Janáček May.
ostrogoths: The Goths appear in Roman records from the third century in the regions north of the Lower Danube and the Black Sea. By then they already had sub-groups, among them the Tervingi, who bordered the Roman Empire. The Ostrogoths are associated with the Greuthungi, who lived further east; Ammianus Marcellinus put the dividing line between the two at the Dniester, with Alans beyond the Greuthungi near the Don.

Scholars disagree on that link. Herwig Wolfram sees Ostrogoths and Greuthungi as two names for one people, while Peter Heather argues that the Ostrogoths who followed Theodoric stand at the end of complex processes of fragmentation and unification, and some historians doubt that any single Gothic ethnicity united them before the Amal clan did. The name comes from a Germanic root meaning 'eastern', although Jordanes took it simply to mean the eastern Goths, as against the Visigoths.

In the late fourth century the Huns subdued many Goths and Alans. Many Greuthungi entered the Roman Empire in 376 with Saphrax and Alatheus, and a group of Ostrogoths and Greuthungi was settled in Phrygia in the 380s. The Amal dynasty, which had fought under Attila, settled in Pannonia after the Hunnic empire collapsed, and around 483 or 484 the Amal kingdom took in the Thracian Goths as its second main component.

Theodoric the Great, born about 454 to Theodemir, was educated as a diplomatic hostage in Constantinople. Backed by the emperor Zeno, he invaded Italy, defeated Odoacer and ruled from Ravenna, keeping Roman administration and law and governing Goths and Romans under parallel systems. He was an Arian but allowed freedom of religion.

After his death in 526, his grandson Athalaric reigned under the regency of Amalasuntha, but Theodahad killed them both. In 535 Justinian I began the Gothic War. Totila revived Gothic fortunes but was killed at the Battle of Taginae in 552, and the kingdom had collapsed by 554. Survivors were absorbed by the Lombards, who had their own kingdom in Italy by 568.

The Gothic language, best attested in Ulfilas's translation of the Bible, is the only eastern Germanic language with continuous surviving texts. The Edict of Theodoric of about 500 and the Variae of Cassiodorus, which can be read as the state papers of Theodoric and his successors, also survive. The historian Ian Wood stresses that Gothic identity in the West was a flexible, politicised construct formed through Roman political categories, military patronage and court ritual rather than a stable lineage.
ostrogozhsk: Ostrogozhsk is the administrative centre of Ostrogozhsky District in Voronezh Oblast, Russia. It stands on the Tikhaya Sosna River, a tributary of the Don, 142 kilometres south of Voronezh. It is a historical centre of Eastern Sloboda Ukraine. Its name means little fortress, from the ostrog, or fortress, around which it grew.

The town was established in 1652 by the Belgorod voivode Fedor Arsenyev and a Cossack leader, Ivan Zevkovsky or Dzenkovsky, who brought about 2,000 settlers from the Chernigov and Nezhin regiments. It grew around an ostrog on the Belgorod Defensive Line of Russia. During Stepan Razin's revolt against Aleksey Mikhailovich it was under the control of rebellious Cossacks. In 1696 Peter the Great stopped there to meet Ivan Mazepa, the hetman of the Zaporizhian Host, and the Cossacks of the Ostrogozhsk regiment, an event commemorated by a memorial in the town square. In 1708 it was incorporated into the Azov Governorate.

The town was the headquarters of a Sloboda Ukrainian Cossack territorial and military regiment until the 1760s, when Catherine II abolished it. In 1765 it was incorporated into the new Sloboda Ukraine Governorate, and in 1802 it passed to the new Voronezh Governorate and received town rights.

In the 1897 Russian census a small majority of its inhabitants were Little Russians, or Ukrainians, and nearly as many were Great Russians, and the townspeople kept Ukrainian customs and Cossack traditions well into the 20th century. In 1918 it was controlled by the Ukrainian People's Republic and the Ukrainian Hetmanate, from 1919 by Anton Denikin's White army, and from 1920 it was part of Soviet Russia, though the border between Soviet Russia and Soviet Ukraine was not finalised until 1925. In 1926 Ukrainians were 74.1 per cent of the town's population.
Nazi Germany occupied the town from 5 July 1942 until 20 January 1943, when it was liberated in the Ostrogozhsk–Rossosh Offensive. The Germans operated a forced labour battalion for Jews there.
ostsiedlung: The Ostsiedlung followed a large rise in population across Europe in the High Middle Ages. From the 11th to the 13th centuries the population of the kingdom of Germany grew from about four to twelve million, and arable land was expanded at the expense of forest. Demand for land still could not be met. Landless younger sons of noble families, who could not inherit property, were among those who sought new holdings on the edges of the Empire, especially after the success of the First Crusade.

East of the Elbe and Saale lived Slavic peoples known as Wends or Elbe Slavs, who seldom formed large political units. A Slavic revolt in 983 ended imperial rule and Christian missions between the Elbe and the Baltic, and the area stayed under Polabian tribes into the 12th century. A call for a crusade against the Wends in 1108, offering land to new settlers, had no noticeable effect.

The first settlers, mostly Flemish and Dutch, arrived in 1124 and settled south of the Eider. The conquest of the land of the Wagri in 1139 and the founding of Lübeck in 1143 followed. In 1152 many Flemish and Dutch people were brought to marshland east of Magdeburg near the Havel, and Henry the Lion settled Mecklenburg with Flemish people. Dutch settlers were valued as hydraulic engineers who drained land with networks of ditches.

Settlement spread to Bohemia, where German traders, miners, farmers and monks arrived and Germans came to make up almost a quarter of the people of Prague. In 1149 Géza II invited German settlers to southern Transylvania, where the name Saxons became the official term for local Germans in 1231. Most settlers were Germans of the Holy Roman Empire, with some Dutch, Danes, Scots, Walloons and local Wends. Towns were founded or enlarged with regular street plans and central market places, and Cistercian monasteries joined faith and settlement.

Settlers brought heavier ploughs, half-timbered building and hard-fired pottery, and Slavic place names such as those ending in -ow or -witz remain common in eastern Germany. Assimilation ran in both directions: Germans in Kraków and Poznań were assimilated into the Polish population over about two centuries, while small Sorbian communities were absorbed by German speakers. About 25 per cent of German family names are estimated to be of Slavic origin.

The movement slowed after 1300. Explanations include the worsening climate from about 1300, the agricultural crisis of the mid-14th century and the plague of 1347, though no single cause can be weighed against the others. In the 19th and 20th centuries nationalists used the Ostsiedlung to support the idea of a German drive to the east, and after the Second World War it was reversed east of the Oder.
osun-state: Osun State lies in south-western Nigeria, bounded by Ekiti and Ondo states to the east, Kwara State to the north, Ogun State to the south and Oyo State to the west, mostly across the Osun River. It takes its name from the river, which bisects the state's interior before forming much of its south-western border, and the Erinle and Oba are tributaries. Most of the state lies in the Nigerian lowland forests, with the drier Guinean forest–savanna mosaic in the north. The people are primarily Yoruba, of the Ibolo, Ife, Igbomina, Ijesha and Oyo subgroups, and the climate is tropical wet and dry.

In the pre-colonial period the area was divided among various western Yoruba states, some based on a single town and some part of larger empires such as the Oyo Empire. From 1877 to 1893 the Kiriji War was fought among Yoruba states and ended in a stalemate brokered by the British, after which the area was colonised and incorporated into the British Southern Nigeria Protectorate, merged into British Nigeria in 1914. After independence in 1960 it belonged to the Western Region, and from 1967 to the Western State. In 1976 the west of the Western State became Oyo State, and on 27 August 1991 Osun State was formed from the south-east of Oyo State, with its capital at Osogbo.

The name comes from the River Osun, the venerated spring that is the manifestation of the Yoruba goddess of the same name. Every August adherents and others travel from many countries to the Osun-Osogbo festival, among them visitors from Brazil, Cuba, Trinidad and Grenada, and the Osun-Osogbo Grove, the shrine of the annual rites and an important artistic centre, was declared a World Heritage Site in 2005.

Yoruba and English are the official languages, and the people practise Christianity, Islam and the traditional faith. The economy rests largely on agriculture, with cocoa, cassava, millet, cashew, banana, maize, potato and yam, along with services, artisanal mining and livestock. Obafemi Awolowo University stands in the ancient town of Ile-Ife, an important early centre of Yoruba political and religious development. The state also holds many ancient kingdom capitals, among them Ila Orangun, Iragbiji, Ikirun, Ede, Iwo and Ilesa, and festivals such as Olojo in Ife and Iwude Ijesha in Ilesa. Erin-Ijesha Waterfalls, with seven levels, is a tourist attraction.
oswestry: Oswestry (Welsh: Croesoswallt) is an ancient market town and historic railway town in Shropshire, England, about five miles from the Welsh border, at the junction of the A5, A483 and A495 roads. It has a mixed English and Welsh heritage and is the largest settlement within the Oswestry Uplands. The name is first attested in 1191 as Oswaldestroe, from the Old English personal name Ōswald and trēow, meaning tree. The traditional Welsh name, first attested in 1254, means Oswald's cross, and since trēow may also mean cross, the name may have meant Oswald's cross in both languages.

The earliest known settlement is Old Oswestry, one of the best-preserved Iron Age hill forts in Britain, with evidence of construction and occupation between 800 BCE and 43 CE. The Battle of Maserfield, between the Anglo-Saxon kings Penda of Mercia and Oswald of Northumbria, is widely thought to have been fought at Oswestry, although scholars debate its location. The Domesday Book of 1086 records a castle built by Rainald, a Norman sheriff of Shropshire. Henry I later granted the feudal barony of Oswestry to Alan fitz Flaad, a Breton knight.

The town changed hands between the English and the Welsh a number of times in the Middle Ages and still keeps some Welsh-language street and place names. In 1190 it was granted the right to hold a market each Wednesday. It built walls for protection, but Parliamentarians took the town from the Royalists after a brief siege on 22 June 1644 and tore the walls down in the English Civil War, leaving only the Newgate Pillar visible. Oswestry School, founded in 1407 by David Holbache, is the second oldest free school in the country.

Oswestry had a population of 17,509 at the census of 2021. The railway station, opened in 1840 on the main line of the Cambrian Railways, closed in 1966. St Oswald's Church, first mentioned in the Domesday Book, is Grade II* listed, with a tower from the late 12th or early 13th century. Old Oswestry dominates the northern and eastern approaches to the town. The poet Wilfred Owen (1893–1918) and the novelist Barbara Pym were born in Oswestry, and Park Hall, east of the town, served as an army training camp and military hospital from 1915.
oswiecim: Oświęcim lies 33 kilometres south-east of Katowice, near the confluence of the Vistula and the Soła. Its old town is east of the Soła, around the Main Market Square. The name is Slavic, possibly from the owner of a Slavic gord that stood here in the Middle Ages, or from the Polish word oświęcić, 'to sanctify'. Fourteenth-century German-speaking merchants called the town Auswintz, which by the 15th century had become Auschwitz. Both Polish and German names were in official use under Habsburg rule, and the town has been called Oświęcim since 27 January 1945.

Oświęcim was one of the oldest castellan seats in Poland, dating from the 12th century. After the fragmentation of Poland in 1138 it passed to the Duchy of Opole, and the first Mongol invasion destroyed it in 1241. Around 1272 the rebuilt town received a municipal charter, confirmed on 3 September 1291.
A separate Duchy of Oświęcim was established around 1315; in 1327 Duke Jan I the Scholastic joined it with the Duchy of Zator, and it became a vassal of the Kingdom of Bohemia for over a century.

In 1454 Duke Jan IV pledged allegiance to Poland, and in 1457 King Casimir IV Jagiellon bought the rights to the town. In 1564 Sigismund II Augustus integrated the duchies of Oświęcim and Zator into the Kingdom of Poland.

The town traded in salt from Wieliczka, and the Swedish invasion burned it in 1655. In 1772 it passed to the Habsburg Empire as part of Galicia and Lodomeria, where it stayed until 1918, and in the second half of the 19th century it became an important rail junction.

About 8,000 Jews lived in the town on the eve of the Second World War, fewer than half its people. Germany annexed the area in October 1939 and expanded former Polish barracks into the Auschwitz concentration camp. In 1941 a large IG Farben chemical plant was built on the eastern outskirts.

To keep the area around the camp empty, the Germans planned a 40-square-kilometre buffer zone and expelled the Polish residents in 1940 and 1941; some 17,000 people left their homes, eight villages were wiped off the map, and the town's population shrank to 7,600 by April 1941. The Red Army liberated the camp on 27 January 1945. The Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, preserves the camp site, and the town remains a railway junction and a centre of the chemical industry.
otago: Otago covers about 32,000 square kilometres in the southern half of the South Island. The name is the southern Māori pronunciation of Ōtākou, the name of the Māori village near the entrance to Otago Harbour. Its meaning is disputed, with common translations being isolated village and place of red earth, the latter referring to the reddish-ochre clay around Dunedin.

From the west the land rises to high alpine mountains, where Mount Aspiring / Tititea is the highest peak outside the Aoraki / Mount Cook area. Glacial lakes, among them Wakatipu, Wānaka and Hāwea, feed the Clutha River / Mata-Au, the largest river in New Zealand by discharge, which is used for hydroelectric power. East of the mountains lie the dry Central Otago basins, where the climate is the closest in New Zealand to a continental one.

Like the rest of New Zealand, Otago was first settled by the Māori, mostly on the coast and around the Otago Peninsula. A European settlement named Otago was established on the harbour by the Weller Brothers in 1831. The settlement that gave the region its character was founded in March 1848, when the ships John Wickliffe and Philip Laing arrived from Greenock with colonists of the Free Church of Scotland. Captain William Cargill was its secular leader, and he was elected provincial superintendent after the provinces were created in 1853. Otago Province covered all of New Zealand south of the Waitaki River.

In 1861 Gabriel Read discovered gold at Gabriel's Gully near Lawrence, and the Otago gold rush followed. Veterans of the goldfields of California and Australia and fortune-seekers from Europe, North America and China poured in, eroding the province's Scottish Presbyterian character. Further finds at Clyde and on the Arrow River brought a boom, and for a period Otago was the cultural and economic centre of New Zealand. The Otago Daily Times, the country's first daily newspaper, dates from this time, as does New Zealand's first university, the University of Otago, founded in 1869 in Dunedin.
Southland separated from Otago in 1861 and was re-absorbed in 1870. The provincial governments were abolished on 1 November 1876, and from then on the national limelight gradually shifted northwards.

Dunedin is the principal city, and Oamaru, Balclutha, Alexandra, Queenstown and Wānaka are other major centres. Most of the population of European lineage is of Scottish stock, and a large proportion of the Māori population belongs to the Ngāi Tahu iwi. Sheep farming gave way in parts to dairying, and the Central Otago wine region is known for its Pinot noir.
otepaa: Otepää lies in Valga County in southern Estonia, in the hilly, lake-filled region known as the Otepää Upland. At up to 171 metres above sea level it is the highest of Estonia's towns, and Lake Pühajärv lies nearby. The name means Ott's Head in South Estonian, where ott is a euphemism for bear. The town was formerly called Nuustaku and is nicknamed the winter capital of Estonia.

The first settlement dates to the sixth century BCE, and the site has been inhabited continuously since the sixth or seventh century CE. It was the site of an Ugandi County hill fort. Rus' sources first mention the fortress in 1116, when the princes of Novgorod and Pskov marched against Tartu and Otepää. The conquest of Estonia in the Northern Crusades began with an attack on the fortress in 1208, and in 1217 Christianized southern Estonians stopped the advance of Kievan Rus' there. German crusaders finally conquered the fort in 1224.

Hermann of Dorpat, the first Prince-Bishop of the Bishopric of Dorpat, built an episcopal castle there, the first stone fortress in Estonia. Its importance declined in the fourteenth century as Tartu, the bishopric's seat, grew. It is commonly believed that the Livonian Order razed the castle in 1396 during a conflict with the bishopric, although archaeologists have argued that it was inhabited as late as 1477. The earliest surviving firearm in Europe was found in the castle and dates to at least 1396.

The settlement was named Nuustaku and given town privileges in 1862. The first agricultural fair was held at the church manor in 1876, and on 4 June 1884 the flag that became Estonia's national flag was dedicated in Nuustaku Church as the flag of the Estonian Students' Society. The name changed to Otepää in 1922, and it officially became a town in 1936.

St Mary's Church stands in the town; its oldest parts date to the 1860s, and it was largely rebuilt in 1889 and 1890. Otepää is a popular skiing resort and hosted FIS Cross-Country World Cup events from the 2005 to 2006 season.
othello: Shakespeare's main source was the seventh story of the third decade of Gli Hecatommithi, a collection of one hundred novellas published in 1565 by Cinthio, whose plot he borrowed and substantially reworked. In Cinthio only Disdemona is named, a name that means ill-omened in Italian; the others are called the Moor, the Ensign and the Corporal. There the Ensign falls in love with Disdemona, turns to hatred when she is indifferent, and persuades the Moor of her unfaithfulness. It cannot be later than 1604, since a performance that year is recorded in the accounts of Sir Edmund Tilney, the Master of the Revels, and it cannot be earlier than 1601, when Holland's translation of Pliny's Natural History, one of its sources, was published.

The play was not published in Shakespeare's lifetime. It survives in a quarto of 1622 and, a year later, in the First Folio. The Folio has about 160 lines that the quarto lacks, among them Desdemona's Willow Song.

The play is set in Venice and Cyprus. In the first act Roderigo, a wealthy and dissolute gentleman, complains to his friend Iago, an ensign, of the secret marriage of Desdemona, the daughter of the senator Brabantio, to Othello, a Moorish general in the Venetian army. In Cyprus, Iago has Cassio, Othello's lieutenant, made drunk, so that Othello strips him of his rank, and then persuades Othello to suspect Cassio and Desdemona.

The handkerchief that Othello gave Desdemona is found by Iago's wife, Emilia, and passed to Iago, who plants it in Cassio's lodgings. Othello, convinced of his wife's unfaithfulness, vows with Iago to kill her and Cassio. The action is continuous from the wedding night, apart from the voyage to Cyprus, and the time spent on the island is estimated at about 33 hours, which leaves no time for the supposed affair. The play's earliest critics already noted its reliance on the handkerchief; Thomas Rymer, in 1693, suggested it be called the Tragedy of the Handkerchief.

The King's Men performed Othello at the Globe, and at Court on 1 November 1604 and again in 1612 and 1613 for the wedding of Princess Elizabeth and Frederick V of the Palatinate. The first professional appearance of a woman on the English stage was as Desdemona on 8 December 1660. Originally performed by white actors in dark makeup, the title role began to be played by black actors in the 19th century; the first known was James Hewlett in New York in 1822, and Ira Aldridge played it at the Royalty Theatre in London in 1825.
otho: Marcus Salvius Otho was born on 28 April 32 into a noble Etruscan family. His grandfather Marcus had been a senator, and Emperor Claudius granted patrician status to his father, Lucius Salvius Otho. Suetonius describes him as moderate in height and bandy-legged but almost feminine in his care of his person, wearing a carefully fitted wig, and the satirist Juvenal mocks his vanity. An aged freedwoman brought him into the company of the young Emperor Nero, whose friend and courtier he became.

Otho married Poppaea Sabina, but Nero took her for himself, forced a divorce and exiled Otho to Lusitania as governor, in 58 or 59. Otho governed capably, yet never forgave Nero. In 68 he allied himself with Galba, governor of neighbouring Hispania Tarraconensis, in his rebellion against Nero. Nero committed suicide that year, the Senate proclaimed Galba emperor, and Otho accompanied him to Rome in October 68.

On 1 January 69 the legions of Germania Superior refused to swear loyalty to Galba, and the next day the soldiers of Germania Inferior proclaimed their governor, Aulus Vitellius, emperor. Galba adopted the nobleman Piso Licinianus as his successor, which angered Otho. On 15 January the praetorians killed Galba, then Titus Vinius and Piso, and proclaimed Otho emperor. The crowd acclaimed him as Nero Otho, and Nero's statues were set up again. He showed clemency to the consul-designate Aulus Marius Celsus and shared the consulship with his brother Lucius Salvius Otho Titianus until 1 March.

Otho soon found it easier to overthrow an emperor than to rule. Vitellius's forces under Aulus Caecina Alienus and Fabius Valens crossed the Alps into northern Italy, and Otho summoned troops from Pannonia and Dalmatia. The two armies met at the Battle of Bedriacum, near Cremona, where the Praetorian Guard performed poorly and Otho's force was defeated.

Otho still commanded a large force, with the Dalmatian legions at Aquileia, and his soldiers urged him to fight on. He chose instead to end the war. After a farewell speech, in which he said it was more just that one should perish for all than many for one, he stabbed himself in the heart with a dagger. He had reigned three months, from 15 January to 16 April 69. A plain tomb was raised at Brixellum, and his reign of 91 days was the shortest until that of Pertinax in 193.

Many Romans came to respect him in death. Tacitus wrote that some soldiers killed themselves beside his funeral pyre because they loved their emperor, and the poet Martial admired his choice to spare the empire a civil war. Otho appears as a character in the operas of Monteverdi (1643), Handel (1709) and Vivaldi (1713).
oto-manguean-languages: The Oto-Manguean family has existed in southern Mexico since at least 2000 BCE and probably several thousand years earlier. Some estimates using glottochronology, a controversial method, suggest that Proto-Oto-Manguean split around 4400 BCE. The Tehuacán Valley has been proposed as the original home, and although this is now uncertain, the Tehuacán culture (5000 BCE to 2300 BCE) was likely made up of Oto-Manguean speakers.

The internal diversity of the family is comparable with that of Indo-European. Its speakers were among the first in Mesoamerica to form highly complex cultures. Monte Albán, with remains dated as early as 1000 BCE, is believed to have been in continuous use by Zapotecs, and the undeciphered Zapotec script is one of the earliest forms of Mesoamerican writing. In the Post-Classic period the Mixtecs were prolific artisans and codex painters, while Oto-Manguean cultures of central Mexico were marginalised by the intruding Nahuas.

The family has two main divisions. The western branch includes Oto-Pamean (Otomi, Mazahua, Matlatzinca and Pame), Chinantecan and Tlapanec-Mangue. The eastern branch includes Popolocan (Popoloca, Chocho, Mazatecan and Ixcatec), Zapotecan (Zapotec and Chatino) and Mixtecan-Amuzgoan (Mixtec, Trique, Cuicatec and Amuzgo). The largest numbers of speakers live in the state of Oaxaca, where Zapotecan and Mixtecan languages are spoken by almost 1.5 million people combined.

Every Oto-Manguean language is tonal, which makes the family unique among those of North America, Mesoamerica and Central America. Tone distinguishes the meanings of roots and marks grammatical categories. Some languages have two level tones and others up to ten tone contrasts. The languages are also more analytic than other Mesoamerican languages and almost all use verb-subject-object order. Whistled speech, which carries the tones of words over distances, is common in Chinantec, Mazatec and the Zapotecan languages.

A relationship between Zapotecan and Mixtecan was first proposed by Manuel Orozco y Berra in 1864. Later scholars added further groups, and the Oto-Pamean and Oaxacan groups were joined into one family in Edward Sapir's classification of 1929, which placed them in Hokan. Reconstruction work began in the 1950s, with Proto-Oto-Pamean reconstructed by Doris Bartholomew and Proto-Zapotecan by Morris Swadesh. Lyle Campbell's classification of 1997 was the first to give a unified view of the family.

The family is widely accepted by specialists, though a reconstruction of Proto-Oto-Manguean remains incomplete: only about 350 vocabulary items have been reconstructed. In 2015 the linguist Brown argued that the reconstructed vocabulary lacks regular sound correspondences and proposed that Oto-Manguean might instead be a Sprachbund. Several languages are endangered or extinct. All Manguean languages have died out, and Chiapanec was declared extinct after 1990.
otranto: Otranto lies on the east coast of the Salento peninsula in the province of Lecce, in Apulia. The Strait of Otranto, named after it, connects the Adriatic Sea with the Ionian Sea and separates Italy from Albania. The harbour is small and has little trade. About five kilometres to the south-east the lighthouse of Faro della Palascìa marks the most easterly point of the Italian mainland. The surrounding region was long known for its breed of horses.

Otranto occupies the site of the Greek city of Hydrus, in Latin Hydruntum, which was of Messapian origin. Under the Roman emperors it was perhaps more important than Brundisium as a port of embarkation for the East, since the crossing to Apollonia was shorter. A Fatimid fleet sacked it on 17 August 928 and carried its inhabitants to North Africa as slaves. It remained Byzantine until it was among the last cities of Apulia to surrender to the Norman Robert Guiscard, in 1068.

In 1480 Sultan Mehmed II sent an Ottoman fleet under Gedik Ahmed Pasha, which reached Apulia on 28 July and took the city in two weeks. The invaders had the commander of the defenders executed by being sawn in half, and about 800 residents were beheaded after refusing to convert to Islam. They were canonised in 2013, and Archbishop Stefano Pendinelli was also killed. The Ottomans held the city for 13 months and abandoned it on 11 September 1481, after the Pope called a crusade joined by troops of the Hungarian king Matthias Corvinus. In 1537 the corsair Barbarossa recaptured Otranto, but the Ottomans were again repulsed.

The town's main sights include the Aragonese Castle, rebuilt in the late 15th century, and the cathedral, consecrated in 1088, with a mosaic pavement of 1166 showing the months and Old Testament subjects. Bones and relics of the Martyrs of Otranto surround its high altar. Horace Walpole set The Castle of Otranto, generally held to be the first Gothic novel, in the town, though he had chosen it from a map for its well-sounding name.
otrar: Otrar, also called Farab, lay at the junction of two great rivers on the Silk Road, at the centre of a large oasis. The Syr Darya supplied water for irrigation, and the oasis lay near the foothills of the Karatau Mountains, which made it a supporting fortress for the nomads of the steppes. Roads ran from Otrar along the Arys to Taraz, Balasagun and Xinjiang, along the Syr Darya up to Shash, Sogd, Merv and Nishapur, and across the Kyzylkum desert westward to Khorezm, the Volga region and the Black Sea. The oasis is a series of towns, not one site.

The city dates to the Achaemenid Empire, when it was known as Parab. In the 9th and 10th centuries it submitted first to the Caliphate and then to the Samanids, and minted its own coinage. In 1218 a Mongol trade caravan of about 450 men, including an ambassador of Genghis Khan, reached Otrar. Its governor Inalchuq, an uncle of Sultan Muhammad II of the Khwarazmian Empire, accused them of spying and, with the Sultan's assent, executed the whole caravan. Genghis Khan besieged Otrar for five months in 1219, breached its walls, executed Inalchuq and massacred the inhabitants.

Many towns of the oasis were abandoned, but Otrar rose again and by the middle of the 13th century was a large trade centre between West and East. In February 1405 Timur caught a cold while gathering troops at Otrar and died in one of its palaces. In the 16th and 17th centuries the Kazakh Khanate and Dzungar lords feuded over the area. As the Silk Road lost its importance, so did the city, and the irrigation system fell out of use. By the end of the 18th century only 40 families remained, against perhaps 5,000 to 7,000 between the 14th and 17th centuries.

The oasis lies in the Kusulkum district of South Kazakhstan Province, 120 km northwest of Shymkent and 50 km from Turkistan. Only ruins overgrown with grass remain. The settlement covers about 2 square kilometres, and its lowest layers date from the 1st century CE. The central fortress and the fortified city formed a five-cornered hill about 18 metres high. Excavations show a densely populated town with monumental buildings, two bathhouses of the 9th to 12th centuries and evidence that Otrar was a centre of ceramic production in Central Asia.
ottawa: Ottawa lies in the south-eastern part of the province of Ontario, at the confluence of the Ottawa River and the Rideau River, with a third major river also meeting within the city. Across the river is Gatineau, Quebec, and the two form the Ottawa-Gatineau metropolitan area and the National Capital Region. The name was chosen in 1855 after the Ottawa River, whose name comes from the Algonquin adawe, meaning to trade. In modern Algonquin the city is called Odàwàg. The city's land area is 2,788.2 square kilometres.

The Ottawa Valley became habitable about 10,000 years ago, after the Champlain Sea drained. The first evidence of people there is spearpoints dated 8,000 to 8,500 years before the present. Settlements are documented at the mouth of the Gatineau River from 3,000 to 3,500 years ago, suggesting that the Algonquin people foraged, hunted, fished and traded there. The three rivers made the area an important route for trade and travel. In 1610 Étienne Brûlé became the first documented European to navigate the Ottawa River, and three years later Samuel de Champlain wrote about the waterfalls and the Algonquin people he met.

The city was founded in 1826 as Bytown, incorporated in 1850 and renamed Ottawa in 1855. In 1968 the Region of Ottawa-Carleton was formed as a two-tier municipality out of eleven townships, two cities and three villages, and in 2001 it became a single-tier city. As the national capital it has hosted events such as the first visit of a reigning Canadian sovereign, King George VI, to his parliament on 19 May 1939, the first raising of the new national flag on 15 February 1965, and the centennial of Confederation on 1 July 1967. Queen Elizabeth II issued the royal proclamation of the Constitution Act there on 17 April 1982.

Ottawa is the capital of Canada and the seat of the federal government. It houses the Parliament of Canada, the Supreme Court, the residence of the Governor General at Rideau Hall, and the Office of the Prime Minister. The 2021 census counted 1,017,449 people in the city and 1,488,307 in the metropolitan area. Its institutions include the University of Ottawa, Carleton University, founded in 1942, the National Arts Centre and the National Gallery of Canada. The Ottawa Public Library was created in 1906 as part of the Carnegie library system.
otto-i: Otto was born on 23 November 912, the eldest son of Henry the Fowler, Duke of Saxony, and his second wife Matilda, daughter of the Saxon count Dietrich of Ringelheim. In May 919, at the Imperial Diet of Fritzlar, Frankish and Saxon nobles elected Henry king, so that for the first time a Saxon reigned over the kingdom. Otto gained military experience in campaigns against the Wends on the eastern border, and by about 929 his father was probably preparing the succession. Henry died on 2 July 936, when all the German tribes were united in a single realm.

Otto was crowned on 7 August 936 at Aachen, Charlemagne's former capital, by Hildebert, Archbishop of Mainz. Though a Saxon, he wore Frankish dress to assert his authority over Lotharingia and his role as Charlemagne's true successor. He put down rebellions by dukes, among them Eberhard of Bavaria, whom he exiled in 938, and he installed members of his own family in the great duchies. Loyalty to Otto, not lineage, became the way to advancement. He also made bishops and abbots his instruments of government, granting them land and the title of Prince of the Empire; because these offices fell back to the crown at death, hereditary claims were avoided.

Otto's son Liudolf, Duke of Swabia, and his son-in-law Conrad, Duke of Lorraine, rebelled in 951, resenting Otto's marriage to Adelaide, Queen of Italy, and the power of his brother Henry. During the civil war the Magyars ravaged Bavaria and Franconia. Otto defeated them at the Battle of Lechfeld in 955, which ended the Hungarian invasions of Western Europe and earned him a reputation as a saviour of Christendom.

By 961 Otto had conquered the Kingdom of Italy. On 12 February 962, as emperor, he and Pope John XII held a synod in Rome, which approved his long-desired Archdiocese of Magdeburg. Relations with the papacy soon soured: in 964 Otto besieged Rome, forcing the Romans to accept his appointee Leo VIII as pope. Seeking peace with the Byzantine Empire, which opposed his claim to emperorship, he arranged the marriage of his son Otto II to the princess Theophanu in April 972.

Otto returned to Germany in August 972 and died at Memleben on 7 May 973; Otto II succeeded him. His patronage helped create several cathedral schools and the Ottonian Renaissance of manuscripts and architecture. Hrotsvitha, a poet and dramatist, was raised at his court. Historians have long depicted him as a successful ruler and a gifted commander, though the realm he built was too vast for the administrative structures of the time and could only be governed as a confederacy.
otto-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Otto II was born in 955, the third son of Otto the Great and his second wife, Adelaide of Italy. By 957 his older brothers Henry and Bruno had died, as had Liudolf, his father's son by his first wife, and the two-year-old Otto became heir apparent. His father entrusted his literary and cultural education to Archbishop William of Mainz, while Odo, margrave of the Eastern March, taught him the art of war and the kingdom's legal customs. He was made joint ruler of Germany in 961. On 25 December 967 Pope John XIII crowned him co-emperor in Rome, a step that was a prerequisite for his marriage to the Byzantine princess Theophanu, whom he married on 14 April 972.

Otto the Great died in 973, and the 18-year-old Otto II succeeded peacefully. The nobles assembled on 8 May and, according to Widukind of Corvey, elected him. During his first seven years he was constantly occupied with internal rivals and external enemies. His cousin Duke Henry II of Bavaria came into conflict with him over the see of Augsburg, and Otto invested Henry's candidate as bishop on 22 September 973 rather than risk civil war. In 974 Harald Bluetooth of Denmark rebelled and crossed into Germany with Norwegian support, but Otto countered him at the Danevirke when his Norwegian allies sailed home.

After a revolt of other Ottonians he excluded the Bavarian line from the imperial succession. In the west he granted the sons of Reginar III their confiscated inheritance in Lorraine and in 976 appointed his cousin Charles as Duke of Lower Lorraine.

From 980 Otto turned to Italy, supporting Pope Benedict VII and planning to annex the whole of the south, under the influence of Theophanu. This meant war with the Byzantine Empire and the Muslim Fatimid Caliphate. His campaigns ended in 982 with a disastrous defeat at Stilo. A rising of the Lutici Slavs followed in 983, which destroyed the bishoprics of Havelberg and Brandenburg and forced the Empire to abandon its holdings east of the Elbe.

Otto II died suddenly in his palace at Rome on 7 December 983, aged 28, after a malaria outbreak had halted his preparations to resume the campaign in the south. He was buried in the atrium of St. Peter's Basilica, the only Holy Roman emperor so buried. His three-year-old son Otto III succeeded him, which plunged the Empire into political crisis. Together with Theophanu he had founded the Benedictine Memleben Abbey, which became one of the richest imperial abbeys.
otto-iii-duke-of-bavaria: Otto was born in Burghausen on 11 February 1261, the son of Henry XIII, Duke of Bavaria, and Elizabeth of Hungary. He succeeded his father in 1290 as Duke of Lower Bavaria, together with his younger brothers Louis III and Stephen I. He was in opposition to Habsburg and tried to regain Styria, which Bavaria had lost in 1180. He supported Adolf, King of Germany, and fought on his side in the Battle of Göllheim. In January 1279 he married Catherine, a daughter of Rudolf I of Germany; their twin sons were born in 1280 and died the same year, and Catherine died on 4 April 1282.

The Hungarian crown was offered to Otto, a grandson of Béla IV of Hungary, in 1301, but he did not accept it before 1305. In August 1305 Wenceslaus III of Bohemia renounced his own claim on Otto's behalf. Because the Habsburg Albert I of Germany blocked the way through Austria, Otto disguised himself as a merchant and reached Buda in November 1305. He was crowned with the Holy Crown of Hungary at Székesfehérvár on 6 December 1305.

He was unable to strengthen his rule. In 1306 Charles of Anjou occupied Esztergom and other fortresses in the north, and the next year he took Buda. In June 1307 Otto visited the Voivode of Transylvania, Ladislaus Kán, who imprisoned him. The magnates at Rákos proclaimed Charles king on 10 October 1307, though some of the most powerful ignored him as well. At the end of the year Kán released Otto, who left the country, but Kán still refused to hand the Holy Crown to Charles. Otto abdicated in 1308.

While Otto was in Hungary his brother Stephen I ruled Lower Bavaria, and his involvement in Austrian and Hungarian affairs weakened his position there. In 1310 a new war against Habsburg devastated Burghausen. On 18 May 1309 he married Agnes of Glogau, and their children were Agnes and Henry XV. Otto died in Landshut on 9 November 1312, and Henry XV succeeded him. Hungarian historiography counts him as an anti-king of the interregnum of 1301–1310.
otto-iii-holy-roman-emperor: Otto III was born in June or July 980 somewhere between Aachen and Nijmegen, the only son of Otto II and Theophanu. He was crowned king of Germany in 983 at the age of three. His cousin Henry II of Bavaria, who had been deposed as duke in 976 and imprisoned, claimed the regency, and the Archbishop of Cologne granted it without substantial opposition; Theophanu objected, as did Adelaide of Italy. When Henry's rebellion in 984 failed to win the aristocracy's support, Theophanu became regent until her death in 991, and Adelaide then governed until the Imperial Diet at Solingen in September 994 allowed the 14-year-old king to rule without a regent.

Otto III set out for Italy from Ratisbon in March 996 to be crowned and to restore imperial control of Rome, where Crescentius II had revolted. He put down the rebellion and installed his cousin as Pope Gregory V, the first pope of German descent. After Otto left, Crescentius revolted again in 997 with the support of the Byzantine emperor Basil II, deposed Gregory and installed John Philagathos as the antipope John XVI. Otto returned in 998, reinstated Gregory and executed Crescentius and John XVI. When Gregory died in 999, Otto installed Sylvester II. He made Rome the administrative capital of his Empire.

In the east the Lutici had forced the Empire to abandon its lands beyond the Elbe in 983, and Otto fought to regain them with limited success. He supported mission work in Poland and the crowning of Stephen I as the first Christian king of Hungary. In December 999 he left Italy on a pilgrimage from Rome to Gniezno to pray at the grave of Adalbert, bishop of Prague, who had been martyred by the Old Prussians in 997 and whom Otto and Bolesław I of Poland worked to have canonised.

In 1001 the Roman aristocracy rebelled and forced Otto to flee the city. While marching to reclaim it in 1002 he suffered a sudden fever and died, aged 21, near Civita Castellana. Medieval sources speak of malaria. With no heir, he left a succession crisis, and Henry II of Bavaria was elected king in June 1002.

Contemporaries called him mirabilia mundi, the wonder of the world. Nineteenth-century historians portrayed him as an over-idealistic dreamer, while modern historians generally see him positively and still debate the intentions behind his Imperial Renovation programme.
otto-iv-holy-roman-emperor: Otto was the third son of Henry the Lion, Duke of Bavaria and Duke of Saxony, and Matilda of England. He grew up in England in the care of his grandfather, King Henry II, and became the foster son of his uncle, King Richard I. In 1190 Richard appointed him Earl of York, but the vassals of Yorkshire doubted the grant and prevented him from taking possession. In 1196 Richard, as Duke of Aquitaine, gave him the county of Poitou.

After the death of Emperor Henry VI most of the southern princes elected his brother Philip of Swabia king in March 1198. The opponents of the Hohenstaufen, on Richard's initiative, chose Otto, who was elected at Cologne on 9 June 1198 and crowned at Aachen on 12 July. The civil war drew in England and France, and Pope Innocent III, who wished to prevent the union of Sicily with the Empire, backed Otto. Philip gained ground, and Otto was defeated at Wassenberg in 1206. Philip was murdered on 21 June 1208, Otto was elected by all the princes at Frankfurt on 11 November 1208, and Innocent crowned him emperor on 4 October 1209.

Otto then broke his promises to the pope, taking back Ancona and Spoleto and declaring Frederick of Sicily's fiefs forfeit when Frederick refused homage. Innocent excommunicated him on 18 November 1210, and in 1211 several princes elected Frederick king. Allied with King John of England, Otto fought Philip II of France at Bouvines on 27 July 1214. His army broke when his wounded horse carried him from the field, and in 1215 he was deposed.

Otto spent his last years on his estates between the Harz Mountains and the heathlands. He fell ill at Harliburg Castle in early May 1218 and died on 19 May, after naming his brother Heinrich heir and executor. He married Beatrice of Swabia and then Maria of Brabant, and neither marriage produced children. He was the only German king of the Welf dynasty.
otto-of-greece: Otto was born on 1 June 1815 at Schloss Mirabell in Salzburg, the second son of Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria, a prominent philhellene who gave financial aid to the Greek cause during the War of Independence. As a teenager he was tutored in Classical Greek and Latin by the philhellene scholar Friedrich Thiersch, who first suggested him as a candidate for the Greek throne. The London Protocol of 1829 required that Greece be a monarchy under a prince not drawn from the ruling families of Britain, France or Russia. Prince Leopold of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha was chosen but rejected the crown, and after the assassination of Ioannis Kapodistrias in 1831 the Great Powers met in London and offered it to the 17-year-old Otto.

Otto's reign is usually divided into the regency of 1832 to 1835, absolute monarchy from 1835 to 1843 and constitutional monarchy from 1843 to 1862. His title was King of Greece, not King of the Hellenes, since the latter would have implied a claim to Greeks still under Ottoman rule. He arrived at Nafplio with 3,500 Bavarian troops and was welcomed warmly, wearing Greek costume and using the name Othon. The regency council of Bavarian officials under Count Josef Ludwig von Armansperg imposed financial stringency, and many Greeks saw its government as a foreign bureaucracy, the Bavarocracy. Otto moved the capital from Nafplio to Athens, then a small town of about 4,000 to 5,000 people, and the University of Athens was founded in 1837.

Otto married Duchess Amalia of Oldenburg in 1836, and the marriage produced no heir. As a Catholic he was viewed with suspicion by many pious Greeks. Greek politics turned on parties tied to Britain, France and Russia, and he tried to balance them. On 3 September 1843 infantry led by Colonel Dimitris Kallergis and General Yiannis Makriyiannis gathered in front of the palace in Athens and refused to leave until he granted a constitution. The square was renamed Constitution Square. British naval blockades in 1850 and 1854 damaged his standing, and in October 1862 he was deposed while in the countryside.

Otto died in exile in Bavaria on 26 July 1867. He saw himself as an enlightened absolutist and established educational institutions and several state services, but could not resolve Greece's poverty or the economic meddling of outside powers. Among the buildings of his reign are the Old Royal Palace, now the Greek Parliament Building, the National Library and the National Observatory of Athens. Because of Greek hostility to non-Greek rule, this side of his reign has received little historical attention.
otto-von-bismarck: Otto von Bismarck was born on 1 April 1815 at Schönhausen, a noble estate west of Berlin in Prussian Saxony. His father was a Junker estate owner and former Prussian officer, and his mother came from a family of senior civil servants in Berlin. In 1816 the family moved to its Pomeranian estate at Kniephof. He studied law at the University of Göttingen from 1832 to 1833 and then at the University of Berlin, and he knew English, French, Italian, Polish and Russian.

Others took him for a typical backwoods Prussian Junker, an image he encouraged by wearing military uniforms. In 1847 he was chosen as a representative to the newly created Prussian legislature, the Vereinigter Landtag, where he gained a reputation as a royalist and reactionary with a gift for stinging rhetoric.

In 1861 Wilhelm became King of Prussia and soon clashed with the Landtag, which in 1862 refused funds for a reorganisation of the army. On the advice of Albrecht von Roon he appointed Bismarck Minister President and Foreign Minister on 23 September 1862. Bismarck argued that the constitution had a legal loophole where a budget failed to pass, and kept collecting taxes on the basis of the 1861 budget for four years. With Roon's reorganisation of the army and Moltke's military strategy, his diplomacy brought wars with Denmark, Austria and France, and the creation of the German Empire.

In 1871 he was made a prince and the first Imperial Chancellor of the German Empire, while keeping his Prussian offices, so that he had nearly complete control of domestic and foreign policy. That year he began the Kulturkampf in Prussia, partly from fear of papal power; it failed, and the Catholics formed the Centre Party. His diplomacy aimed to keep Germany's position in a peaceful Europe.

Wilhelm I died in 1888 and Frederick III after 99 days. The new emperor, Wilhelm II, wanted rapid expansion and a larger German place in the sun. The final split came over Bismarck's attempt to make the Anti-Socialist Laws permanent. Wilhelm refused to open his reign with a bloody campaign against his own subjects, and Bismarck was forced to resign. Historians have praised him as the statesman who united Germany, and have also criticised his authoritarian rule.
otto-wille-kuusinen: Otto Wilhelm Kuusinen was born on 4 October 1881 at Laukaa in the Grand Duchy of Finland, the son of a village tailor. His mother died when he was two years old, and the family moved to Jyväskylä. He graduated from the Jyväskylä Lyceum in 1900 and entered the University of Helsinki, studying philosophy, aesthetics and art history, and took his degree as a candidate of philosophy in 1902. As a student he was interested in Fennoman conservatism and Alkioism.

In 1906 Kuusinen toppled the more moderate party chairman J. K. Kari and came to dominate the Social Democratic Party of Finland, of which he was chairman from 1911 to 1917. He sat in parliament in 1908 to 1910, 1911 to 1913 and 1916 to 1918. He was a leader of the January 1918 revolution that created the short-lived Finnish Socialist Workers' Republic, in which he was People's Commissar of Education. After the Reds were defeated in the Finnish Civil War he fled to Moscow and helped form the Finnish Communist Party. He became a prominent official of the Comintern and a leader in Soviet military intelligence, where he set up a network against the Scandinavian countries.

Finnish emigrants who went to the Soviet Union to build socialism suffered heavily in the Great Purge. Kuusinen's reputation in Finland was damaged because he was one of the very few not targeted by show trials, deportations and executions. When the Red Army advanced in the Winter War on 30 November 1939, he was pronounced head of the Finnish Democratic Republic, or Terijoki Government, a puppet regime through which Stalin meant to turn Finland into a socialist state. A treaty with the Soviet Union was signed in Moscow on 2 December 1939 by Molotov and Kuusinen. The war went otherwise than planned, and the Soviet leadership negotiated peace with Finland's legitimate government.

After the Winter War Kuusinen chaired the presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the Karelo-Finnish SSR from 1940 to 1956. He was a member of the Politburo in 1952 to 1953 and from 1957 to 1964, and a secretary of the Central Committee from 1957, and he kept his place under Nikita Khrushchev's de-Stalinization. He was an editor of the textbook Fundamentals of Marxism-Leninism and in 1958 was elected to the Soviet Academy of Sciences. He died in Moscow on 17 May 1964, aged 82, and his ashes were buried in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis. His 1926 report on work among the masses spoke of a solar system of organisations around the Communist Party.
ottokar-i-of-bohemia: Ottokar I (Czech: Přemysl Otakar I.) was the son of Vladislaus II, Duke of Bohemia, and Judith of Thuringia. His early years were passed amid the anarchy that prevailed across the country. After several military struggles he was recognised as ruler of Bohemia by Holy Roman Emperor Henry VI in 1192, but he was soon overthrown for joining a conspiracy of German princes to bring down the Hohenstaufen dynasty. In 1197 he forced his brother, Duke Vladislaus III, to abandon Bohemia to him and to content himself with Moravia.

Taking advantage of the civil war in Germany between the Hohenstaufen claimant Philip of Swabia and the Welf candidate Otto IV, Ottokar declared himself King of Bohemia in 1198 and was crowned in Mainz. Philip supported the title, as he needed Czech military support. In 1199 Ottokar divorced his wife Adelheid of Meissen to marry Constance of Hungary, daughter of King Béla III. In 1200, with Otto IV in the ascendant, he declared for the Welf faction, and Otto and later Pope Innocent III accepted him as hereditary king.

The imperial declaration of a new duke of Bohemia, Děpolt III, forced him back into Philip's camp, on condition that his divorced wife be allowed to return to Bohemia. He later supported the young Frederick II.

In 1212 Frederick II granted the Golden Bull of Sicily, which recognised Ottokar and his heirs as kings of Bohemia. The king was no longer subject to appointment by the emperor and had to attend diets only near the Bohemian border. Though a subject of the Holy Roman Empire, he was to be its leading electoral prince and to furnish emperors with a bodyguard of 300 knights when they went to Rome for their coronation. Two earlier Bohemian kings had held the title only for life.

His reign was also notable for the start of German immigration into Bohemia and the growth of towns in what had been forest land. In 1226 he went to war against Duke Leopold VI of Austria, who had wrecked a plan to marry Ottokar's daughter, Saint Agnes of Bohemia, to Frederick II's son Henry II of Sicily. She later entered a convent with the help of the pope.
ottokar-ii-of-bohemia: Ottokar was the second son of King Wenceslaus I of Bohemia and of Kunigunde, daughter of Philip of Swabia, through whom he was related to the Hohenstaufen emperors. He was first educated for an ecclesiastical career, while his elder brother Vladislaus was designated heir. When Vladislaus died in 1247, Ottokar became heir and was appointed Margrave of Moravia, residing in Brno and working on the reconstruction of lands devastated by the Mongol raids of 1242.

In 1248 discontented nobles who supported Emperor Frederick II drew him into a rebellion against his father. He was elected the younger king on 31 July 1248 and briefly expelled Wenceslaus from Prague Castle. Pope Innocent IV excommunicated him, and Wenceslaus defeated the rebels and imprisoned his son at Přimda Castle before the two were reconciled.

The father and son turned to the Duchy of Austria, left without a ruler after the last Babenberg duke, Frederick II, was killed in 1246. In 1251 the Austrian estates acclaimed Ottokar as duke, and on 11 February 1252 he married the duke's sister Margaret of Babenberg, who was much older than he. He succeeded to the Bohemian throne in 1253. Papal mediation settled a conflict with his cousin King Béla IV of Hungary over Styria, and in July 1260 Ottokar defeated the Hungarians at the Battle of Kressenbrunn. He then married Kunigunda of Halych, Béla's granddaughter, and she became the mother of his children, among them Wenceslaus II.

During the imperial interregnum he occupied the Egerland in 1266, inherited Carinthia and Carniola from Ulrich III of Carinthia in 1269 and acquired Friuli in 1272. His bids for the imperial crown failed, and in 1273 the electors chose Rudolf of Habsburg. Rudolf ordered the return of imperial lands, placed Ottokar under the imperial ban in 1275 and besieged Vienna. A rebellion led by Záviš of Falkenstein weakened Ottokar, and in November 1276 he gave up Austria and its neighbouring duchies, keeping Bohemia and Moravia. In 1278 he tried to regain them and was killed at the Battle on the Marchfeld on 26 August.

Ottokar's body was laid out in the Minorites Church in Vienna and moved to St Vitus Cathedral in Prague in 1297. His six-year-old son Wenceslaus II succeeded him. He founded about thirty towns, granted them charters and encouraged German-speaking settlers. He built or promoted castles such as Zvíkov, Křivoklát and Bezděz. The Zemské desky, the oldest preserved source of Czech law, dates from his time.
ottoman-empire: As the Rum Sultanate declined in the 13th century, Anatolia became a patchwork of independent Turkish principalities known as the Anatolian Beyliks. One of them, in the Bithynia region on the Byzantine frontier, was led by Osman I, a figure of obscure origin from whom the name Ottoman is derived. His early followers were Turkish tribal groups and Byzantine renegades, not all of them Muslim. A Byzantine defeat at the Battle of Bapheus in 1302 contributed to his rise.

How the early Ottomans came to dominate their neighbours is not well understood, because sources are lacking. The Ghaza thesis, popular in the 20th century, credited their success to rallying religious warriors, but it is no longer generally accepted.

Osman's son Orhan captured the city of Bursa in 1326 and made it the capital.
