The Ottomans expanded into the Balkans in the mid-14th century, and their victory in Kosovo in 1389 effectively ended Serbian power in the region. Mehmed II ended the Byzantine Empire with the conquest of Constantinople in 1453. Further conquests by Selim I led the sultans to adopt the title of caliph, and in the 16th century, in the reign of Suleiman, the empire became a global power.

Modern scholarship holds that the empire began to decline after its defeat at the Second Siege of Vienna in 1683, though it kept a flexible economy, society and military into much of the 18th century. The Tanzimat reforms of the 19th century made the state more powerful and organised. The Young Turk Revolution of 1908 re-established a constitutional monarchy. During the First World War the empire engaged in genocide against Armenians, Assyrians and Greeks. The Allies occupied and partitioned it afterwards, and the Turkish War of Independence under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk ended the sultanate in 1922.

Before the reforms of the 19th and 20th centuries the state had two dimensions, a military and a civil administration, with the sultan at the top. It first divided its territory into provinces with governors appointed by the sultan in the late 14th century, and the Vilayet Law of 1864 established the vilayet as the top of a new hierarchy. The empire granted varying levels of autonomy to its confessional communities, or millets, to manage their own affairs under Islamic law.

Mehmed II and Bayezid welcomed Jews fleeing persecution in Europe and settled them in Istanbul and Salonica. The empire's annual income quadrupled between 1523 and 1748, adjusted for inflation. Turkish was the predominant literary language, though Persian was the preferred vehicle for the imperial image. Slavery was part of Ottoman society, mostly as domestic service, and it was never abolished in the empire.
ottonian-dynasty: The family's earliest known member is the Saxon count Liudolf (d. 866), who held large estates on the Leine river west of the Harz and in the Eichsfeld of Thuringia. About 852 he and his wife Oda, with Bishop Altfrid of Hildesheim, founded Brunshausen Abbey, which after its move to Gandersheim became the family monastery and burial ground. In 869 his daughter Liutgard married Louis the Younger, son of the Carolingian king Louis the German.

Liudolf's son Otto the Illustrious was, according to the Saxon chronicler Widukind of Corvey, already a candidate for the East Frankish crown in 911, when it passed instead to the Franconian duke Conrad I. Otto died in 912, and his son Henry the Fowler succeeded him as Duke of Saxony.

Elected king in May 919, Henry won the support of the Franconian, Bavarian, Swabian and Lotharingian dukes and in 933 defeated the Hungarians at the Battle of Riade. Otto I put down revolts by his brother Duke Henry I of Bavaria and his son Duke Liudolf of Swabia, reducing the dukes to royal subjects, and made the Church in Germany a base of royal power. He was crowned emperor by Pope John XII, married his heir to Theophanu, niece of the Byzantine emperor John I Tzimiskes, and in 968 established the Archbishopric of Magdeburg.

Otto II was defeated by the Saracens at the Battle of Stilo in 982, faced the Great Slav Rising in 983 and died that year aged 28, leaving a three-year-old son for whom Empress Theophanu acted as regent. Otto III installed his confidants Bruno of Carinthia and Gerbert of Aurillac as popes and in 1000 travelled to the Congress of Gniezno; expelled from Rome in 1001, he died the next year aged 21. Henry II, of the Bavarian line, was crowned king on 7 June 1002 and emperor by Pope Benedict VIII on 14 February 1014, and founded the Bishopric of Bamberg in 1007.

Henry II's marriage to Cunigunde of Luxembourg was childless, and with his death in 1024 the dynasty became extinct. The crown passed to Conrad II of the Salian dynasty, a great-grandson of Liutgarde, daughter of Otto I; the Salians held the imperial throne until 1125. Pope Eugene III canonized Henry II in 1146. Historians disagree about how the Ottonians governed: those following Karl Leyser stress oral and ritual means, while others, such as David Bachrach, argue for the continued use of writing in administration.
ouadane: Ouadane, also written Wādān, is a small town in the desert region of central Mauritania, on the southern edge of the Adrar Plateau, 93 kilometres north-east of Chinguetti. It was a staging post in the trans-Saharan trade and for caravans carrying slabs of salt from the mines at Idjil. The old town, a World Heritage Site, is in ruins but still substantially intact, and a small modern settlement lies outside its gate. The commune has a total area of 118,210 square kilometres, mostly desert.

The early history of Ouadane is uncertain, though the town may have prospered from the trans-Saharan gold trade. In the middle of the 11th century the geographer al-Bakri described a route for gold in the time of the Ghana Empire, but historians disagree on whether it passed through Ouadane. Caravan traffic would have declined from the beginning of the 13th century, when the oasis of Oualata replaced Aoudaghost as the southern terminus of the route.

The first written reference is by the Portuguese writer Ca' de Mosto in the middle of the 15th century. Gomes Eanes de Zurara described Ouadane as the most important town of the Adrar and the only one with a surrounding wall. Fifty years later Valentim Fernandes wrote of the salt trade and of the town's role as an entrepôt, giving a population of 400. Duarte Pacheco Pereira, writing in 1505–1508, reckoned about 300 hearths, which suggests 1,500 to 1,800 people. According to Pereira, the Portuguese built an entrepôt there in 1487, probably short-lived.

In the 16th century the Moroccans tried to take control of the trans-Saharan trade, especially in gold from the Sudan. They sent expeditions to occupy Ouadane in 1543–44 and again in 1584, and in 1591 their victory at the Battle of Tondibi led to the collapse of the Songhay Empire.

Tegherbeyat, the upper ruined section of the town, is almost certainly the oldest. The ruins of the lower section include a mosque probably built in the 15th century, when the town expanded; some horseshoe arches still stand, and the mosque was probably abandoned in the 19th century. Ouadane is the closest town to the Richat Structure, a large circular landmark visible from space.
ouahigouya: Ouahigouya lies in northern Burkina Faso, 182 kilometres north-west of Ouagadougou, to which it is linked by an asphalted road. It is the capital of the Yatenga Province and of the Ouahigouya Department, and the biggest town of the Nord Region. In the Mossi language its name is Wayugyã. The climate is hot semi-arid, and the region depends heavily on rainfall.

The town was the capital of Yatenga, one of a number of Mossi kingdoms, and its name still records that role: it is said to mean come and prostrate yourselves. Its features include the tomb of Naaba Kango and the compound of the Yatenga Naba, together with an artificial lake. In the Christmas War of 1985 the town's marketplace was bombed by Malian forces, and almost 100 people were killed.

The town had a population of 124,587 in 2019 and is the fourth largest in the country. It has a stadium, a private non-profit paediatric hospital with 36 beds for births and 24 beds for children suffering from severe malnutrition, a post office with internet access and an Ecobank branch.

The economy rests mainly on agriculture, with some commerce and craft. Two dams north and west of the town allow irrigated vegetable growing, chiefly potatoes, tomatoes, carrots and onions, while millet and sorghum are the basis of the local diet. Craft work centres on leather and tanneries, and the town buys manufactured goods in Ouagadougou for resale locally. Its one sister city is Decatur in the United States.
ouidah: Ouidah, also written Whydah and known locally as Glexwe, meaning farmhouse, was the chief port of the Kingdom of Whydah. By local tradition Kpassa founded the town, probably towards the end of the 16th century. The Portuguese reached the coast in 1580, and its role in international trade rose after the Royal African Company built a fort there in 1650. Brandenburg established forts between 1682 and 1700, alongside the English and the Dutch. By 1716 the Kingdom of Whydah had become the second largest slave port in the triangular trade, as the crew of the slave ship Whydah Gally noted when it arrived to buy 500 slaves from King Haffon.

King Agaja of Dahomey captured the kingdom in 1727, and a report in The Boston News-Letter of 19 March 1727 described the destruction as so great that it could not be represented. In 1860 the port sent the last recorded shipment of slaves to the United States, aboard the Clotilda to Mobile, Alabama, although the country had prohibited the transatlantic slave trade in 1808; the last shipment to Spanish Cuba was as late as 1873. France captured the town in 1894, by which time it had declined after the outlawing of the slave trade.

Ouidah's importance arose because French, Portuguese and English powers competed for influence, weakening their overall authority. The Portuguese Fort of São João Baptista de Ajudá was built from 1721 on land given by King Haffon, and stayed under Portuguese control until 1961. William's Fort began as an English trading post in the late 17th century. Unlike the forts of the Gold Coast, the forts at Ouidah lacked real authority: they were not sovereign, paid rent to local rulers and deferred to them, first in Hueda and then in Dahomey.

William's Fort relied heavily on African labour, enslaved and free, and its records document wages and prices. Its surrounding population, Sogbadji, was ethnically diverse, and some families there descend from fort employees, such as soldiers, a linguist and a boatswain. A shrine to a local deity stood within the fort, and Dahomian kings sent priests to make offerings at the graves of English governors buried there.

Ouidah is often considered the spiritual capital of the Vodun religion. Its landmarks include the Maison du Brésil, a restored mansion of Brazilian slavers, a Vodun python temple, the Basilique de l'Immaculée Conception and the Sacred Forest of Kpasse, with bronze statues. The Route des Esclaves, by which captives were taken to the beach, has statues and monuments, among them the Door of No Return, a memorial arch. The site was added to UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List on 31 October 1996.
oujda: Oujda is the largest city and the capital of the Oriental region of north-eastern Morocco. It lies about 15 kilometres west of the Algerian border, south of the Beni Iznassen Mountains and about 55 kilometres south of the Mediterranean coast, at an altitude of about 450 metres. The climate is semi-arid, with 300 to 500 millimetres of rain a year. Because it stands on the frontier, the city's economy depends heavily on trade and on the state of the border, which has been closed since 1994.

There is some evidence of a settlement in the Roman period, apparently under Berber rather than Roman control. Ziri ibn Atiyya, a Berber chief of the Zenata Maghrawa, founded the city in 994. He had been authorised to occupy the region of Fes but felt insecure there and wished to be nearer his tribe's homeland in the central Maghrib, so he garrisoned Oujda and appointed a relative as governor. Yusuf ibn Tashfin occupied it in 1079, and in the following century it came under Almohad control.

Oujda held a strategic place between the Marinids of Fes and the Abdalwadids of the Kingdom of Tlemcen. The Marinid sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub destroyed it in 1271 after defeating Sultan Yaghmorasan. In 1296 his successor Abu Yaqub Yusuf took it again and rebuilt the town with new walls, a palace and the Great Mosque that still stands. From the 16th century it was contested between the Saadis and then the Alaouites of Morocco and the Ottoman Empire to the east. It was only in 1795 that the Alaouites retook it and permanently incorporated it into Morocco.

French forces occupied the city in 1859, and in 1907 and 1908 it was taken again and used as a French military base to control eastern Morocco; its modern infrastructure was first developed in that period. Anti-Jewish riots in June 1948 killed 47 Jews and one French person. From 1954 Morocco allowed Oujda to be the logistic centre of the Oujda Group during the Algerian war of independence.

The old city at the centre keeps narrow, winding alleys and markets, and the Grand Mosque of Oujda is among its historically most important. Just outside the city are the ruins of a Roman fort, Bled el Gaada, measuring 175 by 210 metres. Oujda is one of the main Moroccan centres of Gharnati music, a style of Andalusi music, and holds an international festival of it each year.
our-lady-of-guadalupe: According to the Nican Mopohua, a Nahuatl text included in the 17th-century Huei tlamahuiçoltica, the Virgin Mary appeared four times to Juan Diego, a Chichimec peasant, and once to his uncle, Juan Bernardino. The first apparition, on the morning of Saturday 9 December 1531 by the Julian calendar, took place on the Hill of Tepeyac, now part of a suburb of Mexico City. The young woman spoke to him in Nahuatl, called herself the mother of the very true deity and asked for a church to be built on the site. Archbishop Juan de Zumárraga did not believe Juan Diego, and she told him to keep insisting.

The name has a Spanish background. The shrine of Guadalupe in Extremadura was the most important Marian shrine of medieval Castile, and many conquistadors came from the town. Luis Becerra Tanco proposed in 1675 that the name was a Spanish rendering of a Nahuatl word, since Nahuatl lacks the sounds d and g.

One of the first printed accounts of the apparitions was published in 1648 by the priest Miguel Sánchez. The Codex Escalada, a parchment dated to 1548, has been cited as an earlier mention, though the historians Alberto Peralta and Stafford Poole question its authenticity.

The image on Juan Diego's cloak, the tilma, shows a life-sized young woman with dark hair and olive skin, her eyes downcast and her hands joined in prayer. She wears a pink dress with a floral design and a blue-green mantle edged with gold and starred, and she stands on a crescent moon held by an angel, within a golden sunburst. The tilma measures about 1.72 by 1.07 metres and is made of two pieces sewn together.

Miguel Sánchez read the figure as the Woman of the Apocalypse. Virgil Elizondo argues that indigenous people also saw their own deities in it, for the blue-green mantle was the colour reserved for the divine couple Ometecuhtli and Omecihuatl. It hangs above the main altar of the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, in Mexico City.

Pope Benedict XIV declared her patroness of New Spain in 1754, Leo XIII authorised the coronation of the image, carried out in 1895, and Pius X made her patroness of Mexico in 1910. Juan Diego was beatified on 6 May 1990 by Pope John Paul II. The shrine is the most visited Catholic pilgrimage destination in the world. The devotion became a national symbol. The first president of Mexico took the name Guadalupe Victoria, and Miguel Hidalgo in 1810 and Emiliano Zapata in 1910 led their forces under Guadalupan flags. Cesar Chavez led the 1966 farm workers' pilgrimage from Delano to Sacramento under her banner.
ouro-preto: In 1695 Manuel Borba Gato found gold at Rio das Velhas, the start of the Brazilian Gold Rush, and a gold-bearing stream was found at Itacolomi between 1695 and 1696. Vila Rica, meaning Rich Town, was established in 1698, and in 1711 several small settlements were united as a municipality. Vila Rica became the capital of Minas Gerais from 1720 and was the focal point of Brazil's golden age under Portuguese rule. Officially 800 tons of gold were sent to Portugal in the 18th century, not counting what moved illegally or stayed in the colony, as in the gold used to decorate churches.

The wealth drew the intelligentsia of Europe, and the baroque revival known as the Barroco Mineiro flourished, seen in the sculptor Aleijadinho, the painter Manoel da Costa Ataíde, the composer Lobo de Mesquita and the poet Tomás António Gonzaga. It became one of the most populous cities of Latin America, about 40,000 people in 1730 and 80,000 in 1750, when São Paulo had fewer than 8,000.

In 1789 the town was the birthplace of the Inconfidência Mineira, a failed attempt to gain independence from Portugal. Its leader, Joaquim José da Silva Xavier, known as Tiradentes, was hanged as a warning to future revolutionaries. On 20 May 1823 the village was raised to a city and took the name Ouro Preto, meaning Black Gold, from the gold covered with a layer of iron oxide found there. The Escola de Minas was created in 1876. In 1897 the state government moved to the new planned city of Belo Horizonte, because the needs of government had outgrown the town in its valley.

Ouro Preto lies in the Serra do Espinhaço mountains of Minas Gerais, Brazil, and its centre keeps well-preserved Portuguese colonial architecture with few signs of modern development. Its 18th- and 19th-century churches are decorated with gold and with the sculptures of Aleijadinho, and it was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its Baroque colonial architecture. The Museu da Inconfidência occupies the former municipal palace on Tiradentes Square. The Universidade Federal de Ouro Preto has about 10,000 students, many living in communal houses called repúblicas, a tradition shared with the University of Coimbra.
outer-mongolia: Outer Mongolia was the name of a territory of the Manchu-led Qing dynasty from 1691 to 1911. It is contrasted with Inner Mongolia, which was more directly administered by the Qing court. Outer Mongolia lay further from the capital Beijing and had a greater degree of autonomy within the empire. Its administrative region consisted only of the four Khalkha aimags: Setsen Khan, Tüsheet Khan, Sain Noyon Khan and Zasagt Khan. In the late Qing period the name was also used for the Khalkha and Oirat regions together with the directly ruled Tannu Uriankhai, and the territory corresponds to modern Mongolia and the Russian republic of Tuva.

During the Xinhai Revolution the region gained de facto independence from Qing China. The Republic of China claimed it as an integral part of the state, having acquired the legal right to inherit all Qing territories through the Imperial Edict of the Abdication of the Qing Emperor. Most of the region was in practice under the control of the Bogd Khanate, which was largely unrecognised internationally. The Republic of China briefly established de facto rule over most of it from 1919 to 1921. Since 1928 the Kuomintang used the term Mongolia Area to distinguish its claim from Outer Mongolia.

The Nationalist government formally recognised Mongolian independence on 5 January 1946 under Soviet pressure. The Kuomintang government, by then retreated to Taiwan, rescinded the recognition in 1953, after the Soviet Union violated the Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship and Alliance, and Republic of China maps showed the claim until 2002, when a government led by the Democratic Progressive Party recognised Mongolia again. The People's Republic of China has recognised the Mongolian People's Republic since 1949 and has full diplomatic relations with Mongolia.

Outer Mongolia is still sometimes used informally for the independent state of Mongolia. Chinese sources generally call that state Měnggǔ Guó, the State of Mongolia, a translation of its official Mongolian name Mongol Uls, to avoid confusion with Inner Mongolia in China. Mongolian and Chinese also have the terms Ar Mongol and Mobei Mongol, North-of-the-Desert Mongolia, which imply a geographic unity and leave out the history of Qing rule. In English the phrase is also used colloquially for a place very far away.
ouyang-xiu: Ouyang Xiu, courtesy name Yongshu, was born in Sichuan, where his father was a judge, though his family came from present-day Jishui in Jiangxi. The family was relatively poor. His father died when he was three, and his literate mother was responsible for much of his early education. Unable to afford tutoring, he was largely self-taught, and the writings of Han Yu influenced him particularly. He passed the jinshi examination in 1030, on his third attempt, at the age of 22.

His first post was a judgeship in Luoyang, where he found others who shared his interest in Han Yu and founded a group that made his ancient prose style a public cause. In 1034 he became a collator of texts at the Imperial Academy in Kaifeng and came to know Fan Zhongyan, whom he defended when Fan was demoted, and for which he was himself demoted. In 1043 he and Fan spurred the Qingli Reforms, a ten-point platform that included better entrance examinations, an end to favouritism in appointments and higher salaries. The emperor rescinded the changes, and Ouyang was sent to the provinces. He returned to the central government in 1054 and by 1060 was assistant councillor of the state.

He headed the commission that compiled the New Book of Tang, completed in 1060. Around the accession of Emperor Shenzong in 1067 he was charged with several crimes, charges that had no credibility but damaged his reputation, and was sent to posts in Shandong and Anhui. There he refused to carry out Wang Anshi's low-interest loans to farmers. He was allowed to retire in 1071 and died in 1072. Wang Anshi, though his opponent, wrote a moving tribute to him.

Following Han Yu, Ouyang promoted the Classical Prose Movement, and he is counted among the Eight Masters of the Tang and Song. His best-known essay is the Zuiwengting Ji, an account of the Old Toper's Pavilion near Chuzhou, acclaimed as one of the highest achievements of Chinese travel writing. He wrote the Historical Records of the Five Dynasties privately and alone, the only one of the Twenty-Four Histories so written, though it was not discovered until after his death. Critics have found him overly didactic as a historian, but he helped establish epigraphy as a historical method. His poems, in both shi and ci, are relaxed and often self-mocking.
ovambo-people: The Ovambo are a group of kindred Bantu-speaking peoples who inhabit what was formerly called Ovamboland, the flat, sandy and grassy plains of northern Namibia and the Cunene Province of southwestern Angola. In Namibia the groups include the Ndonga, Kwanyama, Kwambi, Ngandjera, Mbalantu, Kolonkadhi, Kwaluudhi and Mbandja, and the Kwanyama are the largest. Seasonal rains flood the area through water courses called oshanas, and the Ovambo adapted their housing, agriculture and livestock practices to the changes between wet and dry seasons. They started migrating to the area from the region of Zambia around the 14th century and expanded further south into Namibia in the 17th century.

Before the 19th century the Ovambo were largely unaffected by Swahili-Arab and European traders. When Germany established a colony in Namibia in 1884 it left them undisturbed and concentrated on the south and the coast. After the First World War South Africa took over the territory as South West Africa and brought plantations, cattle ranching and mining to Ovamboland. In the 1920s and 1930s the Ovambo rose several times against South African rule, and the Union Defence Force suppressed each rising. A veterinary line, the Police Zone, kept the Ovambo from moving south without permits, and the German and later colonial authorities preserved their traditional authorities to work with.

Because of a labour shortage, in part a result of the Herero and Nama genocide of 1907–1908, many Ovambo went south as migrant labourers, under racial segregation and highly restricted rights. South Africa introduced apartheid rule in Ovamboland in 1948. It declared Ovamboland an independent province in 1973 and appointed chiefs aligned with its policies, which the Ovambo rejected, and the appointed chief minister was assassinated in 1975. Together with the SWAPO movement, Namibia and its Ovambo people gained independence in 1990. In 1915 Portugal launched a violent campaign in the Ovambo territories of Angola, in which its forces massacred people and burned villages.

The Ovambo live a settled life based on farming and herding. Millet, sorghum and beans are the staple crops, and cattle, goats and sheep are kept mainly for milk, with hunting, fishing and gathering as supplements. A homestead is a complex of huts, each with its own purpose, inside a fence of large vertical poles. Each tribe had a hereditary chief, and descent is matrilineal, so that chieftainship passes through the maternal line.

Traditional belief names a supreme being, Kalunga, with rites centred on a sacred fire. Finnish Lutheran missionaries arrived in the 1870s, and most Ovambo are now Lutheran, with traditional practices such as the sacred fire and invoking Kalunga continuing in a mixed form of Christianity.
ovid: Publius Ovidius Naso was born on 20 March 43 BCE in the Paelignian town of Sulmo, in an Apennine valley east of Rome, into an important equestrian family. He and his brother, who excelled at oratory, were educated in rhetoric in Rome. Their father wanted Ovid to practise law, but after his brother died at 20 Ovid renounced law and travelled to Athens, Asia Minor and Sicily. He held minor public posts but resigned, probably around 29 to 25 BCE, to pursue poetry, a decision his father apparently disapproved. He belonged to the circle of the patron Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus, claims to have heard Horace recite, and only barely met Virgil. He married three times and had divorced twice by thirty.

For the first 25 years of his career Ovid wrote mainly elegiac poetry on erotic themes. His earliest surviving work is thought to be the Heroides, letters from mythological heroines such as Penelope, Dido and Medea to their absent lovers, perhaps published in 19 BCE. He is ranked with Virgil and Horace as one of the three canonical poets of Latin literature.

He enjoyed enormous popularity, but the emperor Augustus exiled him to Tomis on the Black Sea, the capital of the newly organised province of Moesia, where he spent the last nine or ten years of his life. Ovid blamed a carmen et error, a poem and a mistake, but gave no specifics, and scholars have speculated on the cause since. His last wife helped him during his exile. He died there in 17 or 18 CE.

Ovid's best-known work is the Metamorphoses, a continuous mythological narrative in fifteen books of dactylic hexameters, which remains one of the most important sources of classical mythology. In elegiac couplets he also wrote the Ars Amatoria, or The Art of Love, and the Fasti. Scholars regard his Corinna as an invention rather than a real woman.

In the Middle Ages and the Renaissance he became one of the best known and most loved Roman poets. The French Ovide moralisé moralised the Metamorphoses and influenced Chaucer, and Arthur Golding's translation of 1567 was used in Tudor grammar schools and shaped writers such as Christopher Marlowe and William Shakespeare.
oviedo: The Kingdom of Asturias began in 720 with the revolt of the Visigothic aristocrat Pelagius against the Muslims who held most of the Iberian Peninsula. The hillside where Oviedo stands was then uninhabited, with no Visigothic or Roman settlement before it. It is said that two monks, Máximo and Fromestano, founded the city, and a small church dedicated to Saint Vincent soon followed. In 794 Emir Hisham I sacked and pillaged Oviedo in one of his campaigns against the Christian kingdoms.

Fruela I (757–768) was the first decided promoter of the city and built a palace and a nearby church. Alfonso II the Chaste (791–842) is credited with establishing it as a capital: the court was moved here from Pravia, and the Cathedral of San Salvador and a royal palace formed the nucleus of the city. His reign also saw the church of San Julián de los Prados. Ramiro I (842–850) added Santa María del Naranco, probably planned as a palace, and San Miguel de Lillo, while facing rebellions by the Counts of the Palace.

Oviedo is the capital of the Principality of Asturias and its administrative and commercial centre, with a population of 223,576. It lies between the Nalón and Nora rivers, about 24 km southwest of Gijón, and has a maritime climate. After the royal court moved to León following the death of Alfonso III in 910, the city's life stayed tied to the relics in its cathedral and to pilgrims travelling on to Santiago de Compostela. The Cámara Santa, dating from 802 and attached to the cathedral, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and houses the Arca Santa, which holds the Sudarium of Oviedo.

The University of Oviedo was created in 1574 and inaugurated on 21 September 1608 under the will of Archbishop Fernando de Valdés Salas. In October 1934 about 50,000 workers, mostly miners, captured the city in the Asturian miners' strike, and troops sent by General Francisco Franco retook it, leaving about 3,000 rebels dead. The Siege of Oviedo in 1936 lasted three months, until the garrison was relieved in 1937. The city inspired the fictional Vetusta of Leopoldo Alas's novel La Regenta and hosts the Princess of Asturias Awards.
ovra: After the young Anteo Zamboni tried to assassinate Benito Mussolini in Bologna on 31 October 1926, the Italian government quickly passed repressive laws. All parties and associations opposed to the regime were dissolved. On 25 November 1926 the State Defence Law set up a Special Court to try those accused of being enemies of the state and restored the death penalty. The public security code enacted in 1926 specified a department of political police as a special division of the force. Its existence stayed secret until December 1930, when the official press agency Agenzia Stefani named the OVRA as a special section of the police.

Arturo Bocchini appointed the inspector Francesco Nudi as head of the OVRA; he was later replaced by Guido Leto. The organisation compiled files on around 130,000 potential subversives with the aid of approximately 100,000 informants, and by 1930 it was organising around 20,000 raids each week. About 6,000 of those it arrested, mainly communists and members of Giustizia e Libertà, are believed to have been tried by the Special Court or exiled to remote Mediterranean islands, where conditions were extremely poor. It also kept the Casellario Politico Centrale, an archive of personal profiles of known subversives.

The OVRA spied on Pope Pius XI, blackmailing priests into informing; the historian David Kertzer described its network in the Vatican as robust. Heinrich Himmler met Bocchini repeatedly, and the two police forces signed a secret protocol of cooperation on 2 April 1936. During the Second World War the OVRA was used against resistance groups in the Balkans, and in 1943 it tried to infiltrate the British Special Operations Executive with double agents. Many agents followed Mussolini to the Italian Social Republic, where they were favoured targets of communist partisans.

The OVRA was officially disbanded after the war, but a decree of 26 April 1945 ordered that the central political archive be maintained. A new police division, the Servizio Informazioni Speciali, took over its management, and many former OVRA officers were reinstated in it; its head, Inspector General Santoro, had been one of Leto's deputies. Most of the public security laws of 1931 were kept in force by the Italian Republic, and Leto himself was later reinstated as a police officer and put in charge of supervising the police academies.
owain-glyndwr: Owain ap Gruffudd Fychan was born in or before 1359, the son of Gruffudd Fychan and Elen ferch Tomas. His father's family descended from Madog ap Maredudd, last ruler of a united Powys, and held land by Welsh barony, a tenure that owed the Crown only military service. His father held the lordship of Glyndyfrdwy and half of Cynllaith, and on his death shortly before 1370 Owain inherited both and became known as Owain Glyndŵr.

He may have spent his youth in the household of the Fitzalan earls of Arundel and may have trained in law at the Inns of Court. He married Margaret Hanmer, daughter of the lawyer David Hanmer, and they had five or six sons and four or five daughters.

In the late 1390s a dispute with his neighbour Baron Grey of Ruthin, who had seized land and whose influence at the court of Henry IV blocked Owain's appeals, pushed him towards rebellion. On 16 September 1400 at Sycharth he was proclaimed Prince of Wales by about 300 followers, and he soon attacked Ruthin, Denbigh, Rhuddlan, Flint, Holt, Oswestry and Welshpool. Penal laws passed against the Welsh in response increased support for him across Wales.

By 1404 four royal expeditions into Wales had been repelled and Owain held parliaments at Machynlleth and Harlech, with envoys from France, Scotland and León. In February 1405 he agreed the Tripartite Indenture with Edmund Mortimer and Henry Percy, Earl of Northumberland, dividing England and Wales among the three. In the Pennal Letter to Charles VI of France, written on 31 March 1406, he set out plans for two universities, the laws of Hywel Dda and an independent Welsh church.

From 1405 the rebels suffered defeats, and Owain's brother Tudur ap Gruffudd died at the Battle of Pwll Melyn. By 1409 English forces had taken the last castles, Harlech and Aberystwyth. Owain refused two royal pardons and fought on as a guerrilla, but he was never captured. The circumstances of his death are unknown, and the most credible accounts place his burial in Herefordshire.

In Welsh tradition he became a folk hero, a foretold son who would free his people. Shakespeare portrays him as Owen Glendower in Henry IV, Part 1. Cymru Fydd revived his reputation in the late 19th century as a father of Welsh nationalism.
oxford: Oxford is a cathedral city and the county town of Oxfordshire, at the confluence of the River Thames, known locally as the Isis, and the River Cherwell. The rivers meet south of the city centre, and they and their flood plains constrain its size. Carfax Tower is usually considered the middle of the city, where Cornmarket Street, Queen Street, St Aldate's and the High Street meet. Its name comes from the Old English Oxenaforda, ford of the oxen, a shallow crossing of the river, and the ford and the town's control of the upper Thames gave it strategic importance.

Oxford was founded in the eighth century and was granted city status in 1542. It was historically an important port on the Thames, and the Oxford-Burcot Commission of the 17th century tried to improve navigation to it. The Oxford Canal reached the city in 1790 and linked it with the industrial Midlands, bringing a steady supply of cheap coal. Salters Steamers, founded in Oxford in 1858, helped popularise pleasure boating on the Upper Thames.

Brewing was long established: several colleges had private breweries, one of them at Brasenose surviving until 1889, and in the 16th century brewing and malting appear to have been the most popular trades. By 1874 there were nine breweries in the city. Morris Motors was established in 1910, making Oxford an important centre of motor manufacturing.

Oxford is home to the University of Oxford, the oldest university in the English-speaking world, with buildings in every style of English architecture since late Anglo-Saxon. Its Ashmolean Museum, the world's first university museum, was built in 1678-1683 to house a cabinet of curiosities given to the university in 1677. Joseph Haydn received an honorary doctorate there in 1791, commemorated by three concerts at the Sheldonian Theatre; his Symphony No. 92 is nicknamed the Oxford. The city has been closely associated with religious life: it was the birthplace of the Oxford Movement in Anglicanism and of the Wesleyan Church, and the Lollard movement followed the expulsion of the theologian John Wycliffe from the university in 1381.
oxfordshire: Oxfordshire lies between the River Thames to the south, the Cotswolds to the west, the Chilterns to the east and the Midlands to the north. Its landscape has two bands of hills, in the north and the south, separated by a low clay vale around the Thames. The north-west includes part of the Cotswolds, and the south the Berkshire Downs and the Chiltern Hills, known for the Uffington White Horse. The highest point is White Horse Hill, 261 metres. Many smaller rivers feed the Thames, among them the Thame, Windrush, Evenlode and Cherwell, and the Oxford Canal follows the Cherwell from Banbury to Oxford.

Oxfordshire was recorded as a county in the early years of the 10th century. It had some significance as valuable agricultural land in the centre of the country but was largely ignored by the Romans, and it grew in importance only with the formation of a settlement at Oxford in the 8th century. The name of the county town comes from the Anglo-Saxon Oxenaford, a ford for oxen. Alfred the Great was born across the Thames at Wantage, in the Vale of White Horse. The University of Oxford was founded in 1096, though its collegiate structure developed later.

From the 13th century the area took part in the Cotswolds wool trade, which brought wealth especially to the western part of the county. For most of its history the county was divided into fourteen hundreds, among them Bampton, Banbury, Bloxham, Dorchester and Thame. Morris Motors was founded in Oxford in 1912 and brought heavy industry to an otherwise agricultural county. In 1974, under the Local Government Act 1972, Abingdon, Didcot, Faringdon, Wallingford and Wantage, historically part of Berkshire, were added to the administrative county.

Oxfordshire is a ceremonial county in South East England and is largely rural, with five local government districts. Oxford is the largest settlement, and other towns include Banbury, Bicester, Abingdon-on-Thames, Didcot and Witney. Its buildings include the Sheldonian Theatre, built from 1664 to 1668 to a design by Sir Christopher Wren, and the Radcliffe Camera, built from 1737 to 1749 to a design by James Gibbs. Blenheim Palace, near Woodstock, was designed and partly built by John Vanbrugh for John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough, after the Battle of Blenheim, and is a World Heritage Site.
oxus: The Amu Darya, historically the Oxus, rises in the Pamir Mountains, north of the Hindu Kush, where the Vakhsh and Panj rivers meet on the border between Afghanistan and Tajikistan. It flows north-westwards through or along Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan towards the Aral Sea, and is about 2,400 kilometres long. Its basin covers more than half a million square kilometres, and nearly all its water comes from glaciers in the Pamirs and the Tian Shan, since it rarely rains in the lowlands. It is navigable for over 1,450 kilometres. Use of its water for irrigation has been a major cause of the Aral Sea's shrinking since the late 1950s.

In the late 3rd millennium BCE the watershed was home to a river valley civilisation that was forgotten until Soviet archaeologists found it in the 1970s. The Greeks called the river the Oxus, a derivative of Vakhsh, the name of its largest tributary, and in antiquity it was regarded as the boundary between Greater Iran and Turan. Medieval Arabic sources call it the Jayhun, from Gihon, one of the four rivers of Eden. One southern route of the Silk Road ran along part of the river from Termez before turning west to the Caspian.

The river's course has shifted repeatedly. Most recently, from the 13th century to the late 16th, it emptied into both the Aral and the Caspian seas, reaching the latter through the Uzboy distributary. People settled along the lower Amu Darya and the Uzboy from the 5th century. About 985 the Gurganj Dam at the fork began to divert water to the Aral. Genghis Khan's troops destroyed it in 1221, and the Mongols used the river's water to flood Konye-Urgench. In the 18th century the river turned north again, and by 1720, when the Russian explorer Bekovich-Cherkasski surveyed the region, it no longer reached the Caspian.

In the 19th century the Oxus was a stage of the Great Game. William Moorcroft visited it around 1824, and in 1839 the naval officer John Wood found Lake Zorkul and proclaimed it the source. Some in Britain feared that Russia would find a route to British India from the Oxus valley, but this never came to pass. Russia took over the area in its conquest of Turkestan, and the Soviet Union became the ruling power in the early 1920s. In the 1960s and 1970s the Soviets began using the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya to irrigate extensive cotton fields.
oxyrhynchus: Oxyrhynchus, also known by its modern name Al-Bahnasa, is a city in Middle Egypt about 160 km south-southwest of Cairo, west of the main course of the Nile on the Bahr Yussef. Its Greek name means sharp-nosed. In ancient Egyptian times a city called Per-Medjed stood on the site, named after the medjed, a species of Nile elephantfish worshipped there as the fish that ate the penis of Osiris. It was the capital of the 19th Upper Egyptian nome.

After Alexander the Great conquered Egypt in 332 BCE the city was re-established as a Hellenistic town called Oxyrrhynchoupolis. In the Hellenistic period it was a prosperous regional capital, the third-largest city in Egypt. After Egypt became Christian it was known for its many churches and monasteries. It remained a prominent but gradually declining town in the Roman and Byzantine periods. During the Jewish diaspora uprisings of 115 to 117 CE fighting spread to its nome, and papyri show that a local festival commemorating the Jewish defeat was still held about eighty years later. A papyrus of 291 CE records an active synagogue.

Early Islamic chroniclers report that the Rashidun army under Khalid ibn al-Walid took Bahnasa after a battle against a Christian force led by a patrician named Batlus, and then besieged the city; accounts of the siege differ. After the Muslim conquest of Egypt the canal system on which the town depended fell into disrepair, and Oxyrhynchus was abandoned.

The town of el-Bahnasa occupies part of the ancient site. Because Oxyrhynchus was not considered an Ancient Egyptian site of importance, it was neglected until 1896, when Bernard Pyne Grenfell and Arthur Surridge Hunt of The Queen's College, Oxford, began to excavate it. Grenfell wrote that the flow of papyri soon became a torrent. Dry conditions had left an unequalled archive of the ancient world, with texts from the Ptolemaic Kingdom and Roman Egypt. Eighty large volumes of the Oxyrhynchus Papyri have been published. Their very ordinariness makes them valuable for social and economic history and for the history of Christianity. In 2005 a reconstructed poem by Sappho was published, part of it first published in 1922 from an Oxyrhynchus papyrus.
oyo-empire: According to oral tradition the origins of Oyo lie with Ọranmiyan, the last prince of the Yoruba kingdom of Ile-Ife. He agreed with his brother to launch a punitive raid on their northern neighbours for insulting their father Oduduwa, the first Ooni of Ife, but the brothers quarrelled on the way and the army split up. Ọranmiyan's force was too small to attack, and he wandered along the southern shore of the Niger until he reached Bussa. He became the first oba of Oyo and was succeeded by Ajaka, then by Shango, later deified as the deity of thunder and lightning. The founding is placed at about 1300, but this is only estimated by backtracking through the chronology.

After a defeat by the Nupe, the Yoruba of Oyo spent an interregnum of 80 years as an exiled dynasty. Re-established in the early 17th century, Oyo became more centralised and more militant than before. By 1680 it spanned over 150,000 square kilometres, held together by mutual self-interest and by a combination of local autonomy and imperial authority. Islamic influence in the empire was slight, though some Muslim officials were kept at Oyo.

Many believe the decline began as early as 1754, with the palace intrigues of the prime minister Gaha. With the Oyo Mesi he forced four successive Alaafins to commit ritual suicide, two of them between June and October 1754 alone. Alaafin Abiodun had Gaha executed in 1774, but the instability had further weakened Oyo.

The Alaafin, whose title means owner of the palace, was head of the empire and supreme overlord. He kept tributaries safe, settled disputes between sub-rulers, and received their homage at annual ceremonies, of which the Bere festival was the most important. The Oyo Mesi, who spoke for the politicians, and the Ogboni, an earth cult speaking for the people, kept his power in check. The empire had four layers: metropolitan Oyo, southern Yorubaland, the Egbado Corridor, which secured trade with the coast, and the distant Ajaland, reaching far into Ewe territory in modern Togo.

Its army relied on cavalry, as most of its territory lay in the northern savannah. Horses were bought from the north and kept in metropolitan Oyo, which was partly free of the tsetse fly. Oyo also became the southern emporium of the trans-Saharan trade, exchanging salt, leather, horses, kola nuts, ivory, cloth and slaves, and it often demanded tribute in slaves from its tributaries.
ozurgeti: Ozurgeti lies about 200 metres above sea level, mostly between the Bzhuzhi and Natanebi rivers and bounded by hills to the north and south. The Natanebi is a subterranean river, with a good deal of the town built on top of it, while the Bzhuzhi flows above ground. The town sits on a slope levelled into three broad terraces: the market district at the bottom, most of the public buildings and parks on the middle terrace, and private housing on the highest. The climate is humid subtropical, with significant rainfall throughout the year.

Ozurgeti was founded in the late Middle Ages and is first mentioned by name in 1578 in the New Georgian Chronicles. It soon became the centre of Guria, an important place of trade and the home of the rulers of the Principality of Guria. A later find of a hoard of 270 silver coins under the town, the Ozurgeti Treasure, is regarded as evidence of this.

On 14 December 1846 it was designated a city, with just over 300 residents, and by 1865 the population had grown to over 700. It was a strategic place in the Russo-Turkish War (1877–78), and under the Russian Empire it was the administrative centre of the Ozurgeti Uyezd of the Kutaisi Governorate. The fourth city in Georgia to have a legal printing press, it received one in 1891. A rail line connecting it to the rest of the country was established on 26 December 1923. On 9 July 1934 it was renamed Makharadze in honour of the Georgian Bolshevik Filipp Makharadze, and it took back its original name on 15 May 1989.

Ozurgeti is the capital of the Guria region and the administrative centre of Ozurgeti District, and a regional centre of tea and hazelnut processing. The Ozurgeti Dramatic Theatre, founded in 1868, is named after Alexander Tsutsunava and occupies a five-storey Soviet Neoclassical building of 1962. The History Museum, founded in 1936, holds over 6,000 artifacts. Gurieli Palace, built in 1873, is now the seat of the Shemokmedi Orthodox Bishopric, and the ruins of a two-storey Byzantine-era bathhouse have been found in the centre of the town.
